Readers who like Irish country humor will find a bright, old-style collection, best read a sketch at a time for its voices and its fun.
16775-biographies-of-distinguished-scien:
Francois Arago wrote these lives of distinguished men of science, here in a first series translated by Admiral W. H. Smyth, Baden Powell, and Robert Grant, issued by Ticknor and Fields in Boston in 1859. The volume holds Arago's own life story plus his memoirs of eminent men of science, both continental and British. Translators warn that Arago's self-praise and romance may raise a smile.

Arago writes with ardor and energy, mixing personal adventure with scientific praise. Each life shows a mind at work in an age of discovery. The book gives a lively, 1800s view of science as heroism, useful for readers who want the human side of great discoverers, told by one of their own.
16797-luther-and-the-reformation-the-lif:
Joseph A. Seiss, pastor of the Church of the Holy Communion in Philadelphia, wrote this 1883 book on Luther and the Reformation as life-springs of our liberties, issued by Charles C. Cook in New York. The first part grew from a memorial oration in New York on November 10, 1883, for the four hundredth birthday of Martin Luther. The second part grew from discourses at Pennsylvania's bicentennial.

Seiss links Luther's stand to American liberty, church, and commonwealth, in earnest, sermon-like prose. He did not plan a book, but hearers asked for the talks in lasting form. The volume gives a clear sample of 1883 Lutheran praise for Luther, useful for readers of Reformation history and of American Protestant thought.
16799-dangerous-ages:
Rose Macaulay wrote this 1921 novel, issued by Boni and Liveright in New York and dedicated to her mother, driving gaily through the adventurous middle years. Chapters move from Neville's birthday and Mrs. Hilary's birthday, through family life, roots, seaweed, Jim, Gerda, and Nan, to pace, principles, the mother, the daughter, and time. An epigraph warns that all ages are dangerous to all people in this dangerous life.

Macaulay writes of women at middle age who refuse to fade quietly, with wit, irony, and sharp talk. Neville wakes on her birthday to a summer dawn and a house full of kin and claims. The novel gives a bright, modern portrait of family, age, and freedom, and it remains one of Macaulay's most loved books.
16802-the-ladies-vase-or-polite-manual-f:
An American Lady wrote this polite manual for young ladies, eighth edition, issued in Hartford in 1849 by H. S. Parsons. The preface says many like books cost too much for the girls who need them most, so this short, cheap volume aims to reach them. It stresses the forming of female character and manners as a matter of first importance.

The manual gives rules for speech, dress, visits, letters, and conduct in company, in plain, earnest terms. It reflects 1840s hopes for young women: modest, kind, and well-mannered in a world ruled by morals more than force. Modern readers get a clear view of old manners teaching, and a useful source for social history.
16803-lydia-of-the-pines:
Honore Willsie wrote this 1917 novel of Lydia of the pines, issued by A. L. Burt in New York by arrangement with Stokes. Chapters move from a toy balloon and a heroic day into a cottage and a cooking class. A Republican candidate, an election, and a camp follow. High school, an Indian celebration, and a Harvard instructor appear. An investigation leads to cap and gown. A murmuring pine speaks of being the last of its kind at the book's start.

Willsie sets Lydia, a northern girl, against pines, schools, and politics, with an Indian celebration and a search for truth at its heart. The novel mixes youth, nature, and civic duty in warm prose. Readers who like old girls' tales with a serious core will find a thoughtful, well-told story of growing up among pines and people.
16808-the-story-of-the-guides:
Colonel G. J. Younghusband wrote this 1908 story of the Queen's Own Corps of Guides, issued by Macmillan in London with pictures and dedicated by special leave to King Edward VII, colonel-in-chief. Younghusband thanks past and present officers, and leans on Lumsden of the Guides and Daly's memoirs. The first chapter opens with Sir Henry Lawrence's idea, stocks and tunics, and a new departure in soldiering.

Younghusband tells how the Guides grew on India's frontier, from first steps in war to fame as scouts and fighters. The tone is proud and regimental, full of marches and skirmishes. Readers of empire military history will find a compact, first-hand regimental story, useful for its detail and its view of frontier war.
16860-a-lover-in-homespun-and-other-stor:
F. Clifford Smith wrote this second edition book of Canadian stories, issued in Toronto by William Briggs in 1896 and dedicated to his mother. Contents run from A Lover in Homespun and The Faith that Removes Mountains into A Pair of Boots and A Prairie Episode. A Daughter of the Church, A Perilous Encounter, and Le Loup-Garou follow. A Christmas Adventure, Narcisse's Friend, A Strange Presentiment, and A Memorable Dinner close the set. The title tale opens with Onesime Charest, a happy farmer of L'Orignal, driving to the station.

Smith writes of French-Canadian villages, prairies, and church life with warmth and humor. Each story stands alone, full of local color and kind feeling. Readers who like Canadian regional tales will find a pleasant, old-style collection, rich in village scenes and in the speech of its folk.
1687-parmenides:
A very young Socrates meets a very old Parmenides in this dialogue, and the meeting turns into the hardest argument Plato ever wrote. If each thing has a Form — one, being, likeness — how do Forms relate to each other, and to the things that share in them.

The second half of the dialogue is a long, exacting exercise: suppose the One exists, suppose it does not, and follow each path to its end. It is the most difficult of Plato's dialogues, and interpreters have argued over it ever since. Readers who want Plato at his most rigorous, testing his own ideas rather than defending them, should start here.
16898-green-bays-verses-and-parodies:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, known as Q, wrote this book of verses and parodies called Green Bays. Most verses were written at Oxford and first printed in the Oxford Magazine. A few came from The Speaker and from Cassell fiction. Contents run from a college garden and a splendid spur into Irish melodies and a triolet. An oath, Titania, and measure for measure follow. Retrospection, why the volume is so thin, and Oxford trifles appear. Twilight, Willaloo, a letter, and an envoi as he lay dreaming close the set.

Quiller-Couch mixes light verse, parody, and Oxford memories with wit and ease. His parodies poke at great writers while his lyrics praise gardens, pipes, and old friends. Readers who like light verse will find a charming, slim volume, best read for its humor and its Oxford flavor.
16937-critical-miscellanies-vol-2-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this second volume of Critical Miscellanies, issued by Macmillan in London and New York in 1905, opening with an essay on Vauvenargues. Contents weigh Vauvenargues against Pascal and the votaries of perfectibility, then trace his birth, hard life, Paris days, friendship with Voltaire, faith, reserve, and views on Moliere, Racine, and Corneille. Character, Morley says, is the key to his theory of greatness.

Morley reads Vauvenargues as a moralist who prized spontaneous feeling over cold systems, and human relation over ascetic rules. The essay is a model of Victorian criticism: learned, fair, and full of style samples. Readers who love French moralists will find a fine, short guide to a writer too little read in English.
1696-the-club-of-queer-trades:
Major Brown is an ordinary man who stumbles into a series of wild adventures in London flats. Each one turns out to have been staged by a member of a very odd club. The club's rule is simple: a member must have invented a new trade, and must live by it.

Basil Grant, the club's founder, explains each case after the fact, and the trades, from professional duellists to men who sell adventure itself, turn out to be jokes with a point. Chesterton uses the club to argue that modern work has grown dull, and that imagination, given a living, could make a city strange again.
16960-history-of-the-united-states:
Charles A. Beard and Mary R. Beard wrote this 1921 history for students who needed the whole American story in one volume. It opens with migration and colonial farms, trades, schools, churches, and laws, then moves through war for independence, the making of the Union, and the growth of a continental nation. Each part ends with a short sum of its age.

The Beards stress work, land, and common people beside presidents and battles, which set the book apart in its day. Maps, chapter sums, and clear prose make it easy to follow across centuries. It still serves as a solid, readable frame for US history from first settlements to the modern republic.
16978-dante-the-central-man-of-all-the-w:
John T. Slattery gave these lectures to students at the New York State College for Teachers at Albany in 1919 and 1920, and they appeared in book form in 1920. Five talks cover Dante and his time, Dante the man, and the three parts of his great poem: Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. A preface by John H. Finley opens the set.

Slattery holds that Dante cannot be read apart from the thirteenth century, its faith, its politics, and its art. He guides students through the poem's souls, sins, and hopes in clear, lecture-room prose. The book suits readers who want a first path into Dante, with history and biography kept beside the verse at each step.
16981-old-peter-s-russian-tales:
Arthur Ransome retells Russian peasant tales as told by Old Peter, mostly from memory and from chapbooks and Afanasiev's great set. Baba Yaga, Frost, Sadko, the Fire-Bird, the Golden Fish, and Prince Ivan all appear, with the hut in the forest and the little daughter of the snow beside them. Dmitri Mitrokhin drew the pictures for the book.

Ransome wrote far from home for English children, yet he keeps the Russian plain, forest, and river close in each tale. The stories are short, strange, and kind in turn, with magic that rewards courage and punishes greed. This is a warm first door into Russian fairy lore, told in plain, musical prose for reading aloud.
1703-dead-men-tell-no-tales:
A shipwreck leaves one survivor with a story of hidden treasure and a murdered crew. The men who sank the ship soon close in on the only witness who can name them. Taken in by strangers, he must decide whom to trust while the men who sank the ship close in on the one witness who can name them.

Hornung, best known for his Raffles stories, writes here in the voice of an ordinary man pulled into crime and danger against his will. The novel moves from open water to sickroom intrigue. Its pull comes from a simple question: how does a decent man stay alive when the only people who can help him may also be the ones hunting him.
17034-english-fairy-tales:
Flora Annie Steel retold these English fairy tales, first issued by Macmillan in 1918 with pictures by Arthur Rackham. Contents run from St. George of Merrie England and the three bears into Tom-Tit-Tot and the golden snuff-box. Tattercoats, Lazy Jack, and Jack the Giant-Killer follow. The three sillies, the golden ball, and two sisters appear. The laidly worm, Titty Mouse, and Jack and the beanstalk lead to the black bull of Norroway, Catskin, and the three little pigs. Mr. Fox and Dick Whittington and his cat close the set.

Steel retells old tales in clear, plain prose, keeping their wonder and their moral bite. Rackham's pictures add a second magic to the book. Young readers get a classic English fairy book, rich in giants, beasts, and clever lads. Grown readers get a fine, illustrated treasury of tales told in England for ages.
17045-in-the-roaring-fifties:
Edward Dyson wrote this 1906 tale of the roaring fifties, opening on a bright, cool night at sea. An old East Indiaman moves slowly under a strong full moon, like a wind-blown ghost between sea and sky, with no cloud, no horizon line, and long, lazy green waves. Suddenly the ghost falters, shouting breaks the silence, and men swarm the rigging.

Dyson tells of gold-rush Australia, ships, diggers, and the wild years when fortunes rose and fell in a season. His prose mixes sea poetry with rough, vivid life ashore. Readers who like Australian gold tales will find a stirring, atmospheric novel of ships, camps, and the roaring decade that made a colony.
17065-interludes-being-two-essays-a-stor:
Horace Smith's 1892 volume gathers two essays, a story, and some verses, in Macmillan's plain cloth. The first essay treats criticism as the art of judging, and warns that lazy judgment breeds bad books, bad pictures, and bad buildings. Smith urges readers to hold the scales steady, even when it takes bother, rather than let things slide.

The rest of the book eases from argument to tale and verse, in the same clear, moral voice. Smith writes for thoughtful general readers, not scholars alone. The set suits anyone who likes Victorian essays with bite: short, firm, and fond of good sense over fashion.
17069-a-great-emergency-and-other-tales:
Juliana Horatia Ewing's tales, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, open with A Great Emergency, a boys' adventure of school, cricket, and a runaway barge. Rupert's lectures, a yellow leather book, and a canal carrier's home lead to a coasting voyage, a stowaway aboard the Atalanta, and a glow on the horizon. Other tales in the set follow in the same warm vein.

Ewing writes for children with humor, pluck, and a moral heart, and her boys feel real in speech and scrape. The book is dedicated to the Bishop of Fredericton and his wife, in memory of New Brunswick. Young readers who like old-style school and river tales will find a kind, lively set here.
17120-fashionable-philosophy-and-other-s:
Laurence Oliphant's 1887 shilling volume mixes satire, tale, and play. The title sketch stages a London tea party where fine ladies debate the religion of the future, poking fun at chic faith and its smooth talk. A tale of a brigand's bride in southern Italy, a satire on sisters in Tibet, and a short comedy of affinities fill out the set.

Oliphant warns in his preface that the Tibet piece is not his own life story, but a jab at a system he thought weak in morals. The wit is sharp, Victorian, and fond of drawing-room talk. Readers who like period satire will enjoy its light sting, and its view of what smart London took for deep thought in 1887.
17151-bob-chester-s-grit-or-from-ranch-t:
Frank V. Webster's 1911 boys' book follows Bob Chester from under a cloud to ranch and riches. Bob finds an unexpected champion, gains freedom, and sets out to be his own master, with a kind waitress, a tale of the plains, and a freight engine throttle along the way. Fairfax at last, a job, a dog, a ranch, and a race for life close the road to riches.

Webster writes in brisk, moral series style, with pluck and kind acts rewarded at each turn. The frontispiece shows Bob urging Firefly to greater speed. Young readers who like ranch tales and rags-to-riches plots will find a cheerful, fast-moving story of grit that pays off.
1716-the-copy-cat-and-other-stories:
Two little boys and a little girl can keep a secret — sometimes. And the title story of this volume turns on what happens when a lonely girl named Amelia copies her schoolmate Lily in everything. The title story follows Amelia Wheeler, nicknamed the Copy-Cat, a lonely girl whose whole ideal is her schoolmate Lily Jennings, and the trouble that imitation stirs.

Other tales in the volume turn on a boy in the woods, a man who will not spend his savings, and neighbors who judge too fast. Freeman writes in a plain, watchful style, and the pleasure of the book is in its people: stubborn, tender, and often funnier than they know, in villages where everyone watches everyone else.
17190-greek-and-roman-ghost-stories:
Lacy Collison-Morley's 1912 set gathers Greek and Roman ghost tales from years of browsing among the classics, begun at the suggestion of Marion Crawford. Chapters treat the power of the dead to return, belief in ghosts in Greece and Rome, hauntings, necromancy, visions in sleep, apparitions, and warning apparitions. The opening notes confusion in ancient views of the afterlife, from tomb spirits to souls freed by cremation.

Collison-Morley retells each tale with sources and a scholar's care, yet keeps the shivers intact. The book suits classicists and ghost fans alike. It shows how old peoples feared, honored, and bargained with their dead, in stories that still chill.
17250-mother-west-wind-where-stories:
Thornton W. Burgess's 1918 Mother West Wind Where Stories, pictured by Harrison Cady, explains how animals got their marks. Grandfather Frog got his big mouth, Miser the trade rat set up shop, Yap-Yap the prairie dog used his wits, and Yellow-Wing learned to love the ground. Little Chief made hay, Glutton the wolverine got his name, and Mr. Quack got webbed feet.

Each where tale is short, funny, and kind, with a nature lesson tucked inside the fancy. Burgess writes in gentle storyteller prose for young children. Families who love animal tales will enjoy a classic set where every quirk has a story, and every story ends with a smile.
17371-raggedy-andy-stories:
Johnny Gruelle wrote and pictured these stories of Raggedy Andy, the little rag brother of Raggedy Ann. The book grew from a reader's gift: a woman who had bought Gruelle's Raggedy Ann books and dolls sent him an old doll from her own attic trunk, and Andy was born. Chapters include how Raggedy Andy came, the nursery dance, the spinning wheel, the taffy pull, and the rabbit chase.

Doctor Raggedy Andy, Raggedy Andy's smile, the wooden horse, and making angels in the snow complete the set. Readers get nursery adventures in which rag dolls come alive when children are away, told in Gruelle's kindly, playful style. The book remains a fond classic of American children's fiction.
17391-the-princess-elopes:
Harold MacGrath's 1905 romance opens with a diplomat narrator who cannot place the Grand Duchy of Barscheit or the principality of Doppelkinn. Berlin and Vienna lie near, he notes, and the Carpathians rise three hours off. Barscheit, the meddler and maker of trouble, is ruled by Old Grumpy, a duke with a finger in every pie. Princess Hildegarde, called Gretchen, plays piano in the frontispiece.

From that Ruritanian setting grows a light tale of courts, love, and flight, told in MacGrath's breezy, popular style. Fans of The Prisoner of Zenda's world will enjoy a warm, funny romance of a princess on the run. It is pure Edwardian escapism, best read for its charm and its pretty heroine.
17427-president-wilson-s-addresses:
George McLean Harper of Princeton edited this school collection of President Wilson's addresses, in the English Readings for Schools series under general editor Wilbur Lucius Cross of Yale. The volume gathers Wilson's first inaugural address, his first address to Congress, and addresses on the banking system, at Gettysburg, and on Mexican affairs. Understanding America and an address before the Southern Commercial Congress follow.

Later pieces cover the state of the union, trusts and monopolies, and Panama Canal tolls, among other subjects. Readers get Wilson's public voice in the years before and during the Great War, chosen for classroom use. The book suits students of American oratory and of Wilson's presidency.
1746-new-collected-rhymes:
Lang himself called this book a poor little flutter of rhymes let down the wind at a friend's urging. The verses move between Jacobite loyalty and ballad echoes. The verses move between Jacobite loyalty, ballad echoes, and light pieces on books and friends.

Loyal lyrics for Charles and James and the White Rose sit beside poems on Galloway men who fought for Kirk and Covenant. Lang is careful to say the politics are those of song, not of rebellion. The collection shows Lang the poet rather than the scholar: fluent, traditional, and fond of old causes kept alive in verse.
17490-the-memorable-thoughts-of-socrates:
Xenophon wrote these memorable thoughts of Socrates, translated by Edward Bysshe and published by Cassell and Company in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1888. Bysshe's translation had first appeared in 1712, and this printing follows the revised edition of 1722. Bysshe, author of The Art of English Poetry in 1702, saw his Socrates stay in good repute, with another edition in 1758.

Readers meet Socrates through Xenophon's memories: his talk, his morals, and his way of questioning friends. The book suits readers new to Greek philosophy, since Xenophon's Socrates is plainer than Plato's. Bysshe's old English gives the volume a period flavour.
17560-the-adventures-of-ann-stories-of-c:
Mary E. Wilkins drew these stories of colonial times from original documents and family traditions, publishing them in Boston in 1886 with D. Lothrop and Company. The contents list four tales: The Bound Girl, Deacon Thomas Wales' Will, The Adopted Daughter, and The Horse-House Deed. The first opens with an indenture binding Margaret Burjust of Boston to service.

Readers get colonial New England in short, documentary-flavoured fiction, where wills, deeds, and bindings shape women's lives. Wilkins's spare style and local knowledge give the tales their force. The book suits readers of early American fiction and of the daily law and custom of the colonies.
17572-the-last-spike-and-other-railroad-:
Cy Warman published this set of railroad stories in New York in February 1906 with Charles Scribner's Sons. The contents list runs from The Last Spike and The Belle of Athabasca. It moves through Pathfinding in the Northwest and The Cure's Christmas Gift, to The Mysterious Signal, Chasing the White Mail, and Oppressing the Oppressor. The Iron Horse and the Trolley and In the Black Canon close the set.

Warman, a popular writer of rail life, tells tales of crews, passengers, and frontier lines with the insider's ear. Readers get short, stirring stories of the railroad age, when the last spike still stood for a continent joined. The book suits readers of western and railroad fiction.
17601-masques-phases:
Robert Ross published this collection of essays and reprints in London in 1909 with Arthur L. Humphreys of Piccadilly. Ross thanks Smith, Elder for leave to reprint A Case at the Museum, first seen in the Cornhill of October 1900, and the Westminster Gazette for its account of Simeon Solomon. Former proprietors of the Wilsford Press allowed other pieces to be reissued, including How We Lost the Book of Jasher.

Readers get art-world essays, memoirs, and jeux d'esprit from a central figure of the Wilde circle. Ross writes with wit and insider knowledge of late Victorian art and letters. The book suits readers of Wilde, of Solomon, and of Edwardian literary London.
17603-bert-wilson-in-the-rockies:
J. W. Duffield, author of Bert Wilson at the Wheel and Bert Wilson at Panama, published this boys' adventure in New York in 1914, printed in Racine, Wisconsin, in 1924. Bert Wilson heads for a ranch in the Rockies, and the chapters promise a desperate encounter, busting a broncho, a forest terror, and the grizzly at bay. The ringer's downfall, the wolf pack, teeth and hoofs, and an Indian outbreak follow.

Readers get a brisk, outdoor tale of ranch life, wild animals, and frontier danger, in the style of early twentieth-century series fiction for boys. Duffield keeps the pace quick and the perils frequent. The book suits young readers who like horses, bears, and mountain adventure.
17607-superstition-in-all-ages:
Jean Meslier wrote this attack on superstition. He was a Roman Catholic priest who served thirty years at Etrepigny in Champagne, France. He left the work as his last will and testament to his parishioners and to the world, to be published after his death, under the title Common Sense. Meslier, born in 1678 at Mazerny, son of a serge weaver, wholly abjured religious dogmas at the end of his life. Anna Knoop translated the work from French in 1878.

A life of Meslier by Voltaire fronts the volume. Readers get one of the boldest freethought texts of the Enlightenment, arguing that superstition rules all ages. The book suits readers of atheism, of Voltaire's circle, and of the clandestine literature of dissent.
17618-jethou-or-crusoe-life-in-the-chann:
E. R. Suffling, author of History and Legends of the Broad District, wrote this account of Crusoe life in the Channel Isles, centred on Jethou, with drawings prepared from the author's own sketches. Suffling presents a castaway life on a small island, lived out in the manner of Robinson Crusoe but in the familiar waters of the Channel.

Readers learn how a solitary islander finds food, shelter, and company in a tiny kingdom of rock and sea. The book mixes travel, natural history, and adventure, with the author's sketches to guide the eye. It suits readers of island books and of Victorian Crusoe imitations.
17669-the-three-brides-love-in-a-cottage:
Francis A. Durivage published this volume of tales in Boston in 1853 with Sanborn, Carter, Bazin and Company. He dedicates it to his mother, the first to encourage his efforts and the most indulgent of his critics. The title tales are The Three Brides and Love in a Cottage, with other tales beside. Durivage, a Boston writer of the 1850s, worked in the popular sentimental mode of his day.

Readers get short stories of love, marriage, and domestic feeling, written for the parlour reader. The book suits readers of mid-nineteenth-century American fiction and of the gift-book tale. Its dedication gives a glimpse of the author's family circle.
17762-the-burglar-s-fate-and-the-detecti:
Allan Pinkerton, founder of the famed Pinkerton agency, wrote this 1884 account of a burglary at Geneva and the hunt that followed. Pinkerton had already told tales of expressmen, forgers, and the Mollie Maguires, and here he turns his own case books into a true-crime story.

The case opens with a robbery, a search for the thieves, and a call to Pinkerton's men. Clues lead through a ten-cent coin, a witness named Miss Patton, and a trail to Newton Edwards. Pinkerton writes with the pride of a man who built his trade, and the book reads as both memoir and early detective tale, told by the man who lived it.
17772-mrs-overtheway-s-remembrances:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Mrs. Overtheway's Remembrances for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, with a New York edition from E. and J. B. Young. The book is dedicated to her husband, in memory of 1866 and 1867, and it reads like tales told by a kind old neighbor.

The little old lady over the way goes to morning prayer at eight each day, in black satin bonnet and white shawl. Young Ida watches from her window, and the tales that follow run from Ida to Mrs. Moss, a snoring ghost, and far Kerguelen's Land. Ewing writes with grace and moral warmth, a gentle Victorian book for young readers.
17893-the-best-ghost-stories:
Arthur B. Reeve wrote the introduction to The Best Ghost Stories, printed in New York in 1919 by Boni and Liveright for the Modern Library. Reeve asks what draws us to ghost tales, and he links that pull to the pull of detective tales, where readers flirt with crime they dare not do.

The set runs from Defoe's apparition of Mrs. Veal to M. R. James, Bulwer-Lytton, Kipling's phantom rickshaw, Bierce's damned thing, and some real American ghosts. It is a strong, classic ghost shelf, chosen when the form was at its peak. Readers who love a chill will find much here to read by lamplight.
17901-the-smiling-hill-top-and-other-cal:
Julia M. Sloane wrote these California sketches, printed by Scribner's in 1921 with pictures by Carleton M. Winslow. The book is dedicated to her three road companions, one large and two small, and it reads like a diary of drives, walks, and garden days in the Golden State.

Sketches visit a hill-top home, a poppy field, gardeners at work, thorns, a gypsy trail, a lone night out, a Sabine farm, and the land of Whynot. Sloane writes with a light, fond eye for sun, soil, and the small joys of the road. Readers who love California, gardens, or gentle travel prose will enjoy this warm, old book of place.
17902-sunny-boy-and-his-playmates:
Ramy Allison White wrote Sunny Boy and His Playmates in 1922, printed by Barse and Company in New York and Newark, with pictures by Howard L. Hastings. Sunny Boy, a small, sunny lad, returns for more winter fun with his friends.

Chapters teach him to skate, find Grandpa Horton, build a snow man, brave a blizzard, and set out with explorers on a rescue. Jerry loses his temper, toys go to school, and brave little Sunny Boy saves the day. The tale is sweet, simple fun for young children, in the warm, old style of the Sunny Boy books.
17922-visionaries:
James Huneker wrote Visionaries, first printed in 1905 and reissued by Scribner's in 1916, as a set of strange, dream-like tales. The book is dedicated to Remy de Gourmont in Paris, and its epigraph from Baudelaire sets a mood of clouds and far-off things.

Twenty short pieces move from a master of cobwebs to rebels of the moon, a mock sun, a haunted harpsichord, and a woman who loved Chopin. Huneker's prose is lush, odd, and full of art talk. Readers who like weird tales with a fin-de-siecle air will find this a rich, curious book, best taken one piece at a time.
17932-the-second-class-passenger-fifteen:
Perceval Gibbon wrote The Second-Class Passenger in 1913, a set of fifteen stories first printed by Methuen and reissued in the Abbey Library in 1922. Gibbon, a traveler and tale-teller, sets his stories in ports, ships, and far towns, where strangers meet and fates cross.

The title tale opens at Mozambique, where a party from a German mail-boat buys curios, and a heavy bronze image is left behind at a hotel. Other tales run from a trader and a murderer to a captain's arm and a widower. Gibbon writes with dry wit and a keen eye. It is a strong, worldly story book, best for readers who like tales with a sting.
17934-a-practical-directory-for-young-ch:
Harvey Newcomb wrote A Practical Directory for Young Christian Females in 1833, printed in Boston for the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, in a seventh edition. The book is a set of letters from a brother to a younger sister, approved by the Society's committee.

Newcomb counsels a young woman on faith, conduct, reading, company, dress, and duty, with plain, earnest advice for each stage of youth. The tone is kind but firm, and the rules reflect the piety of early New England. It is a revealing conduct book, best read now as a window on how Christian girls were once taught to live.
18009-sagittulae-random-verses:
E. W. Bowling, rector of Houghton Conquest and late fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge, printed Sagittulae, or Random Verses, in London in 1885. A few pieces had run in Punch, but most were written over twenty-five years for The Eagle, the college magazine, under the name Arculus.

Verses range from the battle of the Pons Trium Trojanorum to Julia, a May term memory, a curate's complaint, and a romance in real academic life. Bowling begs pardon for his light, crude arrows, and hopes they wound no one. The book is a pleasant, witty relic of Cambridge life, best for readers who like light verse with a college air.
18041-celtic-religion-in-pre-christian-t:
Edward Anwyl wrote Celtic Religion in Pre-Christian Times in 1906, printed in London by Archibald Constable. Anwyl, professor of Welsh at Aberystwyth, sets out to explain what Celtic means, and what the old faith of Gaul and Britain truly was.

He warns that Celtic speech does not prove one stock, since men lived in Gaul and Britain long before Indo-European tongues arrived. Chapters then trace gods, rites, and beliefs from the old evidence. Anwyl writes with scholarly care. The book is a clear, early study of Celtic faith, still useful as a first step, though later finds have deepened the field.
18099-donatello-by-lord-balcarres:
Lord Balcarres wrote Donatello, a life of the great Florentine sculptor, printed from Toronto library images. The book keeps old spellings of names like Michael Angelo and Brunellesco, while fixing clear misprints of Verrocchio, Buonarroti, Orcagna, and Vasari.

Donatello's marble and bronze, his saints, prophets, and boys, shaped the Renaissance eye for form and feeling. Balcarres traces his work, his patrons, and his place among Florentine masters. The book is a solid, scholarly life of an artist, best for readers who love Italian art and the story of how sculpture learned to live again.
18150-the-hidden-places:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote The Hidden Places in 1922, put out in New York by A. L. Burt, by arrangement with Little, Brown. Sinclair, author of Big Timber, sets this tale in the shadow of the Great War, where wounds of body and mind hide from sight.

Hollister stands in his room, staring at a door he does not see, gripped by a terror that has loomed for weeks. Soft fingers explore the ruin left by an exploding shell, and hidden places of the heart open. Sinclair writes with force and feeling. It is a strong, post-war novel of trauma, love, and the long road back.
18165-russian-rambles:
Isabel F. Hapgood, author of The Epic Songs of Russia, recorded her stay in Russia in this 1895 volume. Hapgood wrote to correct the common picture of Russian daily life, which she found full of misadvice and prejudice. Her preface attacks books that invent scenes, such as a boy skating to church and singing from an organ gallery in Moscow.

Her chapters take up passports, police, and the post office, the Nevsky Prospekt, the censor, bargaining, a summer resort, and a stroll in Moscow with Count Tolstoy. She also visits a holy city, travels on the Volga, and reports the Nizhni-Novgorod fair. Readers get Russia as a traveler met it: offices, markets, churches, and talk, rather than romance.
18181-the-path-of-duty-and-other-stories:
H. S. Caswell wrote The Path of Duty and Other Stories, printed in Montreal in 1874 by John Lovell. The lead tale, Clara Roscom, or the Path of Duty, gives the book its name, and other stories follow in the same earnest vein.

Clara faces sudden bereavement, wins success at school, boards with Mrs. Wentworth, and serves as governess in Mr. Leighton's family. Willie Leighton's return from England, an evening party, and her mother's failing health test her heart. Caswell writes moral, Victorian fiction for young readers, full of duty, faith, patience, and quiet courage through hard days.
18187-hebrew-life-and-times:
Harold B. Hunting wrote this 1921 history of Hebrew life for general readers. Hunting begins on the borders of the desert, where shepherd peoples lived on the fertile fringes around Arabia's great central waste. Phoenicians, Assyrians, Babylonians, and Canaanites share that world before the Hebrews enter Palestine.

Chapters follow home life in tents, desert pilgrims, a struggle against tyranny, a great deliverance, and the move from desert into Canaan. Later chapters take up farming, village life, government, David and Solomon, wars, prophets, and a new kind of religion centered on one just God. Readers get the Hebrews' story as social history, from tents to nation, told in short, clear chapters.
18190-raggedy-ann-stories:
Johnny Gruelle wrote and drew Raggedy Ann Stories, printed in New York, London, Toronto, and Sydney by Little Simon. Gruelle dedicates the book to the millions who loved a rag doll, and his preface tells of the old doll on his desk.

Raggedy Ann, the doll his mother played with as a child, sits loppy and loose-jointed, her face smeared with chocolate from a tea party. Mice have nibbled her cotton stuffing, yet her painted smile never fades. Gruelle's tales teach kindness and patience through rag-doll play. It is a beloved children's classic, gentle, funny, and full of heart.
18212-arts-and-crafts-in-the-middle-ages:
Julia de Wolf Addison wrote this survey of medieval workmanship in the applied arts, with notes on special artisans of the early Renaissance. Addison, author of books on the Pitti Palace and the National Gallery, treats craft as art: the skill of hands shaping precious and common stuff into things of use and beauty. Plates show church metalwork, the crown of Charlemagne, and Bernward's cross and chalice.

Chapters take up gold and silver, jewelry and precious stones, enamel, other metals, tapestry, embroideries, and sculpture in stone in France, Italy, England, and Germany. Later chapters cover carving in wood and ivory, inlay and mosaic, and the illumination of books. Readers get a clear guide to how medieval makers worked, and why their work still holds the eye.
1824-peace-manoeuvres:
Richard Harding Davis opens this story with a scout standing where three roads cut three green tunnels through pine woods. They meet at his feet, beneath a sign-post pointing impartially to East Carver, South Carver, and Carver Centre. The scout's choice of road is the story's first small drama, and the manoeuvres that follow are fought in peacetime.

A girl with flushed cheeks and guilty eyes, glimpsed across the road, adds a second plot to the military one. Davis writes the tale as a light study of soldiers at play, with the woods, the sign-post, and the watchers all given their part. It is a brief, atmospheric piece, more about mood than about battle.
18264-within-the-enemy-s-lines:
Oliver Optic wrote this Civil War story for boys as part of his Blue and Gray Series, following Taken by the Enemy. The Boston firm Lee and Shepard published it, with a frontispiece showing two men making their way through a grove. Optic, a veteran writer of army, navy, and boat club stories, sets his tale on the blockade, where Union and Confederate loyalties cross.

Chapters open with an unexpected visitor and a difference of opinion, then follow Corny Passford playing another part, Captain Carboneer and his party, the cabin of the Florence, and Midshipman Christy Passford. Signals are arranged, the Vampire approaches, and a shot from the long gun sounds. Readers get a naval adventure of disguise, divided families, and daring inside enemy lines.
18269-pascal-s-pense-es:
Blaise Pascal's Pensées gathers the short notes he left unfinished at his death. This Dutton paperback, published in 1958, opens with an introduction by T. S. Eliot. The notes are grouped into sections on mind and style, the misery of man without God, the need for the wager, the means of belief, justice, philosophers, and morality.

Later sections turn to the Christian religion, prophecy, proofs of Jesus Christ, and miracles, with an appendix of polemical fragments. Pascal writes in brief, pointed strokes rather than long proofs. Readers meet a thinker testing faith against reason, doubt, habit, and human pride, one fragment at a time.
1828-chronicles-of-the-canongate-1st-ser:
A chronicler of the Canongate looks back over Edinburgh life and tells stories of law, love, and local history, pausing now and then for a glass of claret. The first series moves between law, love, and local history, with Scott's notes at the foot of the page filling in the customs and places behind the tales.

Readers who know Waverley will recognize Scott's method. A narrator who has seen the world change, characters caught between old Scotland and new, and a story that pauses for a glass of claret and a memory show it. The volume is less famous than the great novels, but it shows Scott's storytelling at its most relaxed and most Scottish.
18309-emerson-s-wife-and-other-western-s:
Florence Finch Kelly, author of With Hoops of Steel, published this set of western stories at Chicago in 1911, with color pictures by Stanley Wood. The title story, Emerson's Wife, leads a contents list that also holds Colonel Kate's Protegee, The Kid of Apache Teju, A Blaze on Pard Huff, and How Colonel Kate Won Her Spurs.

Other stories give the rise, fall, and redemption of Johnson Sides, plus a piece of wreckage. They also tell the story of a Chinese kid, an old Roman of Mariposa, and a case of the inner imperative. Guns, horses, and frontier towns fill the frontispiece and the plates. Readers get the West in short form: strong women, hard men, sudden choices, and the price of pride on the range.
18405-great-sea-stories:
Joseph Lewis French edited this 1921 anthology of great sea stories, published by Brentano's in New York. French, editor of Great Ghost Stories and Masterpieces of Mystery, gathers sea tales from famous novels. Each is chosen for a single strong scene: a chase, a wreck, a mutiny, or a rescue. The volume serves readers who want the sea in short, stirring pieces.

Contents open with Spanish bloodhounds and English mastiffs from Kingsley's Westward Ho. They give the club-hauling of the Diomede from Marryat's Peter Simple, and the cruise of the Torch from Michael Scott's Tom Cringle's Log. Later pieces give the mutiny of the Bounty and the wreck of the Royal Caroline from Cooper's Red Rover. They give the capture of the great white whale from Melville's Moby Dick, and a storm and rescue from Russell's Wreck of the Grosvenor. Readers get the sea library in one volume.
18426-sunny-slopes:
Ethel Hueston, author of Prudence of the Parsonage, wrote this novel, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1917, with pictures by Arthur William Brown. Sunny Slopes is written in memory of Hueston's husband, eager in service, patient in illness, and unfaltering in death, and dedicated to the St. Louis Presbytery, to which she owes a debt of sympathy and friendship. A frontispiece teases a minister's wife who looks more like a little girl's baby doll.

Chapters open with the beginning, where a tennis ball spins over the net to cries of deuce. Mansers, a baby in business, and a woman in the church follow, with a minister's son and the heavy yoke. Later chapters give the first step, reaction, upheaval, where health begins, the old teacher, the land of lungers, and old hopes and new. Readers get a minister's family novel of health, service, and second chances.
18444-the-story-of-the-hymns-and-tunes:
Theron Brown and Hezekiah Butterworth wrote this 1906 history of hymns and tunes, published in New York. The book takes the motto that tongues are many but joys are one, and it follows hymns from their writers to their tunes and their use in worship. Portraits of Thomas Ken, Oliver Holden, Joseph Haydn, Charles Wesley, and Martin Luther mark its range.

Chapters treat hymns of great witnesses, Christian devotion and experience, missionary hymns, hymns of suffering and trust, Christian ballads, old revival hymns, and Sunday school hymns. Patriotic hymns, sailors' hymns, hymns of Wales, field hymns, and hymns of hope and consolation follow. Readers get the stories behind the songs sung in church: who wrote them, why, and how their tunes carried them round the world.
18449-the-treasure-of-heaven-a-romance-o:
Marie Corelli published this romance with Dodd, Mead in New York in 1906, after an August release, with a frontispiece portrait of the author taken that spring. The book's subtitle, A Romance of Riches, names its theme, and its dedication to Bertha calls a faithful friend better than gold.

The story opens on a night in June in London. The city stands grim and misty, with a million lights gleaming on its blackness like a fortress against heaven. Corelli, author of The Sorrows of Satan and Thelma, sets wealth against faith, asking what riches are worth when measured beside love and the life beyond them.
18450-hawaiian-folk-tales:
Thomas G. Thrum compiled this collection of native Hawaiian legends, published at Chicago in 1907 by A. C. McClurg and Company, with sixteen illustrations from photographs. Thrum gathered tales that had run for years as a feature of The Hawaiian Annual, adding several new ones, including a famous shark legend from the papers of the Hawaiian Historical Society. Contributors included recognized authorities such as Rev. A. O. Forbes and Dr. N. B. Emerson.

Contents open with legends resembling Old Testament history, then exploits of Maui: snaring the sun, the origin of fire, and Pele and the deluge. Later tales give Hiku and Kawelu, the origin of healing in Hawaii, a visit to the spirit land, and the rocks of Kana. Readers get Hawaii's old stories in English dress: gods, heroes, and the spirit world, told by those who knew the islands best.
18462-the-story-of-the-innumerable-compa:
David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, published this 1896 volume of sketches, historical or allegorical, bound by the idea of the higher sacrifice. Jordan dedicates the book to his wife Jessie Knight Jordan, and thanks Professor William R. Dudley for a photograph of a record of Father Serra, secured through Father Casanova of Monterey. The volume appeared in San Francisco from Whitaker and Ray.

Contents give the story of the innumerable company and the story of the Passion. They also give the California of the Padre, the conquest of Jupiter Pen, the last of the Puritans, and a knight of the order of poets. Nature study and moral culture, the higher sacrifice, and the bubbles of Saki follow. Readers get a naturalist president's moral sketches: missions, saints, poets, and the price of devotion, told with California light behind them.
18469-captain-scraggs-or-the-green-pea-p:
Peter B. Kyne wrote this sea adventure, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with illustrations by Gordon Grant and copyrights from 1911 to 1919. It first appeared in Sunset Magazine, and Kyne was already known for Cappy Ricks, The Long Chance, and The Valley of the Giants.

The frontispiece shows Captain Scraggs throwing his brown derby on the deck and leaping upon it, a picture of the captain's temper and humor. The novel follows a rough, comic shipmaster and his crew through a piratical yarn, where bluster, loyalty, and sea-going trouble carry the story from one scrape to the next.
18487-food-remedies-facts-about-foods-an:
Florence Daniel wrote this booklet as number two in the Healthy Life Booklets, published in London by C. W. Daniel, ready in September 1908. The series set Arnold Eiloart's health tracts beside Daniel's food and cookery booklets, offering plain health advice for home readers.

Food Remedies gives facts about foods and their medicinal uses, in three parts: an introduction, the foods themselves, and indices. The book belongs to an early health movement that trusted food over drugs. It lists what common foods were believed to heal, so that a household might treat small ills from the kitchen.
18498-king-john-of-jingalo-the-story-of-:
Laurence Housman wrote this comic fable of kingship, published by Henry Holt in New York in 1912. The story follows King John of Jingalo, a monarch in difficulties, through the troubles of ruling a kingdom that will not stay in order.

Chapters give a domestic interior, accidents will happen, wild oats and widows' weeds, popular monarchy, and church and state. Later chapters bring pace-making in politics, king and council, and a royal commission. A promissory note, heads or tails, and the king's night out follow, as satire and fairy tale meet in a court full of surprises.
18509-nick-baba-s-last-drink-and-other-s:
Geo. P. Goff, a Lancaster writer, gathered these sketches in 1879 after friends urged him to collect pieces written in spare hours. The title sketch opens on Christmas Eve in a small town, where Nick Baba, a poor shoemaker, sits alone at his bench while neighbors feast. Other pieces include a trip to Currituck, a haunted island tale, and a legend of Berkeley Springs.

Humor, local color, and a taste for odd characters mark the whole set. Goff dedicates the book to the Raymond Hall Shooting Club, a sign of its club-room roots. The sketches give a homely picture of small-town life in the late 1800s.
18523-the-poetry-of-wales:
John Jenkins edited this 1873 set of Welsh poems in English dress, hoping to share Welsh verse with English readers. His preface says friends in England had often asked why no one had translated the treasures of Welsh poetry. The book answers with songs and poems from early bards such as Aneurin, Taliesin, and Llywarch Hen. It moves through love poets like Dafydd ap Gwilym to hymn writers led by William Williams of Pantycelyn.

A long introduction traces Welsh history through its verse, from heroic odes and triads to courtly love songs and Puritan hymns. Jenkins took no pay for the work, seeking only to spread knowledge of his native land. The book remains a friendly door into Welsh literary history.
18526-eating-in-two-or-three-languages:
Irvin S. Cobb, author of Paths of Glory, wrote this humorous book of eating, published by George H. Doran in New York in 1919, with copyright in 1918 by the Curtis Publishing Company. Cobb dedicates the book to B. B. McAlpin, who knows a lot about eating. The frontispiece promises no red meats, but only sea foods, a joke on wartime and postwar tables.

Cobb opens on his way home from overseas, mapping a campaign of eating. The day he lands will be great for waiters and hard on cooks, he says. He wrestles green corn like a mouth organ and greets hothouse asparagus with the best work of the late Bosco. Cantaloupes follow in his fancy. Readers get Cobb the humorist at table: travel, appetite, and the languages of menus, told by a man who loved food and the English that describes it.
1853-the-ninth-vibration-and-other-stori:
L. Adams Beck's stories travel the East. A track nine thousand feet up runs from India into Tibet, past Simla of the imperial councils, to China, Burma, and the building of the Taj Mahal. The title story, The Ninth Vibration, sets its mysticism on that high road. The Interpreter, The Incomparable Lady, and The Hatred of the Queen take up love, duty, and revenge.

Beck writes with a sympathy for Eastern faiths that was unusual in her day, and her tales mix romance with moral argument. The collection will appeal to readers who like Kipling's India told from a more inward angle, where a color that strikes a traveller dumb can matter more than a battle.
1855-ban-and-arriere-ban-a-rally-of-fugi:
Verses written here and there and never gathered are rallied here under a military metaphor, pictured in the dedication as a broken host returning like a ghost. In the dedication to Eleanor Charlotte Sellar, they appear as a broken host come back like a ghost from the dead, sad or glad as the verses take them.

The poems wander through graveyards, ruined barges, and haunted tracks, with Lang's usual blend of scholarship and lightness. Readers who know his ballads and fairy books will find the same voice in shorter compass: a man of letters amusing himself. Inviting the reader to walk a thicket dim and sere beside him.
18566-hawthorne-english-men-of-letters-s:
Henry James wrote this short study of Nathaniel Hawthorne for Macmillan's English Men of Letters series in 1879, edited by John Morley. James warns at the start that it is more a critical essay than a full life, since Hawthorne's days were quiet and his papers thin. Chapters follow his early years, early manhood, early writings, Brook Farm and Concord, and his three American novels.

Later chapters cover his years in England and Italy and his last years. James praises Hawthorne as the finest voice of American letters, subtle and modest, yet notes how little his work touched public events. The book remains a classic early judgment on Hawthorne's art.
18604-the-ice-maiden-and-other-tales:
Hans Christian Andersen wrote these tales, translated by Fanny Fuller and published at Philadelphia in 1863. The lead tale, The Ice-Maiden, opens in Switzerland among steep rocks, snow fields, and glaciers near Grindelwald, under the Schreckhorn and Wetterhorn. A boy named Rudy grows up in that grand, harsh country.

Three shorter tales follow: The Butterfly, The Psyche, and The Snail and the Rose-Tree. Fuller keeps Andersen's wonder, charm, and melancholy in plain English for young readers. The book gives young readers a fine sample of his work beyond the best-known fairy tales.
18642-women-of-the-romance-countries:
John R. Effinger, a University of Michigan scholar, published this study at Philadelphia in 1907 and 1908. It surveys women in the Romance lands, starting with Italian women in the age of Countess Matilda of Tuscany. Effinger opens in the eleventh century, when feudal law gave husbands near-absolute rights and some men even debated whether women had souls.

Later parts move across Italy, France, and Spain through later ages, tracing how law, custom, and famed women shaped women's place. Effinger writes with sympathy for his subjects and a scholar's care for sources. The book gives a readable survey of women's history in southern Europe.
18644-the-swindler-and-other-stories:
Ethel M. Dell gathered these ten stories in a Grosset and Dunlap volume, after they first ran in the Red Magazine. The title tale opens aboard a liner, where a girl named Cynthia Mortimer sizes up a quiet stranger called West and guesses his trade at once. Other tales carry titles such as The Nonentity, Her Hero, The Friend Who Stood By, and The Knight-Errant.

Dell writes popular romance with brisk talk, sharp heroines, and men of mystery, set on ships, in country houses, and in town. Questions of trust, honor, and love drive each plot. The set is a pleasant sample of the best-selling romance fiction of its day.
18650-the-war-and-the-churches:
Joseph McCabe published this short work at London in 1915 for the Rationalist Press Association, in the first full year of the Great War. He asks how far the churches could have used their sway to prevent the war, and how far they failed to do so. Chapters take up the churches' share of blame, Christianity and war, the clergy's apologies, the war and belief in God, and a human alternative.

McCabe warns that bias shapes how each side reads the facts, and he presses his case in plain, combative prose. The book gives a sharp freethought view of religion in wartime. Readers studying the war's moral debate will find it a pointed period source.
18679-historical-mysteries:
Andrew Lang published this set of historical puzzles at London in 1905 with Smith, Elder and Company, second edition, frontispiece portrait of Elizabeth Canning. Lang opens with a modern Cheshire parallel: a governess vanishes while skating, then reappears hurt, with a tale of capture no one can verify. He suggests a fall on ice and concussion explain her story better than crime.

Other cases cover the murder of Escovedo, the Campden mystery, Allan Breck, and the cardinal's necklace. Kaspar Hauser, the Gowrie conspiracy, medium Daniel Dunglas Home, Captain Green, the Chevalier d'Eon, and Saint-Germain the deathless follow. Lang weighs each with wit and doubt. The book is a classic of historical detection.
18683-ralph-granger-s-fortunes:
William Perry Brown published this boys' adventure novel with Saalfield in 1902. It opens on Ralph Granger's fifteenth birthday, when his grandfather hands him his dead father's rifle and orders him to settle the feud with the Vaughn family.

Ralph refuses the killing and sets out instead on a road that takes him past moonshiners and railroads to Columbia and Savannah. There he ships aboard the Curlew, faces shipboard discipline and bad weather, and sails toward the Gold Coast. Up a river and into the wilderness, he is left behind, finds a discovery, and endures hard times before reaching his uncle Gideon. The tale values pluck, loyalty, and quick thinking over revenge.
1870-reginald-in-russia-and-other-sketch:
No one would like a rich octogenarian uncle to take Reginald as an ideal of conduct, and yet the sketches keep returning to him, epigram first. The sketches move from London drawing rooms to Russia, with Reginald's epigrams cutting through every scene and his friends left to explain him.

A request for ordinary white blotting-paper, answered with talk of Winks and Pinks, shows Saki's method. A small absurdity, pursued with perfect manners, carries the joke until sense gives way. The collection is short, sharp, and very funny, and it remains the best place to meet Saki's most famous creation outside his short stories.
18713-violets-and-other-tales:
Alice Ruth Moore published this maiden book of sketches and verses in 1895 with the Monthly Review. Moore calls it a little thing that seeks only to amuse, with pieces first printed in newspapers and magazines beside new work. Her introduction owns the risk of a first book in a crowded market, hoping the pieces may lift care for an hour or two.

Contents run from Violets and The Woman to Titee, Anarchy Alley, A Carnival Jangle, A Story of Vengeance, At Bay St. Louis, and Chalmette, with poems such as At Eventide and Amid the Roses. The mix of Louisiana color, musing, and tale gives the book a fresh, personal voice. It is a charming debut.
18729-lourdes:
Robert Hugh Benson, a Monsignor of the Catholic Church, wrote this account of Lourdes, published by Herder of St. Louis and Manresa Press of London in 1914. Benson drew on notes made during his own stay at the shrine, writing first for the Ave Maria and reprinting the pieces six years later.

His preface reports a famous French scientist who studied Lourdes and found no scientific account equal to the cures he had seen or checked. The scientist held that an atmosphere of prayer mattered most, with cures rising and falling as prayer grew strong or weak. He mused on a transfer of vital force from sufferer or bystanders. Benson offers the account without pressing the theory, letting the shrine's story speak for itself.
18732-aesop-s-fables-a-new-revised-versi:
A revised version of Aesop's fables, published by Frank F. Lovell of New York and copyrighted in 1884, carries upwards of two hundred illustrations by Harrison Weir, John Tenniel, Ernest Griset, and others. A life of Aesop opens the volume before the fables begin.

The life places Aesop's birth about 620 B.C., tells of his slavery under Xanthus and Jadmon of Samos, and of the freedom Jadmon gave him for learning and wit. At the court of Croesus in Sardis he met Solon, Thales, and other sages, and his missions for the king took him to Corinth, Athens, and Delphi. There, the life says, his refusal to divide the king's gold angered the Delphians, who had him executed. The fables that follow carry the plain morals of that storied life.
18807-he-walked-around-the-horses:
H. Beam Piper's tale, from Astounding Science Fiction of April 1948, rests on an authenticated fact. In November 1809, the English envoy Benjamin Bathurst vanished at an inn in Perleberg, Prussia, while examining a change of horses on his way from Vienna to Hamburg. He was never seen again, at least not in this continuum.

The story is told through Prussian police papers, opening with Baron von Krutz writing to Chancellor von Berchtenwald about a man held at Berlin who calls himself Bathurst. The man's dispatch case holds papers so extraordinary that local officers sent him on to the ministry. A police report from Perleberg follows, as the tale turns a real disappearance into a story of worlds beside our own.
18811-the-light-princess-and-other-fairy:
George MacDonald's fairy stories gather three tales in one volume, headed by The Light Princess. That tale opens with a king and queen who have no children, until at last a lovely daughter is born and a christening is planned.

The king writes every invitation by hand yet forgets his sister, the sour and clever Princess Makemnoit, a slight the tale soon turns to mischief. The volume also holds The Giant's Heart and The Golden Key, two more tales of wonder in MacDonald's gentle, teasing voice. Together they offer magic that tests courage and kindness, told with humor for children and for older readers who still enjoy a tale told well.
18814-the-mercenaries:
H. Beam Piper's short story, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in March 1950, imagines warfare changed by hired experts and secret weapons work. Its hero, Duncan MacLeod, has spent fifteen years in research and development for a dozen nations and now works inside the guarded Tonto Basin Research Establishment.

There, veterans of the Manhattan Project grumble at rules far stricter than those of Fermi's Chicago or Oppenheimer's Los Alamos days. By 1965, four great power blocs race to put the first spaceship on the Moon and build a lunar fortress to hold world supremacy. The story asks what becomes of soldiers for hire when wars turn on science, secrecy, and machines.
18819-hume-english-men-of-letters-series:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this short study of David Hume for the English Men of Letters series, published by Macmillan in London in 1879. The first half traces Hume's life, from his birth in Edinburgh in 1711 through his literary work and his later years writing the History of England. The second half turns to his philosophy, chapter by chapter.

Huxley explains Hume's account of the mind, sense impressions, and belief, then moves through language, miracles, theism, the soul, free will, and morals. He presents Hume as a clear thinker who tested every claim against experience. Readers get a compact guide to both the man and his ideas, useful as an entry point before tackling Hume's own longer works.
1884-the-exiles:
In Clara Bell and James Waring's translation, Balzac sets The Exiles in Paris in 1308. Few houses yet stood on the island formed by Seine sand above the Cité, behind Notre-Dame. Two strangers arrive in that half-built quarter, and the neighbors, seeing one wear so fair a mien, whisper that the devil himself could look no better.

The tale follows a scholar and a mysterious companion through medieval Paris, with holy water, toads, and gossip as its instruments. Balzac writes the Middle Ages as a world of faith and fear. The story's interest lies in its atmosphere: a city still forming, and two exiles who do not belong in it.
18843-applied-psychology-for-nurses:
Mary F. Porter, a graduate nurse and teacher of applied psychology at Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina, wrote this textbook for nurses in 1921, published by W. B. Saunders in Philadelphia and London. It grew from her conviction, strengthened by years of teaching young people, that nurses needed psychology fitted to ward work, not abstract theory.

The book applies ideas about habit, attention, emotion, and suggestion to daily nursing tasks: calming patients, winning cooperation, and managing one's own temper and fatigue. Porter writes for students on the ward, with cases and plain advice. Readers get a clear record of how early applied psychology entered nurse training, and practical guidance that still reads as humane common sense.
1885-bunyan-characters-1st-series:
Alexander Whyte, D. D. , preached these lectures in St. George's Free Church, Edinburgh, taking the characters of Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress one by one. The introductory lecture starts from Hebrews 1:3, 'the express image,' and the Greek word for character, then turns to Christian, Faithful, and their companions as types of the Christian life.

Whyte's method is pastoral rather than scholarly. Each figure becomes a mirror for the hearer, with anecdotes from Scottish church life, including a dying minister in Aberdeen who wished for one more Sabbath in his pulpit. Readers who love Bunyan will find the lectures a warm companion, and readers new to the allegory will find its people explained.
1886-bunyan-characters-2nd-series:
Alexander Whyte's second series of Bunyan Characters continues his Edinburgh lectures, opening with Ignorance, who says he was alive without the law once, and brisk in his talk. Whyte follows Bunyan's figures through the Pilgrim's Progress, drawing out what each one means for a Christian reader.

A passage on a woman who was shown the way and left to taste the sweetness of prayer alone on her knees shows Whyte's pastoral method. A character becomes a case of conscience, examined with sympathy. Readers who finished the first series will find the same voice here, and newcomers can start with either volume, since each lecture stands alone.
18892-a-thoughtless-yes:
Helen H. Gardener gathered these stories in A Thoughtless Yes, in a tenth edition copyrighted in 1890. Gardener, author of Men, Women, and Gods and Sex in Brain, dedicated the volume to strangers who had written her letters. Their letters were thoughtful, gay, or sad, and came from far and near. They came from rich and poor, from Christian and unbeliever, from a bishop's palace and from behind prison walls.

The contents include A Splendid Judge of a Woman, The Lady of the Club, Under Protest, For the Prosecution, and A Rusty Link. The stories argue, in fictional form, for women's judgment and against double standards. Readers get feminist short fiction from the American freethought movement, plain in style and bold in its questions about marriage, law, and reputation.
18895-at-home-with-the-jardines:
Lilian Bell's household sketches, published by the A. Wessels Company of New York in 1906, tell of life at home with the Jardines. The narrator, a woman of emotional mountain peaks and dark valleys, marries Aubrey Jardine, whom their best man calls the Angel, one vast and sunny plateau.

The book's true heroine is Mary, the cook, who is also housekeeper, nurse, purse-keeper, seamstress, and best friend. Found at the Waldorf on their honeymoon through a billiard-room tip from Mr. Zanzibar, Mary had served her last place twenty-three years. Chapters on janitors, taming the cook, moving, and a first house-party follow the young household she keeps.
18907-holidays-at-the-grange-or-a-week-s:
Emily Mayer Higgins's book of games and stories for parlor and fireside, published by Porter and Coates of Philadelphia in 1886, spends a holiday week at Wyndham Grange. The rambling mansion, built a hundred years before by John Wyndham not many miles from Philadelphia, still keeps its family portraits, armor, antlers, and guitar.

Chapters run from Christmas Eve through New Year's Day, mixing games like Consequences, Rhymes, Cento, Twenty Questions, and Acting Charades with tales. An Indian tale of Orikama, the Spectre of Alcantra, the Orphan's Tale, and the Rose of Hesperus fill the fireside hours. Bible stories and capping verses mark the Sunday, in a week built for company and cheer.
18917-goldsmith-english-men-of-letters-s:
William Black's life of Oliver Goldsmith, in the English Men of Letters series edited by John Morley, appeared from Macmillan in 1878. It opens with Goldsmith's own wisdom: "innocently to amuse the imagination in this dream of life is wisdom." Black sets Thackeray's sweet minstrel beside Forster's darker picture of the hack ground down by booksellers.

Chapters follow school and college, idleness and foreign travel, hack-writing, The Bee, and The Citizen of the World. Beau Nash, The Traveller, The Vicar of Wakefield, The Good-Natured Man, The Deserted Village, and She Stoops to Conquer follow in turn. Goldsmith, happy-go-lucky with a guinea or turning starvation to humor without one, closes his wayward career in increasing difficulties.
1893-song-and-legend-from-the-middle-age:
William D. McClintock and Porter Lander McClintock gather song and legend from the Middle Ages, retelling tales of knights, saints, and minstrels for modern readers. The book pairs story with verse. The McClintocks, father and son scholars, retold medieval tales for American classrooms.

Medieval romance, ballad, and legend appear in clear, readable form, with notes to guide newcomers. The collection serves as a friendly door into the literature of the Middle Ages, for students and general readers alike. Their songs, from troubadours to ballads, give the Middle Ages a voice modern readers can hear.
18969-platform-monologues:
T. G. Tucker, professor of classical philology at the University of Melbourne, published these lectures in Melbourne in 1914. The volume gathers six platform addresses. They cover the supreme literary gift, Hebraism and Hellenism, and criticism applied to two successors of Tennyson. The rest treat the making of a Shakespeare, literature and life, and the future of poetry.

Tucker opens with Longinus and the test of true sublimity: great writing leaves the reader feeling as if he had himself begotten what he read. From that idea, he ranges across ancient and modern literature with a classicist's breadth. Readers get learned, well-spoken essays on what literature does and why it matters, from a scholar who lectured to general audiences.
1941-letters-of-two-brides:
Two school friends leave school together and choose opposite lives. One for love and Paris, one for marriage and the provinces — and they argue about it for years in letters. The novel is told entirely in letters between two young women, Louise and Renée. They leave school together and take opposite paths, one toward love and Paris and the other toward marriage and the provinces.

A Spanish lesson, in which a teacher begs to keep a piece of writing in memory of his pupil, shows the novel's method. Feeling is conveyed through letters, with all the misunderstandings letters allow. Balzac writes the two lives in counterpoint, and the book's interest lies in watching two friends argue, across years, about what a woman's life should be.
19722-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote A Child's Garden of Verses for young readers, first issued in 1885. This 1916 edition gathers his poems of childhood. The contents list reads like a child's day: Bed in Summer, Young Night Thought, Pirate Story. Other favorites include The Land of Counterpane and Farewell to the Farm. Stevenson treats small moments as full adventures.

A sickly child himself, Stevenson knew beds, gardens, and long indoor hours. His verses turn those limits into kingdoms. Soldiers march across a bedspread; shadows become playmates. The poems speak in a child's voice without talking down. Few children's books from the era are still read aloud. This one never left the nursery shelf.
1973-tales-of-troy-ulysses-the-sacker-of:
Andrew Lang's Tales of Troy: Ulysses, the Sacker of Cities, retells the story of Odysseus for young readers. It opens with Ithaca as a good island to live in, where summer was long and winter hardly more than a few cold weeks before the swallows came back. The plains, covered with violets, lilies, narcissus, and roses, set the home Odysseus must leave.

Lang follows Ulysses from Troy to Ithaca, through the Cyclops, the Sirens, and the suitors, in prose that keeps Homer's story clear without losing its wonder. The book is a children's classic of retelling, and its charm lies in Lang's voice: a storyteller who loves the tale and tells it straight.
19762-how-to-eat-a-cure-for-nerves:
Thomas Clark Hinkle, a physician, published How to Eat in 1921. Its subtitle promises a cure for nerves. Hinkle tells of a man who scorned a remedy too simple to respect. He borrows the Bible scene where servants urge a proud sufferer to try the plain cure anyway. If the prophet had demanded something great, they ask, would he not have done it?

Diet cures for nervous illness were a thriving genre then. Hinkle argues eating habits drive much nervous misery. Simple rules, faithfully kept, are his prescription. The book mixes medicine, morals, and common sense. It shows how doctors sold self-discipline as therapy. Modern readers will judge its claims for themselves.
19766-young-lucretia-and-other-stories:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote Young Lucretia and Other Stories in 1892. The title story turns on a village judging a child. One woman, the choir's soprano, sees little to pity in Lucretia's case. Most children, she says sharply, are cared for no better. Freeman lets small talk carry big moral weight. Her New England villages run on such talk.

Freeman was a master of the regional short story. Her women and children live under tight custom and tighter money. Small kindnesses and small cruelties decide their days. These stories show her quiet, exact style. Nothing loud happens; everything matters. Readers who like Chekhov's restraint will feel at home. It is American realism at village scale.
1978-buttercup-gold-and-other-stories:
Ellen Robena Field wrote these short stories for young children in 1894, under the care of a Maine kindergarten group. Gentle lessons about kindness, love, and good conduct run through tales told in plain, warm language. Field wrote for the kindergarten movement, which prized stories that taught by feeling rather than by lecture.

A boy named Maurice meets the Little New Year, and other children learn through small acts, kind words, and everyday wonders. The stories suit reading aloud, and each one ends with a simple moral a child can grasp without strain. Parents and teachers can use the tales one at a time, since each story stands alone and ends cleanly.
19781-sketches:
Benjamin Disraeli's Sketches collect his early short fiction and tales. One scene shows the Lady Imogene leaving Charolois by a postern gate. She is the bereaved count's only remaining child. Her page follows, bearing her book of prayers. She walks the undulating heights toward a sanctuary. The manner is romantic, youthful, and theatrical.

Disraeli wrote these pieces before fame, politics, or the premiership. He was trying voices: the tale, the sketch, the Eastern romance. Editors of the day printed such work in magazines and annuals. The Sketches let readers watch a famous style forming. His later novels keep this love of scene and costume. Here it appears young, lush, and unguarded.
19802-cobwebs-and-cables:
Hesba Stretton wrote Cobwebs and Cables as a novel of conscience and city life. It opens at eleven at night in a handsome office. Roland Sefton sits unmoving by the chimney-piece clock. He has not stirred hand or foot for a long while. He seems bound by many strong cords. The stillness signals a man trapped by his own affairs.

Stretton was famous for tales of street children and quiet sacrifice. Her novels press faith against money and reputation. An office at midnight suggests ledgers that will not balance morally. Sefton's paralysis is the story's first clue. Victorian readers trusted Stretton for earnest, unsparing plots. This opening shows her method: one still figure, much implied.
19813-ade-s-fables:
George Ade published Ade's Fables in 1912, modern fables in slang. One speaker here is a Larva with large ambitions. It wants to grow up to be a Joey, a circus clown. It aches to drive a trick mule behind the band. Little pieces of looking glass would glitter in the harness. Scared country girls peeking from wagon beds are its dream audience.

Ade rewrote Aesop for American towns and boosters. Each fable ends in a moral, often bent sideways. His slang was famous enough to define an era's humor. Politicians, farmers, and climbers all take their turns. The Larva's circus dream mocks every small-town ambition. Ade's fables remain readable because the types remain.
19825-herself-talks-with-women-concernin:
E. B. Lowry, a woman physician, wrote Herself as talks with women concerning themselves. She begins with structure before care. Readers must know something of the female generative organs first, she says. The first talk therefore teaches anatomy plainly. Lowry wrote several such guides for women and girls. Shame kept many readers ignorant of their own bodies.

Plain medical talk for women was a reform cause then. Lowry's books sold widely and were often reprinted. She treats readers as capable students, not patients to frighten. Illustrations and direct language carry her lessons. The series helped normalize women's health education. Herself is a landmark of that popular movement.
19848-woman-and-womanhood-a-search-for-p:
C. W. Saleeby published Woman and Womanhood in 1911, subtitled A Search for Principles. He opens by widening a common saying. Woman is half the human race, he grants. But present woman is also half of all generations to come. That makes her share larger than half, he argues. The book applies biology to women's social place.

Saleeby was a physician and a vocal eugenics supporter. His principles claim scientific ground for social claims. Modern readers will reject parts of that framework. The book still matters as evidence of its moment. Suffrage, motherhood, and race filled its debates. Saleeby shows how science-talk served those arguments. It is a document of Edwardian gender ideology.
1985-men-s-wives:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Men's Wives gathers stories of marriage from the husband's side, with wives who are charming, difficult, and sometimes ruinous. The tales follow men who marry for love, for money, or for beauty, and who learn what their choice costs.

Thackeray writes with the satirist's eye and the moralist's sympathy, and the stories' interest lies in their honesty: no villain is wholly villainous, and no marriage wholly happy. The collection pairs with his novels as a shorter, sharper look at the same world. It shows Thackeray's gift for making a whole life visible in a few scenes.
19867-frank-merriwell-junior-s-golden-tr:
Burt L. Standish was Gilbert Patten's pen name for the Merriwell stories. Frank Merriwell Junior's Golden Trail sends young Frank west. Only Merry and his two chums watch from the grand stand. A practice game pits the Ophir Athletic Club eleven against a scrub team. The game was staged for Frank's exclusive benefit. From football the trail turns toward a fugitive professor.

Frank Merriwell was the dime novel's model college hero. His son inherited the name and the adventures. Sports open most Merriwell tales before mystery takes over. The Golden Trail mixes gridiron, West, and pursuit. Millions of boys followed these stories weekly. Junior's trail shows the franchise passing generations.
19892-the-silver-crown-another-book-of-f:
Laura E. Richards wrote The Silver Crown as another book of fables in 1906. One fable sends a child riding and running his best. He crosses hills and valleys, broad streams and foaming torrents. He looks eagerly at people at work or at play. The journey itself is the lesson in her hands. Richards, daughter of Julia Ward Howe, wrote beloved children's verse.

Her fables dress small morals in bright, brief tales. Kings, children, and talking things share her pages. The Silver Crown followed her earlier fable collections. She aimed at wonder first and teaching second. That order kept her books in print for decades. This volume shows her gentle, musical method.
19906-winning-a-cause-world-war-stories:
Winning a Cause, dated 1919, gathers World War stories edited by John Gilbert Thompson. Its framing notes America's slow road into the war. Her people believed war an evil to be avoided, it says. Peace at any price seemed many Americans' motto. That held even after two years of world war. The stories then show what changed those minds. Thompson wrote and edited school readers for years.

War story collections taught patriotism to the young. Short tales of soldiers and helpers carry the cause. Thompson's framing admits the nation's reluctance honestly. That honesty makes the conversion story stronger. Schools bought such volumes for postwar classrooms. The book is civic instruction in story form.
19962-piccaninnies:
