From such street scenes the novel builds its Los Angeles. Spring Street was then the city's busy financial and shopping spine. Booth and local colour fill the pages in period style. The book survives as a curiosity of regional writing, when Los Angeles was still inventing itself in fiction as fast as in fact.
22195-little-tora-the-swedish-schoolmist:
Little Tora, the Swedish Schoolmistress, and Other Stories gathers tales of Sweden for English readers. The title story concerns Tora, a young schoolmistress in a Swedish village. One scene shows a family dinner laid in state: polished silver, shining glass, porcelain, flowers, and fruit cover the table. The plenty on the table seems, at first, to be all the dinner there is.

Mrs. Woods Baker, who wrote several books of Swedish life, gathered these tales from her years in Sweden. Village customs, schools, and family pride shape the plots. Such translated collections introduced English children to Scandinavian childhood. This one keeps the quiet, moral tone of the Swedish originals.
22198-two-sides-of-the-face-midwinter-ta:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, who signed himself "Q," published Two Sides of the Face as a set of midwinter tales. Quiller-Couch was a Cornish writer, anthologist, and champion of clear English. The title story opens behind a house where fields have cut back a plantation of noble ash trees. The modern farm buildings, shabby as they are, look friendlier than the old mansion brooding above them.

That contrast of faces, cheerful front and lost dignity, runs through the tales. Ghosts, doubles, and old houses suit the midwinter season of the subtitle. Quiller-Couch writes with a storyteller's ease and a scholar's vocabulary. The collection shows his fiction at its most characteristic: Cornish air, quiet uncanniness.
22217-my-reminiscences:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize in 1913, wrote My Reminiscences about his own formation. The English version reached readers through a translator who warns of the task's difficulty. Tagore's manner and matter, the translator says, combine in a way no second language easily carries. The effort was ventured anyway, from admiration for the original.

Tagore recalls a sheltered childhood in a great Calcutta house, servants, lessons, and early verses. He writes of his father's travels, his first songs, and the slow birth of a poet. The book is gentle, musical, and self-knowing. It remains the pleasantest door into Tagore's world for English readers.
22226-the-whispering-spheres:
The Whispering Spheres appeared in Comet magazine in July 1941, in that short-lived pulps attempt at wonder. An alien life form advances on Earth in the tale's opening picture, something like an inner eye glowing for a moment. In a factory town the whistle stays silent when it should blow. Three short blasts meant fire; one long blast, a breakdown; five toots, a layoff — but now nothing sounds.

The spheres whisper, and men must learn what the sound means before worse follows. The story works the classic pulp vein of first contact and strange invasion. Comet lasted only five issues, and tales like this one are nearly all that remains of it.
22278-a-master-of-mysteries:
L. T. Meade and Robert Eustace wrote A Master of Mysteries together, joining girls' fiction's queen to a master of scientific crime. Meade opens with a visitor laughing at his friend's special hobby. Yesterday, he admits, it struck him that those strange experiences might help him in a difficulty. The master of mysteries is that friend: a man whose trade is solving what looks supernatural.

Case by case, the tales explain hauntings, curses, and impossible crimes by science and patience. Eustace, a doctor, supplied the technical tricks; Meade supplied the storytelling. Their partnership fed the magazines with a new kind of detective tale. This set is an early, enjoyable sample of the scientific mystery story.
22290-me-and-nobbles:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote 'Me and Nobbles' as a story for children about a small narrator and her dog. The book opens inside a grand, gloomy house. The drawing room is awe-inspiring, its blinds nearly always down, with a musty, unused scent that says its grandeur is not for daily use. The library is gloomier still, with stained glass and dingy books lining the walls.

Through that gloom the child and Nobbles make their own cheerful world. Le Feuvre, whose Teddy's Button sold by the million, wrote faith and feeling in a child's own voice. This slighter tale shows her domestic vein: a dog, a lonely child, and a house learning to be a home.
22315-slain-by-the-doones:
R. D. Blackmore, famed for Lorna Doone, also wrote Slain by the Doones. The tales return to the wild West Country world of the Doone outlaws. One passage recalls a hard fanatic known as the Brewer.

The narrator's father, disgusted with England and banished from her, lost all his property. He took service on the Continent in exile. There he wandered for many years, until the throne was restored. Such backstory gives these short tales their sweep of loss and loyalty. Blackmore mixes family ruin, old violence, and moorland scenery into compact stories for readers who wanted more of the Doones.
22320-oldtown-fireside-stories:
Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Oldtown Fireside Stories from the tales of old New England. The setting is a hearth, with crickets filling each pause. Aged tellers pass their memories down to the young by firelight.

The stories cover early life, war, and adventure in the forest. They tell of Native captivities and escapes, and of bears and panthers. Rattlesnakes appear, along with witches, wizards, and strange dreams. Appearances and providences round out the stock of tales. Stowe, famous for a very different book, here preserves village storytelling. Readers hear how old communities kept their past alive through winter nights.
22338-the-impossibles:
The Impossibles is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its hero, Malone, is caught lying curled up and daydreaming. He drifts toward a wonderful dream and hates to interrupt it.

In that dream stands a girl more wonderful than anything he had imagined. She has big blue eyes and long blonde hair. Her figure, Malone thinks, shames the average pin-up girl. Such a start mixes fantasy with a wry, male daydream voice. The title hints that impossible things drive the plot. Readers get a light period tale where longing and the impossible meet, told with a wink.
22357-danger-and-other-stories:
Danger and Other Stories gathers short fiction preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its title story opens with a summons to a royal Presence. Horli has been called in, and the narrator goes with him.

Horli knew the narrator had clear ideas on England's weak points. He also had schemes for taking advantage of those points. Only four men sat at that meeting. They were the King, the Foreign Secretary, Admiral Horli, and the narrator. Such a start promises invasion plans and high stakes. The other stories share the volume's taste for risk. Readers get compact tales built around danger at sea and court.
224-a-pair-of-blue-eyes:
Elfride Swancourt, a rector's daughter on the Cornish coast, loves two men and loses her way. Thomas Hardy's Pair of Blue Eyes follows Elfride from first love with Stephen Smith to a later passion for Henry Knight. Church restoration, cliffs, and social rank frame the tale.

Hardy's preface notes the craze for restoring churches that reached even remote western parishes. Elfride's blue eyes and quick heart draw both suitors toward tragedy. The novel's forty chapters build slowly to a bleak end. It shows Hardy's early power with love and fate.
22475-tortoises:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Tortoises, a small book of poems on the tortoise. Lawrence watched these creatures closely during his years in Italy. The opening poem addresses a baby tortoise in tender terms.

Voiceless little bird, he calls the resting creature fondly. Its head rests half out of its wimple in slow dignity. Alone, with no sense of being alone, it pauses eternally. Hence, he writes, it is six times more solitary. It pitches its little round house through immemorial ages. Such lines turn a small animal into a figure of endurance. Readers get Lawrence's intense, wondering nature poetry at close range.
22519-christmas-every-day-and-other-stor:
Christmas Every Day and Other Stories, dated 1892, opens with a father's tale. A papa rouses himself from his writing with great effort. His little girl wants a story before anything else will do.

Well then, he says, he will tell about a certain girl. She was the little girl who wanted Christmas every day. How would you like that, he asks his daughter slyly. The wish granted becomes the tale's comic and moral engine. Too much of a good thing teaches its own sharp lesson. The other stories share that playful, instructive spirit. William Dean Howells wrote the title tale. It remains a holiday favorite about gifts, greed, and enough.
22522-artists-wives:
Alphonse Daudet wrote Artists' Wives, a set of stories about creative men's marriages. Daudet knew Parisian art and literary life from inside its circles. One husband's outburst shows the book's dramatic, teasing tone.

You dare say that, he cries, and the lamp stays lit! The walls, he marvels, do not fall on your head. For two hours, he protests, she has shown him enviable happiness. It is the very happiness she forbids him to enjoy himself. Such scenes probe what artists demand of their wives. Sacrifice, patience, and rivalry run through these marriages. Daudet treats them with wit and a touch of cruelty. Readers get Paris studio life in sharp little portraits.
22559-the-day-of-the-boomer-dukes:
The Day of the Boomer Dukes is a time-travel story with a bored hero. Its narrator peers back and back through the centuries seeking interest. He finds no time better than his own to live in.

Back he peered as far as the Numbered Years themselves. The twenty-eighth century was boredom unendurable to his searching eye. The twenty-sixth was a morass of dullness without relief. Twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth centuries offered the same tedium everywhere. Wherever he looked, the narrator complains, tedium was the finding. That comic despair drives his hunt through future history for excitement. Frederik Pohl wrote the tale. Readers get future ages reviewed by their toughest critic.
22608-a-book-for-all-readers-an-aid-to-t:
A Book for All Readers is a practical guide to forming, using, and preserving libraries, public and private. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Written when public libraries were spreading across America, it taught new librarians and home collectors how to choose, arrange, and care for books.

The author calms the fear that books multiply beyond all use. Truly important books, the text reflects, form only a small share of the mass; most books repeat what has already been written, many times over. Originality is the rarest of literary qualities. Around that sober thought, the manual builds advice on selection and upkeep. It is a handbook from the heroic age of library building.
22660-king-candaules:
King Candaules is a tale by Théophile Gautier, the French master of lush, pictorial prose, set in the ancient kingdom of Lydia. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its subject is the old story told by Herodotus: a king so proud of his wife's beauty that he shows her, unseen, to a favored courtier, with ruin to follow.

The sample paints the royal wedding day in Gautier's richest manner. The road for the procession lies strewn with fine yellow sand, while brazen tripods send up smoke of cinnamon and spikenard, the only clouds allowed in the pure azure sky. Such splendor is the trap's bait. Readers who love gorgeous surfaces with a cold fate beneath them will find Gautier in full flower.
22673-plantation-sketches:
Plantation Sketches is a set of reminiscences of the Old South, written as that world faded from living memory. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its opening sets the tone: as the New South rises with all its changes and improvements, hearts that still cling to the old order look sadly backward.

The Old South, the writer sighs, fades into dimness. Soon it will survive only in the memory of the few who knew it. Sketches of plantation life, its people, and its customs follow from that elegiac start. Such books were written in great numbers after the Civil War, and they must be read with care, since nostalgia softens what slavery made brutal. As a record of how the region chose to remember itself, the volume is revealing.
22682-secret-armies:
Secret Armies is John L. Spivak's exposé of fascist and propaganda networks inside the United States, published on the eve of the Second World War. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Spivak, a muckraking reporter, devoted his pen for years to uncovering evidence of fascist activity in America.

The book's framing credits his reporting with setting off several official investigations into un-American, foreign-run propaganda. Secret Armies is presented as the climax of those exposures. Its pages name agents, front groups, and money trails as Spivak traced them. The book belongs to the alarmed literature of the late 1930s, when Americans first reckoned with organized extremist movements at home. It remains a document of that awakening.
22683-practical-pointers-for-patentees:
Practical Pointers for Patentees is a 1901 guidebook for inventors who hoped to profit from their ideas. The catalog record names no author. America's patent system promised that a good invention could make its maker's fortune. A small industry of guides arose in answer. They explained the path from workshop to patent office to market.

The opening insists there can be no doubt that demand for inventions of merit, ready to sell at a fair profit, is real. Never, the writer claims, was the demand for worthwhile inventions so great as at the present time. Around that promise the book builds cautions and steps: searching prior patents, drafting claims, and avoiding sharp dealers. It is a period handbook from the golden age of the lone inventor.
2278-condensed-novels-new-burlesques:
Bret Harte sharpens his parodist's knife again in this second batch of condensed novels, mocking famous authors by squeezing their styles into tiny plots. New Burlesques takes aim at the mannerisms of popular novelists, with heroes, heroines, and villains reduced to their most recognizable tics. The humor depends on knowing the originals, but the jokes land even without them.

Harte's gift for mimicry shows in every page: dialects, melodrama, and moralizing all get the same brisk treatment. The collection is short, sharp, and very much of its literary moment. Fans of parody will enjoy seeing Victorian fiction sent up by one of its own.
22782-the-buddha-a-drama-in-five-acts-an:
The Buddha is a drama in five acts and four interludes, telling the life of Siddhartha Gautama in verse for the stage. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Western writers of the era, stirred by translations of Buddhist texts, repeatedly tried the Buddha's story in poetry and drama.

The opening scene is set with a painter's care: a tropical garden in Kapilavastu, mountains behind, and in the distance, the Himalayas lift their snow-capped peaks. A marble bench stands among bushes. Behind it rises the Raja's palace entrance. At the left stands a fortified gate with its guard house. All is built in antique Indian style. From that luxury the prince's great renunciation proceeds. The play offers the Buddha's life as pageant and meditation.
2281-the-heritage-of-dedlow-marsh-and-ot:
Bret Harte returns to California in this collection of tales anchored by the title story of a marshland inheritance. The Heritage of Dedlow Marsh and Other Tales mixes courtroom disputes, lost heirs, and frontier romance, with Harte's familiar blend of pathos and dry wit. Each story turns on a document, a debt, or a disputed claim.

The marsh itself, foggy and treacherous, gives the title tale its mood. Other pieces range across mining camps and coastal towns. The volume shows Harte in his later manner, polished and fond of his old territory.
22818-an-alphabet-of-celebrities:
Oliver Herford wrote and pictured An Alphabet of Celebrities, printed in Boston in November 1899. Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue designed the border and initial letters, and E. Bird handled the end papers and cover. The result is a small, handsome gift book built around the alphabet itself.

Letter by letter, famous names of the day get brief, witty treatment in verse and drawing. Herford was known for light satire, and the fun here lies in seeing which celebrity he pairs with each letter and what joke he makes of them. The book doubles as a snapshot of who counted as famous in 1899. Many of its stars have faded, and that fading is half the charm now.
22829-no-animal-food-and-nutrition-and-d:
Meat is the enemy in No Animal Food, a health manual pairing arguments on nutrition and diet with vegetable recipes. Its authorities speak bluntly. One quoted physician warns against cheating. Add butter, cream, cheese, eggs, or lard to vegetables, he says, and the meal stops being vegetarian. It becomes mixed fare, with effects much like meat.

Readers get both doctrine and dinner. The early pages press the case that humans thrive without animal food, drawing on doctors and reform journals. The later pages turn practical, with recipes meant to prove the diet workable at an ordinary table. The book captures the vegetarian movement of its day at full confidence. Modern readers can test its claims, and its menus, for themselves.
2284-animal-heroes:
Ernest Thompson Seton, the naturalist who helped found the Boy Scouts, tells true-to-life stories of animals who showed courage, loyalty, and cunning. Animal Heroes follows dogs, horses, wolves, and other creatures through rescues, wars, and wilderness trials, each tale grounded in Seton's observation of animal behavior. The stories avoid sentimentality in favor of fact.

Seton's woodcraft knowledge gives every episode its texture: tracks, scents, and habits all matter to the outcome. Young readers learn natural history while cheering for animal protagonists. The book remains a classic of animal literature for children.
22885-hindu-gods-and-heroes:
East meets West by design in Hindu Gods and Heroes, part of a series meant to build goodwill and understanding between the two. The editors state their aim plainly in the front matter. Their small books would serve as ambassadors, following, in their own sphere, the highest example in the land.

Inside, the gods and heroes of India take the stage in retelling and explanation. English readers of the period often knew Hindu religion only through mission reports and rumor. A sympathetic survey, written to be read by general readers, filled a real gap. The volume keeps a respectful, introductory tone throughout. It remains useful as both a primer on its subject and a record of early cross-cultural publishing.
22886-cinderella-in-the-south-twenty-fiv:
A barroom question opens Cinderella in the South, Arthur Shearly Cripps's set of twenty-five South African tales. What's the good of him, the bar-tender asks, of a man who might explain how the Ruins came to be. A man who could explain the great ruins, he reckons, might earn a handsome monthly cheque for the knowledge alone.

Cripps lived in Southern Africa as a missionary priest, and his tales grow from that ground. Settlers, Africans, ruins, and veld talk fill the pages, with the great stone ruins of the region haunting several stories. His sympathy often ran against settler opinion of his day. The tales preserve a voice both inside and uneasy within colonial Africa, which gives them interest beyond their plots.
22891-simple-simon-silhouette-series:
Simple Simon meets the pieman in this little silhouette picture book for children. The hosted text presents the old nursery rhyme in the Silhouette Series format, where black paper-cut style figures act out the verses against the page. Simon's simple questions and the pieman's plain answers carry the whole joke.

Silhouette books were a cheap, cheerful staple of the nursery shelf. Their stark black shapes let even very young readers follow the story in pictures alone. Simon, the famous fool of rhyme, asks to taste the wares first and pay later, which never ends well for him. The charm lies in economy. A few lines, a few shapes, and a rhyme children have repeated for centuries.
22893-pygmalion-s-spectacles:
A philosopher argues about sight itself in Pygmalion's Spectacles. Sensations are mental phenomena, he insists. They exist in our minds. How, then, do we know the objects themselves do not exist only there too? That wall is never truly seen, he tells his listener. What reaches us is a visual sensation, and the mind supplies the rest.

Out of that argument grows one of early science fiction's most retold inventions, spectacles that make imagined scenes feel real. The story, first printed in the 1930s, plays with virtual experience long before the term existed. Its talk stays lively because the stakes stay personal. Readers who enjoy ideas dressed as conversation will find a small classic of the form.
22939-the-gypsies:
Charles G. Leland reports a discovery in The Gypsies, published in 1882. The Romanies of the East, he claims, speak a language much like the Gypsy speech of England, in vocabulary and in the slang of the roads. He learned this, he says, from a Hindu man who had himself been a Gypsy in his native land.

Leland traveled, listened, and wrote down lore, tales, and spells as insiders shared them. His book ranges across countries, always chasing the thread of Romany language and custom. Modern scholars treat parts of it cautiously, since Leland loved a good story. Yet few Victorian writers took Gypsy life so seriously. The book remains a rich, flawed, firsthand record of its subject.
22998-janet-of-the-dunes:
Harriet T. Comstock pits Janet against Cap'n Billy in Janet of the Dunes, published in 1907. Facing Janet undoes Cap'n Billy completely. He cannot meet her eyes and still hope to win an argument with her. Honest and simple as he is, he means to hold his course all the same, if she will let him..

The dunes of the title frame a Long Island fishing community, where Janet's will meets older men's custom. Comstock wrote regional fiction steeped in salt air and plain speech. Romance and stubbornness share the helm here. The book rewards readers who like their love stories weather-beaten, with the sea doing half the talking.
23051-the-two-shipmates:
A clever little vessel anchors The Two Shipmates. The little vessel nearly knows her own way through the harbor mouth. Her master knows it better than most traders using the port, and young Ralph Michelmore, his mate, is learning it fast.

Master and mate give the story its pair, age and youth working one small trade together. Sea tales for boys ran on such partnerships, where the junior learns seamanship and character in equal doses. Storms, cargoes, and harbor rivalries supply the incidents. The writing keeps a affectionate eye on the ship herself, treated as a third shipmate. Readers who like their adventure salted but wholesome will find this a snug berth.
23068-my-first-cruise-and-other-stories:
A prank at sea starts My First Cruise and Other Stories. The young narrator laughed just to keep the others company, thinking the joke was over. The crew seized him before he understood the joke. A handkerchief blinded him, and they lashed him spread-eagled in the rigging, arms and legs stretched wide. Then all fell silent.

Initiation, storms, and shipboard society fill this set of sea tales told from a boy's berth. The cruise teaches the green hand what books cannot, at the cost of a few such jokes. Collections like this one fed the great demand for naval yarns. Their value now is double, entertainment then, evidence now, of how the sailing services raised their boys.
23070-clara-maynard-or-the-true-and-the-:
An old sailor loves his yacht in Clara Maynard, or The True and the False, a tale of the times. Two men and a boy crew her, and she measures barely twenty-five tons. Even so, her owner swears he would take her round the world without a moment's doubt, if need arose.

Yachts and character tests give the tale its twin engines. Clara's story sorts the true from the false, as the subtitle promises, among suitors, friends, and fortunes. The sea scenes carry the freest writing, salt air clearing the drawing room's plots. Fiction of this school aimed to improve while it entertained, and the yacht chapters show the method at its best, adventure first, moral riding quietly astern.
23071-the-rival-crusoes:
An editor revives a girlhood book in The Rival Crusoes. Agnes Strickland, already known to readers, wrote the tale in her teens, the editor explains, more than fifty years before this reprint. He remembers the intense delight with which he read it in his boyhood, and was lately surprised to find it so long out of print.

Two castaways compete where Defoe's hero stood alone, and rivalry turns survival into sport and spite. Strickland, later a famous historian of queens, wrote this juvenile Robinsonade in her teens. The reprint frames it as a rediscovery, an old favorite rescued for new boys. Shipwreck fiction rarely shows its roots so plainly. Here readers can watch the Crusoe formula being handed down, girl author to boy readers.
2308-bunyan-characters-3rd-series:
Alexander Whyte, the Scottish preacher, continues his studies of John Bunyan's characters in this third series of lectures. Bunyan Characters takes figures from The Pilgrim's Progress and other works, treating each as a portrait of a spiritual type: the fearful, the faithful, the backsliding, and the steadfast. Whyte's pulpit style is warm, learned, and direct.

The lectures work as both literary criticism and devotion, unpacking Bunyan's allegory for ordinary readers. They show why Bunyan's people still feel alive centuries on. Readers interested in Bunyan or in Victorian preaching will find much to ponder.
23112-the-kitchen-cat-and-other-tales:
A child watches the street from high windows in The Kitchen Cat and Other Tales. From her high window, street traffic below shrinks to toys. Iron bars stop her leaning out for a better view. Her whole world is the facing row of houses and a strip of sky between chimney pots.

Amy Walton wrote these tales for children of the London streets and the houses above them. A kitchen cat, caged views, and small kindnesses carry her stories in the manner of the period's city tales for the young. The barred window does quiet work, childhood observed and confined at once. The collection keeps a tender, observant eye throughout.
23114-our-frank-and-other-stories:
A tired walker climbs home in Our Frank and Other Stories. A friend's talk cheered the first stretch of the walk home. After good-nights at the village edge came the steep chalky hill road. Each step up it tired her more, and the basket dragged heavier with every yard.

Village effort and village kindness fill this collection of tales. Frank, the title's hero, belongs to the world of that chalky road, where small earnings and large duties meet. The stories were written for readers who knew such roads themselves, and they honor endurance without dressing it up. Plain settings, plain people, and carefully kept sympathy make the volume a fair sample of its shelf.
23130-black-white-and-gray-a-story-of-th:
A cat hides in Black, White, and Gray, a story of three homes. At play today, the children spotted a white coat in a dusky hiding place. Madam the cat would rather have stayed hidden. Still, she accepted discovery calmly, even when Dennis reached in gently and drew out her black kitten.

Kittens sort the three homes of the title by color and fortune in this tale for young readers, credited to Amy Walton. A white cat, a black kitten, and the gray shades between carry a gentle plot about kindness to animals. Walton wrote many such stories for the era's children's lists. The hiding scene shows her method, small creatures, soft hands, and morals that arrive as naturally as the kittens do.
23171-the-tipster-1901-from-wall-street-:
Edwin Lefèvre studies a honest face in The Tipster, dated 1901, from Wall Street Stories. A great tenderness for the customer rises in Gilmartin, the narrator says, since the man's own credulity stings the lie out of the lie. Relief smiles on the tipster's lips. Three-and-thirty, pleasant in face and voice, he breathes health and an easy conscience. Honesty, it seems, shines in his eyes. People liked to shake hands with him.

A tipster with an easy conscience is Wall Street's perfect animal, and Lefèvre, the Street's great storyteller, dissects him gently. Tips, credulity, and the commission on both fill the tale. Lefèvre later wrote Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, the traders' bible. This early story shows the same eye at work, watching a smile do the work of a prospectus.
23250-the-skeleton-on-round-island-from-:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood's The Skeleton on Round Island comes from her Mackinac and Lake Stories. A hard-bitten lake traveller tells what hunger on the ice means. Sometimes, he says, he waits two or three days for a chance to move, drawing his belt in tighter as he waits.

Ice floes can carry a man miles, since they all drift east down the lakes when they start. He has landed on the far side of Drummond that way. But travel with a woman along, he adds, is different. Readers get a stark winter tale of ice, hunger, and hard choices.
23257-clair-de-lune-a-play-in-two-acts-a:
Michael Strange's Clair de Lune, from 1921, is a play in two acts and six scenes. Its talk is polished and teasing. One character, asked a question, glances about the room and remarks that everyone looks very much in tune with the Almighty, as if He had been telling them secrets.

The same speaker confesses a lasting weakness: a prey to the desire to hear what is said just before entering a room, and just after leaving it. Strange builds scenes from such drawing-room wit. Readers get a slight, elegant drama where conversation, curiosity, and social poise carry the action.
2327-some-short-stories-by-henry-james:
Henry James gathers five of his finest short tales in this volume, from the devoted servant of Brooksmith to the artists and patrons of The Real Thing. Some Short Stories by Henry James shows the master in miniature: social observation, moral ambiguity, and sentences that coil around their subjects. Each story turns on a small social fact with large consequences.

The collection suits readers who want James without committing to a long novel. Its pieces reward slow reading and rereading. For an introduction to James's art, few books serve better.
2395-the-golden-fleece-and-the-heroes-wh:
Padraic Colum retells the Greek myths of Jason and the Argonauts for young readers in The Golden Fleece and the Heroes Who Lived Before Achilles. The book follows Jason from his youth through the gathering of heroes, the building of the Argo, and the quest for the fleece in Colchis. Colum's prose is clear, musical, and faithful to the old tales.

The volume also introduces Heracles, Orpheus, and other heroes before Achilles' age. Its storytelling has charmed generations of children. Mythology lovers will find a classic retelling. Colum also retold the myths of Troy and of Odysseus for children.
2412-the-categories:
Aristotle's Categories opens the Organon, his works on logic, by sorting the ways things can be said to exist. The short treatise defines substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, and other categories, laying the groundwork for Western logic and metaphysics. Aristotle writes with terse, systematic care.

The work is technical but foundational: centuries of philosophers began here. Modern readers will find it demanding yet short, and its influence enormous. Students of philosophy meet it as a first text of the tradition. Medieval schoolmen built their whole logic course on this short text.
2428-an-essay-on-man-moral-essays-and-sa:
Alexander Pope's Essay on Man, with his Moral Essays and Satires, gathers the great Augustan poet at his most philosophical and his most biting. The Essay argues that the universe is ordered and that human pride blinds us to our place in it, in couplets of unmatched polish. The satires skewer dunces, flatterers, and the follies of his age.

Pope's verse rewards readers who love wit, balance, and epigram. His lines have passed into proverb: hope springs eternal, fools rush in. The volume serves as an ideal introduction to his art.
243-the-forged-coupon-and-other-stories:
A forged coupon, passed from hand to hand, spreads crime and ruin through Russian society. Leo Tolstoy's Forged Coupon and Other Stories opens with that chain of small sins growing into murder. Later tales follow its moral logic in reverse, toward repentance.

After the Dance, Alyosha the Pot, and The Young Tsar join the set, with essays on guilt and power. Tolstoy's late prose is plain, stern, and searching. The introduction frames spiritual power against an age of materialism. The volume shows Tolstoy the prophet in story form. Tolstoy's chain of sin and grace still challenges readers about moral cause.
2436-the-marriages:
Henry James's tale The Marriages follows a young woman caught between her father's remarriage and her own engagement, in a tangle of money, loyalty, and social appearance. The story watches a family negotiate two weddings at once, with James's irony exposing every polite evasion. The heroine must choose between duty to her father and honesty to herself.

The tale is compact and psychologically acute, with James's late attention to motive. Readers of his short fiction will enjoy its quiet tension. It pairs well with his other tales of marriage and money.
2458-sermons-on-the-card-and-other-disco:
Hugh Latimer, the Reformation preacher and martyr, delivers his Sermons on the Card, using a deck of cards as a teaching tool for a congregation that knew games better than doctrine. The discourses preach repentance, honesty, and the Christian life in plain, vigorous Tudor English, with Latimer's famous directness. The sermons show why he moved crowds.

The volume preserves a voice of the English Reformation at its most popular and bold. Latimer's plain speech still strikes home. Readers of religious history will find a vivid primary text. Latimer was burned at Oxford in 1555 under Queen Mary.
2459-trent-s-trust-and-other-stories:
Bret Harte's Trent's Trust and Other Stories returns to California for tales of inheritance, trust, and frontier honor. The title story follows a man entrusted with a fortune and the temptations that follow, while the other pieces mix mining camps, romance, and Harte's familiar ironies. The collection shows his late style at its most polished.

Harte's California remains vivid even as the gold rush recedes into memory. The stories are compact and well-turned. Fans of his work will find a satisfying late volume. Harte wrote these tales near the end of his long career in London.
247-webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-1st-:
Noah Webster's revised unabridged dictionary of 1913 opens with the letter A and a history of the alphabet. This file gives the first hundred pages, from A through early entries, with pronunciation guides. The A entry traces the letter from Phoenician aleph through Greek alpha to Latin.

Definitions, word histories, and usage notes follow the dictionary's full pattern. Readers meet the 1913 editors' care for spelling, sound, and sense. The partial file suits browsing and reference alike. Later pages continue the alphabet beyond this opening stretch. The dictionary's first pages show how American English defined itself in print.
2472-white-lies:
Charles Reade's White Lies is a melodrama of love, deception, and redemption set in France, where a woman's small falsehoods snowball into danger. The novel follows its heroine through a maze of secrets, duels, and revelations, with Reade's energetic plotting and reforming zeal driving every chapter. The lies of the title are white only at first.

Reade's theatrical sense keeps the story moving, and his sympathy for his heroine carries the sentiment. Victorian fiction fans will find a fast, emotional read. The book shows Reade at his most popular. Reade adapted the novel for the stage, as he did with many of his books.
248-webster-s-unabridged-dictionary-2nd-:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary of 1913 continues here past page one hundred. This second hundred pages runs through entries near attract, with full etymologies and usage notes. Attractivity, attractor, and attrahent show the dictionary's Latin roots and careful marking.

Medical, obsolete, and figurative senses appear alongside everyday ones, with quotations from Browne, Glanvill, and Taylor. Pronunciation marks and part-of-speech labels guide the reader throughout. The file suits anyone tracing a word's history in early twentieth-century English. It continues the first hundred pages in sequence. The 1913 dictionary remains a favorite of word lovers and crossword solvers.
2480-under-western-eyes:
Joseph Conrad's Under Western Eyes follows Razumov, a Russian student who betrays a revolutionary assassin and is drawn into the world of spies and exiles he betrayed. The novel moves from St. Petersburg to Geneva, with Conrad's narrator piecing together Razumov's guilt and his doomed love. The book's political vision is dark and unsparing.

Conrad writes from his knowledge of Russian exile politics, and the novel's irony cuts every side. Its atmosphere of surveillance and conscience feels modern. Readers of political fiction will find a masterpiece. Conrad based his Geneva exiles on Russians he had known in London.
2492-orpheus-in-mayfair-and-other-storie:
Maurice Baring's Orpheus in Mayfair and Other Stories and Sketches brings classical myth into modern London, with the title story letting Orpheus walk Mayfair's streets. The sketches range from fables to wartime vignettes, many first printed in the Morning Post, with Baring's light, cosmopolitan touch. The collection is urbane and quietly melancholy.

Baring, a diplomat and man of letters, writes for readers who enjoy allusion and understatement. The book's variety suits dipping in and out. Lovers of the literary sketch will find a refined volume. Baring served as a diplomat in Russia and Persia before turning to letters.
2517-lincoln-s-yarns-and-stories:
Alexander K. McClure gathered this large set of funny and pointed tales about Abraham Lincoln, the president famous for settling hard questions with a story. The book opens with a sketch of Lincoln's life, from a Kentucky log cabin in 1809 to the White House and his murder in April 1865.

The anecdotes that follow show Lincoln teasing rivals, calming his cabinet, and answering critics with jokes drawn from farm life, courtrooms, and the army. Some tales are tall, some are sharp, and all show why his humor won friends and disarmed foes. Readers get Lincoln the man, not just Lincoln the monument, in his own best weapon: a well told story.
2518-the-hungry-stones-and-other-stories:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet and storyteller, wrote the tales gathered here, most of them turned into English by several hands, with one version by Tagore himself. Their settings run from old palaces and country villages to the streets of Calcutta, and their people include kings, priests, children, and travelers.

Ghosts haunt a ruined palace in the title story, a fruit seller from Kabul befriends a small girl, and a baby king rules a kingdom of cards. Across the set, Tagore blends folk wonder with sharp looks at pride, devotion, and family duty. The stories stay short, strange, and warm, and they show why his fiction traveled far beyond Bengal.
2525-john-ingerfield-and-other-stories:
Jerome K. Jerome opens this set with the title story of John Ingerfield, an oil and tallow refiner of Limehouse. Tales of a Norwegian mountain farm, stage patter, silhouettes, and the lease of a country inn called the Cross Keys follow. Jerome warns readers up front that the first three stories are serious, not comic.

That warning matters, because the book shifts between quiet tragedy and music hall jokes with ease. The Ingerfield story traces a hard family line, while the lighter pieces show Jerome's gift for talk and character. Together they show a writer wider than his comic fame, able to move from laughter to sorrow in a few pages.
2545-when-god-laughs-and-other-stories:
Jack London published this story set in 1911, opening with a tale of Carquinez, a man who claims Aztec, Inca, and Spanish blood and lives by a wise, instinctive temperance. The gods, London suggests, laugh hardest at men who think they have mastered fate.

An apostate factory boy, a wicked woman, a boxer past his prime in A Piece of Steak, and the crew of the Francis Spaight follow. The stories hit hard on labor, hunger, and pride, with London's blunt naturalism at full strength. Readers get a dozen sharp blows, each asking what a person is worth when luck turns.
2597-mrs-skagg-s-husbands-and-other-stor:
Bret Harte opens this set with Mrs. Skagg's Husbands, as the sun rises over the Sierra foothills east of Angel's camp. The tales that follow bring Santa Claus to Simpson's Bar, Princess Bob and her friends, the Iliad of Sandy Bar, and a prodigal Mr. Thompson.

A romance of Madrono Hollow, the poet of Sierra Flat, and a Christmas gift for Rupert round out the volume. Harte mixes camp humor with holiday feeling, and his miners, wives, and wanderers feel like old friends. The book shows his gift for turning rough California life into warm, surprising stories.
2598-urban-sketches:
Bret Harte turns from mining camps to city streets in these sketches, opening with a venerable impostor glimpsed across his table. From a balcony, among melons, and along sidewalks, Harte watches neighbors, boys, dogs, and steamers with a journalist's eye.

A boy's dog, charitable reminiscences, and the act of seeing a steamer off each get a short, sharp scene. The sketches show Harte as a city observer, fond of small frauds and small kindnesses alike. Readers get a lighter Harte, sketching modern life in quick strokes rather than full tales.
2599-legends-and-tales:
Bret Harte gathers California legends in this volume, and warns the cautious reader himself that documentary evidence for them is thin. The Legend of Monte del Diablo, the adventure of Padre Vincentio, and the Legend of Devil's Point lead a parade of haunted hills and holy tricksters.

The Devil meets a broker, an ogress haunts Silver Land, and the ruins of San Francisco rise in a prophetic vision. A night at Wingdam closes the set with campfire color. Harte blends Spanish folklore, mining camp talk, and sly humor, and the tales work best read as fireside inventions, not history.
2603-questionable-amusements-and-worthy-:
J. M. Judy wrote this book for readers worried about the amusements of a new century, with an introduction by George H. Trever. The manuscript was never sent to a publisher; friends put it into print in Chicago in 1904 through Jennings and Pye.

Judy weighs dances, theaters, cards, and other pastimes, judging which harm character and which wholesome substitutes might take their place. His tone is earnest and pastoral, aimed at parents, teachers, and church workers. The book now reads as a window on Edwardian moral worry, and on the search for clean fun.
2636-the-historical-nights-entertainment:
Rafael Sabatini set himself a task in this first series: to rebuild famous and bizarre events in full detail, with all the color surviving records allow. He chose episodes strange in themselves and born of intrigue, passion, or crime, rather than familiar textbook scenes.

Each night's entertainment retells a historical moment as a vivid tale, with courts, conspirators, and doomed lovers. Sabatini's preface owns his method plainly: color where records allow it, invention never where fact speaks. The book suits readers who like history as story, told by a master of adventure.
2639-villa-rubein-and-other-stories:
John Galsworthy gathers stories in this volume, led by Villa Rubein, a long tale of love and art in twenty nine chapters. A Man of Devon, A Knight, Salvation of a Forsyte, and The Silence follow, each showing Galsworthy's early range beyond the Forsyte clan.

Galsworthy writes of country houses, artists, soldiers, and families under strain, with the irony and pity that mark his best work. The preface to Villa Rubein frames a young writer finding his voice. The set offers a fine way into Galsworthy before the saga, and several stories that stand on their own.
2675-burlesques:
William Makepeace Thackeray parodies the popular novels of his day in these burlesques, with notes by eminent hands. George de Barnwell, Codlingsby, Phil Fogarty of the fighting Onety Oneth, and Barbazure each take a famous style and push it over the edge.

Lords and Liveries, Crinoline, and other pieces mock romance, fashion, and heroic history with glee. Thackeray writes as a critic in costume, showing how easily grand styles turn absurd. The book delights as literary satire, and as a young master's exercise in voices. Thackeray's targets knew themselves at once, and laughed anyway.
2676-the-bell-ringer-of-angel-s-and-othe:
Bret Harte opens this set at Angel's, where the North Fork of the Stanislaus River broadens from mountain youth into the plain. The bell ringer, Johnnyboy, young Robin Gray, and the sheriff of Siskiyou each take a story, with a rose of Glenbogie and a hacienda mystery to follow.

Chu Chu and Harte's own My First Book close the volume, mixing camp legend with literary memory. Harte writes with his familiar blend of dialect, irony, and sudden pathos. The stories show California in many moods, from comedy to quiet tragedy, all under a western sky.
2684-five-tales:
John Galsworthy gathers five tales in this 1919 volume, opening with his motto that life calls the tune and we dance. The First and Last, A Stoic, The Apple Tree, and The Juryman each study a life caught by fate, duty, or desire.

Indian Summer of a Forsyte closes the set, and later became the opening of the second Forsyte volume. Galsworthy's prose is restrained and ironic, letting small choices carry large weight. The book offers a compact introduction to his art, and a bridge into the saga itself. Each tale turns on a single hard choice.
2692-a-protegee-of-jack-hamlin-s-and-oth:
Bret Harte returns to Jack Hamlin in this set, opening as the steamer Silveropolis cleaves the broad shallows of the Sacramento River. Hamlin's protegee, an ingenue of the Sierras, and the reformation of James Reddy each test the gambler's code.

The heir of the McHulishes, an episode of West Woodlands, and the home coming of Jim Wilkes round out the volume. Harte mixes river travel, camp society, and sentimental turns with his usual skill. The stories show his late California still rich in rogues, orphans, and second chances. Hamlin's gallantry toward the protegee anchors the set.
2715-the-real-thing-and-other-tales:
Henry James gathers tales in this 1893 Macmillan volume, issued for circulation in India and the British Colonies. The title story studies artists, models, and the difference between the real thing and its imitation, a theme James knew from life.

Other tales follow writers, painters, and society folk caught between art and commerce, truth and pose. James writes with his late subtlety, in sentences that turn like conversations. The book rewards readers who like fiction about fiction, and about the price of being genuine. James's artists and models debate what truth in art requires.
2721-eric-brighteyes:
H. Rider Haggard sets this saga in Iceland, opening with Asmund the priest finding Groa the witch, and Eric telling his love to Gudruda in snow on Coldback. Asmund bids Eric to his Yule feast, Eric comes down Golden Falls, and Eric wins the sword Whitefire.

Betrothals, feuds, and a fight with Skallagrim the Baresark on Mosfell follow, in the manner of the old sagas Haggard loved. The prose is archaic and bold, full of snow, blood, and oath keeping. The novel stands as Haggard's most Norse romance, and a tribute to the saga age.
2741-the-borgias-celebrated-crimes:
April 8, 1492, in a Vatican bedroom, opens this Celebrated Crimes history of the Borgias. The prologue opens on April 8, 1492, in a bedroom of the Vatican, as Rodrigo Borgia moves toward the papacy that will make his family infamous.

Pope Alexander VI, his son Cesare, and his daughter Lucrezia preside over murder, simony, and splendor in Renaissance Rome. Gusto turns chronicle into dark romance, and the Vatican scenes glitter with menace. The book remains the classic popular history of a family whose name became a byword for corruption. Dumas spares neither pope nor prince in his telling.
2742-cenci-celebrated-crimes:
Dated 1598, this entry in Dumas's Celebrated Crimes turns to the Cenci family of Rome, whose name became a byword for a father's tyranny. A visitor to Rome who seeks shade under the tall pines of the Villa Pamphili will descend toward the Janiculum by a charming road, and there the tale begins.

Beatrice Cenci, her tyrant father, and a murder born of abuse drive one of history's most famous trials. Romantic fire turns records into drama here, and the trial scenes carry the horror. The story remains a harrowing classic of crime, family horror, and justice in Renaissance Rome.
2743-massacres-of-the-south-1551-1815-ce:
Nearly three centuries of religious killing in southern France fill this Celebrated Crimes volume, spanning 1551 to 1815. The reader whose memory reaches back to the Restoration will recall a France still bleeding from religious war.

Catholics and Protestants slaughtered each other across the Midi for nearly three centuries, in towns like Nimes and Avignon. Partisan fire chronicles mob murder, reprisal, and royal indifference across the Midi. The book stands as a grim history of sectarian hatred, and of its long French shadow. Dumas counts the cost in villages, churches, and broken families.
2744-mary-stuart-celebrated-crimes:
Some royal names are predestined to misfortune, Dumas warns at the start of this Celebrated Crimes volume on Mary Stuart, dated 1587. Dumas begins with that warning, and in France the name Henry carries poison, while Mary's own name carries tragedy.

From her French girlhood to her English prison and scaffold, Mary moves through plots, lovers, and rival queens. Sympathy for the doomed queen and fire for her enemies mark the telling. The book offers a romantic history of a life that still divides readers, four centuries on. Dumas writes her fall as high tragedy, not cold chronicle.
2745-karl-ludwig-sand-celebrated-crimes:
A German student with a dagger opens this Celebrated Crimes portrait of Karl Ludwig Sand, murderer of Kotzebue in 1819. Sand, a young German student fired by nationalist dreams, murdered the writer August von Kotzebue in 1819, believing him a traitor to Germany.

Idealistic youth gives way to assassin, trial, and scaffold, and the telling holds both sympathy and horror. The murder shocked Europe and brought repression down on German universities. The book remains a classic portrait of political fanaticism in a young man. His scaffold speech made him a martyr to German students.
2746-urbain-grandier-celebrated-crimes:
Loudun in November 1631 opens this Celebrated Crimes account of Urbain Grandier, a priest accused of sorcery. On Sunday, November 26, 1631, great excitement seized Loudun, and a priest stood accused of sorcery, demonic possession, and a pact with the devil.

Grandier's trial, with nuns, exorcists, and Cardinal Richelieu's agents, became a byword for judicial murder. Indignation drives the narrative, turning documents into a story of power crushing a man. The book remains a classic account of witch panic and political revenge. Loudun's devils and judges share the blame in Dumas's telling. The nuns' possessions and the exorcists' theater made the trial a spectacle.
2747-nisida-celebrated-crimes:
Naples in 1825, the city of the see Naples and die proverb, sets this Dumas crime tale of Nisida. Readers tempted by the proverb to see Naples and die are advised to land at the mole or at Mergellina on a fine summer day. The tale begins in that enchanted city.

Nisida, a beautiful Neapolitan woman, becomes the center of love, jealousy, and murder in a city of sun and shadow. Southern color and romantic passion fill a city of sun and shadow. The story offers a vivid Neapolitan crime tale, where beauty and violence walk side by side.
2748-derues-celebrated-crimes:
A September afternoon in 1751 at Chartres opens this Dumas true crime tale, as schoolboys burst from their school like partridges. One September afternoon in 1751, toward half past five, some twenty small boys burst from a religious school at Chartres, chattering like a covey of partridges.

From that innocent scene grows a tale of a poisoner, a swindler, and a murderer whose pious face hid cold calculation. Schoolboy tricks lead, step by step, to the scaffold, and the horror grows with each crime. The book stands as a classic of true crime, and a study of evil in respectable dress.
2749-la-constantin-celebrated-crimes:
Dumas warns readers not to search the records before this 1660 tale begins, for La Constantin keeps her own counsel. Before beginning, Dumas warns readers not to bother searching contemporary records, for the tale that follows keeps its own counsel about names and places.

A woman known as La Constantin moves through a world of gallantry, betrayal, and murder in the France of Louis XIV. Romantic mystery lets legend fill gaps where documents fail. The story charms as a tale of passion and crime, half history and half invention. The tale keeps its mystery to the final page.
2750-joan-of-naples-celebrated-crimes:
Naples asleep on January 15, 1343, opens this Celebrated Crimes life of Joan, queen from 1343 to 1382. In the night of January 15, 1343, while Naples lay wrapped in peaceful sleep, a queen's reign began in murder and storm.

Joan, beautiful, passionate, and ruthless, ruled Naples through husbands, lovers, and wars, until her own violent end. Romantic sweep turns chronicle into tragedy, and Joan's reign reads like a play. The book offers a vivid portrait of a medieval queen who defied popes, kings, and custom. Naples, Avignon, and Rome all play parts in her stormy reign.
2752-martin-guerre-celebrated-crimes:
Why should two faces not match, Dumas wonders at the opening of this Celebrated Crimes tale of Martin Guerre. We marvel at the likeness of strangers, Dumas begins, yet it is the difference that should surprise us, for why should two faces not match.

A man vanishes from his village, another takes his place, wife, and life, and only a trial can tell true husband from impostor. Wonder and legal suspense carry one of history's strangest cases to its verdict. The book remains the classic telling of an identity stolen and unmasked.
2753-ali-pacha-celebrated-crimes:
Audacious enterprises and strange turns of fortune mark the early nineteenth century, and Ali Pacha's career fits the age, in this Celebrated Crimes volume. The early nineteenth century, Dumas begins, was a time of audacious enterprises and strange turns of fortune, and Ali's career fits the age.

Ali Pasha of Janina rose from banditry to rule Albania as a near independent prince, defying sultans and courting Europe. His fall, siege, and murder close a life of cunning and cruelty. Epic sweep turns an Ottoman strongman into a romantic tyrant. Janina's lion ruled by terror, tribute, and cunning diplomacy.
2754-the-countess-of-saint-geran-celebra:
Horsemen riding into an Auvergne village at midday near the end of 1639 open this Dumas tale of the Countess de Saint Geran. Toward midday, a troop of horsemen rode into a little village at the northern edge of Auvergne, from a direction no one expected.

A stolen child, a substituted heir, and a countess fighting for her son drive a tale of aristocratic crime. Romantic indignation turns a lawsuit into a melodrama of stolen childhood. The book stands as a classic of family conspiracy, and of a mother's long fight for truth.
2755-murat-celebrated-crimes:
Waterloo decided Europe's destiny on June 18, 1815, while a beggar walked the road from Toulon to Marseilles in this Dumas tale. On June 18, 1815, as Europe's destiny was decided at Waterloo, a man dressed like a beggar followed the road from Toulon to Marseilles.

The beggar was Joachim Murat, once King of Naples and Napoleon's dashing cavalry chief, now a fugitive. His flight through Corsica to Pizzo, and his execution there, close a career of glory and folly. Sympathy follows a brave, reckless king who outlived his star. His white plumes and brave charges made him a legend first.
2756-marquise-brinvillier-celebrated-cri:
A crowd on the Pont Neuf on a fine autumn evening near the end of 1665 opens this Celebrated Crimes portrait of the Marquise de Brinvilliers. Toward the end of 1665, on a fine autumn evening, a crowd gathered on the Pont Neuf where it turns down to the rue Dauphine.

The marquise, a poisoner of husbands and kin, moved through Paris society with beauty and piety as her mask. Her crimes, her trial, and her scaffold end unfold with fascinated horror. The book remains a classic of true crime, and a portrait of evil in high places.
2757-vaninka-celebrated-crimes:
Four o'clock sounding from St. Peter and St. Paul above the ramparts opens this Dumas tale of Vaninka, set near the end of Paul I's reign. Toward the end of Paul I's reign, as four o'clock sounded from the church of St. Peter and St. Paul above the ramparts, a St. Petersburg drama began.

Vaninka, a Russian woman of fierce pride, pursues vengeance through love and murder in the court of a mad emperor. Northern color and romantic intensity carry a court where passion meets despotism. The story offers a rare Dumas excursion into Russia, where passion and despotism meet. St. Petersburg's winter cold matches the tale's chill heart.
2758-marquise-de-ganges-celebrated-crime:
A plain carriage with no arms painted on it stops one evening near the close of 1657, opening this Dumas tale of the Marquise de Ganges. Toward the close of that year, a carriage bearing no painted arms stopped one evening before a house in the rue Hautefeuille.

The marquise, a young widow of beauty and fortune, fell victim to her husband's family and their greed. Romantic horror turns a famous murder into a tale of innocence destroyed. The story remains a classic of French true crime, and of aristocratic cruelty.
2771-the-island-pharisees:
John Galsworthy wrote this novel of a young Englishman, Shelton, born to go a journey like every man. At first he sits in the dust with chubby hands reaching at nothing, then he toddles onto the high road of life, where society waits to shape him.

Shelton's engagement, his travels, and his quarrels with convention expose the pharisaism of island England, polite, smug, and cruel. Galsworthy writes with irony and pity for a hero learning to see. The book stands as an early satire of English respectability, and a portrait of conscience waking.
2783-the-trampling-of-the-lilies:
Rafael Sabatini sets this romance in revolutionary France, opening under the old rule with a secretary, lords of life and death, and the word of Bellecour. Disciples of Rousseau gather as the old order cracks.

Under the new rule, sheep turn wolves, a citizen commissioner rules, and La Boulaye discharges a debt, with invalids at Boisvert caught between. Sabatini writes with his usual sweep about revolution's promises and terrors. The novel offers a vivid tale of France trampling its own lilies. Sabatini's lilies fall beneath the Revolution's marching feet. The lilies never rise again.
2791-essays-and-tales:
Joseph Addison wrote these essays and tales, gathered in the 1888 Cassell edition, with an introduction on his life and art. Public credit, household superstitions, opera lions, and women and wives open a set that ranges from finance to fashion.

The Italian opera, lampoons, and true and false humour follow, with Sa Ga Yean Qua Rash Tow's impressions of London. Addison writes with the easy politeness that made the Spectator famous. The volume offers a fine sample of Augustan essay writing, urbane, witty, and humane. Addison's Spectator manner made the essay a daily companion.
2843-little-travels-and-roadside-sketche:
William Makepeace Thackeray, writing as Titmarsh, records short journeys in Little Travels and Roadside Sketches, starting from Richmond in Surrey toward Brussels. He leaves the Rose Cottage Hotel, which he prefers a thousand times to the Star and Garter, where a sneering waiter and a ten-shilling bottle of claret await the lone traveler. Ghent, Bruges, and Waterloo follow on the road.

Thackeray's sketches blend guidebook detail with jokes about fellow travelers, innkeepers, and national pride. He teases Belgians for brawling over politics while France, England, and Prussia spare them the trouble of thinking. The book charms as travel writing by a novelist, observant, funny, and fond of the small scenes beside the road.
2852-the-hound-of-the-baskervilles:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Hound of the Baskervilles as another adventure of Sherlock Holmes, crediting a West-Country legend told to him by his friend Robinson. Sir Henry Baskerville comes to a hall shadowed by a family curse, and Dr. Watson reports from the moor while Holmes works from London. Chapters move from the curse and the problem to Baskerville Hall, the Stapletons of Merripit House, and a light upon the moor.

Watson's diary and reports carry the dread, as footsteps, strange neighbors, and the man on the tor build toward a rational answer. The novel's fog, mire, and hound made it the most famous Holmes tale after the detective's supposed death. It still works as both a ghost story and a detective puzzle.
2862-the-twins-of-table-mountain-and-oth:
Bret Harte's Twins of Table Mountain and Other Stories opens on a vast stony plateau above the California country. A river roars far below, and winds spend their force before the summit. The title story follows twins raised in that high isolation. The volume adds An Heiress of Red Dog, The Great Deadwood Mystery, A Legend of Sammtstadt, and Views from a German Spion.

Harte's California runs through the whole book, from ferry mansion houses and sleepy barkeepers to mining camps and river towns. The tales mix rough humor with sentiment, and the mountain setting gives the twins' story its stark mood. Readers who enjoy Harte's gold-country sketches will find the same voice here, broadened across several kinds of tale.
2873-the-prehistoric-world-or-vanished-r:
E. A. Allen wrote The Prehistoric World, or Vanished Races, as a popular survey of early humanity, reviewed chapter by chapter by leading scholars of the day. The reviewers included Peabody Museum curator F. W. Putnam, Smithsonian curator Charles Rau, Michigan geologist Alexander Winchell, and Bureau of Ethnology scholar Cyrus Thomas. Their names signal a book meant to carry current science to general readers.

Allen compares ancient races with living peoples, arguing that widely scattered groups such as the Turanian or Mongoloid peoples follow patterns seen in geology. The prose moves from stone tools to migrations across Asia and northern Europe. The book now reads as a period piece of anthropology, valuable for how the nineteenth century imagined deep human history.
288-the-certain-hour-dizain-des-poe-tes:
James Branch Cabell gathers ten portraits of poets at their certain hour in this 1916 volume. The Certain Hour, subtitled Dizain des Poètes, takes its epigraph from criticism's limits: it can only note the impression a work made at a moment. Cabell dedicates the book to Robert Gamble Cabell.

Each tale shows a poet meeting love, death, or chance, with Cabell's ironic, musical prose. The framing verse insists that love, God-born, outlasts hourly change. Copyright pages trace the stories through magazines from 1909 to 1915. The volume introduces Cabell's Poictesme world to new readers.
2884-the-mason-bees:
Jean Henri Fabre gathered his essays on mason bees in this volume, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos from the Souvenirs entomologiques. The book covers the Chalicodomae, the mason bees proper, and adds essays on Fabre's cats and on red ants, both bearing on the bees' sense of direction. A separate volume treats the Osmiae, also mason bees by habit, under the title Bramble-bees and Others.

Fabre tests popular stories with patient experiment, asking how far a cat deserves its fame for finding home across tiles and haylofts. He distrusts casual observers and children's natural histories, preferring trials he can repeat. The essays remain a model of close insect observation, written with a naturalist's curiosity and a storyteller's ease.
2892-irish-fairy-tales:
James Stephens retold Irish legend in Irish Fairy Tales, gathering stories of Finn, Tuan mac Cairill, Bran, Becfola, and Mongan. The book opens with Finnian, abbot of Moville, hurrying south and east on hearing that people in his province still honor gods he does not approve. The abbot learns of a powerful gentleman who keeps neither saint's day nor Sunday, and the old tales unfold from that clash.

Stephens writes the Fenian cycle with humor and poetry, letting heroes, enchanted caves, and frenzied kings share the stage. A later passage lists torments for a miscreant so ingenious that listeners' blood runs chill. The collection remains a favorite doorway into Irish myth, told in prose that feels both ancient and newly made.
2910-the-little-dream-an-allegory-in-six:
John Galsworthy's The Little Dream is an allegory in six scenes about a mountain girl named Seelchen and a climber named Lamond. The dream characters include mountains as horns, flowers as the edelweiss, alpenrose, and gentian, and voices such as cowbells, mountain air, and a far view of Italy. Things in books, moth children, dancing youths, and forms of workers and their work also appear.

Seelchen asks Lamond whether she will be safe, and he answers by asking whether she is safe in her mountains. The Town then enters in dance, with girls in white satin and rags paired with youths in velvet and poverty. The play uses dream logic to weigh country innocence against city life, and it rewards readers who enjoy symbolic theatre.
2918-the-first-and-the-last-a-drama-in-t:
John Galsworthy's short drama The First and the Last uses only three characters and three scenes to stage a moral crisis. Keith Darrant, a King's Counsel, sits in his dark-curtained study on a November evening, lamplight falling on a Turkey carpet, books, and a blue-and-gold coffee service. His brother Larry and a woman named Wanda draw him into a secret that tests law against loyalty.

Thirty hours pass between the first two scenes, and two months between the second and third. Wanda begs Keith not to take Larry from her, kissing his hand and recoiling when he draws it away. The play's tension lies in what a respectable lawyer will do for family, and it ends as a compact study of conscience under pressure.
2919-the-little-man-a-farcical-morality-:
John Galsworthy's farcical morality The Little Man plays out at an Austrian railway station, where travelers of several nations wait on a departure platform. An Englishman, an Englishwoman, an American, a German, and a Dutch boy sit at buffet tables served by a pale young waiter. A woman of lowly station sits beside two large bundles, with her baby swathed in a black shawl on one of them.

The little man of the title charms the company by tending the baby, which sucks his finger while the American wonders whether he has created babies in his leisure moments. National pride, kindness, and absurdity collide in three scenes. The play works as a small moral fable about how strangers judge one another in transit.
2928-time-and-life-mr-darwin-s-origin-of:
Thomas Henry Huxley's Time and Life takes Darwin's Origin of Species as its subject and opens with the earth's thin accessible crust, hardly ten miles thick. That film holds beds of stone, the consolidated muds and sands of former seas and lakes, laid one upon another so that deeper layers are older. Geologists group those strata into formations, and formations into primary, secondary, and tertiary assemblages.

Huxley then asks what it means that some animal types persist with little change across vast stretches of time while the world's population as a whole changes greatly. The bearing of that fact on the history of life becomes the lecture's question. The essay remains a fine popular statement of deep time and the fossil record.
294-the-captain-of-the-polestar-and-othe:
A medical student keeps a journal aboard a whaler locked in Arctic ice. Arthur Conan Doyle's Captain of the Polestar and Other Tales opens at latitude 81 degrees 40 minutes north, amid enormous ice fields. The captain's strange visions haunt the crew.

Other tales follow: J. Habakuk Jephson's statement, the Great Keinplatz Experiment, and the Ring of Thoth. Doyle thanks Cornhill, Temple Bar, and other magazines for first printing them. The collection mixes horror, science, and adventure. It shows Doyle before Sherlock Holmes took over. Doyle's Arctic horror shows the imagination that built Holmes.
2942-two-penniless-princesses:
Charlotte Yonge wrote Two Penniless Princesses as a historical romance of fifteenth-century Scotland and England. The story opens at Dunbar Castle, standing on steep rocks above the North Sea, where battlements served as the only recreation ground for ladies in disturbed times. Lady Margaret walks the walls looking over a sea purpled by cloud shadows, with sails fleeting before the wind.

The princesses of the title move through courts, churches, and palaces, including a quiet unveiling before a noontide meal in a tapestry-hung room called Paradise. Yonge follows their fortunes without fortune, relying on rank, kinship, and conduct. The novel appeals to readers who enjoy Yonge's gentle historical fiction and its attention to medieval manners.
299-tales-from-two-hemispheres:
Hjalmar Hjorth Boysen's tales cross between Norway and America, as he himself did. Tales from Two Hemispheres, published in 1877, opens with a young Norseman, Halfdan Bjerk, landing at Castle Garden on June 2. A gruff officer demands name, birthplace, and money.

Later tales follow an outcast, a good-for-nothing, a scientific vagabond, and Truls the nameless. Asathor's vengeance closes the set with Norse myth. Boysen writes immigrant life with humor and sympathy. The collection introduced Norwegian America to English readers. Boysen later became a Columbia professor and a bridge between literatures.
2990-never-again-a-protest-and-a-warning:
Edward Carpenter wrote Never Again! as a protest and warning to the peoples of Europe after the First World War. Carpenter asks which path Europe will follow, and whether the barbarities of war have become more abhorrent to common humanity. His question is addressed to peoples, not merely governments, who must ponder and decide the future.

The pamphlet recalls bodies of men in the trenches of northern France and on the eastern front, where war happened a hundred times over in mud and slaughter. Carpenter argues that the peoples themselves, not their rulers alone, must refuse another war. The tract remains a short, earnest statement of postwar pacifism from a veteran socialist voice.
2997-time-s-laughingstocks-and-other-ver:
Thomas Hardy's Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses gathers poems first published in 1909, in the Macmillan edition reprinted through 1928. Hardy thanks editors and proprietors of periodicals where certain poems first appeared, and the collection shows his lyric voice turning on irony, memory, and lost love. The poems are short, plain, and musical.

One poem, dated Weymouth 1869, finds four footprints on sand where two lovers stood heart to heart and hand to hand the evening before. The morning sun has baked them dry, and the woman confesses she married another a week ago, showing her ring. The book rewards readers who enjoy Hardy's verse at its most compressed and bleakly tender.
304-rio-grande-s-last-race-and-other-ver:
A. B. Paterson's Rio Grande runs his last race in the title poem, as told by Macpherson. Rio Grande's Last Race and Other Verses, from the original 1902 Sydney edition, gathers verses printed from London to Bloemfontein to Sydney. War poems, drought poems, and horse poems share the book.

Contents list Mulga Bill's Bicycle, the Pearl Diver, Saltbush Bill's gamecock, and Hay and Hell and Booligal. Paterson's galloping lines suit cattle, railways, and surveyors. The collection followed his Man from Snowy River fame. It keeps Paterson's bush voice at full stride.
3044-desperate-remedies:
Thomas Hardy's first novel, Desperate Remedies, unfolds through chapters titled by time, from the events of thirty years down to the events of three hours. The structure itself tells the story, as a long past compresses into a fortnight, eight days, one day, twelve hours, and eighteen days of crisis. Hardy later called the book a sensation novel, and its machinery of secrets, wills, and disguises shows it.

A scene of organ music in a small room, loud and soft, simple and complicated, weird and grand, moves a listener out of proportion to the notes themselves. Light and sound strive outside while the music swells within. The novel appeals to readers who enjoy Hardy before Wessex hardened into tragedy, with melodrama handled by a master.
3049-a-group-of-noble-dames:
Thomas Hardy collected A Group of Noble Dames, first in 1891, in the 1920 Macmillan edition with a map of Wessex. The dames include the first Countess of Wessex, Barbara of the House of Grebe, and the Marchioness of Stonehenge. Lady Mottifont, Squire Petrick's lady, the Lady Icenway, Anna Lady Baxby, the Lady Penelope, the Duchess of Hamptonshire, and the Honourable Laura complete the company. Milton's line about ladies whose bright eyes rain influence serves as epigraph. The tales are told by a club of antiquaries.

Barbara's story turns on a frightened woman creeping from a room while her husband sits down to a supper he cannot eat, his worst surmises confirmed. Barbara sinks on her bed and buries her face in the coverlet. The collection shows Hardy's gift for scandalous history told with sympathy.
3052-complete-works-of-plutarch-volume-3:
Plutarch's Complete Works, volume three, gathers his essays and miscellanies, translated in this edition by several hands. Philosophical essays ask whether one can live pleasurably by Epicurus, whether a philosopher should converse with great men, and whether the Stoics speak greater improbabilities than the poets. Symposiacs, common conceptions against the Stoics, the eating of flesh, and fate follow. Literary essays take up the life and poetry of Homer.

Table talk ranges from why air cools water to why stones and iron resist air's passage where bronze and earthen vessels let it through. Plutarch's curiosity runs through every page. The volume suits readers who want the Greek moralist in his essayistic mood, conversational and wide-ranging.
3056-wessex-tales:
Thomas Hardy collected Wessex Tales with a preface apologizing for presenting two consecutive stories of hangmen in so small a book. Hardy explains that tales of executions formed a large part of local tradition near county towns. As a boy he knew a man who applied for the hangman's office and sank into incurable melancholy at failing to get it. The contents include An Imaginative Woman, The Three Strangers, The Withered Arm, Fellow-Townsmen, Interlopers at the Knap, and The Distracted Preacher.

The Withered Arm follows Gertrude to a lonely cottage by a deep slow river under prison cliffs, seeking the Casterbridge hangman. The stream waters Stickleford and Holmstoke meads lower down, though Gertrude does not know it. The tales show Hardy's Wessex at its darkest, where folklore and fate meet.
3058-a-changed-man-and-other-tales:
Thomas Hardy collected A Changed Man and Other Tales in 1920, reprinting a dozen minor novels from periodicals at various dates. The contents include A Changed Man, The Waiting Supper, Alicia's Diary, The Grave by the Handpost, Enter a Dragoon, A Tryst at an Ancient Earthwork, and Master John Horseleigh, Knight. Hardy reprints them to make them accessible in the complete series from his publishers.

A passage from one tale has a listener hidden at the back of an upper landing, hearing a lighter step than her father's cross the hall into a drawing room. Caroline's sweet face in a black gown, weeping, touches her lover deeply. The collection shows Hardy's short fiction at its most varied, from Wessex romance to historical irony.
307-three-elephant-power-and-other-stori:
Banjo Paterson's chauffeur Alfred taps a speed indicator and tells of Henery and an elephant. Three Elephant Power and Other Stories, in the 1917 edition, gathers Paterson's journal tales with one piece by Knott Gold. The Oracle, the Cast-Iron Canvasser, and the Merino Sheep follow.

Stories cover bullocks, dogs, steeplechase riders, and a cat sitting in judgment. Paterson's Australian voice is dry, fast, and fond of rogues. Done for the Double, by Knott Gold, closes the book. The collection suits readers who love Paterson's verse in prose form. Paterson's prose tales are less known than his ballads, but just as lively.
3070-the-hound-of-the-baskervilles:
This edition of Arthur Conan Doyle's Hound of the Baskervilles presents the novel in fifteen chapters. They run from Holmes and the curse through Sir Henry Baskerville, Baskerville Hall, the Stapletons, Watson's reports, the man on the tor, death on the moor, fixing the nets, and a retrospection. Holmes sends Watson to Devon while he works the case from afar. Suspicion gathers around Barrymore, the pale-faced, handsome, black-bearded man who first found Sir Charles's body, with only his word for the circumstances of the death.

Watson wonders whether Barrymore was the man seen in a cab in Regent Street. The novel's moor, fog, and hound carry the terror until reason closes the net, and the tale remains Doyle's finest long Holmes story.
3134-backlog-studies:
Warner builds these fireside studies around a fading New England custom. The backlog once burned on the hearth while the family gathered round it. That hearth has gone out, he laments, and the family's center with it. Age earns less respect, and old rites like toast and cider have faded. Roasting apples and mince pies at ten at night belong to a world slipping away.

Each study starts at the fireside and turns to manners, morals, and change. The book is no manual for winter evenings. It is a quiet protest against hurry and new ways, in the plain, companionable style that made Warner a favorite fireside author.
3152-the-junior-classics-volume-1-fairy-:
William Patten selected and arranged this first volume of The Junior Classics. Charles W Eliot, president emeritus of Harvard, wrote the introduction, and William Allan Neilson supplied a reading guide. The whole set was planned in ten volumes and about five thousand pages, sorting tales, stories, and poems for young readers, both ancient and modern.
