The messages turn from war debts and disarmament to domestic normalcy. Readers get a primary record of the early 1920s, when a war-weary country tried to return to ordinary life.
5036-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Calvin Coolidge's annual messages gather the thirtieth president's reports to Congress, opening in tribute to his predecessor. Coolidge speaks of Warren Harding's humanity, greatness, and character. Justice grew more certain under him, and peace more secure. A surpassing tribute marked his journey across the continent to rest at home.

Those who knew and loved Harding, Coolidge says, need no long account of the man. But his associates cannot resume office without pausing to rededicate themselves to service in his memory. Later messages address tax cuts, economy, and business prosperity. Readers get Coolidge's laconic presidency, beginning with a eulogy and proceeding by restraint.
5037-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Herbert Hoover's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-first president's annual messages, opening with a nation grown in strength, comfort, and knowledge. Education spreads more widely, moral and spiritual forces hold, and peace grows more assured, Hoover emphasizes, while the problems ahead are problems of growth and progress.

The later messages, delivered as the Depression deepens, turn to unemployment, farm relief, and public works, with Hoover insisting on facts and relative importance before action. Read in order, the set traces optimism meeting crisis. Readers get a primary record of 1929 to 1933, from a president who trusted engineering and voluntary effort over federal expansion.
5038-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Franklin D. Roosevelt's annual messages gather the thirty-second president's reports to Congress, opening in January 1934 with a call to counsel rather than to request. Roosevelt tells Congress he comes not for special or detailed laws. He seeks joint work without party strife to continue national recovery. He aims to build, on the ruins of the past, a new structure for modern civilization.

Later messages cover the New Deal, the Four Freedoms, and war mobilization, in Roosevelt's confident and expansive voice. The set spans 1934 to 1945, the longest run in the collection. Readers get a primary record of depression and war, from the president who redefined what Americans expected of their government.
5039-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Harry S. Truman's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-third president's annual messages, from the postwar years through Korea and into the 1950s. One message explains the new executive budget: no longer piecemeal department programs, but a single comprehensive budget the president presents for Congress to act on, with tighter controls as federal programs grow.

Truman argues that budget and general policy are inseparable, since the president bears responsibility for recommending both. Later messages cover containment, civil rights, and the Fair Deal. Readers get a primary record of the early Cold War presidency, practical and plainspoken about government's new size.
5040-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Dwight D. Eisenhower's State of the Union addresses gather the thirty-fourth president's annual messages, opening with his first message to the Eighty-third Congress. Eisenhower welcomes the honor and states the joint purpose of congressional leadership and administration: to justify the summons to responsibility issued by voters the previous November.

That purpose involves applying American influence abroad with fortitude and foresight to deter aggression and secure peace, and establishing an administration of integrity and efficiency at home. Later messages cover the Cold War, interstate highways, and civil rights. Readers get a primary record of the 1950s, from a general turned president who prized steadiness.
5041-state-of-the-union-addresses:
John F. Kennedy's annual messages collect the thirty-fifth president's reports to Congress, opening with a return to the House he calls his oldest home. Kennedy recalls taking the federal oath there more than fourteen years earlier. He learned from leaders of both parties. He heard Churchill's eloquence, Nehru's idealism, and de Gaulle's steadfast words.

The messages that follow set out the New Frontier: Cold War rivalry, space, civil rights, and economic growth, in Kennedy's polished rhetoric. Readers get a primary record of 1961 to 1963, brief but consequential, from a president whose addresses shaped how America described its purposes.
5042-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Lyndon B. Johnson's annual messages gather the thirty-sixth president's reports to Congress, opening with a challenge to make the session historic. Johnson asks that it be known for civil rights above all. He wants it to do more for civil rights than the last hundred sessions combined. He also seeks the most far-reaching tax cut of the time. He declares all-out war on poverty and unemployment.

Health needs of older citizens, education, and conservation follow in the same ambitious program. The messages trace the Great Society from promise to legislation, and then to the strains of Vietnam. Readers get a primary record of the mid-1960s, when a president tried to remake American society by statute in a single session.
5043-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Richard Nixon's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-seventh president's annual messages, and the 1970 message breaks deliberately with tradition. Nixon tells Congress that the address usually offers a lengthy account of past deeds and future requests, with election-year politics in between, but profound events command a different course.

The year 1970, opening a new decade, finds America rethinking Vietnam, the economy, and government's role, and Nixon uses the occasion to set a broader agenda. Later messages cover detente, wage and price controls, and Watergate's shadow. Readers get a primary record of a presidency that began with ambition and ended in crisis.
5044-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Gerald R. Ford's annual messages gather the thirty-eighth president's reports to Congress, opening with a memory of his own beginnings. Ford recalls a young idealist who swore the House oath before Sam Rayburn. Two days later that freshman stood at the back of the chamber. President Truman then reported to the Eighty-first Congress that the state of the Union was good.

Ford's own messages, delivered after Watergate and the pardon, address inflation, energy, and restoring trust in government. The reminiscence frames a presidency that began without election and sought legitimacy through candor. Readers get a primary record of the mid-1970s, from a president governing in a predecessor's shadow.
5045-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Jimmy Carter's State of the Union addresses collect the thirty-ninth president's annual messages, opening with a personal note about saving energy and a constitutional duty to report on the Union. Carter declares the Union sound militarily, politically, economically, and in spirit, and describes Americans as confident, hardworking, decent, and compassionate.

The messages that follow address energy, inflation, human rights, and the hostage crisis, in Carter's earnest and moralizing style. Read together, they show a president appealing to national character as a policy resource. Readers get a primary record of the late 1970s, when energy and confidence both ran short.
5046-state-of-the-union-addresses:
Ronald Reagan's annual messages gather the fortieth president's reports to Congress, opening with a first address that recalls the tradition itself. Reagan notes that Washington began the custom in 1790. Washington reminded the nation that self-government was staked on the experiment entrusted to the American people. The sacred fire of liberty, he said, depended on that experiment.

From the same podium, Reagan adds, Churchill once asked the free world to stand together. His messages then address tax cuts, defense buildup, and the Cold War's final phase, in his warm and confident rhetoric. Readers get a primary record of the 1980s, from a president who told America's story as a tale of freedom renewed.
5047-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George H. W. Bush's annual messages collect the forty-first president's reports to Congress, opening with a claim about dates that divide history. Bush notes that for most lives in the chamber, the world was defined in 1945. That year's events set the shape of nations, the pace of progress, and freedom or oppression for millions.

His messages then address the Cold War's end, the Gulf War, and a new world order, in measured and managerial prose. Readers get a primary record of 1990 to 1992, when an old frame of reference dissolved and a president tried to describe what would replace it.
5048-state-of-the-union-addresses:
William J. Clinton's annual messages gather the forty-second president's reports to Congress, opening with a tribute to Tip O'Neill. Clinton jokes that he is not sure what speech sits in the TelePrompTer. He asks the chamber to recall the giant who presided over it with force and grace. O'Neill was a bricklayer's son who helped build the great American middle class.

O'Neill never forgot who he was, where he came from, or who sent him, Clinton says, and smiles down from the Lord's gallery for the first time. Later messages address health care, welfare reform, and the economy. Readers get a primary record of the 1990s, from a president who framed policy as a story about ordinary Americans.
5049-state-of-the-union-addresses:
George W. Bush's annual messages collect the forty-third president's reports to Congress, from 2001 through 2008. An early message opens with a new budget and a new approach to governing. It thanks Congress for its invitation. It jokes that the vice president may have had to break a tie to secure it.

Later messages address the September 11 attacks, the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, tax cuts, and the financial crisis, in Bush's direct and plainspoken style. Read in sequence, the set traces a presidency transformed by terror and war. Readers get a primary record of the 2000s, from the president who governed through them.
5055-plays-first-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, First Series, gathers the dramatist's earliest stage works, opening in a well-furnished London dining room at Rockingham Gate. John Barthwick's household anchors the first scenes. The Jones family's lodgings in Merthyr Street follow. A London police court closes the action across Easter Tuesday and the Wednesday of the following week.

Little girls left homeless, a relieving officer, a magistrate's clerk, and an usher fill out a drama of class and justice. A small act in a dining room ends before the law. Galsworthy's early plays already show his method: social questions argued through private lives. Readers get the playwright at his debut, sharp and compassionate.
5056-plays-second-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Second Series, gathers the dramatist's middle-period plays. One is a country-house drama set on December 7 and 8 at the Cheshires' house in one of the shires. Its cast lists Joan and Old Studdenham the head-keeper. Freda the lady's-maid and Young Dunning the under-keeper appear. Jackson the butler completes the household. Action moves from hall to morning room to smoking room.

Galsworthy's drama of class, property, and conscience unfolds through such households, where servants and masters watch each other closely. Readers get the playwright who would write The Forsyte Saga, working in the sharper, shorter form of the stage, with social criticism inside drawing-room manners.
5057-plays-third-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Third Series, gathers middle-period dramas set in flats, lodgings, and restaurants. One play opens in George Dedmond's flat in the evening. It moves to the rooms of Malise across mornings and afternoons three months apart. It closes in a small supper room at The Gascony. Waiters, managers, ladies in large hats, and a languid lord fill the company.

Galsworthy's characters argue loyalty, love, and reputation across those rooms, with time itself doing much of the dramatic work. The series shows the playwright's mature craft, compressing social judgment into dialogue. Readers get three acts of Edwardian life, polished and quietly devastating.
5058-plays-fourth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Fourth Series, gathers later plays including A Bit o' Love, set on Ascension Day in a West Country village. In the Burlacombes' low panelled farmhouse hall sits Michael Strangway. He is a clergyman of about thirty-five in collar and Norfolk jacket. He plays the flute before a large framed photo of a woman, the room's only picture.

Strangway's rooms, the village inn, the church, and a barn carry the action through three acts of love, faith, and village judgment. Galsworthy's later drama grows quieter and more spiritual than his early social plays. Readers get a playwright turning from property and class to conscience and forgiveness.
5059-plays-fifth-series:
John Galsworthy's Plays, Fifth Series, gathers later dramas set in the Midlands town of Breconridge. Its cast includes Builder and his French maid Camille. Topping serves as Builder's manservant. The mayor and his secretary appear, with a justice of the peace, a constable, and a police sergeant. A journalist from The Comet joins them, with the figure of a poacher and the voices and faces of small boys.

Action moves between Builder's study after breakfast and at lunchtime and a studio, where respectability meets the wild figure from outside. Galsworthy's later plays probe conscience in provincial life. Readers get a playwright in his final manner, still finding drama in the collision of order and freedom.
5061-the-children-s-book-of-christmas-st:
Asa Don Dickinson's Children's Book of Christmas Stories gathers tales acceptable to parents, teachers, and librarians, marked for younger and older children. Dickens's Christmas at Fezziwig's Warehouse and Andersen's Fir-Tree open the collection, followed by Freeman's Christmas Masquerade, The Shepherds and the Angels, and Olive Thorne Miller's Telltale Tile.

Younger children get starred stories, older children double-starred ones, with Susan Coolidge's Toinette and the Elves and a voyage of the wee red cap among the later entries. Dickinson edited the book for family and classroom reading. Readers get a Christmas treasury that mixes classics with lesser-known seasonal tales, ready for December evenings.
5074-aunt-judy-s-tales:
Aunt Judy's Tales gathers stories for children, told by an elder girl amusing the little ones of a large family. The contents list Vegetables out of Place and Cook Stories. Rabbits' Tails, Out of the Way, and Nothing to Do follow. The Little Victims opens the collection in verse about thankless eyes and saved blessings.

Mamma can nap by the fire because Aunt Judy, as the children call her, keeps the little ones entertained, and the tales mix nonsense, morals, and domestic comedy. The record names no author for this work. Parents and young readers get a Victorian storybook, gentle and imaginative, written for reading aloud to a nursery full of listeners.
508-twice-told-tales:
Nathaniel Hawthorne gathers early tales of New England in this volume, twice told from magazine print. The Gray Champion defies a tyrant governor; the Minister's Black Veil hides a secret sin; Dr. Heidegger's experiment gives old folk a taste of youth. Legends of Province House, Wakefield, and the Great Carbuncle fill the rest.

Hawthorne writes in rich, shadowed prose, mixing history with moral allegory. Guilt, pride, and hidden sin recur in tale after tale. The book marks his rise as America's master of the short tale, where a single image can carry a whole moral world.
5195-cape-cod-stories:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cape Cod Stories, also published as The Old Home House, gathers tales told in the voice of Cape Cod folk. Its contents include Two Pairs of Shoes, The Count and the Manager, The South Shore Weather Bureau, The Dog Star, The Mare and the Motor. The Love of Lobelia 'Ankins appears among them, each story turning on a local character or a small deception.

Lincoln writes with affectionate humour about fishermen, captains, and summer visitors, in dialect that gives the stories their flavour. The collection offers a gentle, nostalgic portrait of Cape Cod life before the motor age fully arrived. It remains a favourite among readers of American regional humour.
5223-the-satyricon-volume-06-editor-s-no:
This sixth volume of the Satyricon is not narrative but apparatus: the editor's notes to W. C. Firebaugh's translation of Petronius. It gathers chapter-by-chapter commentary, explaining Roman customs, words, and allusions, from gladiators and silver skeletons at Trimalchio's dinner to the gods, prostitution, and social habits of the Roman world.

The notes also discuss the forgeries and additions that entered the text over centuries, helping readers tell Petronius apart from later hands. The volume serves students and curious readers of the Satyricon who want the background that makes its jokes, obscenities, and satire intelligible.
5224-the-satyricon-volume-07-marchena-no:
This seventh volume of the Satyricon gathers six notes by Marchena, addressed to the Army of the Rhine, on the text of Petronius. Marchena writes of how the French conquests brought Egyptian monuments and convent manuscripts to light, enriching knowledge and letters, and he applies that learning to the puzzles of the Roman novel.

The volume holds only Marchena's notes, not the narrative itself, and it belongs with Firebaugh's translation as scholarly apparatus. Readers interested in how the Satyricon reached the modern world, through discovery, forgery, and emendation, will find here a compact record of that history.
5324-the-book-of-were-wolves:
Sabine Baring-Gould's Book of Were-Wolves, published in London in 1865, gives an account of a terrible superstition. Chapters trace lycanthropy among the ancients, from Marcellus Sidetes, Virgil, Herodotus, Ovid. Pliny leads to a story from Petronius and Arcadian legends, then the book turns to the were-wolf in the North, with Norse traditions, the Volsung Saga, and Hrolf's Saga.

Baring-Gould, a clergyman and antiquary, collects folklore, history, and explanation in a single survey. The book offers readers a thorough, if Victorian, study of how men came to believe they turned into wolves. And it remains a classic of folklore scholarship.
535-travels-with-a-donkey-in-the-cevenne:
Robert Louis Stevenson walks the Cévennes hills with a donkey named Modestine in this beloved travel book. Starting at Le Monastier, fifteen miles from Le Puy, he packs, prods, and argues with his stubborn beast through highland valleys. A dedication to Sidney Colvin frames the trip as a search for honest friends.

Stevenson writes with wit and warmth, noting monks, shepherds, and Protestant memories of the hills. Modestine steals every scene she enters. The book endures as a classic of walking prose, where a man, a donkey, and a pack prove that travel's best reward is friendship.
5403-short-stories-for-english-courses:
Rosa M. R. Mikels's Short Stories for English Courses, edited with introduction and notes for Shortridge High School in Indianapolis, gathers classic short stories for classroom use. Its contents include Henry van Dyke's First Christmas-Tree, Joel Chandler Harris's French Tar-Baby, Ruth McEnery Stuart's Sonny's Christenin', John Fox Jr.'s Christmas Night with Satan, and James Whitcomb Riley's Nest-Egg.

Later stories include Kipling's Wee Willie Winkie, Poe's Gold Bug, O. Henry's Ransom of Red Chief, and Ralph D. Paine's Freshman Full-Back, with notes on the requirements of the short story. The book offers students a varied anthology, with guidance on how each story may be used in class.
5426-princess-polly-s-playmates:
Amy Brooks wrote Princess Polly's Playmates as another book about Polly, following earlier volumes such as Princess Polly at School and Princess Polly by the Sea. The story begins in a garden, where Polly imagines enchanted castles around her home at Sherwood Hall. Friends, visitors, and small adventures fill the chapters that follow.

Polly visits Rose, meets an unexpected guest, spends time at the shore, and deals with a runaway dog named Gyp. Chapters like The Village Nuisance and The Little Green Door show the gentle humor of the series. Young readers get a sweet, old-fashioned story of friendship, play, and everyday kindness.
546-under-the-andes:
Rex Stout, later famed for Nero Wolfe, writes this early adventure of a lost Inca world under the Andes. A New York gambler, bored at a Fifth Avenue club, is drawn into a quest for a hidden kingdom, a king's sweetheart, and a dance of the sun. Caves, courts, whirlpools, and an Inca spear mark the descent.

Stout writes with brisk, romantic flair, mixing modern talk with ancient rite. The hero must win a verdict before a strange court or die. The book charms as a lost-world romance, where gold, love, and danger wait beneath the mountains of Peru.
556-rewards-and-fairies:
Rudyard Kipling continues Puck's tales in this sequel, where Dan and Una meet folk from English history in field and wood. Cold Iron, Gloriana, King Henry VII and his shipwrights, a doctor of medicine, and Simple Simon each bring a song and a story. Puck's charm opens each visit with earth and flowers.

Kipling writes in rich, musical prose and verse, teaching history through talk and craft. The book, like its predecessor, treats the past as a living neighbor. It endures as a beloved companion to Puck of Pook's Hill, where England's makers speak again to children.
5603-seven-icelandic-short-stories:
Seven Icelandic Short Stories, published in Reykjavik by the Ministry of Education, gathers Icelandic fiction across centuries, with an introduction by Steingrimur J. Porsteinsson. The anonymous thirteenth-century Story of Audunn and the Bear opens the set, followed by Einar H. Kvaran's A Dry Spell from 1905, Gudmundur Fridjonsson's The Old Hay from 1909, and Jon Trausti's When I Was on the Frigate from 1910.

Gunnar Gunnarsson's Father and Son from 1916, Gudmundur G. Hagalin's The Fox Skin from 1923, and Halldor Kiljan Laxness's New Iceland complete the book, each in translation. Readers get a compact survey of Icelandic storytelling, from saga to modern tale.
5609-the-corporation-of-london-its-right:
William Ferneley Allen, sheriff of London and Middlesex and alderman of the ward of Cheap, wrote The Corporation of London: Its Rights and Privileges as a defense of the City's civic system. His preface apologizes for a newcomer to civic affairs standing forth as champion. Yet he insists no man of spirit could tamely submit to insulting charges and coarse insinuations long aimed at the Corporation.

Allen admits the system is not free from spot or blemish, but argues its rights and privileges deserve fair hearing. Readers get a Victorian civic tract, part history and part polemic, about London's ancient self-government.
5651-dreams-and-dream-stories:
Anna Kingsford wrote Dreams and Dream Stories, a collection of vivid, symbolic dreams with a preface. Part one runs from The Doomed Train and The Wonderful Spectacles through The Counsel of Perfection and The City of Blood. The Bird and the Cat and The Treasure in the Lighted House follow, then The Forest Cathedral, The Enchanted Woman, and The Banquet of the Gods.

Later dreams include The Difficult Path, A Lion in the Way, A Dream of Disembodiment, The Perfect Way with Animals, and The Laboratory Underground. Kingsford, a mystic and vegetarian reformer, reads dreams as spiritual teaching. Readers get strange, earnest dream visions, part diary and part allegory.
5685-the-conservation-of-races:
Du Bois delivered The Conservation of Races in 1897 as Occasional Paper number two of the American Negro Academy. The paper argues that educated Black Americans bear a duty to their people. They should use learning and culture for uplift. It names two blocks to that work: disunity within the race, and persistent opposition to Black progress. Du Bois writes at a moment when the future relations of Black and white Americans stood at the center of public debate.

The essay's force comes from its plain claim about races. It treats them as real human groups with distinct gifts to preserve. Progress, it says, needs unity of purpose and honest facing of prejudice. Readers get a foundational text of African American thought, short enough to read in one sitting and rich enough to repay study. It still speaks to questions of identity, leadership, and collective duty.
5758-many-cargoes:
Jacobs gathers sea stories and shore comedies in Many Cargoes, a second edition published in New York in 1894. Contents include A Change of Treatment and A Love Passage. The Captain's Exploit, Contraband of War, and A Black Affair follow. The Skipper of the Osprey, In Borrowed Plumes, and The Boatswain's Watch add further tales of low water, inquests, elopements, and cooks. Sailors, skippers, and Thames-side folk fill every page.

The stories thrive on trickery, mistaken identity, and the gap between a sailor's plan and its outcome. Jacobs tells them in brisk, plain prose with a dry comic eye, letting dialogue carry the humor. Readers who enjoy short sea fiction will find a lively, old-fashioned collection, and fans of Jacobs will recognize the small boats and smaller ambitions that made his name.
5767-the-fireside-chats-of-franklin-dela:
Franklin Delano Roosevelt speaks directly to the American people in his Fireside Chats, radio addresses broadcast between 1933 and 1944. The first chat, on March twelfth, 1933, opens with banking, as Roosevelt promises to talk for a few minutes about a subject few fully understand. Later chats take up recovery, war, and the duties of citizenship, always in a calm, neighborly voice.

Readers hear a president explain policy as if sitting by a fire, turning complex measures into plain talk. The chats show radio as a new instrument of leadership, building trust in crisis. Historians, students, and general readers will find here the words that shaped American morale through Depression and war, in the informal style that made them famous.
5779-the-crushed-flower-and-other-storie:
Leonid Andreyev gathers stories of childhood, fear, and inner life in The Crushed Flower and Other Stories. The opening tale follows Yura, six years old, for whom the world is enormous, alive, and bewitchingly mysterious. Yura knows the sky by day. He knows its deep azure and its white-breasted clouds drifting slowly. He watches them lying on his back on grass or roof, though much of the world stays unknown.

Readers meet Andreyev's psychological realism, where a child's wonder borders on dread and adult certainties fail. The stories favor mood and inner vision over tidy plots, with images that linger after reading. Lovers of Russian short fiction will find a powerful, unsettling collection, and readers new to Andreyev will meet a writer who treats the soul as his true subject.
5797-youth-challenges:
Clarence Budington Kelland opens Youth Challenges with Bonbright Foote the Sixth rising behind a long table that serves as his desk, extending a hand across it. The elder Foote welcomes his son to his place in the firm with historic gravity, smiling as only he can smile. From that formal welcome, the novel follows a young man challenging his father's world, its business, and its values.

Here is a business and coming-of-age story, where youth tests tradition, ambition tests loyalty, and a family firm becomes a stage for character. Kelland writes with energy and clear moral stakes, favoring action and dialogue over introspection. The book suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century American novels of work, family, and the price of independence.
582-a-collection-of-beatrix-potter-stori:
Beatrix Potter's original Peter Rabbit books gather in this volume, with starred tales included here. Peter Rabbit, Benjamin Bunny, Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, Mr. Jeremy Fisher, Jemima Puddle-Duck, the Flopsy Bunnies, Two Bad Mice, Timmy Tiptoes, Mr. Tod, Pigling Bland, and Ginger and Pickles lead the set.

Potter writes and draws small animal tales with plain words and keen country detail. Peter, warned against Mr. McGregor's garden, runs straight there and eats lettuces till sick. The book charms young readers as a treasury of Potter's best, where naughty rabbits learn, gently, that rules have reasons.
5843-the-young-step-mother-or-a-chronicl:
Charlotte Yonge tells a chronicle of mistakes in The Young Step-Mother, opening as Albinia Kendal drives down the steep hilly street of Bayford on a March evening. The equinoctial sun has long set. Blue haze has deepened into twilight and darkness. The town, not large nor modern enough for gas, is lit here and there by a shop of more pretension. A young stepmother's trials begin in that dim light.

Readers follow Albinia through marriage, stepchildren, and household errors, as good intentions meet real family friction. Yonge writes with moral care and domestic detail, letting small mistakes grow into serious tests of character. The book suits readers of Victorian domestic fiction, and those who enjoy long novels where patience and humility are the true heroics.
5867-rataplan-a-rogue-elephant-and-other:
Ellen Velvin gathers animal stories in Rataplan, a Rogue Elephant and Other Stories, with illustrations by Gustave Verbeek. Velvin, author of Tales Told at the Zoo and Jack's Visit, dedicates the book affectionately to Grace Gallatin Thompson Seton, and to the author coming as a stranger to this country. The title story follows a rogue elephant, with further tales of zoo and wild creatures.

Young readers join animals as individuals, with tempers, tricks, and troubles of their own. Velvin writes with naturalist care and storyteller warmth, favoring observation over sentiment. The book suits children who love elephants and zoo tales, and families reading animal stories aloud, where a rogue's mischief teaches respect for wild strength.
5956-gallegher-and-other-stories:
Richard Harding Davis gathers newspaper and city tales, headed by the story of Gallegher, an office boy. The newsroom has seen many boys come and go, sleepy ones, lazy ones, and smart ones who grew too familiar too fast. Gallegher stands apart from that composite of small boys in blue coats and nickel badges.

Alongside the title tale come Van Bibber stories, a walk up the avenue, and sketches of a disreputable friend and a cynical Miss Catherwaight. Davis writes with a reporter's eye for offices, streets, and sharp talk. The collection favors quick scenes and vivid figures over long plots.
6005-celibates:
George Moore's Celibates returns in a 1915 edition with an introduction by Temple Scott, twenty years after its first publication. Scott finds the Moore of 1895 and the Moore of 1915 one and the same. He sees a novelist more concerned with how the world appears to him than with how it appears to casual observers.

Moore, Scott insists, was never a reporter or a philosopher, but always an artist expressing himself through facts and figures that stirred his imagination. That self-expression is not mere private sensation, but a shaping vision. The novel studies lives held apart from union, with suffering and privilege intertwined.
6051-stella-fregelius-a-tale-of-three-de:
H. Rider Haggard tells a tale of three destinies, opening with Morris, Mary, and the aerophone, then the colonel and some reflections, poor Porson, and Mary preaching while the colonel prevails. A proposal and a promise lead to good days at Beaulieu, sunk rocks, and a singer.

Miss Fregelius herself enters, with dawn and the land, a morning service, Mr. Layard's wooing, and two questions with one answer. Stella's diary, the evil gate, dreams and sleep, and Stella's coming carry the tale toward its close. Haggard mixes romance with strange invention and the pull of fate.
6054-mrs-caudle-s-curtain-lectures:
Douglas Jerrold presents Mrs. Caudle's curtain lectures, and his preface answers gentlewomen who asked in wonder, pity, and reproof what could have put Mrs. Caudle into any man's mind. He says some subjects fall like raindrops on a head, and the book grew like a night flower from a small seed.

The scene that sparked it was a thick, black wintry afternoon before a suburban school playground, where boys full of Saturday holiday ran, jumped, hopped, and shouted under leaden skies. Jerrold turns that chance sight into comedy. Mrs. Caudle's night-time lectures scold, tease, and rule the house from behind the curtain.
6073-smith-and-the-pharaohs-and-other-ta:
H. Rider Haggard opens Smith and the Pharaohs by teasing scientists who claim to know all worth knowing about man, tracing his bones and shape and intelligence from humble origins. Haggard doubts the dissecting table explains aspirations toward another life, rooted, some say, in fear of death, earthquake, or thunder.

The volume adds Magepa the Buck, The Blue Curtains, Little Flower, and Only a Dream. It also gives Barbara Who Came Back, whose chapters run from a rectory blind and a new year feast through wedded, parted, sin, and atonement. Haggard mixes Egypt, ghosts, and moral reckoning, letting the past press hard upon the present.
6106-definitions-essays-in-contemporary-:
Henry Seidel Canby, editor of The Literary Review and Yale English teacher, gathers essays in contemporary criticism under the title Definitions. He thanks the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, Century, The Bookman, The Nation, and other journals for permission to reprint pieces first seen in their columns.

Canby says the book's unity lies in his point of view, not in chapters building one theme toward categorical conclusions. Literature in a civilization trying to be sophisticated and democratic at once has many sources and manifestations, tangled with social background. The essays open many doors before judging art and life.
6144-report-of-commemorative-services-wi:
The Church in Connecticut kept a record of rites and talks for the Seabury hundred-year mark of 1883 to 1885, with an added part at the end. The list marks the hundred years since Bishop Seabury was picked, with thanks on Easter Day, 25 March 1883, and a rite at Woodbury two days later.

Bishop Williams gives talks and sermons, Dr. Beardsley gives talks, and church meets of 1883, 1884, and 1885 fill the book. Rites at Hartford and Middletown, a show of Seabury keepsakes, and an Aberdeen event close the record. The book keeps a church's mind on its first bishop. The added part gives the Aberdeen event of 1884.
6157-what-men-live-by-and-other-tales:
Leo Tolstoy opens What Men Live By and Other Tales with epistles of St. John: we have passed from death into life because we love the brethren, and he who loves not abides in death. Love in deed and truth, not word or tongue, marks the passage, for God is love.

The title tale begins with Simon the shoemaker, who has neither house nor land, lives with wife and children in a peasant's hut, and earns his living by his work. Tolstoy asks what truly keeps men alive: not goods or strength, but love shown to a brother in need. The tales teach by parable and plain life.
6168-fifty-famous-people-a-book-of-short:
James Baldwin offers Fifty Famous People as short stories that, although not biographical, concern real persons who actually lived and played parts in the great drama of world history. Some were more famous than others, yet all left enduring footprints on the sands of time.

Each story holds a basis of truth and an ethical lesson of wholesome influence, with interest enough to disprove the doctrine that children delight only in tales of the imaginative and unreal. A few more than fifty famous people appear in the volume. Baldwin writes history as story, meant to teach and to please.
623-the-battle-of-the-books-and-other-sh:
Jonathan Swift satirizes the war between ancient and modern learning in this volume, with other short pieces. The Battle of the Books stages a fight in a library, where ancients and moderns clash over wit and worth. An introduction traces Swift from Dublin birth, seven months after his father's death, to Trinity College and fame.

Swift writes with cold, brilliant irony, mocking pride on both sides of the quarrel. The short pieces add wit and bite. The book serves as a fine entry to Swift, where a library brawl becomes a lasting joke on how ages judge each other.
633-the-golden-mean-or-ratio-1-sqrt-5-2-:
This volume prints the golden ratio, (1+sqrt(5))/2, to twenty thousand decimal places, with a trove of other constants beside it. Catalan's constant, Artin's constant, the Feigenbaum numbers, Khinchin's constant, and zeta values share the pages, each to thousands of digits. The golden ratio itself opens at 1.6180339887 and runs on for pages.

The book serves less as reading than as a reference store for mathematicians, artists, and the curious. Its digits, checked and printed in blocks, let workers test code, art, and theory against a true value. For most readers it stands as a monument to precision, where beauty meets long arithmetic.
6330-amanda-a-daughter-of-the-mennonites:
Anna Balmer Myers opens on a scorching midsummer day in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, where a little red haired girl wades barefoot in a tree bordered creek. Her gingham skirt is tucked unevenly, her laughter breaks the Sabbath calm, and she declares the wading the best fun, with pebbles to pick and cool water against the heat. Amanda Reist, daughter of the Mennonites, grows up in that world of farms, markets, and plain speech.

Chapters follow a snitzing party, apple butter boiling, a visit to Martin's mother, school days, and Amanda as teacher, with a spelling bee, a market day, pink moccasins, and a boarder. A frontispiece shows her rescued from fire, still feeling the wonder of it. Myers writes Pennsylvania Dutch life with affection and detail, as a girl becomes a teacher and a woman in a community that values work, faith, and family.
6340-literary-lapses:
Stephen Leacock's Literary Lapses runs from a financial career and Lord Oxhead's secret to boarding house geometry and the awful fate of Melpomenus Jones. A Christmas letter, how to make a million dollars, and how to live to be two hundred follow. How to avoid getting married, how to be a doctor, new food, and a new pathology come next. The poet is answered, statistics exert force, and men who have shaved the author take their turn.

A barber, Leacock jokes, pins his customer in the chair and covers his face with soap. He plants a knee on his chest and asks about yesterday's Detroit game, not as a question at all. Getting the thread, telling faults, winter pastimes, and number fifty-six keep the comedy coming, with a conjurer's revenge and hints to travellers. Leacock writes short, sharp humour, Canadian in setting and universal in its targets.
6381-two-years-in-the-french-west-indies:
Lafcadio Hearn dedicates his West Indian book to Leopold Arnoux, notary at Saint Pierre, Martinique, in memory of walks, voyages, and talks. On an unshadowed day in Saint Pierre, a visitor with poetry and study in mind feels he has seen it all before, in a happy dream half recalled. Quaint architecture and bright narrow streets aglow with warm colour fill the view. Roofs and walls streaked with mould greens and greys, and no window sashes, glass, gas lamps, or chimneys, make the scene feel past rather than present.

Chapters follow porteuses, Grande Anse, a revenant, la guiablesse, washerwomen, Mount Pelee, little canoes, and a coloured girl, with bonnes haggling for first fish as boats return. Hearn writes Martinique as colour, sound, and custom, with a French epigraph on the passion to return. The book is travel as portrait, tender toward a city soon to vanish.
6434-a-brief-history-of-the-united-state:
Barnes's One-Term History offers a brief history of the United States for school pupils, with a preface on why children dislike history books. Teachers testify, the preface says, that pupils prefer real incidents to improbable tales, yet find their books dry. The remedy is method, not shorter facts: each pupil first draws an outline map of North America, at least eighteen by twenty four inches, showing only coast line, mountains, lakes, and rivers.

Six epochs carry the story: early discoveries and settlements, development of the colonies, the Revolutionary War, development of the states, the Civil War, and reconstruction with passing events. An appendix adds questions for class use, historical recreations, the Declaration of Independence, and the Constitution. A mid passage shows Washington's Princeton feat kindling patriotism afresh, with expiring enlistments renewed and Howe alarmed.
6465-short-cruises:
W. W. Jacobs gathers twelve cruises, with drawings by Will Owen. The tales are The Changeling, Mixed Relations, His Lordship, Alf's Dream, A Distant Relative, The Test, In the Family, A Love Knot, Her Uncle, The Dreamer, Angels' Visits, and A Circular Tour. The tales run on sailors, families, and talk, from a voice demanded in one illustration to a lordship exclaiming over eyes in another. Jacobs writes in cockney voice and humour, where a joke lands like a rope's end.

A mid passage shows Alf questioning his uncle: why sign them so, and never mind, it is his handwriting and good enough for her. The uncle tried writing backwards once, but would not do it again for fifty pounds, and Alf muses that if her first husband were alive she could not marry him. Jacobs writes short stories where folk scheme, blunder, and talk their way out of trouble.
6487-the-new-boy-at-hilltop-and-other-st:
Ralph Henry Barbour gathers The New Boy at Hilltop and other stories. It opens with Hilltop School closing its fall term at ninety five students and reopening two weeks later, January third, with ninety six. Kenneth Garwood, booked for autumn but delayed by family plans, journeys to Moritzville on a cold January afternoon. Curled in a heated day coach, he wonders why the Connecticut Valley runs colder than Cleveland, Ohio.

Other tales follow. They are the proving of Jerry, McTurk le, the band, the triumph of Curly, and Patsy. Then come a first assignment, Pemberton's fluke, the seventh tutor, a race with the waters, a college Santa Claus, the triple play, and the dub. A mid passage shows Jerry on a bridge, grasping Welch's wrist as the boy hangs swinging over water, praying for strength and endurance while his shoulder hurts worse every moment. Barbour writes schoolboy sport and pluck.
6562-the-pretentious-young-ladies:
Molière turns his eye on Parisian ladies who aped high style in speech and manners, and made a fashion of fine words. His one-act comedy, first played in 1659, marks the point where he left Italian and Spanish plots behind and began to paint living people as they were. The note that opens the text sets that shift out with care.

Two young women, keen to seem grand, fall for false suitors and fine talk, and the fun comes from the gap between their airs and plain sense. Molière keeps the jokes sharp but the target clear: a craze for polish that had grown coarse in the civil wars. The play is short, brisk, and still easy to grasp today.
6577-the-junior-classics-volume-6-old-fa:
Volume six of The Junior Classics, chosen for boys and girls, gathers old-fashioned tales from writers young readers still know. Mary Mapes Dodge opens with a race for silver skates, Louisa Alcott follows with a hospital tale, and Lucretia Hale, Sophie May, and Mary Freeman add their own stories. A reading guide and a Harvard introduction frame the set.

Each tale stands alone, yet all share a plain, moral warmth and a love of home, work, and play. The book was made as a library for the young, not as a school text, and its tales reward reading aloud. Old-Fashioned Tales gives families a solid shelf of classic short stories in one handy volume.
6655-tom-slade-boy-scout-of-the-moving-p:
Percy Fitzhugh sends Tom Slade, boy scout, into a tale adapted from the photo play The Adventures of a Boy Scout. The story starts in Barrel Alley, where Tom, as usual, is the one who does it, picking up a barrel stave for a scrape. Sticks and stones, hats off, jail and out again, and Camp Solitaire follow in brisk order.

Tom turns detective, faces revenge, rescues Roy, and learns first aid by wireless, all with scout honor as his guide. Fitzhugh keeps the action clean and the jokes boyish. Tom Slade, Boy Scout of the Moving Pictures, is a lively early scout book, tied to the new thrill of the movies.
6658-owindia-a-true-tale-of-the-mackenzi:
Charlotte Selina Bompas tells the true tale of Owindia, a girl born on a pretty open spot by the great Mackenzie River. Pine woods stand behind the camp, low shrubs and willows ring it, and mossy grass carpets the ground. Her father Michel the Hunter pitched his lodge where the banks rise sixty feet above the river, near other camps drawn by abundant fish.

The story follows Owindia's life among the Mackenzie River Indians, with its hunts, camps, and hard northern ways. Bompas writes with missionary warmth and a keen eye for place. Owindia is a short, vivid true tale of the Canadian north, told for readers far from its cold rivers.
6694-in-midsummer-days-and-other-tales:
August Strindberg, in a translation by Ellie Schleussner, opens with midsummer in the north, when the earth is a bride and brooks still run. A dove flies from the wood to a cottage where a ninety-year-old granny, bedridden twenty years, watches through her window. Flowers, birds, and untouched meadows frame the scene.

Other tales follow: a big gravel-sifter, a sluggard, a pilot's troubles, a photographer and a philosopher, and a tree-swallow's song. Strindberg mixes folk fancy with sharp, modern observation. In Midsummer Days is a varied, lovely set, full of northern light and strange, short wonders.
675-american-notes:
Charles Dickens paired two travel works in this volume: his notes on a visit to America and his sketches of Italy. The American part records what he saw on his 1842 tour, from cities and prisons to hotels, courts, and daily manners. The Italian part follows his later stay in that country, with scenes of streets, churches, and country life.

Dickens writes as a keen-eyed visitor, quick to praise warmth and wit and just as quick to fault slavery, boast, and harsh jails. He dedicates the American notes to friends in the United States who could bear plain truth told in good humour. Read together, the two halves show a famous novelist testing his own first views against places he knew only by report.
6758-the-adventures-of-sir-launcelot-gre:
Smollett's Sir Launcelot Greaves opens with a set of personages introduced to the reader, then brings its hero onto the stage of action. A chapter the reader may wish were the last, a knight hard to wake, and a recapitulation that draws to a close follow in Smollett's teasing chapter titles. Madness, it seems, may prove catching.

Launcelot, a modern knight-errant, rides to right wrongs in a world of lawyers, madhouses, and rogues. Smollett mixes Don Quixote with English satire, to comic effect. The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves is a lively, odd novel, for readers who like a knight out of time.
6765-mogens-and-other-stories:
Jens Peter Jacobsen's Mogens and Other Stories, in Anna Grabow's 1921 translation from Danish, opens with a decade of ferment in Denmark, 1870 to 1880. Georg Brandes lectured on main currents of literature, Ibsen probed from Norway, and Darwin's ideas echoed from England. Old and new fought with bitterness, each side going to extremes.

The stories that follow, Mogens, The Plague at Bergamo, There Should Have Been Roses, and Mrs. Fonss, show that new spirit in human terms. Jacobsen writes with a poet's eye for mood and a scientist's care for detail. Mogens and Other Stories is a fine, short gateway to Danish realism at its most lyrical.
6768-the-man-upstairs-and-other-stories:
Wodehouse gathers short stories under the title The Man Upstairs, with Something to Worry About, Deep Waters, When Doctors Disagree, and Ruth in Exile among them. The title tale opens with Annette Brougham, composing a waltz, and the knocking from above in three stages: vague discomfort, physical pain like red-hot pincers, and at last insult.

Other tales follow: a man who disliked cats, a tuppenny millionaire, a goal-keeper and a plutocrat, and Sir Agravaine. Wodehouse's wit, light and precise, runs through them all. The Man Upstairs is a delightful, varied set of comic stories from a master of the form.
6807-pickle-the-spy-or-the-incognito-of-:
Andrew Lang traces Pickle the Spy, the secret agent who shadowed Prince Charles, from papers he found in the British Museum. The Pelham Papers held letters of Pickle and of James Mohr MacGregor, transcripts of which Lang sent to Robert Louis Stevenson for a novel Stevenson did not live to finish. Pickle, like the Master of Ballantrae, tempts romance writers.

Lang resists that temptation, telling Pickle's woeful history as fact, not as fiction's villain. His preface sets out sources with scholarly care. Pickle the Spy is a vivid, true tale of Jacobite intrigue, spies, and a prince in hiding.
684-worldwide-effects-of-nuclear-war-som:
A 1975 report from the United States Arms Control and Disarmament Agency sums up what was then known about the wide, long-term effects of nuclear war. It draws on a National Academy of Sciences study and related agency work, and it is frank that much stayed unsure. Its aim was to give the public a clear, plain account, not a technical one.

The chapters cover how nuclear blasts work, local and worldwide fallout, dust high in the air, and harm to the ozone layer. Short notes add facts on yields, bomb design, and radioactivity. The value lies in its scope. It looks past the blast zone to effects that could touch the whole globe, and it warns that statecraft should aim to never learn these lessons from real war.
6864-average-jones:
Samuel Hopkins Adams opens Average Jones in the Cosmic Club, where three men ask what is the matter with Jones. Waldemar, owner of an important newspaper, wears a look of good-humored power; Robert Bertram, the club idler, sits slender and languid; Jones himself is the third. His nickname, Adams notes, was foreordained by parents who gave him an average name.

Chapters on a B-flat trombone, a red dot, an open trail, mercy signs, blue fires, and a million-dollar dog follow, each a small mystery Jones solves by keen, average sense. Adams writes with wit and pace. Average Jones is a delightful set of detective tales, where plain logic beats showy brilliance.
6874-canada-and-the-states:
Sir Edward Watkin recalls his work in Canada and the United States between 1851 and 1886, years spent crossing the Atlantic on railway and trade business. He opens with an American report urging that the Maritime Provinces, with their hardy folk, harbors, fisheries, and seamen, would strengthen the United States at sea. That bold claim frames his own hope for Canada as a great part of the British Empire.

Dedicating the book to his wife, who bore long absences while he traveled the continent, Watkin mixes personal memory with public argument. He writes of routes, deals, and the men he met, and he keeps returning to one theme: Canada's place in the Empire and its ties, friendly and rivalrous, with its southern neighbor.
688-the-goodness-of-st-rocque-and-other-:
Alice Dunbar wrote these stories of Creole life in and around New Orleans, where French, Spanish, and African roots mix. The title tale follows Manuela through the streets of the old city, and the other pieces move between bayous, fishing towns, feast days, and small shops. Love, faith, pride, and hard luck run through them all.

Dunbar gives close portraits of women and men who live by custom and by heart, from a praline seller to a violin player. The local speech, food, and rites are part of the scene, not mere colour. The book is prized as an early, insider view of Louisiana Creole society, told with warmth and a sharp eye for social rank.
689-the-kreutzer-sonata-and-other-storie:
Leo Tolstoy wrote the title novella as the confession of a man who murdered his wife in a fit of jealousy, told to a fellow traveller on a train. Music, marriage, lust, and rage are argued through at length, and the narrator's guilt gives the tale its force. Benjamin Tucker's translation carries the work into English.

The volume adds further short tales, including the folk fable "Ivan the Fool", in which simple goodness defeats cunning and greed. Together they show Tolstoy's late moral fire: plain stories that preach against pride, wealth, and sexual vanity. The book remains a stark, unsettling read, and a key to Tolstoy's thought after his great novels.
6896-a-brief-history-of-the-united-state:
John Bach McMaster wrote this history for elementary schools, on the view that most Americans learn their country's past at school. The text proper gives the essentials in as few words as truth and fairness allow, so young readers meet the main line of progress first. Notes carry matters of less weight, with outline lives of men whose deeds need mention.

Teachers may set the notes as lessons or leave them to be read alone, as they judge best. The preface stresses fairness over flourish, and it aims to give every young American both the facts all should know and useful things beside. Portraits, including Washington by Rembrandt Peale, add a visual thread to the narrative.
6911-the-majesty-of-calmness-individual-:
William George Jordan, author of The Kingship of Self Control, offers seven essays on calmness and the conduct of life. He calls calmness the rarest quality in human life, the poise of a great nature in harmony with itself and its ideals. It is not the stillness of stone, he warns, for petrifaction is death, nor is it the surrender of the fatalist, whom he calls a coward slave of fate.

Later essays attack hurry as the scourge of America, praise personal influence and the dignity of self reliance, and read failure as a form of success. Doing our best at all times and the royal road to happiness close the set. Jordan writes in short, plain maxims, urging readers to meet each crisis with singleness of purpose and quiet power.
6917-the-gerrard-street-mystery-and-othe:
John Charles Dent, born at Kendal in Westmorland in 1841, came to Canada as a youth when his parents emigrated. He learned in Canadian schools, studied law, and joined the Upper Canada Bar, but practice in an obscure village soon felt uncongenial. Dreams of literary labor drew him to London, the world's literary center, once he could afford the move.

The tales that follow show the Canadian author and historian in a stranger vein, with mystery and the weird as their matter. The title tale of Gerrard Street leads a set that trades on secrets, shadows, and sudden turns. Dent's own restless move from law to letters mirrors the unease his stories stir in their readers.
6956-in-divers-tones:
Charles G D Roberts sings in divers tones in this collection, dedicating its medley to his friend Edmund Collins. His opening verses invite a friend who can rightly hear to listen, promising serious things, light laughter, and here and there a tear. Roberts, professor of English at King's College in Windsor, Nova Scotia, and author of Orion and Other Poems, gathers themes far and near.

The contents range from a collect for Dominion Day and poems on Canada to Actaeon, the pipes of Pan, and scenes out of Pompeii. Fredericton in May time, September, the Tantramar revisited, and a ballade of Calypso sit beside a serenade off Pelorus and a poem on a slave woman. The book is a varied songbook from a young Canadian voice.
6974-tomaso-s-fortune-and-other-stories:
Henry Seton Merriman gathers short stories here, from Sister and A Small World to Tomaso's Fortune, Stranded, and Putting Things Right. The contents run through a crooked way, a tale of a scorpion, life on the rocks, Golossa, a mule, and love and war. Later pieces follow Juanita's sake, the front, the end of the Mooroo, a caravan, and the track of the wandering Jew.

The opening story, Sister, begins with a guard: it does not matter where it was, and the narrator does not want those around them to know Sister or himself. That note of discretion runs through the set, as Merriman sketches soldiers, travelers, and lovers in far places. The stories favor incident, irony, and a quiet moral turn.
6978-made-over-dishes:
Sarah Tyson Rorer, author of the Philadelphia Cook Book and Bread and Bread Making, offers a revised and enlarged book on made over dishes. Her contents run from stock and cooked fish through beef, mutton, chicken, and game, both cooked and uncooked, to bread, eggs, potatoes, cheese, sauces, salads, cereals, vegetables, and fruits. Sour milk and cream close the list, showing how far thrift can reach.

Rorer opens with a rule: wise forethought, which means economy, stands first among domestic duties, and poverty need not dull skill in cooking. The cook's aim is to draw out each ingredient's proper flavor and make it easy to digest, using little leftovers that too often reach the garbage bucket. Buy small amounts of the best, use them wisely, and waste nothing.
7027-a-hive-of-busy-bees:
Effie Williams writes A Hive of Busy Bees as a children's book of virtues, each chapter named for a bee: obedient, honest, truthful, kind, polite, gentle, helpful, grateful, loving, content, and prayerful. The tale opens after Christmas, with Grandpa calling cheerily that the sun has gone under a cloud, while Grandma laughs that it is the brightest day in two weeks. Don's face and Joyce's tell another story.

The children, Daddy explains at last, are thinking about next summer already, borrowing trouble months ahead. Grandpa throws back his white head and laughs at such little trouble borrowers, amid dolls, trains, and pictures from the holiday. The chapters that follow teach each virtue through home scenes, closing with home again.
7057-david-poindexter-s-disappearance-an:
Julian Hawthorne tells of David Poindexter's disappearance and other tales, opening with a note on English state trials. Strange stories there would make a modern novelist's fortune, he says, yet other cases, known only locally and barely touched by law, stir as much wonder. Among them none is better worth recalling than Poindexter's, which he aims to tell simply and briefly, much as he heard it years ago near the scene.

The contents add Ken's Mystery, When Half Gods Go the Gods Arrive, Set Not Thy Foot on Graves, and My Friend Paton. Hawthorne writes as a collector of half forgotten mysteries, where law stops and talk begins. The tales favor quiet dread, odd circumstance, and a past that will not quite explain itself.
7067-the-magnificent-lovers-les-amants-m:
Moliere's Magnificent Lovers, given by Louis the Fourteenth, was acted before the king at Saint Germain en Laye on February 4, 1670. It was never played in Paris, and it was printed only after Moliere's death. Wall calls it one of Moliere's weakest plays, since the whole weight of court entertainment then rested on him. Its attack on astrology stands as the most interesting part, and Moliere himself played Clitidas.

The author's preface notes the king wanted nothing but what is magnificent, and wished his court an entertainment gathering all the stage could furnish. Linking so many different things into one vast idea taxed the playwright hard. The play remains a court spectacle of love, splendor, and star reading, curious for its royal occasion.
7073-specimens-of-greek-tragedy-aeschylu:
Goldwin Smith translates specimens of Greek tragedy by Aeschylus and Sophocles in this 1893 volume. His preface traces Greek drama to the festival of Dionysus, god of wine, celebrated with dance, song, and recitative. Recitative in character grew into drama, chiefly through Thespis, tradition says, while dance and song remained as the chorus, that peculiar feature of the Greek play.

Thirlwall, still perhaps the soundest and most judicious historian of Greece, traces drama to great choral compositions joining music and action to lofty poetry. Smith's specimens let English readers hear the lyric and dramatic elements combined, through the mist of an unrecorded age. The book serves students and lovers of the ancient stage.
710-love-of-life-and-other-stories:
Jack London gathered stories of men and women tested by cold, hunger, and gold in the far north. The title tale follows a prospector left alone in the wild, who crawls toward life with a broken leg while a sick wolf stalks him. Other tales turn on claims, dogs, boats, and the hard code of the trail.

London writes with stark force about hunger, fear, and the will to live. His people are not heroes in fine clothes; they are workers and wanderers pushed to the edge. The book shows his gift for the short tale of survival, where nature is foe and judge, and where life itself becomes the prize.
7114-une-vie-a-piece-of-string-and-other:
Guy de Maupassant's Une Vie, the history of a heart, leads this volume in translations by McMaster, Henderson, Quesada, and others. The contents follow Jeanne from the home by the sea through happy days, Monsieur de Lamare, marriage and disillusion, and Corsica and a new life. Disenchantment, Jeanne's discovery, maternity, the death of La Baronne, and retribution follow, with the development of Paul, a new home, Jeanne in Paris, and light at eventide.

Shorter stories join the novel: A Vagabond, The Fishing Hole, The Spasm, In the Wood, Martine, All Over, The Parrot, and the famous Piece of String. A study by Pol Neveux recalls Maupassant's boast that he entered literary life as a meteor and would leave it like a thunderbolt. The volume gathers his art at its sharpest.
7120-knock-knock-knock-and-other-stories:
Ivan Turgenev's Knock, Knock, Knock and other stories appear here in Constance Garnett's translation. The contents list the title study, The Inn, Lieutenant Yergunov's Story, The Dog, and The Watch. The first story opens in a circle of friends. Alexandr Vassilyevitch Ridel, German by surname but Russian to the marrow, promises a brief tale from the eighteen thirties, forty years past, and begs not to be interrupted.

Ridel, fresh from university and living in Petersburg, often stayed with his brother, a lieutenant in the horse guard artillery whose battery stood at Krasnoe Selo. The brother lodged in a neighboring village, where Ridel met his circle. Turgenev's tales that follow mix the uncanny, the comic, and the military, in Garnett's clear English.
7128-indian-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs selects and edits Indian Fairy Tales, illustrated by John Batten, with an illustration of Princess Labam among its plates. Jacobs, editor of Folk Lore, draws on Indian story tradition for English readers, with page images from the Internet Archive behind the text. A transcriber's note explains a letter after a carat marks a superscript, as in 2e, and notes a fuller HTML version with the original illustrations.

The tales themselves bring princes, princesses, beasts, and magic from the Indian story store, told in Jacobs's clear, scholarly style. Batten's pictures give the book its visual charm, from palace scenes to forest paths. The volume stands as a classic gathering of Indian wonder tales for children and for students of folk lore.
7141-suburban-sketches:
William Dean Howells sketches suburban life in pieces named for Missus Johnson, doorstep acquaintance, a pedestrian tour by horse car to Boston, and a day's pleasure. A romance of real life, scene, jubilee days, lessons from the school of morals, and flitting complete the contents. Illustrations, not available in this edition, once showed a potent pipe lit, a young lady in black alighting, and a sweet young blonde arriving by most trains.

Missus Johnson opens on a morning of lovely New England May, when the narrator leaves the horse car, spreads an umbrella, and walks down toward a suburban scene. Frank and Lucy stalk ahead with shawls dragging, while questioners skirmish about a gaunt figure of forlorn and curious smartness. Howells writes Boston's suburbs with gentle humor and a close eye.
715-the-moon-endureth-tales-and-fancies:
John Buchan gathered tales and fancies in this volume, ranging from the Pentland hills of Scotland to Avignon in 1759. Some pieces are short stories of folk, soldiers, and wanderers; others are songs and sketches, such as the grove of Ashtaroth and the ride of Ninemileburn. A lucid interval, a gipsy's song, and a tale of Babylon sit side by side.

Buchan writes with a love of border country, old faiths, and plain folk, and with a storyteller's pace. The mix is uneven by design, moving from eerie fancy to homely tale. The book shows the lighter, more fanciful side of the man later known for thrillers, and it rewards readers who enjoy short, atmospheric fiction.
7153-elder-conklin-and-other-stories:
Frank Harris gathers Elder Conklin and other stories, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1894. The contents list the title tale, The Sheriff and His Partner, A Modern Idyll, Eatin Crow, and The Best Man in Garotte, with Gulmore the Boss. Elder Conklin opens as the elder leaves the supper table and his daughter walks out with the new schoolmaster onto the stoop, or verandah, running round the frame house.

The day was warm, but evening chill betokened the near approach of Indian summer. The house stood on the crest of a prairie roll. The pair leaned on the railing looking over a small peach orchard to Cottonwood Creek, two hundred yards away at the bluff's foot, fringed by the trees that named it. Harris writes prairie life with sharp, unsentimental eyes.
7182-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's great collection gathers the voyages, traffics, and discoveries of English seamen, keeping the spelling of his sixteenth-century original while expanding old manuscript short forms for modern eyes. The editor's notes explain that footnotes follow later spelling, while Hakluyt's own sidenotes stay his, marking the line between the old text and new help.

Readers meet a vast store of sea tales, trading ventures, and coastal claims, told in the voices of captains, merchants, and chroniclers. Hakluyt built the book as a record of English enterprise abroad, and its bulk still shows how wide that enterprise ran. This text preserves both the journeys and the manner of their first telling.
7187-seven-english-cities:
William Dean Howells walks through seven English cities in this illustrated book of travel and comment, opening with a view of Monk Bar. Howells was already known for books on Rome, English towns, and London, and here he turns the same easy eye on streets, buildings, and local life in a set of linked sketches.

The charm lies in observation rather than in guidebook fact: a gate, a market, a quiet lane, and the talk that rises around them. Howells writes as a friendly visitor, noting what pleases him and what puzzles him without pretending to master each place. The result reads like good company on a slow tour, full of small scenes that stay in mind.
7212-memories-of-canada-and-scotland-spe:
The Marquis of Lorne gathers speeches and verses on Canada and Scotland in this volume, dedicated with respect and affection to the members of the Royal Society of Canada. Verses on Canadian subjects lead the way: a Canadian national hymn, river rhymes, a robin, legends of the St John river, Mohawk guides, prairie roses, Cree fairies, and the Qu'Appelle valley.

Speeches follow the poems, joining public voice to private verse, and the whole book moves between two northern lands the author knew well. Lorne writes as a statesman with a poet's ear, praising lakes, rivers, and peoples in measured lines. The collection preserves a late Victorian view of Canada from inside its public life.
7255-cambridge-sketches:
Frank Preston Stearns sketches Cambridge men he knew without ever seeking them out. His preface owns a regret: he never introduced himself to distinguished persons or sought their notice, and only later wished he had seized chances his youth let pass. Knowing these men, he writes, gave him a more elevated idea of human nature than he might otherwise have held.

Charles Sumner faces the volume, and the sketches that follow mix memory with portraiture, letting talk and habit reveal character. Stearns writes as a neighbour rather than a biographer, fond and frank by turns. The book preserves a Cambridge of friends, teachers, and talk before fame fixed them in print.
7306-autobiographic-sketches:
Thomas De Quincey's Autobiographic Sketches gathers selections, grave and gay, from writings published and unpublished, chosen for an American edition he was revising in 1853. His letter from Lasswade that January explains his plan: to revise and considerably alter, for republication in England, such of his writings as it seemed proper deliberately to avow.

De Quincey stresses that he does not disown anything he published, only that some pieces served a transient occasion and need not stand unchanged. The sketches that follow mix memory, confession, and wit in his famous winding prose. Readers meet a master of the personal essay sorting his own past for a new public.
7366-three-comedies:
Björnstjerne Björnson was Norway's leading writer and a public voice in its national life, and these three plays show him turning from peasant tales to the stage. The volume opens with The Newly-Married Couple, follows with Leonarda, first performed in 1879, and closes with A Gauntlet, written in 1883. An introduction traces Björnson's life from a remote parsonage in the north to literary fame.

The plays take up marriage, reputation, and the rules society sets for women and men. Leonarda and A Gauntlet stirred sharp controversy in Norway, since they pressed social and religious questions that audiences were not used to hearing on stage. Read together, the three comedies show a dramatist using domestic life to argue about freedom, duty, and the cost of defying convention.
7368-lifted-masks-stories:
Susan Glaspell, a playwright and novelist of the American Midwest, writes here about people caught between who they seem and who they are. The stories often place Americans abroad, as in the Paris scene where a young woman's clothes, bought in France, still cannot hide that she is American. Manners, money, and marriage all act as masks her characters wear.

The title points to the moment each story builds toward: a mask lifted, a pretense dropped, a truth spoken at last. Glaspell's people are plain speakers in elegant rooms, and their small rebellions carry real weight. Readers who know her plays will find the same interest in women's inner lives, told here in compact, quietly dramatic fiction.
7399-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
This last volume reaches back to Holmes's oldest portfolio, to verses first printed in The Collegian in 1830 and in illustrated annuals of his youth. The Meeting of the Dryads, The Toadstool, The Spectre Pig, and The Ballad of the Oysterman show a student poet trying on masks: classical fancy, comic parody, and Yankee humor in turn. A poem called The Poet's Lot already wonders what a life in verse will cost.

The charm of the book is its earliness. These are the experiments of a young man who did not yet know he would become Boston's beloved doctor-poet. One of the poems, the preface hints, won kind words from Thackeray. Read after the later volumes, the collection shows where Holmes began: playful, curious, and already fond of the odd corners of New England life.
7437-a-peep-behind-the-scenes:
Mrs. O. F. Walton, author of Christie's Old Organ, looks behind the fairground in this moral tale for young readers. The show people, who seem gay and carefree from the front of the booth, live hard lives in their caravans, grumbling at the weather and counting their takings. The story follows Rosalie, a girl of the little theatre, through the day after the fair and the actress's story.

Later chapters bring a circus procession, a doctor's visit, a family secret, and a lone lamb lost and found, as Rosalie learns what lies behind the painted scenes. Walton writes plainly and kindly, with a Victorian evangelical's eye for suffering and hope. The book's charm is its backstage view: the fair as work, home, and hardship, not only as a holiday show.
7438-friends-in-council-first-series:
Sir Arthur Helps was a Victorian civil servant who wrote his way into literature, and Friends in Council, first published in 1847, was the book that made him known. Born at Streatham in 1813, educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, Helps served as private secretary to the Chancellor of the Exchequer before turning to letters. The book takes the form its title promises.

Friends meet in council and talk through the questions of life: conduct, work, friendship, and the duties of ordinary people. The dialogue form lets Helps argue with himself, giving each side a fair voice. Later series followed, but this first one sets the pattern: thoughtful, good-tempered conversation as a way of thinking, written for readers who enjoy ideas at leisure.
7439-english-fairy-tales:
Who says that English folk have no fairy tales of their own? Joseph Jacobs opens his collection with that challenge, and answers it with a selection from some 140 tales of which he found traces in England. He admits the oddity in his title: few of these stories actually speak of fairies, just as few in Grimm speak of them. The name covers a wider kind of folk tale.

Jacobs invites the child reader in with a playful key and door, then tells the tales plainly, in the voice of the storyteller. Giants, clever youngest sons, talking beasts, and tricksters all appear, in stories that had lived by word of mouth long before they were printed. The collection stands as the classic English counterpart to Grimm, and the source of many tales children still know.
7466-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations is the great Elizabethan collection of English voyages, traffics, and discoveries, and this volume is one part of it. The edition retains the spelling of Hakluyt's sixteenth-century original, expanding only old manuscript abbreviations, so readers meet the accounts in something close to their first form. Editor's footnotes in modern spelling guide the way.

This volume opens amid grim eastern history: Tartar chieftains and their followers destroying whole provinces without respect for condition, fortune, sex, or age. From such accounts the collection builds its picture of a world opening to English ships and traders. For readers of travel history, Hakluyt remains the first source, vast, vivid, and unmistakably of its age.
7471-the-man-with-two-left-feet-and-othe:
P. G. Wodehouse's 1917 collection takes its title from a story about a man who cannot dance, but its pleasures run wider. The contents include Bill the Bloodhound, about Henry Pifield Rice, a detective whose trade is not quite what it seems; Extricating Young Gussie; Wilton's Holiday; and two parts of The Mixer. Crowned Heads at Geisenheimer's and The Romance of an Ugly Policeman add restaurant and street comedy.

Dogs, chorus girls, policemen, and young men in scrapes fill these stories, all told in Wodehouse's bright, effortless voice. The book shows him between his school stories and his mature Jeeves and Blandings work, already master of the comic short story. Readers who want Wodehouse in small, perfect doses will find this collection ideal.
7476-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
This volume of Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations opens with its author's own preface, a defense of recording English deeds at sea. Hakluyt notes how nations love to blaze abroad their pedigrees, painting ancestors' arms on their walls, while poets trace obscure heroes back to the gods themselves. Against fable, he sets the undoubted truth of voyages, traffics, and discoveries, gathered from sailors and merchants.

Like its companion volume, this edition retains Hakluyt's sixteenth-century spelling, expanding only manuscript abbreviations, with editor's footnotes in modern spelling. The collection as a whole remains the foundation of English travel literature. This volume's preface is the place to start for readers who want to know why Hakluyt gathered his vast library of voyages at all.
7505-half-past-seven-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson wrote these stories for half-past seven, the bedtime hour, and the Toyman tells them. That is what the Toyman used to say, the book promises. If you ever go to the White House with the Green Blinds by the Side of the Road, the Toyman will say it still, whatever the weather. Dorothy Hope Smith's color illustrations picture the tales.

The contents run from The Little Lost Fox and The Big Bobsled to The Jolly Roger. Then come The Blue Croaker, the Bright Agate, and the Little Gray Mig, and the old woman who lived on the canal. Anderson dedicates the book to Sarah Davis Anderson, the youngsters' Aunt Sally. The stories are gentle, funny, and just strange enough for bedtime, told for children who are not quite ready to sleep.
7506-the-huge-hunter-or-the-steam-man-of:
Edward S. Ellis wrote one of America's first science-fiction adventures in this dime novel of the prairies. A colossal figure strides across the plains, looking like some Titan taking giant steps, with a black volume of smoke issuing from its mouth or the top of its head. At a distance no one can scrutinize the phenomenon closely, and terror spreads before it.

The terror is the Steam Man, a giant machine built by a genius. It travels with a trapper and an artisan up the Yellowstone, among miners and Indians, on buffalo hunts and against a grizzly bear. Chapters promise the steam man as hunter, in wolf ravine, and in an appalling danger. Ellis's huge hunter is the ancestor of the robot tale, a wonder of steam and iron loose on the frontier.
7515-the-glory-of-the-trenches:
Coningsby Dawson, author of Carry On: Letters in Wartime, wrote this interpretation of the trenches from his own service as a Canadian officer. His father, W. J. Dawson, introduces the volume. The epigraph gives its thesis: the glory is all in the souls of the men, nothing external. Dawson had been wounded, removed to a base hospital and then to a military hospital in London, where amputation of his right arm was gravely feared but happily avoided.

As soon as he could use his hand, he was asked to write for Canada about its forces. The book opens with letters from home carried by runners through battle smoke, up Death Valley spouting flame, and down roads no one uses by day. Dawson writes for those at home, to show what the trenches meant to the men who held them. It is a soldier's book, earnest and unsentimental.
7516-crucial-instances:
Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers seven stories in which a single moment decides a life. The contents run from The Duchess at Prayer and The Angel at the Grave through The Recovery, a dialogue called Copy, and on to The Rembrandt, The Moving Finger, and The Confessional. Italy, art, and old houses provide much of the scenery.

The opening story asks the reader to question the shuttered front of an old Italian house, a motionless mask behind which buzz the secrets of the confessional. Other houses declare the lives they shelter, Wharton writes, but the old palace in its narrow street is as impenetrable as death.
