Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this night sketch for Twice-Told Tales, praising a rainy winter's day indoors. The best study for such a day, he says, is a book of travels, unlike the sombre scene misted through the windows. Fancy then gives shape and color to the author's page, and strange lands glimmer through familiar walls.

An Arabian desert, a caravan, and outlandish figures crowd his small chamber, summoned by words like spells. Hawthorne celebrates reading as travel of the mind. The sketch remains a delightful praise of books on a wet night.
9217-the-lily-s-quest-from-twice-told-ta:
Two lovers plan a little summer-house shaped like an antique temple, meant for refined and innocent joys. There they would hold pleasant talk, give feasts of fruit, hear music, and read poetry, letting minds flit away in daydreams. Hawthorne, in Twice-Told Tales, sends Adam Forrester and Lilias Fay out on a ramble to seek that dream.

On a breezy, cloudless afternoon they set forth, and the quest for the lily becomes a search for pure delight itself. Hawthorne blends romance with moral fancy, as sunshine gathers round the pillars of hope. The tale remains a tender allegory of love and the ideals youth builds.
9218-footprints-on-the-sea-shore-from-tw:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this seashore sketch for Twice-Told Tales, on the need for solitude. At times the forest and ocean summon him from the haunts of men, one with waves, one with boughs. No primeval forest lies near his daily walk, only a wood or two by a farmhouse. So he turns to the sea.

On the shore he walks alone, musing on footprints left and washed away. The sketch joins nature writing to moral reflection, as Hawthorne often does. It remains a quiet, lovely piece on rest, thought, and the pull of wild places.
9219-edward-fane-s-rosebud-from-twice-to:
Gazing at a figure of melancholy age, can fancy restore its youth? Hawthorne poses that hard exercise at the start of this Twice-Told Tales sketch. Some old people, above all women worn by grief, seem never to have been young and gay. Their sable widow's weeds look essential to their being, as they watch at death-beds.

Yet Hawthorne takes one such doleful creature and seeks the girl she once was, beneath time's marks. The sketch is a gentle act of imaginative mercy. It still moves readers as a meditation on age, loss, and the youth hidden in every old face.
9220-the-threefold-destiny-from-twice-to:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this fairy legend for Twice-Told Tales, blending fairy mechanism with New England life. He hoped to give an old-style allegory a warmer, more lifelike hue, without losing nature's sober colors. The tale opens on a summer evening with a tall, dark figure, and a destiny threefold in shape.

Hawthorne lets wonder touch plain folk and plain scenery, as a subdued tinge over the real. The legend asks how fate and choice intertwine. It remains a charming early experiment, showing Hawthorne learning to mix the marvelous with the familiar.
9236-main-street-from-the-snow-image-and:
Hawthorne's Main Street opens with a showman bowing to the public and promising a panorama of time. Walking his native town's main street daily, he dreams of showing its growth from infancy upward, with scenes of two centuries passing along one thoroughfare. He contrives a pictorial show, somewhat like a puppet show, worked by turning a crank.

Ghosts of forefathers file past in historic incidents, called up with no more trouble than that crank. Hawthorne turns local history into theater. The sketch remains a brilliant fancy on time, memory, and the street as a stage of American life.
9239-old-news-from-the-snow-image-and-ot:
Old News, by Hawthorne, opens on a volume of once-new newspapers, now yellow and time-stained. Each small half-sheet, in rude old type, once served the present moment alone. Yet these frail leaves outlived printer and subscribers, and proved more durable than much timber, brick, and stone of their town.

More than that, they alone record the government, interests, and opinions of their day, now passed away. Hawthorne praises editors whose ephemeral work outlasts monuments. The sketch is a witty meditation on news, time, and what truly endures.
9245-biographical-sketches-from-fanshawe:
Hawthorne's biographical studies, from Fanshawe and Other Pieces, treat five figures of early New England. Mrs. Hutchinson leads, then Sir William Phips, Sir William Pepperell, Thomas Green Fessenden, and Jonathan Cilley. The Hutchinson sketch opens with a train of thought on public women, and on how the press now feeds feminine ambition.

Hawthorne writes with moral care, seeking character behind controversy, and weighing faith against dissent in each life. These studies show his early historical mind at work, before his great romances. They remain valuable for readers of colonial New England, and for students of Hawthorne's growth as a writer.
9249-dr-bullivant-from-the-doliver-roman:
Dr. Bullivant was no great man, Hawthorne admits at once, and deserves no public memorial for his own sake alone. Yet his character can sharpen remarks on New England society, seen a century and a half after his time. That society changed with new folk from the east, and with sixty years of wear on Puritan edges.

We paint early Puritans too darkly, Hawthorne warns, because we judge them from afar, by their severest traits alone. Bullivant's life lets him soften that picture. The sketch is a wise, humane essay on how history should judge ordinary people, not just saints and sinners.
9252-time-s-portraiture-from-the-doliver:
Hawthorne's Time's Portraiture is the carrier's address to patrons of the Salem Gazette for January 1, 1838. Kind patrons, the carriers call themselves Time's errand boys, sent all year from door to door to tell what the old gentleman talks of and does. Each New Year's morning they break into rhyme, in hideous strains that might frighten the infant Year.

Patrons never fail to reward them with bounty, whether for verses or for respite from verses. Hawthorne turns a begging custom into wit. The piece remains a delightful New Year's jeu d'esprit, on time, custom, and the press.
9309-in-a-steamer-chair-and-other-shipbo:
Robert Barr, writing as Luke Sharp, gathered these shipboard stories from voyages between England and America. He dedicates them to the Vagabond Club of London and the Witenagemote Club of Detroit, joking that fifty members each can swear they heard his tales from his lips first. The contents range from Mrs. Tremain to a stowaway.

A society for reforming poker players, a man not on the passenger list, and a captain's feat all get their turn. Barr's humor is breezy and worldly. The book still reads as a cheerful companion for a crossing, full of talk, jest, and sea air.
9368-welsh-fairy-tales:
William Elliot Griffis wrote these Welsh fairy tales in 1921, in a preface-letter to his grandfather, Captain John Griffis. The captain died in 1804, having opposed King George the Third, sailed the American flag round the world, and lain buried near Benjamin Franklin among Free Quakers and patriots. Griffis claims Welsh blood with pride.

He links Wales to Roger Williams, William Penn, and Thomas Jefferson, prophets of spiritual liberty. The tales that follow draw on Welsh lore and fancy. The book remains a charming collection, patriotic, learned, and full of old Welsh magic.
9370-tiverton-tales:
Alice Brown published these Tiverton tales in 1899, set in a town of breezy upland roads and damp, sweet valleys. A summer there might waste excursions abroad, Brown says, once you gain the freedom of family living. Dooryards, those outer courts of domesticity, hold the town's true life, where homely joys spill over and children riot.

Contents include Dooryards, A March Wind, The Mortuary Chest, and The Experience of Hannah Prime. Monday washings move outdoors in bright weather. Brown's tales remain a gentle, exact portrait of New England domestic life, its work, grief, and quiet humor.
9379-a-woman-intervenes:
Robert Barr wrote this novel in 1896, opening in the office of the New York Argus. Its managing editor sits frowning, looking from under shaggy eyebrows at a young man before his desk. Eight illustrations by Hal Hurst show Wentworth, Miss Jennie, and Edith Longworth, with a frontispiece protesting an insult. Barr dedicates it to Horace Hart.

A woman intervenes in the affairs of men, turning business and romance with a prodigious head for business. Barr writes briskly, with newspaper pace. The novel remains a lively tale of love, work, and a woman who refuses to stay in the background.
9382-grandma-s-memories:
Mary D. Brine wrote this illustrated verse memoir in 1888, dedicated to dear ones whose faces turn toward sunset. Its pictures trace a life: Grandma as a maiden, as a bride, as a mother hearing a lullaby, soft and low. The young head is lain, farewells are merry yet sad, and a grandchild's gift closes the circle.

Evening and the bells head the book, as the mantle of evening veils the sky. Brine's verse is sentimental in the Victorian manner, tender rather than sharp. The book remains a sweet relic of family piety, meant to be read aloud by the fire.
9458-questionable-shapes:
W. D. Howells, a leading American novelist, published Questionable Shapes in May 1903, three tales of ghosts and doubt. The tales are His Apparition, The Angel of the Lord, and Though One Rose from the Dead. Howells treats the supernatural with quiet dignity, far from the cheap thrills of stage spiritualism. Each tale asks what a sane person should make of a sight beyond sense.

His Apparition opens with Hewson, calm at first, then torn between sense and reason as he weighs what he saw. The other tales press the same doubt in new forms: angels, return from death, and the wish to believe. A reader gets subtle, literate ghost fiction, where the true chill lies in doubt itself, not in shocks.
9460-camps-quarters-and-casual-places:
Archibald Forbes, a famed war correspondent, gathered Camps, Quarters and Casual Places in London in 1896. The book collects his pieces from magazines on war, travel, and odd corners of life. Titles range from Matrimony Under Fire and A Version of Balaclava to Bismarck during the Franco-German War. Forbes writes as a man who saw camps and courts at first hand.

Other sketches recall Christmas in a cavalry camp, the Cawnpore and Lucknow of his day, and the warfare of the future. Some pieces are grave, some comic, all brisk and sure. A reader gets a veteran reporter's scrapbook, rich in war lore, travel talk, and sharp portraits of the age's great men.
9468-anna-st-ives:
Thomas Holcroft wrote Anna St. Ives in 1792, a long novel in letters from the age of revolution. Anna, a bright young heiress, writes to her friend Louisa Clifton as she sets out southward with her kin. The party means to stay in London, then cross to Paris. Anna's fancy runs ahead to Calais, Abbeville, and the gay scenes Sterne made famous.

Told through letters across seven volumes, the novel tests love, rank, and new ideas of freedom against old custom. Anna's warm, eager voice carries the tale, as suitors, kin, and French scenes press her choices. A reader gets a key radical novel of the 1790s, full of debate, feeling, and the hopes of a changing Europe.
9485-a-little-book-of-profitable-tales:
Eugene Field, a Chicago poet and humorist, published A Little Book of Profitable Tales in 1901. Field dedicated the book to his daughter Mary French Field, his severest critic and most loyal admirer. Tales inside include The First Christmas Tree, The Mouse and the Moonbeam, The Symbol and the Saint, and The Coming of the Prince. The prose and verse mix fancy, humor, and moral point.

Other tales range from a robin and a violet to an oak and ivy, a pearl named Margaret, and a cyclopedia clerk. Each tale teaches gently, through wit or wonder, rather than preaching. A reader gets a charming, old-style story book for family reading, full of Field's whimsy and warmth.
9488-the-line-of-love-dizain-des-mariage:
James Branch Cabell wrote The Line of Love in 1921, a book of linked tales about love, chivalry, and marriage. The subtitle, Dizain des Mariages, points to ten tales of wedlock, told in Cabell's ornate, mock-heroic style. An opening essay recalls how long Cabell wrote in neglect, praised by few, while critics passed him by. The tales that follow play with knights, lovers, and vows.

Episodes range from Adhelmar at Puysange to love letters in Falstaff's voice and a tale of porcelain cups. Each asks what love costs, and how honor, wit, and folly mix in courtship. Cabell writes with irony and rich prose, half romance and half jest. A reader gets a clever, old-world fantasy of love's many shapes, from the gallant to the absurd.
9492-understanding-the-scriptures:
Francis J. McConnell, a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church, gave the Mendenhall Lectures at DePauw University on understanding the Scriptures. His book asks how a plain reader should read the Bible, when its tales seem far from daily life. McConnell grants the English is clear, yet notes that Genesis alone soon poses hard problems. The lectures seek a path between blind literalism and vague doubt.

Chapters, including The Book of the Cross, weigh how to read narratives, laws, and parables with sense and faith. McConnell speaks to church folk who want honesty and reverence at once. A reader gets a sane, early modern guide to Bible reading, still useful for those who ask how an old book speaks today.
953-tom-swift-and-his-big-tunnel-or-the-:
An appeal for aid sends Tom Swift to Peru in this tale by Victor Appleton, to build a big tunnel and find a hidden city of the Andes. A face at the window, a bearded man, and a bomb warn him that rivals are near, while Professor Bumper aids the search. Tom's experiments test rock, air, and nerve.

The tunnel leads toward a lost city, with Inca gold and ancient wonders in the offing. Appleton blends engineering detail with lost-world adventure, and Tom's pluck carries the party through. The book is a rousing Tom Swift quest, where science and exploration meet in the high Andes.
9624-directions-for-cookery-in-its-vario:
Miss Leslie, a famed Philadelphia cookery writer, published Directions for Cookery in its Various Branches, here in its tenth edition of 1840. The book covers soups, meats, poultry, game, fish, sauces, and vegetables, with pickles, sweetmeats, pastry, and cakes beside. Warm cakes for breakfast, bread, yeast, butter, and cheese get their own sections. Home liquors, sickroom dishes, and perfumery round out the volume.

Leslie writes with plain, firm guidance for a household cook, naming cuts, times, and methods in clear order. Her receipts shaped American kitchens for decades. A reader gets a rich window on 1840 cooking, and a working cookbook whose dishes still suit a modern table with care.
970-uncle-josh-s-punkin-centre-stories:
Cal Stewart wrote these stories of Uncle Josh Weathersby of Punkin Centre, in rural dialect humour. Stewart states his object plainly in his preface: to furnish the reader with an occasional laugh, and himself with an occasional dollar, a fair bargain if the laugh arrives. Uncle Josh is a purely imagined countryman.

Josh tells of farm, town, and city folk in his own drawling voice, with jokes on new inventions, politics, and neighbours. Stewart's humour, first heard on phonograph records, made Uncle Josh famous across America. The book charms readers who enjoy old-time country comedy, told by a master of the dialect tale.
977-american-notes:
Rudyard Kipling wrote these notes on America, gathered from his travels in the United States in 1889. The introduction recalls a paragraph in the London World of April 1890. It named Kipling, the literary hero of the hour, the man who came from nowhere, in two small rooms joined by a tiny hall.

Kipling writes of American cities, trains, and people with a young reporter's eye, praising energy while mocking boast and bad manners. His notes are vivid, opinionated, and sometimes harsh, as a visitor's notes often are. The book gives readers Kipling's America at first sight, before fame softened his pen.
9777-riley-child-rhymes:
James Whitcomb Riley wrote Riley Child-Rhymes, a book of Hoosier childhood verse with pictures by Will Vawter. Dedicated to children everywhere, the book gathers poems from Little Orphant Annie to The Bumblebee, Circus-Day Parade, and Our Hired Girl. A frontispiece shows a child listening to witch tales Annie tells. Riley's verse favors dialect, laughter, and tender memory.

Poems range from aunty's house and farm boys to grandfathers, naughty Claudes, and down-around-the-river days. The Hoosier pictures match the rhymes' warmth. A reader gets a beloved children's classic, rich in Indiana speech and the magic of small days.
9790-traffics-and-discoveries:
Rudyard Kipling wrote Traffics and Discoveries, a book of tales and verse on empire, sea, and modern war. Contents include The Captive, The Bonds of Discipline, A Sahibs' War, and Their Lawful Occasions, with Steam Tactics, Wireless, and The Army of a Dream. Mrs. Bathurst and They add mystery to the mix. Kipling opens with a captive's march, chained yet nobly at ease.

Tales move from barracks and ships to wireless rooms and dream armies, with verse woven between. Kipling writes with terse craft and imperial confidence, shadowed by doubt. A reader gets a strong, varied Kipling collection, where soldiers, sailors, and signals tell the age's story.
9806-mr-justice-raffles:
E. W. Hornung wrote Mr. Justice Raffles in 1909, a tale of Raffles the gentleman thief turned judge of rogues. The book opens with Raffles vanished, then cabling his friend to meet the 7.31 at Charing Cross from Carlsbad. Chapters promise an inaugural banquet, a council of war, and our Mr. Shylock, with Camilla Belsize and a triple alliance. A dash in the dark and trial by Raffles follow.

Later chapters bring a secret service, the death of a sinner, and an apologia, as Raffles rights wrongs his own way. Hornung writes with light, daring wit. A reader gets a charming Raffles adventure, where a thief plays justice with style.
9815-the-principal-navigations-voyages-t:
Richard Hakluyt, an English preacher and collector, gathered the accounts of his countrymen's sea voyages in the sixteenth century. This eighth volume, edited by Edmund Goldsmid, covers the English in Asia, from early trading ventures to longer stays in eastern ports and markets.

Sailors, merchants, and envoys describe storms, markets, rulers, and customs they met far from home. The spelling keeps the flavor of Hakluyt's age, with notes to help modern readers follow old names and terms. Together the reports show how England first learned Asia by ship, bargain, and hard travel.
9867-riders-of-the-silences:
Max Brand's 1919 western opens on the legends of the old West: gunmen whose bullets never missed, and stallions faster than the wind. Greatest of these legends, the prologue says, is the tale of Red Pierre and the phantom gunfighter McGurk.

The two men, unlike in every way, share one trait: neither can be beaten. Their rivalry drives the novel through mountain deserts, chases, and showdowns. Brand writes with speed and a storyteller's relish for myth. Fans of classic westerns get a tale that knows it is a legend and enjoys being one.
9888-the-spread-eagle-and-other-stories:
Gouverneur Morris published this story collection in 1910, with The Spread Eagle as its title tale. Morris, author of The Footprint and other stories, sets his characters in drawing rooms, Swiss winters, and Nice holidays, where pride, love, and money collide.

The title story opens with a youth spoiled by the praise of everyone around him, and the other tales follow men and women learning what praise and position are worth. Morris writes with wit and a light hand. Readers get polished, early twentieth-century short stories about society people discovering their limits.
9959-the-armourer-s-prentices:
Charlotte M. Yonge's 1889 novel follows prentice lads in an armourer's household in an earlier England of craftsmen, guilds, and faith. Published by Macmillan in London and New York, with illustrations by W. J. Hennessy, it belongs to Yonge's long shelf of historical tales for young readers.

The story moves through workshop life, old haunts, and the duties of apprentices learning a trade and a code. Yonge's interest lies in character formed by work, loyalty, and patience. Readers who enjoy historical fiction about ordinary craftspeople will find her earnest, detailed picture of a vanished working world.
9994-the-indian-lily-and-other-stories:
Hermann Sudermann's story collection, translated by Ludwig Lewisohn in 1911, takes its title from The Indian Lily. That story opens at seven in the morning with Herr von Niebeldingk and his dark, weary eyes. Sudermann, a leading German dramatist and novelist, writes of love, guilt, and fate.

The other stories are The Purpose, The Song of Death, The Victim, Autumn, and Merry Folk, each turning on a moral crisis. Lewisohn's translation keeps Sudermann's serious, polished manner. Readers get German short fiction of the naturalist age: somber, thoughtful, and attentive to the costs of desire.
a-brief-history-of-the-united-states:
Joel Dorman Steele wrote his one-term history, Barnes's, on a teacher's complaint: pupils find history books dry, and the interesting ones are too long. His preface promises an attractive book that can be mastered in a single term. The copyright page dates the work 1872. Six epochs organize the whole.

Early discoveries and settlements, development of the colonies, the Revolutionary War, development of the states, the Civil War, and reconstruction and passing events carry the story to his own day. Questions for class use, historical recreations, the Declaration of Independence, and the Constitution fill the appendix. Steele's brief histories taught more American schoolchildren than almost any rival, and this is the pattern book.
a-changed-man-and-other-tales:
Thomas Hardy reprints a dozen shorter tales from the periodical press in this collection, transcribed from the 1920 Macmillan edition. His prefatory note, dated August 1913, says he gathered the pieces so readers could have them in the complete series of his works. The title tale, A Changed Man, opens the volume.

The Waiting Supper, Alicia's Diary, and The Grave by the Handpost follow. Enter a Dragoon and A Tryst at an Ancient Earthwork come next. A committee-man of the French Terror and a duke's reappearance stand among them. Soldiers, shepherds, and waiting women fill the Wessex scenes. Hardy mixes ghostly hints, class-crossed love, and his usual irony about fate in these late, polished stories.
a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these poems for children, many of them from the memory of his own sickly childhood. The volume is dedicated to Alison Cunningham, his nurse, with a verse letter thanking her for the nights she watched over him. The contents group the poems in three parts: the first under his own name as the child speaker, then The Child Alone, then Garden Days.

Short rhymes cover bedtime, rain, swings, shadows, foreign lands, and the land of counterpane, where a sick child turns bedcovers into hills for toy soldiers. Favorites such as My Shadow and The Lamplighter sit beside marching songs and farewells to the farm. The poems speak in a child's voice without talking down, which is why the collection has stayed a nursery classic.
a-collection-of-beatrix-potter-stories:
Beatrix Potter's animal tales are gathered here from her little Peter Rabbit books. A front list names the titles and marks those included: among them The Tale of Peter Rabbit, The Tale of Benjamin Bunny, The Tale of Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, The Tale of the Flopsy Bunnies, The Tale of Two Bad Mice, and The Tale of Mr. Tod.

Peter opens the collection, squeezing under Mr. McGregor's garden gate and losing his jacket and shoes in the chase, as his mother warned. The other tales follow hedgehog washerwomen, fishing frogs, cats, mice, and foxes through small domestic adventures in the Lake District countryside. Potter's exact, unsentimental animal observation carries the charm: the creatures wear clothes and keep house, but they eat and are eaten like real animals.
a-few-figs-from-thistles:
Edna St. Vincent Millay's A Few Figs from Thistles collects short poems and sonnets of love and independence. The title promises small sharp fruit, and the opening poems deliver it. First Fig boasts of a candle burning at both ends. Second Fig builds a shining palace on sand.

Recuerdo remembers a night spent riding a ferry back and forth until dawn. Thursday coolly dismisses a lover who complains of Wednesday's change of heart. Macdougal Street walks a noisy New York immigrant street at night. Other pieces sing of travel, roses, and the not impossible him. Millay's voice is musical, witty, and unrepentant. These brief lyrics made her the emblem of a young generation that meant to live brightly and briefly.
a-group-of-noble-dames:
Thomas Hardy groups ten tales of Dorset ladies of past centuries, first collected in 1891, as the title page of this 1920 edition records. The dames are named like a roll of honor. They include the First Countess of Wessex and Barbara of the House of Grebe. They include the Marchioness of Stonehenge, Lady Mottisfont, and Squire Petrick's Lady. The Lady Icenway, Anna Lady Baxby, the Lady Penelope, the Duchess of Hamptonshire, and the Honourable Laura complete the roll.

A map of Wessex faces the tales, which are told as after-dinner stories among a club of antiquarians, in parts before and after dinner. Each turns on a marriage, a pride, or a strange fate in an old great house. Hardy treats his dames with irony and pity in equal measure.
a-guide-to-the-best-historical-novels-an:
Jonathan Nield sorts the best historical novels and tales ever written so that readers can find their way through a huge field. After an introduction on the rise of the form, his lists run by period: pre-Christian times, then century by century up to the nineteenth. A supplementary list covers semi-historical works.

Each section names authors and titles worth reading for that age, from ancient Rome to the age of Scott and Dumas. Suggested courses of reading for young readers and a bibliography close the volume. Nield's guide served for years as the standard map for readers who wanted the past told as story, arranged so a reader could march through history in fiction.
a-hive-of-busy-bees:
Effie Mae Hency Williams frames her children's book as a visit to Grandpa and Grandma, where Don and Joyce are caught worrying about next summer just after Christmas. The contents tell the plan: after How It Happened and The Sting of the Bee come chapters named Bee Obedient, Bee Honest, Bee Truthful, Bee Kind, Bee Polite, and more.

Each bee chapter tells a small story from the children's days. It turns a fault or a kindness into the lesson of its title. Bee Grateful, Bee Loving, Bee Content, and Bee Prayerful pass in review. The book ends with Home Again. Williams writes for young readers in plain, warm sentences. The book is Sunday-school moral teaching in story dress, gentle and old-fashioned.
a-knight-of-the-white-cross-a-tale-of-th:
G. A. Henty's A Knight of the White Cross tells the first siege of Rhodes through an English boy's eyes. His preface to his dear lads explains the Knights of St. John. Born as hospitallers to pilgrims, they became a great military order. At Rhodes they fortified the town against the Turks.

The tale opens at the chateau of Amboise in June 1470, with a lad of seventeen stroking a hawk. Gervaise Tresham's path leads from English faction fights to the white cross of the order. Page, squire, and knight, he rises through the Rhodes campaigns. The siege itself, against Sultan Mahomet's host, crowns the book. Henty chose the episode, he says, as the most full of incident in the order's history. Research and adventure march together in his most chivalrous tale.
a-modern-cinderella-or-the-little-old-sh:
Louisa May Alcott gathers four stories, opening with the title tale in an ancient, many-gabled New England house, where a brook runs through the orchard and patriarchal elms stand on the lawn. One summer morning a humble history begins there: Nan, a poor relation with a kind heart, and Di, the restless invalid she tends. A little old shoe carries the Cinderella plot into this household.

Debby's Debut, Brothers, and Nelly's Hospital complete the volume, the last drawn from Alcott's own nursing in the Civil War. The stories mix romance, sacrifice, and domestic duty in her early manner. Readers who know her through Little Women will find the same warmth in shorter compass.
a-pair-of-blue-eyes:
Thomas Hardy's novel tells, in his own preface's words, an imaginary history of three human hearts. The preface sets the frame: a craze for restoring old churches had reached the wild coast of western England, and the story grows out of such a restoration. The scene lies near Castle Boterel, at the furthest west of Hardy's Wessex settings, a region he calls one of dream and mystery.

Across forty chapters, the architect Stephen Smith comes to restore a church tower and falls in love with Elfride Swancourt, the vicar's daughter. Her later attachment to the man of letters Henry Knight, and the misunderstandings between the three, drive the tragedy. Hardy mixes cliff scenery, coincidence, and his early interest in how chance governs feeling.
a-peep-behind-the-scenes:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote A Peep Behind the Scenes as a Christian story for young readers, by the author of Christie's Old Organ, as the title page notes. It begins in rain at a fair, where little Rosalie belongs to a travelling theatre company, brightly lit on Saturday night and dreary by Sunday afternoon, when the crowds have gone.

Rosalie's story runs through the little theatre, the actress's own tale, a family secret, circus processions, and lodging-house poverty. Kind and cruel adults cross her path while the book presses its lesson, that the showy world backstage is poor and sad beside a Christian home. Chapter titles like 'The Lost Lamb Found' and 'The Green Pasture' announce the ending Walton's Sunday-school readers expected.
a-protegee-of-jack-hamlin-s-and-other-st:
Bret Harte opens aboard the steamer Silveropolis, cleaving the Sacramento River with foam at her paddle-boxes, where the gambler Jack Hamlin steps quietly from his stateroom. Hamlin, Harte's recurring gentleman of the camps, takes a young woman under his protection, and the title story follows what his chivalry costs him. Five more tales fill the volume.

An Ingenue of the Sierras and The Reformation of James Reddy come next. The Heir of the McHulishes, An Episode of West Woodlands, and The Home-Coming of Jim Wilkes follow. They range across mining towns, ranches, and river landings. Harte writes his California with sentiment and irony in equal measure, and Hamlin remains one of his most graceful creations.
a-ring-of-rubies:
A Ring of Rubies is an 1892 novel by L T Meade. Rosamund Lindley, an English girl, begs a wealthy but eccentric relative to aid her in a cherished project. He puts her off with a promise to answer definitely after a week. Within that week he dies, and his will leaves Rosamund an antique ruby ring.

The ring is the hinge of the story: an unexpected inheritance that changes what Rosamund can do and what others expect of her. Meade, a hugely productive writer of girls' and domestic fiction, builds the tale around the gift and its consequences. The novel shows her gift for turning a single striking object into the engine of a young heroine's fortunes.
a-short-history-of-wales:
Owen Edwards tells the whole story of Wales in twenty-five short chapters, first published in 1906 and in its fifth impression by 1922, as this Fisher Unwin edition records. He begins with what Wales is made of and what it is like, then the wandering nations: Iberians and Celts. Rome, the coming of Christ, and the Welsh kings follow.

The laws of Howel, the Normans, Llywelyn the Great and the last Llywelyn, Owen Glendower, the Tudors, the Reformation, and the Civil War carry the tale forward. Closing chapters treat the religious awakening under Howel Harris, the Reform Acts, education, and self-government. Edwards writes with love and clarity, in a small book meant for every Welsh home.
a-thief-in-the-night-a-book-of-raffles-a:
A Thief in the Night, subtitled A Book of Raffles' Adventures, is E W Hornung's 1905 collection of stories about A J Raffles. It is the third book of the series and the last of the short story collections. In it, Raffles, the gentleman thief, commits his crimes behind the perfect cover of an England cricketer admired by the society he robs.

Bunny Manders, his devoted friend, shares the dangers and tells the tales. This edition gathers those adventures under the book-of-adventures subtitle, with the full original content. For new readers it serves as a complete entry into the Raffles world: elegant theft, loyal friendship, and the police forever one step behind.
acres-of-diamonds-our-every-day-opportun:
Russell H. Conwell, founder of Temple University as the title page notes, built his fame on a single lecture, Acres of Diamonds, delivered thousands of times across America. This volume prints that lecture together with Robert Shackleton's account of Conwell's life and achievements and an autobiographical note. The contents trace the life first: the story of his sword, his start at Lexington, and the fifty-seven cents that began his work.

The lecture itself argues that wealth and opportunity lie close at hand, in one's own town and trade, rather than in distant strikes. Its title story tells of a man who sold his farm to hunt diamonds abroad, while diamonds lay under his own land. Shackleton's biography then shows the doctrine financing a university built for working students.
aeroplanes:
James Slough Zerbe explains the flying machine while it is still new, in chapters that move from theory to practice. His contents begin with theories and facts about flying: gravity, momentum, resistance, lift and drift, and the flight of birds. Later chapters take up the shape of machines, fore and aft control, and lifting surfaces.

Construction, power, propellers, and accessories follow, with chapters on experimental gliders and model aeroplanes for the beginner. A chapter on the aeroplane in the Great War brings the subject up to its military present. Zerbe writes in plain terms for curious readers and amateur builders, and his tables and arguments show an inventor thinking on paper.
after-a-shadow-and-other-stories:
T. S. Arthur's After a Shadow, and Other Stories appeared in New York in 1868. The title tale begins on a bright June morning with baby Arty. The child escapes his nurse and runs laughing down the pavement. He is chasing his own long shadow on the ground.

Seventeen stories follow, among them In the Way of Temptation and Andy Lovell. Coffee versus Brandy brings Arthur's temperance cause into the parlour. A Good Name, Little Lizzie, and An Angel in Disguise treat children and disguise. Which Was Most the Lady tests manners against worth. Arthur writes short fiction for family reading, each piece turning on a small incident with a moral inside it. The shadow of the title is the kind adults chase too, an emptiness mistaken for a prize.
ali-pacha-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas tells the true story of Ali Pacha of Janina in this volume from his Celebrated Crimes set, printed here in the 1910 edition. His first chapter sets the scene: while Napoleon remade the West, the old Ottoman East crumbled, and bold adventurers carved pieces from its ruins. Ali, a brigand's son, carved the largest piece in Greece.

Eleven chapters trace his rise from robber chief to pasha ruling Albania and much of Greece, his courts, cruelties, and wars, and his long defiance of the Sultan. Dumas writes history like a novel, with scenes, speeches, and a villain of real grandeur. The fall of Ali, besieged in Janina, closes the tale in fire.
alice-of-old-vincennes:
Maurice Thompson's novel Alice of Old Vincennes opens under the Roussillon cherry tree, a French seedling old Vincennes remembered into statehood days. The Wabash town of French habitants and British soldiers is the stage: Fort Sackville flies the British flag over the Illinois country. Alice Tarleton grows up among priests and traders while George Rogers Clark's Virginians move toward the river forts. The contents promise an attack, a flag of Alice's making, and Clark's counsel.

Inside, the novel follows the 1778-79 campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes for Virginia and lost and retook the fort. Alice's flag, sewn for the American cause, gives the romance its emblem of women's part in the frontier war. Thompson fills his pages with French patois, river weather, and the diplomacy of the old Northwest. Readers get the standard American historical romance of its decade, the book that made Vincennes famous in fiction.
alonzo-fitz-and-other-stories:
Mark Twain gathers stories and sketches, opening with The Loves of Alonzo Fitz Clarence and Rosannah Ethelton. Alonzo sits in snowbound Eastport, Maine, on a bitter winter morning, courting by the new telephone a Rosannah he has never seen in California. The contents continue with On the Decay of the Art of Lying, Punch Brothers Punch, and The Great Revolution in Pitcairn.

The Canvasser's Tale, An Encounter with an Interviewer, Paris Notes, a legend of Sagenfeld, and speeches on the babies and the weather fill out the volume. Twain mixes tall tale, satire, and platform humor, much of it from his earlier years. The telephone courtship, with its cross-country mix-ups, remains the best-known piece in the set.
amanda-a-daughter-of-the-mennonites:
Anna Balmer Myers sets her novel in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, opening on a scorching midsummer day with children splashing in a small stream. Amanda Reist grows up Mennonite, plain in dress and strict in church, in a farm world of snitzing parties and apple butter boiling. Helen Mason Gross illustrated the book, as the title page notes.

Twenty-six chapters follow Amanda through school days to work as a teacher, a spelling bee, the market, a boarder, a trouble maker, and Aunt Rebecca's will. Martin, the boy of the farm, and Lyman, a voice from the wider world, divide her heart. Myers writes the Pennsylvania Dutch country from inside, with affection for its faith and food alike.
american-fairy-tales:
L. Frank Baum, fresh from The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, wrote American Fairy Tales as a set of comic wonder stories. Baum sets his magic in modern American homes, attics, and streets rather than old European kingdoms. The first tale leaves little Martha alone in a big house. She opens a brass-studded chest from Italy and lets out trouble.

Twelve tales follow, among them The Glass Dog, The Queen of Quok, and The Enchanted Types. A dummy comes alive, a boy captures Father Time, and magic bonbons cause chaos. A laughing hippopotamus and the king of the polar bears join the company. Baum mixes slang, satire, and nonsense with his enchantments. The stories gently mock fashion, wealth, and pride while keeping a child's view of wonder at the centre.
american-notes:
Charles Dickens wrote this travel book after his first tour of the United States, published here in an edition that also carries Pictures from Italy. His dedication thanks the American friends who welcomed him and left his judgment free, and who can bear the truth told good-humouredly. A preface to the cheap edition insists, years on, that his opinions stand unaltered.

Dickens travels through Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Washington, and the West, touring prisons, asylums, factories, and schools, riding steamboats and trains, and watching Congress and frontier manners with the same sharp eye. He praises American energy and kindness and attacks slavery, the press, and the national habit of spitting. The book made him enemies in America and remains a vivid outsider's portrait of the young republic.
among-malay-pirates:
Among Malay Pirates, published in 1893 by G A Henty, is a collection of short adventure stories for boys. Henty was the era's best-known writer of such tales, and this volume ranges widely. Its title story takes readers among the Malay pirates of the East, and other stories turn to India and to a shipwreck around the Channel Islands.

The collection also includes a tale of a dam within California and an escape from Chinese captors. Each story delivers the brisk danger and resourceful heroes that made Henty famous. Together they show the full spread of his adventure map, from Eastern seas to American engineering, in the short form his young readers devoured.
an-essay-on-man-moral-essays-and-satires:
Alexander Pope's poems fill this 1891 Cassell volume, whose introduction divides his career by reigns: original poet under Anne, translator of Homer under George I, and moral poet as his genius ripened. The Essay on Man stands first, a poem in heroic couplets that surveys man's place between angels and beasts and argues that whatever is, is right.

The Moral Essays take up the characters of men and women, riches, and taste, through portraits of real people thinly veiled. The Satires close the book with Pope's attacks on dunces, hirelings, and corrupt taste. Line after line has passed into common quotation, and the volume shows why Pope defined poetry for his century.
andersen-s-fairy-tales:
Hans Christian Andersen's tales fill this collection, opening with The Emperor's New Clothes. The contents list nineteen stories, among them The Swineherd, The Real Princess, The Fir Tree, The Snow Queen, The Shadow, and The Little Match Girl. Andersen wrote as a Dane telling stories aloud, and the voice stays close and warm.

Some tales are funny, like the emperor parading in invisible clothes. Others are sad: a match girl freezing on New Year's Eve, a fir tree longing for greatness, a mother searching for her dead child. Andersen mixed folk material with stories wholly his own, and his blend of wonder, humor, and sorrow changed children's books for good.
angling-sketches:
Andrew Lang writes as a fisherman in sketches first printed in periodicals such as Macmillan's Magazine and the Fishing Gazette, gathered here from the 1895 Longmans edition. The Confessions of a Duffer opens the book honestly: Lang owns his failures with rod and line. Loch Awe, Loch Leven, and Tweedside supply the waters.

The Lady or the Salmon, The Bloody Doctor, and The Complete Bungler mix fishing fact with story and joke. Lang salts his sport with classical learning and Border memories from his boyhood. The result is sporting literature for readers who may never cast a fly: a book about patience, hope, rivers, and the tales fishermen tell.
animal-heroes:
Ernest Thompson Seton tells the life stories of animals he calls heroes, and his note to the reader insists each tale rests on a real animal's life. The contents list the Slum Cat and Arnaux the homing pigeon. They list Badlands Billy the wolf and the Boy and the Lynx. Little Warhorse the jack-rabbit, Snap the bull-terrier, the Winnipeg Wolf, and the White Reindeer complete the set.

Seton, a working naturalist, follows each animal's habits, enemies, and escapes with a tracker's knowledge. Some tales end in triumph, others in the hard deaths nature deals. He wrote the White Reindeer in Norway with herds in sight, and Arnaux's flight from people who knew the bird. The stories helped create the realistic animal story as a form.
anne-of-green-gables:
Lucy Maud Montgomery wrote this novel about Anne Shirley, an orphan sent by mistake to Green Gables, the Prince Edward Island farm of Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert. The brother and sister had asked for a boy to help with work. Anne, talkative and full of imagination, wins Matthew over at once and slowly softens Marilla. The contents list thirty-eight chapters following her first years in Avonlea.

Anne renames places, befriends Diana Barry, feuds with Gilbert Blythe, and lands in scrapes at school and at tea. Later chapters take her through the Queen's class, examinations, and a scholarship path, ending with loss at home and a bend in her road. Warmth and comedy carry the story of a child remaking a strict household.
april-hopes:
William Dean Howells dates his novel 1887 on the title page and opens at Harvard's Class Day, in the Hemenway Gymnasium. Tall Mr. Elbridge G. Mavering watches the gaiety from the floor, struck by how young the students look. Among the promenading girls is Alice Pasmer, and young Dan Mavering's April hopes begin.

The courtship runs through a Newport summer and a winter of misunderstandings, family pride, and second thoughts on both sides. Alice's mother, a widow with a sharp tongue, and Dan's easy nature complicate every step. Howells studies the small change of feeling — a word, a visit, a silence — with his famous fineness. The novel is a comedy of manners with real pain under it.
arizona-sketches:
Joseph A. Munk wrote these sketches of Arizona from his own trips and ranching experience there. The contents list fourteen chapters. The first, A Romantic Land, warns the newcomer that Arizona judged by Eastern standards looks a disappointment: it seems all desert at first glance. Munk answers that the country must be taken on its own merits, for its scenery, climate, minerals, and strange plants and animals.

Following chapters describe his first trip, the open range, ranch life and the round-up, and a model ranch. Others treat desert plants, Hooker's Hot Springs, echoes in the canyons, and the fallen star at Meteorite Mountain. The ancient cliff dwellers and the Moqui Indians come next, and the climate closes the book. The book is part travel narrative, part settler's handbook for a territory still new to most American readers.
ars-ne-lupin-versus-herlock-sholmes:
Arsène Lupin versus Herlock Sholmes is a 1908 book by Maurice Leblanc, pitting his gentleman thief against a great detective. Arsène Lupin is everything expected of a French aristocrat: witty, charming, brilliant, and sly, and possibly the greatest thief in the world. Against him stands Herlock Sholmes, the British gentleman detective, the one man who may be able to stop him.

The book stages their duel of wits across a set of linked cases. Each man reads the other's moves and answers with a bolder stroke, so the contest stays open to the end. It remains a classic of the Lupin series, loved for the rare pleasure of watching thief and detective test each other at full strength.
artemis-to-actaeon-and-other-verses: Edith Wharton's 1909 book of verse opens with Artemis to Actaeon, in which the goddess speaks to the hunter who saw her and must die for it. Later poems take up Vesalius in Zante, Margaret of Cortona, Chartres, tombs and grief, then Orpheus, autumn sunsets and All Souls. Classical myth, Italian places and mourning run through a collection written in strict, musical verse.
asser-life-king-alfred-giles:
Asser, a Welsh monk from St David's, wrote his Life of King Alfred in 893, during the king's lifetime. J. A. Giles's English translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Asser had joined Alfred's court in 885 and wrote as a friend and daily companion.

The life mixes a chronicle of the Viking wars with intimate detail: Alfred's childhood, his illnesses, his hunger for learning, and his program of translating Latin books into English. Asser shows the king dividing his income and his hours with a monk's exactness. It is the first biography of an English king by a man who knew him. Its authenticity has been debated; its charm has not.
aunt-judy-s-tales: Mrs. Alfred Gatty's 1859 children's book gathers stories told by Aunt Judy to the little ones of a large family. The Little Victims, Vegetables Out of Place, Cook Stories, Rabbits' Tails and Out of the Way mix drollery with gentle moral teaching. Each tale is framed as fireside talk, with an elder girl amusing younger children while their mother rests nearby.
autobiographic-sketches:
Thomas De Quincey's Autobiographic Sketches gathers selections, grave and gay, from his published and unpublished writings. De Quincey writes to his American editor from Lasswade in January 1853, as he revises his works for republication in England.

He does not disown anything he has published, De Quincey insists, though some pieces served only a transient occasion and others might as well have been suppressed. Even pure levities, he adds, may lack any justifying principle of life within them. The sketches that follow mix memory, confession and wit. Readers of De Quincey will find here the opium-eater in reflective, autobiographical mood.
average-jones:
Samuel Hopkins Adams's Average Jones introduces a hero nicknamed by his own initials. Average Jones, whose parents gave him the initials A. V. R. E. before the surname Jones, seems a composite photograph of a thousand well-conditioned, clean-living young men.

Three men at the Cosmic Club open the book by asking what is the matter with Jones, and the stories that follow answer them case by case. Chapters include The B-Flat Trombone, Red Dot, Open Trail, The Mercy Sign, Blue Fires, Pin-Pricks, and The Million-Dollar Dog. Adams writes crisp, witty detective stories in which an apparently ordinary man notices what others miss. Readers who like clever, short mysteries will enjoy Jones immensely.
b-b-e-or-two-little-wooden-shoes: Bébée, or Two Little Wooden Shoes, Ouida's tale of the Flemish flower girl. Its sad story unfolds. This book preserves that Victorian novel. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
b09-luther-95theses:
Martin Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses on October 31, 1517, under the formal title Disputation on the Power and Efficacy of Indulgences. An indulgence was a church grant that cut the penalty for sin, and its sale had grown into a trade. Luther, a monk and teacher at Wittenberg, wrote in Latin for debate among scholars.

The theses attack the sale point by point and deny that the pope can free souls from purgatory at will. Luther asks what true sorrow for sin is worth next to a bought pardon. Few short texts have changed so much: this one lit the spark of the Reformation. It remains the most cited single document of that break.
b09-melanchthon-loci-communes:
Philipp Melanchthon was only twenty-four when his Loci Communes appeared in 1521. The Latin title means commonplaces, the main topics of theology set in order. No one had yet given the young Reformation a full, ordered system of teaching, and this book did it first.

Melanchthon builds the system straight from Paul's letter to the Romans, topic by topic. Sin, law, grace, and faith stand at the center of the scheme. The Latin text here follows the first form of the work, in the edition of G L Plitt as revised by Th Kolde. Students of the Reformation still treat it as the movement's first dogmatics.
back-to-god-s-country-and-other-stories:
James Oliver Curwood collected Back to God's Country and Other Stories from his tales of the Canadian north. The title story opens forty years before its climax, with Shan Tung travelling up the Fraser River. His Great Dane Tao, the biggest dog on the Height of Land, pulls his sledge alone. A drunken man's shot at Copper Creek Camp starts the long fuse.

Tao's blood survives in Wapi, a giant fighting dog of Coronation Gulf, born generations later. Other stories include The Fiddling Man, Peter God, and The Honor of Her People. Curwood sets gold camps, fur trails, and Eskimo igloos against each other. Dogs and men alike fight cold, hunger, and each other. His north is violent and romantic, a God's country judged by endurance and loyalty.
backlog-studies:
Charles Dudley Warner named these essays studies, and the first of them studies a disappearance: the open fire on the New England hearth. The hearth has gone out, he writes, and the family has lost its centre. No more toast-and-cider, no roasting apples before the coals, no grey-haired sires dozing in the chimney corner.

Warner builds the study into a small philosophy of the home. A house without a fire has no soul in it, nothing to rally round, and people move between rented rooms as they change clothes. The gas log with painted iron logs he calls a fraud and a blasphemy, because a fire you cannot poke is no fire. The later studies work the same vein of domestic observation, half lament and half comedy.
ban-and-arriere-ban-a-rally-of-fugitive-:
Andrew Lang rallied his fugitive rhymes in Ban and Arriere Ban, printed at Edinburgh in 1894 and dedicated to Eleanor Charlotte Sellar. His verses, ghosts returning from dusty papers, are offered for the sake of other times. The contents open with A Scot to Jeanne d'Arc and a ballad of how Jacobites held the Bass Rock for King James in 1691 to 1693.

Three portraits of Prince Charles, versions from Omar Khayyam and Meleager, a haunted tower, and a ballade of Yule fill the middle. Poems address Stevenson and mourn places like the deserted spa hotel of the mid-book sonnet. Lang's occasional verse mixes Jacobite sentiment, Greek translation, and pure play with his usual polish.
baring-gould-curious-myths-1867-second-s:
Sabine Baring-Gould, a Devon priest with a vast store of lore, made this second set of his Curious Myths in 1867. The text here is the 1868 print. He dealt with the odd tales of the Middle Ages and sought their roots.

One long part traces the tale of Melusina, the fairy bride, from land to land. Swan maids and the Fortunate Isles, the isles of the blest in the west sea, fill other parts. The set was the main Victorian guide to such tales, read far past its own age.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-part-1:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History reaches the Middle Ages in this third volume's first part, an older lecture-order edition whose note points readers to a later renumbering. The lectures open with Mohammed and the Saracenic conquests, reviewing his early life, his wife Cadijeh, his meditations, and the flight to Medina. Lord tracks the astonishing triumph of Islam against older Arabian religions.

Later lectures treat the medieval church, Charlemagne's age, and the scholastic world, ending near Abelard, who died at Cluny in the arms of Peter the Venerable after condemnation. Lord, a popular American lecturer, wrote history as moral biography for lyceum audiences. His medieval volume shows both his narrative gift and his century's Protestant frame.
beyond-these-voices: Beyond These Voices, by Mary Elizabeth Braddon. Its tale unfolds. This book preserves that novel. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
boethius-consolation-philosophy-james:
Boethius, a Roman senator and scholar, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison in 524, awaiting execution under King Theodoric. H. R. James's English translation is the text here. Boethius had been the king's chief minister; now, stripped of office and wealth, he wrote his way toward calm.

Lady Philosophy visits his cell and talks him out of self-pity, step by step. She shows that fortune's gifts were never truly his, and that the good cannot be taken by force. The famous wheel of fortune turns through the book. Verse and prose trade places as the argument climbs. It was among the most loved books of the Middle Ages.
brazilian-sketches:
T. B. Ray's Brazilian Sketches reports his travels in Brazil for American church readers. Ray, Educational Secretary of the Southern Baptist Foreign Mission Board, dined with a businessman ignorant of missions and resolved to write what missions do. His contents run from the country and its capital, Rio de Janeiro, to a visit to a country church. Two presidents, saint worship, and penance frame his argument. Brazil is Catholic in form, hungry in fact, and open to the Bible carried by native Christians whose mettle he praises.

Inside, travel alternates with testimony: converts like Jose Barretto, persecution endured, and the Bible as a missionary factor. The urgent call and the last stand of the Latin race close the appeal. Readers get a primary document of Protestant missions in South America, part travelogue, part fundraising sermon, wholly certain of its cause.
bryusov-the-republic-of-the-southern-cro:
A polar republic dies of a mysterious disease of contradiction in the title story of Valery Bryusov's story collection, given here in English. Bryusov led the Russian Symbolists, and his tales mix utopias, plagues, and the occult with decadent polish. Madness spreads through a perfectly planned Antarctic city like a logical infection.

Other stories in the set range across history and fantasy with the same stylish control. Bryusov wrote prose the way his movement wrote verse: dense, musical, and deliberately strange. English readers meet a side of Russian fiction far from the great realist novels. The collection shows symbolism attempting the short story with full ambition. Strange and unlike anything else of its period, it rewards adventurous readers.
bunyan-characters-1st-series:
Alexander Whyte, minister of St George's Free Church in Edinburgh, delivered Bunyan Characters as lectures on the people of The Pilgrim's Progress, printed in 1893. His introduction lingers on the word character, used once in the New Testament for Christ as the express image of the Father. From that text he builds a method: study Bunyan's persons to study souls.

The first series treats Christian himself, the Interpreter, Evangelist, Obstinate and Pliable, Faithful, Talkative, and Hopeful among others. Whyte quotes Goodwin, Pusey, and Thomas Shepard on truth without love making hypocrites. His lectures became devotional classics in Scotland, read as seriously as Bunyan himself, and they assume a congregation that knew the allegory by heart.
bunyan-characters-2nd-series:
Alexander Whyte continued his St George's lectures in Bunyan Characters, second series, printed in 1894, opening with Ignorance, the brisk young talker in religion who was alive without the law once. Whyte warns that a few more such gentlemen would make pilgrimage fashionable. The series turns to the second part of Bunyan's allegory, Christiana's journey.

Christiana, overcome by the King's letter bidding her follow her husband, begs her visitor to carry her and her children to worship the King. Mr Fearing trembles at the wicket gate until Goodwill takes him by the collar and bids him peace. Whyte's pulpit psychology treats Bunyan's figures as parishioners he has counseled for years.
bunyan-characters-3rd-series:
Alexander Whyte, minister of St. George's Free Church in Edinburgh, devoted this third series of Bunyan Characters lectures to John Bunyan's Holy War. Whyte opens by ranking the books: Pilgrim's Progress tells the soul's journey, while Holy War, published in 1682, tells its battles. The town of Mansoul is besieged, taken, and retaken, and Whyte reads the siege as a map of the Christian life.

Lecture by lecture he walks through Bunyan's soldiers, captains, and assaults, drawing lessons for faith under attack. Macaulay's praise of Holy War as nearly the best allegory ever written gets quoted early. Whyte writes as a preacher to preachers, warm, urgent, and certain that Bunyan's war still describes his hearers.
burlesques:
William Makepeace Thackeray collected his Burlesques, the parodies that first showed his comic gift in magazines. Notes by Eminent Hands mimics the novelists of the day in fake masterpieces: George de Barnwell after Bulwer-Lytton, Codlingsby after Disraeli, and others in the manners of popular romancers and military tale-tellers. A Plan for a Prize Novel gives the recipe away.

Then come the Jeames papers, the diary and letters of C. Jeames de la Pluche, a footman speculating in railway shares and writing his lords-and-liveries English. Major Gahagan's tremendous adventures in India close the volume in tall-tale style. Thackeray's targets are literary humbug and social climbing, and the imitations are so exact that the laughter doubles as criticism. Few parodists have loved their victims this knowingly.
buttercup-gold-and-other-stories:
Ellen Robena Field dedicated Buttercup Gold and Other Stories, copyrighted in 1894 by the Bangor Kindergarten Association, to the dear kindergarten children and her little friend Alice Caro Wing. Longfellow and Lowell supply the mottoes about children as living poems and God's apostles. The tales are nature stories for the very young.

Flowers, birds, and seasons speak in short chapters meant for kindergarten telling: a homesick bird is cheered by a singer promising the sun is smiling and trying to make the flowers glad. Field wrote from the Froebel kindergarten movement, which taught through story, song, and garden. The book preserves that movement's voice at its most earnest and sweet.
buttered-side-down-stories:
Edna Ferber published Buttered Side Down in 1912, her first book of stories, after years as a newspaper reporter in Wisconsin and Chicago. The title states her rule of life: things tend to fall buttered side down, and her heroines, mostly working girls, learn to laugh and carry on anyway. Her pages fill with salesgirls, stenographers, actresses, and traveling saleswomen in small hotels and city shops.

Ferber writes with quick wit and a warm eye for the talk and dress of her time. The tales mix romance with rent money, and success, when it comes, is earned at a counter or a desk. The book launched a career that led to Show Boat and a Pulitzer Prize for So Big.
cambridge-pieces:
Cambridge Pieces collects Samuel Butler's earliest published writings, most of them written while he was an undergraduate at St John's College, Cambridge. R A Streatfeild edited the volume, issued in London in 1914, long after Butler's death. Several pieces first appeared in the Eagle, a college magazine, in 1858. They show a clever student testing his voice.

An essay on English composition argues for clear, plain prose over swollen style. A tour narrative and a mock translation from Herodotus follow. Butler offers variations on the shield of Achilles and a playful prospectus for a Great Split Society. Skits on examinations, two deans, and Napoleon at St Helena add satire. A memoir by A T Bartholomew on Butler and the Simeonites, a college religious group, closes the book.
cambridge-sketches:
Frank Preston Stearns's Cambridge Sketches recalls the distinguished men he knew in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Stearns regrets that he never introduced himself to more of them, since at the time he had no expectation of writing about them, yet their acquaintance raised his idea of human nature.

Some of his subjects enjoy world-wide celebrity, Stearns notes, while others, famed in their day, now seem headed for oblivion. All, he insists, deserve honour from humankind and from their age. Charles Sumner fronts the volume, and the sketches that follow mix memory, anecdote and character. Readers of New England history will find Stearns warm, unpretentious and observant.
canada-and-the-states:
Sir E. W. Watkin's Canada and the States gathers his recollections from 1851 to 1886, years spent crossing the Atlantic on railway and political business. Watkin dedicates the book informally to Lady Watkin, who bore the anxieties of home life during his many long absences on the American continent.

The recollections touch the Maritime Provinces, their hardy population, harbours, fisheries and seamen, and the question of their place beside Canada and the United States. Watkin writes as a businessman and member of Parliament, not as a detached historian, and his pages carry the practical concerns of railways, trade and empire. Readers interested in Anglo-Canadian relations will find his first-hand view unusually concrete.
canterbury-pieces:
Samuel Butler's Canterbury Pieces gathers short early writings from his years in New Zealand, edited by R A Streatfeild and published in London in 1914. Butler had emigrated to Canterbury in 1859, just as Charles Darwin's Origin of Species appeared. That book seized his attention at once. The pieces here grew out of colonial newspaper debates that followed.

A dialogue on Darwin's theory opens the volume, dated from Christchurch in 1862. Letters from 1863 argue with a newspaper leader called Barrel-Organs. Darwin Among the Machines then imagines machines evolving like living things, an idea Butler later expanded. A note on Shakespeare's Tempest and a piece on English cricketers close the set. Readers see a young Butler learning to argue, joke, and doubt in print.
cape-cod-stories:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cape Cod Stories, also published as The Old Home House, opens at the Orham post-office. Cap'n Jonadab Wixon and Barzilla Wingate each find a long envelope sealed with a crest and a letter D. The two old salts narrate the tales in thick Cape dialect. Two Pairs of Shoes leads the contents.

The Count and the Manager, The Mare and the Motor, and The Love of Lobelia 'Ankins follow, with The Antiquers and His Native Heith among the twelve. Lincoln's Cape is a place of retired sea captains, summer visitors, and small schemes. Motors meet mares, antiquers meet their match, and the post-office stove hears all. His humour is gentle and his dialect lovingly phonetic. The stories made Lincoln the chronicler of a vanishing Cape Cod, read aloud in parlours for a generation.
captain-cook-his-life-voyages-and-discov: Captain Cook, his life, voyages, and discoveries. The great navigator's story. This book preserves that biography. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
carlyle-reminiscences:
Thomas Carlyle, the Sage of Chelsea, wrote his Reminiscences in bursts of grief right after his wife's death in 1866. His friend and biographer James Froude published them in 1881. The pieces were never meant as a finished book, which gives them their raw force.

Carlyle recalls his father, his early friend Edward Irving, and the Scotland of his youth, now vanished. He writes of London fame and of Jane Welsh Carlyle with love and regret. The prose is tender, gloomy, and vivid by turns. Publication stirred scandal, since Carlyle spared neither himself nor others in these pages.
catalan-s-constant-to-1-500-000-places:
Thomas Papanikolaou computed Catalan's constant to 1,500,000 digits on October 26, 1996, and this file prints them. The run used a Sun Sparc20 and took seven days, seven hours, and about a quarter of an hour. Papanikolaou says he verified the earlier million-digit value by LiDIA comparison before extending it.

The method is Greg Fee's algorithm from the 1990 ISSAC proceedings, using the standard series for Catalan's constant sped up by an Euler transform and only integer arithmetic in the main loop. A companion file gives 300,000 places by Fee himself. The digits fill the file in long blocks, a reference monument to 1990s computational number theory rather than a text to read.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-ferr:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Ferrières describes a Benedictine abbey in the diocese of Orléans. It has been most unfortunate for historians, having lost its archives, charters and all that would aid a reconstruction of its history. Legend has therefore had full play around its origins.

The most accurate account available, the entry says, comes from an obscure eighteenth-century Benedictine, Dom Philippe Mazoyer. Mazoyer traces a chapel of Our Lady of Bethlehem at Ferrières, dates the abbey no earlier than King Dagobert's reign, and dismisses the Acts of St. Savinian and a Clovis charter dated 508 as false. The entry weighs these claims against the church's ancient stonework.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-s:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Solesmes describes a Benedictine monastery in the Sarthe, near Sablé in France. Geoffrey, lord of Sablé, founded it in 1010 as a priory under Le Mans' St-Pierre de la Couture. War with England brought two pillagings and one fire that almost wholly burned it.

Apart from those disasters its history ran uneventfully for centuries, until rebuilding began late in the fifteenth century. Prior Philibert de la Croix changed the church from basilica to Latin cross form. His successor Jean Bougler, prior from 1505 to 1556, finished the church, added the tower, and rebuilt cloisters, sacristy and library. Under Bougler the two famous Saints of Solesmes statue groups were set in the transept chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abipones:
The Abipones were an Indian tribe of Guaycuru stock who once roamed the east bank of the Parana. They were later gathered between the Bermejo, the Salado, and the Parana in present-day Argentina. Their customs matched those of South American tribes generally: clanship, elaborate animism, and great sway for medicine men over private and tribal affairs. Chiefs were chosen or imposed through striking deeds and shaman craft, and the lance was their favoured weapon.

By 1641 they had horses from Spanish settlers, and mounted raids made them dangerous to colonization. Jesuits undertook to tame them in the early eighteenth century. Fathers Casado and Sanchez laboured at the task, and above all Martin Dobrizhoffer, a missionary in Paraguay for eighteen years, whose history of the Abipones remains the chief source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abrahamites:
Abrahamites is a name borne by three distinct groups, and this entry keeps them apart. First came Syrian heretics of the ninth century, called Brachiniah by the Arabs after Ibrahim of Antioch, their head, who denied Christ's divinity and was linked by some to the Paulicians. Second were Bohemian Deists who claimed Abraham's religion before his circumcision, believed in one God, and rejected the Trinity, original sin, and endless punishment.

From the Bible those Bohemian Abrahamites accepted just the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer. When they refused to adopt a tolerated religion, Joseph II banished them in 1783 to Transylvania, though some later became Catholics. Third were monks of St. Abraham's in Constantinople, martyred in 832 under Emperor Theophilus for defending holy images against the Iconoclasts. The entry cites the Kirchenlexikon for all three.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-a:
Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament in the accepted order, and this long entry questions whether its title came from the author at all. Cornely thought the author affixed it, but the entry judges it far more likely added later, like the Gospel headings. The title itself misleads, since the book holds neither the acts of all apostles nor all the acts of any one apostle.

It opens with the forty days after the Resurrection, when Christ spoke of the kingdom of God, promised the Holy Ghost, and ascended. Peter advises choosing a successor to Judas, and Matthias is chosen by lot. At Pentecost the Holy Ghost descends with the gift of tongues, Peter explains the miracle as the power of Jesus Christ, and many converts are baptized. The entry then follows authorship, sources, and text through modern scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adamites:
Adamites were an obscure sect, perhaps from the second century, professing Adam's primeval innocence regained. St. Epiphanius and St. Augustine mention them by name and describe their practices; their church they called Paradise, condemned marriage as foreign to Eden, and stripped themselves naked during common worship; they cannot have been numerous.

Accounts of their origin differ. Some make them an offshoot of the Carpocratian Gnostics, with a sensual mysticism and complete emancipation from moral law, a view Theodoret held, linking them to licentious sects Clement of Alexandria describes. Others see misguided ascetics striving to kill carnal desire by simpler manners and abolishing marriage. Similar practices revived in Europe later, among the Brethren of the Free Spirit, the Beghards, and Bohemian Picards, whom Ziska nearly exterminated in 1421.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-admiral-sands:
Benjamin F. Sands was a rear-admiral of the United States Navy, born at Baltimore on 11 February 1812. He died at Washington on 30 June 1883, of non-Catholic parents, and became a convert in 1850 after marrying Henrietta French, a Catholic. Appointed midshipman on 1 April 1828, he rose through successive grades to rear-admiral on 27 April 1871, retiring at sixty-two in 1874.

In the Civil War he commanded several important posts with conspicuous success; in 1867 he became superintendent of the Naval Observatory at Washington. Under him until 1874, the observatory rose to equal the most celebrated in Europe. His notes became From Reefer to Rear Admiral. Son James Hoban Sands, born in 1845, also became a rear-admiral, famed for daring and seamanship, and the entry follows both careers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aguas-calient:
Aguas Calientes, Latin Aquae Calidae, is a Mexican see dependent on Guadalajara. Leo XIII erected it by decree on 27 August 1899, carving it from Guadalajara. The province of Aguas Calientes forms it. Its first bishop, Jose Maria Portugal, a Friar Minor, was born in Mexico on 24 January 1838.

Portugal had been made Bishop of Sinaloa in 1888, transferred to Saltillo in 1898, and to Aguas Calientes on 9 June 1902. An inland Mexican state, it covers 2,950 square miles. Its capital, also Aguas Calientes, lies 300 miles northeast of Mexico City on a 6,000-foot plateau, with a population of 30,000 in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albanenses: The Albanenses were a Manichaean group, followers of a dualist faith built on two eternal powers, good and evil. They lived in Albania probably around the eighth century. Little is known about them beyond their place among the sects that kept the original Manichaean teaching alive. They held a strict, unyielding form of that teaching, refusing any softening of the claim that the evil power is eternal and fully equal to the good. The entry points readers to related groups such as the Bogomiles, the Cathars, and the Paulicians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albigenses:
The Albigenses, named from Albi in southern France, were a medieval religious movement whose entry sets out their beliefs, history, organization, and the Church's response. They held that two opposed powers coexist: a good power that made the spiritual world and an evil power that made the material world. Their doctrines and morals followed from that stark division.

The sect divided its members into the perfect, the few who had received the initiation rite called the consolamentum, and the ordinary believers. The entry traces the movement's origin and history, its organization and liturgy, and the attitude of the Church toward it. It covers the sect's system whole, from its dualist first principles to its clash with the medieval Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Hales was a Franciscan theologian and philosopher, counted among the greatest scholastics. He was born at Hales in Gloucestershire toward the end of the twelfth century and died at Paris in 1245. Schooled at home and probably at Oxford, he went to the University of Paris, where he took master's degrees first in arts and then in theology. Later writers styled him the Irrefragable Doctor, the Fount of Life, and the Monarch of Theologians.

His chief work, the Summa of Universal Theology, was begun about 1231 and left unfinished. It made him the first to attempt a systematic account of Catholic doctrine after Aristotle's metaphysical and physical works reached the schools. His theology broadly matches that of Bonaventure and Thomas, beginning from what the mind can know of God. In psychology he kept to the older Augustinian teaching, with its threefold division of the soul's powers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-de-:
Alexandre de Rhodes was a French missionary and author, born at Avignon in March 1591 and dead at Isfahan in Persia in November 1660. He entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in April 1612, intending to devote his life to converting the infidels, and was sent to the East Indies. He began mission work in 1624, winning great success in Cochin China. By 1627 he went to Tongking, where he converted 6,000 people in three years, including several bonzes, Buddhist monks.

When persecution drove Rhodes from Tongking in 1630, his new converts carried on the work of evangelization. Recalled to Rome, he gained permission to work in Persia instead. Amid a busy missionary life he still wrote. His works include a two-book history of Tongking published at Lyons in 1652 and an account of the glorious death of Andrew the Catechist in 1653. He also wrote a catechism in Latin and Tongkingese printed at Rome in 1658.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-de-va:
Alfonso de Valdés was a Spanish humanist and chancellor of Emperor Charles V, born at Cuenca about 1500, dead at Vienna in October 1532. His talents won early advancement, and he accompanied Charles to the coronation at Aachen in 1520 and the Diet of Worms in 1521. From 1522 he was secretary of the imperial chancellery. He drafted state papers including the 1525 Pavia report and a sharp 1526 letter to Clement VII urging an ecumenical council.

After Rome's capture and sack in 1527, Valdés wrote the dialogue Lactantius, attacking the pope as a disturber of peace. The papal nuncio accused him before the Inquisition, but Charles protected him. Valdés admired Erasmus and spread his ideas in Spain. He travelled with the emperor through Italy, Germany, and the Netherlands in 1529, and in October 1531 wrote from Brussels congratulating the Swiss Catholics on their victory over Zwingli. His brother was Juan Valdés of the Naples movement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-breadbo:
Altar breadboxes hold the unleavened hosts used at Mass, made of wood, tin, britannia, silver, or other metal. A round flat weight, covered if needed with silk or linen and fitted with a knob, rests on the breads to keep them from bending or curving. The cover must fit tightly, so the breads stay dry and clean.

The box for the large hosts is sized to fit them, while a larger box holds the small particles given at the communion of the laity. Together these plain vessels keep the breads flat, dry, and clean until the moment of consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-candles:
Altar candles at Mass and other liturgical functions must be beeswax. The pure wax from flowers stands for Christ's pure flesh from his Virgin Mother, the wick for his soul, and the flame for his divinity. Only beeswax carries the first meaning, though other candles share the other two.

Seven candles burn at a pontifical high Mass, the seventh somewhat higher than the rest. A solemn high Mass takes six, a sung high Mass at least four, and a low Mass by a priest only two. A bishop's low Mass usually takes four, and bishops may use a hand candle, the bugia, before Mass except on Good Friday and Holy Saturday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altars-in-the:
In Old Slavonic and Russian, altar, sometimes spelled oltar, means the whole space behind the iconostasis around the altar, matching the Greek bema and the Latin sanctuary. The Russian Orthodox or Ruthenian Greek Catholic altar is thus the sanctuary, not merely the Latin altar, which Slavonic and Russian call prestol, the throne.
