Juan Donoso Cortés was a Spanish author, diplomat, and Marquess of Valdegamas. Born in Extremadura in 1809, a descendant of the conquistador Cortés, he finished humanities at eleven, took a law degree at sixteen, and taught literature at eighteen. Swept up by French rationalism, he embraced liberalism and Rousseau, then turned against revolution after 1834.

Donoso Cortés served Queen Maria Cristina and the young Isabella II, became her secretary and tutor, entered the Senate, and was made Marquess of Valdegamas. His eloquent defense of the Spanish marriages won him the Legion of Honor. A brother's death deepened his faith, and his later writings became a leading voice of Catholic conservatism. He died at Paris in 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-luis-viv:
Juan Luis Vives was a Spanish humanist and philosopher who fled the Inquisition for Flanders. Born at Valencia in 1492, he left Spain forever in 1509, studied at Paris, and settled at Bruges in 1512. He taught at Louvain, tutored Cardinal Guillaume de Croy, and in 1523 joined Corpus Christi College, Oxford, under Wolsey.

Vives defended Queen Catherine of Aragon against Henry VIII's divorce plans and was arrested and banished for it. Back in Flanders, he wrote on piety, education, and political economy, with his Introduction to Wisdom running to fifty editions. His commentary on Augustine's City of God annoyed theologians and Erasmus alike. He died at Bruges in 1540.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-martinez:
Juan Martínez Montañés was a Spanish sculptor in wood called the Sevillian Phidias. Born, by rival accounts, at Seville or Alcalá la Real, he trained under Pablo de Rojas at Granada and settled at Seville, where most of his work still stands. He died in 1649.

Montañés carved a charming Infant Jesus in 1607, a lifelike St. Ignatius for the saint's beatification in 1610, and a masterly penitent St. Jerome in 1612. His large crucifix for the Carthusians and his St. Bruno of 1620 show his power. In 1635 he modeled Philip IV's portrait in Madrid for Tacca's equestrian statue, and Velázquez painted his likeness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-melendez:
Juan Meléndez Valdés was a Spanish poet and judge ruined by politics. Born at Ribera del Fresno in 1754, he studied law at Salamanca, won the Academy's prize in 1780 for his eclogue Batilo, and took a Salamanca chair through his friend Jovellanos. His comedy on Camacho's wedding won Madrid's prize in 1784 but failed on stage.

Meléndez rose to judge at Saragossa, Valladolid, and Madrid's supreme court, then fell with Jovellanos and was exiled from the capital. After 1808 he served Joseph Bonaparte's government as councillor of state, and in 1813 he fled to France. He died poor and neglected at Montpellier in 1817, remembered for delicate, graceful eclogues and romances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judges:
Judges is the seventh book of the Old Testament and the second of the Hebrew Early Prophets. Its Hebrew name, Shophtim, first meant to act as God's judge, a title given to God, to Moses, and then to Israel's leaders. A judge differed from a king only in lacking hereditary succession.

The book opens with a summary of the conquest of Canaan and a reproof for leagues with strangers, then tells the deeds of the judges, chiefly Gideon and Samson across seven chapters. It closes with the migration of Dan and its idol worship and the Benjamites' crime and punishment. The entry defends the book's place in the canon and its history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kantes-marial:
Kantes Mariales was a Dominican of a noble Venetian family, born about 1580 and dead at Venice in April 1660. While young he joined the Dominicans at Sts. John and Paul, and his versatility and prodigious memory soon sent him to Spain to finish his studies. He taught first at Venice, then at Padua, where he held the regency three times. From 1624 he lived a retired life at Venice, giving himself wholly to prayer, reading, and study.

His writings showed such zeal for the Holy See that the Venetian senate exiled him twice. At Milan, Ferrara, and Bologna, his refuges, he was highly esteemed for learning and holiness. He died of apoplexy, and Venetian nobles honored his obsequies. Two works stand out: his Controversiae on the whole Summa of St. Thomas, published at Venice in 1624, and his vast Amphitheatrum of all arts and sciences, published at Bologna in 1658.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-langres:
Langres is a French diocese covering the Haute-Marne department. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1801 and joined to Dijon, it kept a pro-vicar-general and two seminaries at Langres. It was re-established in 1817 and definitively restored by the bull Paternae charitatis on 6 October 1822.

The new bishop governed 360 parishes of old Langres plus parishes from Chalons, Besancon, Troyes, and Toul. Duchesne counts Senator, Justus, and St. Desiderius, martyred in the Vandal invasion about 407, as its first bishops, putting its founding near the mid-fourth century. Later bishops include St. Gregory, great-grandfather of Gregory of Tours, who moved St. Benignus's relics, and Betto, who helped draft Charlemagne's capitularies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lares:
Lares, a walled town in ancient times named by Sallust in his Jugurtha, was once a titular archiepiscopal see of proconsular Africa, later receiving the name Colonia Aelia Augusta Lares.

At least five bishops are known. Hortensian attended Carthage councils in 242 and 255. Victorinus appeared with his Donatist colleague Honoratus at the Carthage conference. Quintian lived in Huneric's persecution about 480, and Vitulus lived in 525 under King Hilderic. Augustine, Victor of Vita, Procopius, and Arab historians all mention the town. It is today's Lorbeus, between Tunis and Tebessa, where wide ruins mark a once considerable town. A mosque now stands where a church stood, and a basilica's ruins remain visible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-law-of-guaran:
The Law of Guarantees, La Legge delle Guarentigie, was the Italian parliament's law of 13 May 1871. It settled the Holy See's prerogatives and State-Church relations after Rome's capture. Its chief terms made the pope's person sacred and inviolable, ranked insults to him with insults to the king, and freed discussion of religious matters.

Royal honours and customary guards accompanied the deal, with a yearly endowment of 3,225,000 lire for the Holy See, cardinals, congregations, embassies, and church upkeep. Vatican, Lateran, and Castel Gandolfo palaces stayed as papal property. Letters and papers of church government passed free of interference, clergy assembled freely, and bishops owed no allegiance oath. The state dropped Sicily's Apostolic Legation and most nomination rights. It kept the exequatur only for major benefices and property acts. Civil courts judged only the legal effects of church sentences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-tithes:
Lay tithes, as treated here, are church tithes alienated in time to lay owners. They stand against secular tithes, which tenants paid princes and landlords on crown or leased lands. Merovingian secularizations began the transfer, and bishops, abbots, and violent seizures passed more church land and tithes to laymen seeking servants, vassals, and protectors.

The Church fought back from the ninth century, at Diedenhofen in 844 and Beauvais in 845. Gregory VII in 1078 demanded return of all tithes, even those given by bishops or kings, branding refusers as sacrilegious. Later popes and synods called church tithes of divine right, inalienable parish income that no layman could gain by prescription or inheritance. Yet centuries-old lay possession proved impossible to undo, and later rulings let laymen give tithes to a monastery instead, with the bishop's approval.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lebrecht-bluc:
Lebrecht Blucher Dreves (1816-1870) was a Hamburg poet, named for his baptismal sponsor, the famed Prussian General Blucher. At fifteen he wrote German and Latin verse faultless in rhyme and metre, and at nineteen he laid a stout volume before Chamisso and Gustav Schwab, both of whom praised it.

A second volume, Lyrische Anklange, grafted on his favourites Chamisso, Uhland, Heine, Ruckert, and Schwab, kept a sweetness of its own. Law studies and a doctorate summa cum laude did not kill his love of verse, and Vigilien fulfilled his early promise. Money troubles and a bleak view of life followed, until his reception into the Catholic Church at Candlemas 1846 lifted him. Notary work freed him from want, and his Church Hymns made him a model hymn translator, with a history of Hamburg and Altona's Catholic congregations beside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-legacies:
A pious legacy, legatum pium, is the assigning by a last will of one particular thing from an estate to a church or church institution. It differs from a pious testament, which makes the institution the testator's true heir over the whole property. It also differs from a deathbed gift, which is a contract, while a legacy is a one-sided act.

It also differs from a foundation, which may arise in life or by will. A foundation always lays lasting obligations on the favoured house, whereas a legacy need not found anything. The Church's right to receive legacies rests, the article argues, on natural and divine law. As a necessary and perfect society meant to lead men to their last end, it may hold temporal goods for worship, ministers, propagation of the faith, and care of the poor. Pious bequests count among its legitimate means.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-levi-silliman:
Levi Silliman Ives (1797-1867) was a noted convert to the Church through the Tractarian Movement of 1848-49. Born at Meriden, Connecticut, in 1797, he served a year in the army. In 1823 he was ordained an Episcopal minister. In 1831 he was elected Bishop of North Carolina.

There he cared for the schooling and training of the coloured people. Moved by the Oxford Movement, he founded the Brotherhood of the Holy Cross. Its few clergymen and laymen kept a rule and preached Tractarian ideas. His advocacy brought him before the Episcopal convention on charges.  In 1852 he went to Rome and submitted to the pope, leaving thirty years as minister and twenty as bishop. He sought admission as a layman into the Catholic Church, for peace of conscience. Back in the United States he taught rhetoric at St. Joseph's Seminary, lectured convent pupils, founded New York's Catholic Protectory, and served as its president.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-levites:
The Levites were the subordinate ministers of the Mosaic Law for Tabernacle and Temple service. Levi, whose name is read as joined to, was Jacob's third son by Lia. With Simeon he avenged their sister Dinah by slaughtering Shechem and his people. That deed was reproved at the time and in prophecy.

Leaving debate aside, the next point is Levi's link with the priesthood. By the Biblical account, all Levi's male descendants were set apart by Moses for sanctuary work. That mark may owe to the tribe's zeal at the golden calf worship. As Moses's own tribe, it could be trusted to uphold his institutions. Numbers describes the tribe standing before Aaron to minister to him. Numbers 18:23 calls the tribe's mission mediation between the Lord and his people. The Levite of Judges 17 and 18 acts as priest. Many hold that early on priests and Levites grew distinct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-libraries:
The ancients knew libraries before Christ came: collections of books gathered for public or private use. Probably the oldest library of exact knowledge is that of Tello in Mesopotamia, now largely in the Louvre. It seems to have held more than 20,000 cuneiform tablets from Gudea's time, about 2500 B.C. Still larger was Nineveh's royal library, formed by Sargon (722-705 B.C.) and Ashurbanipal (668-628 B.C.).

Ashurbanipal sent scribes to old cities to copy rare works for him, and the collection covered every branch of learning known to his day. The weightier texts bear a formula claiming them for Ashurbanipal's palace, closing with a curse on any carrier-off or name-adder. II Machabees ii, 13 states plainly that Nehemias founded a library and gathered the books of the prophets, of David, and the kings' epistles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liessies:
Liessies was a Benedictine monastery near Avesnes, in Cambrai's diocese, France (Nord), founded about the middle of the eighth century, dedicated to St. Lambert. Theodoric of Avesnes and his wife Ada firmly established the monastery about 1110.

Louis de Blois became a monk there at fourteen. In 1530 he became abbot and began his well-known reforms against the slide from strict observance. After Blosius's death the next six abbots kept up his observance, but Lambert Bouillon, the forty-first abbot, was another type. Fenelon, Archbishop of Cambrai, held a visitation in 1702, of which the abbot spread a largely fictitious account. In 1791 Dom Mark Verdier, the last abbot, and his community signed a declaration affirming their wish to stay in religion, but suppression followed all the same. The abbey's valuable paintings, including a series of religious founders, burned or dispersed, a few still in nearby churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limoges:
Gregory of Tours names St. Martial, founder of Limoges's church, as one of seven bishops dispatched from Rome to Gaul in the mid-third century.

An anonymous Vita primitiva, published by Abbé Arbellot, presents him as dispatched to Gaul by St. Peter. Père de Smedt and Mgr Duchesne hold the Vita primitiva much later, and M. de Lasteyrie gives 800. The Abbey of St. Martial at the start of the eleventh century held a fuller life. Martial numbered among the seventy-two disciples witnessing the Passion and Ascension, stood at the first Pentecost, then followed St. Peter to Antioch and Rome, and was sent to Gaul. They moved toward Limoges, where Martial raised a shrine to St. Stephen. A pagan priest, Aurelian, sought to jail Martial, but was struck dead, then revived and baptized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linares:
Linares, or Monterey or Nuevo León, is an archdiocese erected as a see in 1777, when Pius VII made it suffragan of Mexico's archdiocese at Charles III's request. Leo XIII raised it to archiepiscopal rank on 23 June 1891, its suffragans being San Luis Potosi, Saltillo, and Tamaulipas. Monterey, the cathedral town, is Nuevo León's capital, with 62,266 people in 1900.

In September 1846, during the United States-Mexico war, General Taylor with 6,700 men assaulted Monterey, held by General Ampudia's 10,000 Mexicans. The archdiocese takes its name from the town of Linares, standing on the Tigris's left bank about fifty miles from Monterey. The archdiocese counts 327,937 people across Nuevo León, 23,592 square miles, with eighty priests, seventy-five churches, and twenty seminarians. The present archbishop is Leopold Ruiz y Flórez, an Amealco native born 13 November 1865, appointed to León in 1900, and transferred to Monterey in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-list-of-popes:
Popes from St. Peter onward fill this long reference list. Each pontiff gets a name and years in office, set down in plain sequence. It runs from the first century through the early twentieth century, with brief notes where a rival claimant, an antipope, opposed the sitting pope.

Readers can trace the whole succession at a glance. They can spot long and short reigns, and see how often disputed elections broke the line. Alternate names are noted where a pope is known by two forms. Cross links point to fuller entries on the papacy and on how popes were chosen, making the list a quick map rather than a set of life stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lithuanians-i:
Lithuanians in the United States are the story of a Baltic people who kept their tongue and faith under Polish rule, then Russian rule, and carried both across the Atlantic. Their language, unlike Polish or Russian, has two genders and three numbers, singular, dual, and plural, with a rich verb system.

Famine in 1867 and 1868 drove the first wave abroad. Early arrivals farmed near New York, worked Hudson brickyards, built railroads in north-east Pennsylvania, and dug anthracite coal near Shamokin and Shenandoah. Others settled in Chicago after the 1872 fire, or took up tailoring in New York, Brooklyn, and Baltimore, building parishes and papers as they went.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-los-hermanos-:
Los Hermanos Penitentes, the Penitent Brothers, are a brotherhood of flagellants among Spanish settlers in New Mexico and Colorado. To atone for sin they scourge themselves, haul heavy crosses, bind their bodies to crosses, and tie limbs to slow the blood.

Public until 1890 and largely secret since, each local fraternity stands alone under a hermano mayor, elder brother, who rules for life. Initiation in Holy Week ends in a harsh test: cross-shaped cuts below the shoulders, made with flint. Women and children later formed separate, smaller groups, and the morada, or meeting house, remains the centre of their rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-antoine:
Louis Antoine de Noailles was a French cardinal and Archbishop of Paris, born in Auvergne in 1651 and dead in 1729. Son of the first Duke de Noailles, he studied at the College du Plessis beside Fenelon, took his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1676, and held Cahors, then Chalons, before Paris.

Louis XIV raised him to Paris in 1695, where his piety, zeal, and plain manners won rich and poor alike. In famine year 1709 he sold his silver plate to feed the hungry, and spent his own fortune adorning Notre-Dame. He reprinted Paris liturgical books, ordered seminary residence before ordination, and organized clergy conferences across his diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-de-carr:
Louis de Carrieres was a French Oratorian priest and Bible scholar, born at Avrille in 1662 and dead at Paris in 1717. He entered the Oratory when masters like Malebranche, Thomassin, and Richard Simon flourished, and made Scripture his chosen field.

His fame rests on a French Bible with a literal commentary woven into the translation itself, using Sacy's version as a frame. Short paraphrase glosses, printed in italics, clear hard places without breaking the narrative, and no notes pile up to distract the reader. Bossuet praised the first volumes, and the work, finished in 1716, ran to twenty-four small volumes with many later editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-hector-:
Louis Hector de Callieres was the thirteenth governor of New France, born at Cherbourg in 1646 and dead in 1705. A captain in the Navarre regiment, he reached Canada in 1684 and became governor of Montreal at the Sulpicians' call.

Colony affairs stood at a low ebb, with Iroquois chiefs wrongly shipped to French galleys. Callieres urged a strike on New England, won Frontenac's return, and helped defend Quebec against Phipps in 1690. Succeeding Frontenac in 1698, he laboured for Indian peace, crowned by the Montreal treaty of 1701, signed by all tribes, and sent Cadillac to found Detroit that same year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lourdes:
Lourdes, in the Hautes-Pyrenees, is France's famed pilgrimage town, built on the apparitions of Mary to fourteen-year-old Bernadette Soubiroux in 1858. Eighteen visions came between 11 February and 16 July at the rock of Massabielle, where a hidden spring gushed at the lady's word.

Clergy doubted at first, but the bishop in 1862 judged the faithful justified in believing the apparitions real. A basilica rose on the rock, national pilgrimages began in 1873, and the Rosary church followed in 1901. Leo XIII gave the feast a special office, Pius X spread it Church-wide in 1907, and by the fiftieth year throngs unmatched by any shrine poured in.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-moral:
Luis de Morales was a Spanish painter of devotion, born at Badajoz about 1509 and dead there in 1586. His whole life went to sacred pictures for churches and oratories, since painting for him meant voicing the faith of his age, not merely pleasing the eye.

Early work shows Florence's mark, with studies after Michelangelo, including a Crucifixion copied at Evora. Later he thinned his scenes to two or three figures, often busts, repeating Ecce Homo, Christ at the Column, and the Virgin holding the dead Christ. Clean drawing, correct anatomy, slender grace, enamel-bright colour, and minute care for beard, blood, and tears gave his sacred figures an intense, infectious feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-vaz-de-c:
Luis Vaz de Camoes was Portugal's greatest poet, born in 1524 or 1525 and dead on 10 June 1580. His fame rests on the epic Os Lusiadas, with lyrics of high art beside it and lesser dramas, and exile dogged much of his life, while fame after death bred legends.

Likely born at Coimbra to a reduced noble house kin to Vasco da Gama, he studied there under his chancellor uncle. He loved Catherina de Athaide at Lisbon's court, and was banished for his passion. He fought in Africa from 1546 to 1549, losing an eye to a splinter, then sailed to India, where shipwreck, prison, and poverty dogged him. The Lusiads, published in 1572, sang Portugal's sea empire in verse that outlived its maker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macarius-magn:
Macarius Magnes is a Christian apologist of the late fourth century. He is generally taken as Macarius, Bishop of Magnesia, who at the Synod of the Oak in 403 charged Heraclides of Ephesus with Origenism. His Apocritica stages a dispute with a pagan philosopher who mocks passages of the New Testament.

Four centuries later Iconoclasts twisted his words to defend image-breaking, prompting Nicephorus to write an account and prove Macarius meant only heathen idolatry. Forgotten again, he surfaced in the sixteenth century when Turrianus quoted a Venice copy against Protestant Eucharist doctrine. The text, lost from St. Mark's, was found at Athens in 1867 and printed at Paris in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madianites-mi:
The Madianites, or Midianites, are an Arabian tribe whose name Genesis and Judges use interchangeably as Madian and Madianites. Their eponym Madian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, whose name means incense, and his five sons, Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abidah, and Eldah, anchor the tribe in genealogy.

Haupt's recent claim that Madian meant a religious association like a Greek amphictyony is called specious but inconclusive. Delitzsch linked Shuah, another son of Keturah, to Suhu, the desert between Euphrates and Syria, and the last two sons appear as names in Sabaeo-Minaean inscriptions. The entry weighs these identifications and the tribe's place in Israel's neighbour history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malabar-rites:
Malabar Rites was the label for customs of inland South India that Jesuit missionaries let converts keep. Rome later banned those customs. Despite the name, the missions lay not on the Malabar coast. They lay inland, in the old kingdoms of Madura, Mysore, and the Carnatic.

Roberto de Nobili, born at Rome in 1577, founded the approach. He won a hearing among Hindus by adapting to local ways. Step by step he taught Christian doctrine. Accusations followed, and Rome heard his defence. The dispute flared again at Pondicherry under Tournon, whose decree condemned many usages. Hard rules were softened by a regulation of 1734. One point stayed bitter, however. Priests had to bring the sacraments openly to sick pariahs at home. Madura Jesuits felt that demand made work among higher castes near impossible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manasses:
Manasses is a name shared by seven Bible figures, a tribe of Israel, and one apocryphal writing. This entry sorts them out one by one. First comes Manasses, son of Joseph, whose name the tribe bears. Judith's husband, who died of sunstroke at Bethulia, is second. A figure in the Ahikar story told by Tobias is third.

Fourth and fifth are companions of Esdras who married foreign wives, sons of Bani and Hasom. Sixth is the ancestor of Jonathan, priest of Dan. Seventh is Manasses, thirteenth king of Judah, ruling 692 to 638 B.C. The tribe itself split into eastern and western half-tribes. Last comes the Prayer of Manasses, an apocryphal piece in Greek that claims to give the prayer cited in Second Chronicles 33. Nestle dates its present form no earlier than the Apostolic Constitutions, and notes its path into some Septuagint manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcellinus-c:
Marcellinus Comes was a Latin chronicler of the sixth century, Illyrian by birth, who spent his life at Constantinople's court. Under Justin I he served as chancellor to Justinian, the emperor's nephew and chosen heir. When Justinian took the throne in 527, his chancellor stayed in favour and rose to high government posts. Little else is known of his life, and he died soon after 534.

His only surviving work is his chronicle, the Annales, a continuation of Eusebius covering 379 to 534. He first carried it to 518, then added a sequel to 534, and an unknown hand later stretched it to 566. Though written in Latin, it treats almost only the East, as its author says he followed only the Eastern Empire. Court anecdotes crowd it, Eastern church history is full, heretics get no kind word, and slips occur, such as placing Theodoret of Cyrus in 466, ten years after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcionites:
Marcionites were a heretical sect founded at Rome in A.D. 144 by Marcion. They lasted in the West for 300 years and longer in the East, above all beyond the Byzantine Empire. They rejected the Old Testament writings. They taught that Christ was Son not of the Jews' God, but of a higher good God, distinct from the God of the old covenant.

Marcion, son of the Bishop of Sinope, was himself likely a bishop there. His church organisation mirrored the Catholic Church, making his sect perhaps Christianity's most dangerous early foe. Doctrine and discipline follow his life: he barred marriage and cut the New Testament to fit his views, keeping a trimmed Luke and Paul's letters. Later followers drifted toward Gnosticism, and the sect at last dissolved into Manichaeism. Foes from Irenaeus to Tertullian, whose five-book Against Marcion of 207 is the chief source, answered him at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maronites:
Maronites were a Syrian people and church, numbering about 300,000 souls across Syria, Palestine, Cyprus, and Egypt. For centuries their mountaineers kept themselves half independent of the Ottoman Empire. 

Their church splits into nine dioceses, from Gibail and Batrun with 60,000 souls to Tyre and Sidon with 47,000. Its head bears the title Patriarch of Antioch of the Maronites, bishops are named by the patriarch, and clergy include chorepiscopi, archdeacons, stewards, and periodeutes. Liturgy is Syrian, Syriac in rite, though the Gospel reaches the people in Arabic. History turns on their origin and unbroken orthodoxy, traced to Maro, a fifth-century Syrian monk praised by Theodoret, and his monastery before the Monothelite dispute. All agree from the sixteenth century onward, when Lateran 1516 opened their brightest age, with national councils in 1596 and 1736 reshaping manners and discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marseilles:
Marseilles was a diocese in Bouches-du-Rhone, suffragan of Aix, covering the Marseilles district. Phoenicians founded the city about 600 B.C., Caesar took it in 49 B.C., and Visigoths, Burgundians, Ostrogoths, and Franks held it in turn. Medieval Marseilles owed allegiance to three sovereignties, its episcopal town swearing fealty only to the emperor.

Duchesne showed the St Lazarus first-bishop tradition dates only from the thirteenth century. Notable bishops ran from Honoratus I about 495, an ecclesiastical writer, to St Theodore, St Serenus, and Honoratus II, who began restoring St Victor Abbey. Cassian founded St Victor's twin monasteries about 415, and Benedict IX dedicated its church in 1040. Councils met in 533, 1040, and 1103. William de Grimoard became St Victor abbot in 1361 and pope as Urban V next year. St Vincent de Paul visited in 1605 and 1622, and Bishop Mazenod made St Joseph diocesan patron in 1839, with Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde pilgrimage dating from 1214.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathieu-nicol:
Mathieu-Nicolas Poillevillain de Clemanges, or Clamanges, was a French humanist and theologian, born in Champagne about 1360 and dead at Paris between 1434 and 1440. He studied at Paris's College of Navarre, took licentiate in 1380 and Master of Arts later, learned theology under Gerson and Pierre d'Ailly, and won a theology bachelor's degree in 1393.

The Western Schism agitated the Church, with compromise, concession, and general council proposed as cures. The letter failed, discussion was banned, and Clemanges resigned the rectorship. Antipope Benedict XIII, admiring his Latin, made him secretary in 1397 until he left Avignon in 1408 over Benedict's clash with Charles VI. Retiring to Valfonds and Fontain-du-Bose, he wrote De Fructu eremi, De Fructu rerum adversarum, De novis festivitatibus, and De studio theologico, scorning scholastic method. Schubert showed he did not write De corrupto Ecclesiae statu, though sometimes counted a Wyclif-Hus type reformer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-blast:
The Syntagma of Matthew Blastares, a fourteenth-century Basilian monk, gave the Greek Church a handier book of church law. Earlier collections by John the Scholastic, Photius, Zonaras, and Balsamon left a gap. Blastares filled it about 1335 with an alphabetical digest of church rules in Greek, with a long preface and chapters grouped under the first letters of their topics.

Each chapter states the church rule first and then any civil rule that bears on it. It gives the sense rather than the exact words and notes where each rule can be found. Topics range from marriage and kinship to wills, deacons, justice, and church trials. Widely used ever since, and still current in the Greek Church, the work earned the nickname Nomocanon, and by metaphor the rudder, for steering church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-media-and-med:
Media and the Medes cover an ancient Asian land and its people. The Hebrew and Assyrian form Madai matches the Mada of the earliest Persian cuneiform texts, though the word's origin is unknown. Genesis lists Madai among Japheth's sons, between Magog and Javan. Second Kings tells how Salmanasar carried Israel away to the cities of the Medes, and Isaiah names the Medes as Babylon's coming destroyers. Acts mentions them between Parthians and Elamites.

The earliest facts about their land come from Babylonian and Assyrian texts, which call it Anshan. It likely stretched from Armenia in the north-west to the Caspian Sea in the north, the great desert in the east, and Elam in the south. It held far more than the later Persia, which formed its south-eastern part toward Carmania. The entry gathers Scripture, cuneiform, and classical witness to map a people who helped end Assyria and Babylon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchites-mel:
The Melchites, or Melkites, are the people of Syria, Palestine, and Egypt who stayed loyal to the Council of Chalcedon in 451 when most turned Monophysite. The name at first meant opposition to Monophysism. While Nestorians held eastern Syria until Zeno closed their Edessa school in 489 and drove them into Persia, the west split another way. Western Syria, Palestine, and Egypt divided between Chalcedonian Melchites and Monophysites, called Jacobites in Syria and Palestine and Copts in Egypt.

The Monothelite heresy of the seventh century tangled matters further. After the schisms of Photius in 867 and Cerularius in 1054, two kinds of Melchites stood in these lands: Catholic Melchites in Rome's communion and schismatical, or Orthodox, Melchites following Constantinople. Today the name commonly means only the Eastern-rite Catholics. The entry traces origins and name, history before the schism, the road to union, and the Melchite Church's constitution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-memorial-bras:
Memorial brasses, whose first use is unknown, survive in dated examples from the thirteenth century. They sprang from a wish for memorials tougher than incised stone and marble slabs. Time has proved their worth: they lie in far better shape than contemporary slabs of the hardest stone. The metal, called laton, an alloy of copper, zinc, lead, and tin, was beaten into thick plates at Cologne and shipped across Christendom.

England used the most, and despite Reformation plunder, Puritan violence, and neglect, between three and four thousand brasses from the thirteenth to sixteenth centuries survive. The dead were usually shown life size on the plates, in deep incised lines with little shading. Architectural and heraldic dressings and inscriptions framed them. Some lines were stressed with black and red enamels, others enriched with Limoges enamels. The art peaked in the fourteenth century, then faded under Elizabeth and James I.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mennonites:
The Mennonites, a Protestant denomination of Europe and America, arose in Switzerland in the sixteenth century and took their name from Menno Simons, their leader in Holland. Menno was born in 1492 at Witmarsum in Friesland, ordained to the Catholic priesthood in 1515 or 1516, and made assistant at Pingjum. In 1532 he became pastor of his birthplace, but on 12 January 1536 he resigned and became an Anabaptist elder.

The rest of his life served the new sect he had joined. Though no commanding figure, he wielded real influence as speaker and still more as writer among moderate Anabaptists. He died on 13 January 1559 at Wustenfelde in Holstein. Mennonite views began at Zurich, where Grebel and Manz founded an Anabaptist community in 1525. Persecution dogged the sect in Switzerland until 1710 yet could not crush it. About 1620 the Swiss split into Amish and Lowland Mennonites, differing on marriage after excommunication, buttons, and shaving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-middle-ages:
The Middle Ages is the term commonly used for the stretch of European history between the fall of the Roman Empire and about the middle of the fifteenth century. Its precise beginning, height, and end are fixed more or less arbitrarily, according to the viewpoint adopted. The period is usually taken to open with the German tribal migrations that destroyed the Western Roman Empire.

The conventional starting point is 375, when the Huns fell upon the Gothic tribes north of the Black Sea and drove the Visigoths across the lower Danube into Roman territory. A later date is sometimes preferred, namely Odoacer's deposition of Romulus Augustulus. The article surveys the whole span, from the barbarian invasions through the medieval centuries to the threshold of the modern age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-midwives:
Midwives fall under the Church's canon law in their relation to two sacraments, baptism and matrimony. For marriage, their testimony is often required in cases of non-consummated marriage, whether through the impediment of impotence or because a dispensation is sought over a ratified but unconsummated union. In such cases the testimony of three midwives is held sufficient in practice.

The number seven named in the Corpus Juris Canonici is not considered obligatory in law, though some older canonists insisted on seven. For baptism, the midwife's office matters most when a newborn child is in danger of death, since she may baptize in necessity. The article sets out the canonical rules governing her evidence and her baptismal duty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miracle-plays:
Miracle plays and mysteries are the names for the religious drama that developed among Christian nations at the end of the Middle Ages. Mystery has often been applied to all Christian dramas before the sixteenth century. It should be confined to those of the fifteenth century, which represent the great dramatic effort before the Renaissance. Before that period dramatic pieces were called plays or miracles.

The embryonic representations, first given inside churches, are called liturgical dramas. The origin of medieval drama was in religion, growing from the liturgy's dramatic elements, such as the Easter Quem quaeritis dialogue. The article follows the liturgical drama, twelfth- and thirteenth-century plays, miracles of Our Lady, the mysteries, and the drama's course in England, Germany, and the Netherlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moab-moabites:
Moab, in the Old Testament, designates first a son of Lot by his elder daughter. It also names the people descended from him, also called the Moabites, and possibly the territory they occupied east of the Dead Sea. Its etymology, from my father, added by the Septuagint to the Hebrew text of Genesis 19:37, is more probable than any derivation modern scholars have suggested.

The Moabites' origin and race need no separate discussion, since Genesis 19 makes them the same as the Ammonites'. Their history is one of rivalry with Israel. Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, Ruth the Moabitess became David's ancestress, and Mesha's rebellion against Israel is recorded both in Kings and on the Moabite Stone, discovered in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mohammedan-co:
Muslim lands in the early twentieth century teemed with secretive religious brotherhoods. They also acted as political forces, and this entry surveys their orders, rites and reach. The oldest, the Kadriya, dates from the twelfth century, when united counsel was needed against the Crusades. It takes its name from the Persian founder Sidi-abd-el-Kader-el-Djilani, who died at Bagdad in 1166.

Members went by different names by region. They were khouans in North Africa, dervishes in Turkey and Central Asia, fakirs in India and mourids in Egypt, Arabia and Syria. Daily prayers were followed by order-specific devotions, often repeated thousands of times with swaying, bowing or head movements. Some groups sought trance states in retreat. The entry puts total membership near 170 million and warns that the orders could turn troublesome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monothelitism:
Monothelitism was a seventh-century heresy, condemned by the Sixth General Council. It taught that Christ has only one will and one kind of activity. It grew as a compromise meant to win back the Monophysites. They tied personhood to will and action, so a single divine-human person seemed to require a single divine-human will.

Catholic teaching answers that willing belongs to nature, not to person. Christ, having a complete human nature alongside his divine nature, must have both a human will and a divine will. The entry traces the dispute from Emperor Heraclius and Patriarch Sergius through Pope Honorius. It covers the Ecthesis and the Type, the council's condemnation, and the heresy's slow fading in the East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monterey-and-:
The Diocese of Monterey and Los Angeles covers the part of California south of 37 degrees 5 minutes north. It spans some 80,000 square miles, embracing eighteen of the twenty-one Indian missions that made California famous. At first the whole state with Lower California formed the Diocese of Both Californias. Its bishop was Francisco Garcia Diego y Moreno, seated at Santa Barbara Mission.

In 1850 Pius IX organised Monterey under Joseph Sadoc Alemany. When San Francisco became an archdiocese in 1853, Thaddeus Amat took Monterey. He moved his residence to Los Angeles in 1859 while keeping the old title. Around the former missions and four military garrisons, immigrants from nearly every land settled. The entry follows parishes, schools and religious orders across the growing southland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses:
Moses, Hebrew liberator, leader, lawgiver, prophet and historian, lived in the thirteenth and early twelfth centuries BC. His name's origin remains unsettled. Exodus hints at Hebrew drawing, Josephus and the Fathers split it into Coptic water and saved, and Egyptologists favour Egyptian mesh, meaning child. To doubt his historic reality, the entry argues, would leave Israel's later history unintelligible.

Born of Levite stock under a king's edict drowning Hebrew boy babies, the goodly child spent three months hidden. He then lay in a basket on the Nile until Pharaoh's daughter found him. The entry follows him from Midian and the Burning Bush through the Exodus, the Red Sea, Sinai and the Law. It ends with his death within sight of the Promised Land, weighing sources, rabbinical legends and the figure's lasting force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-of-beat:
The Mount of Beatitudes is the traditional place where Christ delivered the Sermon on the Mount, opening with the Beatitudes. Tradition sets the scene on Karn Hattin, the Horns of Hattin, named for the village at its northern base and the two cones crowning its summit. It lies in Galilee within easy reach of Nazareth, Cana, Tabor, Tiberias and Capharnaum.

The mountain stands 1,816 feet above the lake and 1,135 feet above sea level. It is a low ridge a quarter mile long ending in two horns, the taller only sixty feet above the ridge. Between the horns lies an uneven platform that could hold the crowd following Jesus. The discourse itself is thought to have been given lower down, on level ground on the southern side matching Luke's description of a level place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-musical-instr:
For almost a thousand years Gregorian chant without instrumental or harmonic addition was the only music of the liturgy. The organ in primitive, rude form was the first and long the sole instrument to accompany it, giving pitch and adding brilliance and sonority. Secular music, by contrast, used instruments from an early date.

Troubadours, trouveres and jongleurs of France, Italy and Spain, English minstrels and German minnesingers accompanied their songs on many instruments. They used diminutive harps, vielles ancestral to the violin, the ancient crwth, hurdy-gurdies, flutes, trumpets, horns and sackbuts. The entry follows instruments into church use, the debates over their fitness for worship, and the organ's rise to its commanding place in Catholic music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nahanes:
The Nahanes, People of the Setting Sun, are a tribe of the great Dene family, living east and west of the Rocky Mountains just north of latitude 58 north. They divide broadly into eastern and western branches. The western branch splits into the Thalhthans, named for their rendezvous at the Thalhthan River's meeting with the Stickine, and the Takus of the Taku River basin.

The Kaskas west of the Rockies count as eastern Nahanes by speech, physique and sociology, while another subdivision roams the Mackenzie mountains east of the range. The whole tribe numbers little more than 1,000 souls: 175 Thalhthans, 200 Kaskas, 150 Takus and 500 eastern Nahanes proper. Eastern Nahanes and Kaskas are pure nomads with patriarchal descent, while the westernmost have taken up the matriarchal clans, petty chiefs and potlatches of their Pacific neighbours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nantes:
Nantes is a French diocese covering the whole department of Loire-Inferieure, re-established by the Concordat of 1802 and suffragan of Tours. Late traditions make Saint Clarus, first Bishop of Nantes, a disciple of Saint Peter. De la Borderie showed the 1263 ritual ignores that apostolic mission, and that Saint Peter's nail reached the cathedral only after the tenth-century Northmen invasions.

Saint Felix of Nantes, writing with six bishops in 567, gives Saint Martin the chief role in converting the Nantais. The earliest bishop list, from the early tenth century, favours no bishop before Constantine. The entry follows the diocese through its martyrs Donatian and Rogatian, its medieval bishops, the wars of religion, and its parishes, schools and orders into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-naples:
Campania's province in southern Italy has Naples for its capital, a role the city once filled for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies as well. Its site lies on the north shore of the Bay of Naples, across the Capodimonte, Vomero, and Posilipo heights, in a setting among the loveliest on earth. No Italian town holds more people, and its outlying districts run beside the bay to Torre Annunziata.

Work and trade drive the city: fishing, shipping, and commerce all thrive, and only Genoa stands ahead of it commercially in Italy. A Royal Navy arsenal stands there. Vines and food crops fill nearby fields; fruit and vegetables leave in bulk, and silk counts as a major trade. Vesuvius has battered Naples many times, most memorably in 72, and again in 1631 and 1904, the last ruining Ottaiano and San Giuseppe. The city also holds churches, palaces, a university, and museums.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natchitoches:
Natchitoches is the former title of the present Diocese of Alexandria, covering all northern Louisiana above 31 degrees north, some 22,212 square miles. The Venerable Antonio Margil, whose canonisation is in process, was the first priest to minister in that territory. Hearing from the Ays Indians of the Adayes, he located them near Spanish Lake in March 1717 and founded the mission of San Miguel de Linares.

That mission probably held Louisiana's first church, since Charlevoix reaching New Orleans in 1721 found only cabins, houses and a storehouse once used as chapel. Leaving Father Gusman in charge, Margil walked to Natchitoches to serve French Catholics there, then returned to Texas. In 1718, during the brief war with Spain, Saint Denis plundered the Adayes mission, and Margil came back in 1721, regathered the refugees, and rebuilt their church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nathinites:
Nathinites, or Nathineans, from Hebrew for the given ones, were an inferior class of Temple servants. The name occurs in seventeen Old Testament passages, and the Vulgate always renders it by the adapted transcription Nathinaei. Josephus renders the Hebrew Nathinim by sacred servants.

The Nathinites appear under this title only in post-Exilic writings. Jewish tradition in the Talmud traces their origin to Joshua's time. In the first ordering of Mosaic ritual, no provision existed for menial services, since Levites performed them all. After the Midianite defeat, Moses gave one in fifty of 16,000 prisoners to the Levites for night service of the Tabernacle. Joshua first officially deputed slaves for the sanctuary, sparing the Gibeonites for oath's sake but making them hewers of wood and drawers of water. The Temple's growth later increased their number.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-necrologies:
Necrologies, more often called obituaires in France, are registers where religious communities entered the names of the dead. They listed their own dead, associates and chief helpers, so prayers could be offered for their souls. The bodies keeping them varied almost as much as the entries' forms.

Some necrologies belonged to cathedral chapters, most to monasteries and religious houses, others to colleges such as the Sorbonne, collegiate churches and parishes. Some took the form of marginal entries in martyrologies or calendars, others formed a separate book ordered by days of the month, others were jumbled lists written as names arrived. The commonest name was martyrologium, since they often merely extended the saints' list. The entry surveys examples, uses and editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-hebrides:
The New Hebrides, a vicariate apostolic in Oceania, comprise the New Hebrides with Banks and Torres islands. They lie between 13 and 21 degrees south and 166 to 170 degrees east, covering about 580 square miles. The indigenous population, considerably decreased, numbers about 75,000, mostly of olive or brown complexion. Their many languages belong to the Malay stock, and their worship centres on the souls of the dead, though they also recognise a higher, good Being.

About 1,000 whites live there, nearly 650 French, under the Anglo-French Condominium. Quiros discovered the group in 1606 and named it Tierra Austral del Espiritu Santo, Bougainville called them the Grandes Cyclades in 1768, and Cook gave the present name six years later. Franciscan chaplains celebrated Mass on Quiros's shore chapel, but Catholic missionaries waited until January 1887, when four Marists arrived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nikolaus-nill:
Luxembourg Jesuit Nikolaus Nilles, born in 1828, became the leading canon lawyer of Innsbruck and a guide to North American clergy. After brilliant school years, he studied at the German College in Rome from 1847 to 1853, taking doctorates in theology and canon law amid the terrors of 1848.

Entering the Jesuits in 1858, he took the Innsbruck canon law chair the next year and held it for life. His commentaries on church law, his work on Eastern rites, and his counsel to American theologians after 1898 made him an authority until his death in 1907. He left Rome in 1853 with grey hair and a heart ailment from the terrors of 1848.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nimes:
Nîmes, a diocese in southern France covering the Gard, joins Roman splendor to an old Christian see. Its Maison Carrée, amphitheatre ruins, and the Pont du Gard nearby show a great Roman city, and a council letter proves a bishop there by 396, with Sedatus dated to 506.

Tradition names Celidonius or Honestus as founder, but the entry favors Baudilus as true apostle. Rebuilt as a separate diocese in 1821 after the Concordat merged it with Avignon, Nîmes kept Alais and Uzès in its bishops' style from 1877. Late traditions credit Celidonius, the man born blind, or Honestus with founding the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notaries:
Notaries, in church and civil usage, are officials appointed to draw up authentic documents that courts and chanceries can trust. The name comes from taking notes, short signs that capture spoken words for later writing in full, and early notaries served as private secretaries to great men.

From the imperial court the office spread to royal chanceries, papal bureaus, and every bishopric, though the title faded in time. The entry follows Roman regional notaries, their ranks and duties, and the later notaries apostolic who served the Roman curia. Seven regional notaries, one for each district of Rome, served the early Roman church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de:
Our Lady of the Angels, a shrine near Lure in France, grew from a Roman road station into a pilgrimage center. The site, ancient Alaunium founded in 150 BC, lay on a road between early evangelized cities, and tradition credits a disciple of Christ with an oratory to Mary there.

Chapels rose and fell on the spot, yet an old tablet survived, and after a cure in 1665 a choir of angels was heard singing. Renamed for the angels, the shrine passed to Recollect friars, was despoiled in 1791, and drew pilgrims again once churches reopened.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nueva-caceres:
Nueva Cáceres, a Philippine diocese created by Clement VIII in 1595, serves the southern Luzon provinces under Manila. Covering Camarines Sur and Norte, Albay, and Tayabas, with Ticao, Masbate, Burias, and Catanduanes, it spans 13,632 square miles and nearly 600,000 people.

Augustinian friars of the Legazpi expedition found islanders worshipping sun, moon, stars, and ancestors, yet within a few years thousands converted in Albay, Camarines, and Masbate. Gathering converts into villages, friars and lay helpers taught faith and settled civic life, and the entry lists later bishops and parishes. Its cathedral and episcopal residence stand in Nueva Caceres, capital of Camarines Sur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obedientiarie:
Obedientiaries were the lesser officials of a medieval monastery, appointed at the superior's will to run its departments. The name usually excludes prior and sub-prior, covering officers who held real power in their spheres yet remained subject to appeal to the abbot and to the house customary.

The entry lists them in order: cantor and sub-cantor for chant, sacrist with subsacrist, treasurer, and revestiarius for church and vessels. The cellarer or bursar kept stores, and further officers served kitchen, infirmary, guesthouse, and alms, with local titles varying by house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oblates-of-sa:
The Oblates of Saint Francis de Sales, a congregation of priests, trace their design to Francis de Sales himself at Jane de Chantal's prompting. His death blocked the plan, Raymond Bonal carried it out for a time, and that early congregation died out in the early eighteenth century.

Two centuries later Mother Marie de Sales Chappuis and Abbé Louis Brisson revived it, opening Saint Bernard's College near Troyes in 1869. Temporary approval came in 1875, first vows in 1876, and definitive approval in 1897, with clerics and lay brothers under annual then perpetual vows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orate-fratres:
Orate Fratres, the celebrant's call Pray brethren in the Roman Mass, asks the people to join his sacrifice before the Secrets. The people answer that the Lord receive the sacrifice from his hands for God's praise, for their benefit, and for all the holy church, and the priest adds Amen.

Merely an expansion of the usual Oremus, the form is a medieval addition, always spoken, never sung aloud. Jacobite, Nestorian, Gallican, and Mozarabic rites hold near parallels, and old Roman Secrets carry the same plea in other words. In his Rationale, Durandus prints the Orate Fratres in a somewhat different form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-gilb:
The Gilbertines, founded by Saint Gilbert of Sempringham about 1130, formed England's only native monastic order and its double houses for nuns and canons. Gilbert, parish priest of Sempringham, first gave a rule to seven girls he had taught, built them a convent north of his church, and won Bishop Alexander of Lincoln's support.

Copying Cistercians, he added lay sisters for housework and lay brothers from poor serfs for farm labor, and Haverholm followed in 1139. The order grew to houses across England, governed by a prioress and canons under Gilbert's rule, until Henry VIII dissolved it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-serv:
The Servites, or Servants of Mary, rank fifth among mendicant orders, devoted to members' holiness, Gospel preaching, and devotion to Mary's sorrows. Seven Florentine patricians of the Laudesi confraternity saw Mary on the Assumption of 1233, left the world, and settled near the Friars Minor at La Camarzia.

Seeking stricter seclusion, they moved to Monte Senario, took the Augustinian rule, and spread across Italy and Europe. The entry covers their foundation, devotions like the Seven Sorrows, affiliated groups, and distinguished Servites through later centuries. Their first home lay beside the Friars Minor at La Camarzia, outside Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orientation-o:
Orientation of churches means building with apse and altar toward the east, a custom Tertullian already notes when pagans mistook Christians for sun worshippers. Christians turned east in prayer, and the Apostolic Constitutions direct that church heads face east, while Tertullian calls churches homes of the dove in high, open places facing light.

Gregory of Nyssa traced the custom to Paradise in the east, Aquinas added Christ's eastern life and his return from the east to judge. Great Roman basilicas like the Lateran and Saint Peter's break the rule, and the entry weighs those exceptions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orphans-and-o:
Orphans and orphanages are traced here from ancient custom to the child-care systems of the early twentieth century. A child left without one or both parents became a charge on the whole community. Law laid the duty of support on parents and grandparents, but on no other kin. Scripture, Greek practice, and Roman neglect each shaped how that duty was viewed.

Early Christians took fatherless children into homes and church care. Medieval houses, guilds, and hospitals carried the work forward. England's workhouses and indenture system drew sharp criticism in the nineteenth century. Reformers built private asylums instead. Boarding-out placed children with paid foster families. Placing-out settled them in free homes. Both are weighed against the large orphanage, with notes on law and practice in several countries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osorio-franci:
Francisco Meneses Osorio was a Spanish painter born at Seville in 1630 and probably dead there in 1705. Very little is known of his life, yet he stands as the finest imitator of Murillo, his master and friend. Many works long given to Murillo likely came from his brush. He worked with Juan Garzon, served as secretary and later president of the Seville Academy, and won high repute for skill and personal devotion.

That repute dimmed after his death, since his copies of Murillo ran so true that some said he should have signed the master's name. Two copies were even taken for genuine Murillos, though one Spanish writer calls the charge a slur. His chief work, the Prophet Elijah for Saint Martin's church at Madrid, heads a short list. It includes pictures at Cadiz and Seville, among them a piece on the Order of Saint Francis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-overpopulatio:
Overpopulation theories are surveyed here from ancient Greece to the early twentieth century, asking whether people tend to outgrow their food. Down to the late eighteenth century, little heed was paid to the link between numbers and subsistence. Plato and Aristotle urged legal curbs on marriage and births in a communal state, lest support run short, and some Greek cities practised abortion and infanticide to the same end.

Most ancient and medieval peoples prized growth, since it bred soldiers, and Frederick the Great called population the wealth of the state. Malthus then argued that numbers tend to rise in geometric steps, 2, 4, 8, while food can grow only slowly. Later writers softened or fought his view, with some tying lower birth rates to better living standards. The entry weighs Malthus, Spencer, and Italian sociologists, and the moral questions their theories raise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parables:
A parable is a comparison, a likeness drawn from real, earthly incidents to carry an ideal, spiritual, or heavenly sense. The Hebrew mashal and Greek parabole both mean a setting beside, a story made up to give a lesson and hide it at once. As saying one thing and signifying another, the parable resembles a riddle, with a light side and a dark side, stirring curiosity and demanding ears to hear.

Its root sense is likeness, but a likeness that judges, shading into the maxim or proverb, of which Proverbs is the chief inspired example. The entry follows the parable from Old Testament and rabbinic use to Christ's teaching, sorting its kinds, its aims, and its rules of reading. It weighs how parables reveal truth to the willing and veil it from the dull, and why simple tales could bear the weight of ethics and religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paralipomenon:
Paralipomenon, or Chronicles, names two Bible books that sum up sacred history from Adam to the end of the Captivity. The Greek title means books of things passed over, passing from the Septuagint into old Latin and the Vulgate. It is often read as saying the books fill gaps in Kings, but their contents hardly bear that out, and the present participle is left unexplained.

Jerome's reading is likelier: Paralipomenon means an epitome of the Old Testament, with many things passed over. The Hebrew title, Words of the Days, means annals, and most Bibles call them Chronicles. The two books form one work in Hebrew manuscripts, split first in the Septuagint for ease, and the entry weighs their unity, canon place, sources, and kinship with Ezra and Nehemiah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-offic:
Passion offices, also called offices of the Instruments of the Passion, were first granted as a body to the Passionist Fathers, whose aim is spreading devotion to the Sacred Passion. Other communities and dioceses soon won the same grant, and the United States received it on 12 December 1840, at the Fourth Provincial Council of Baltimore's plea. The offices cling to set days and cannot be moved, save by special indult, and then not beyond Lent.

They rank as secondary doubles major, yielding to higher feasts and to primary feasts of equal rank. The list runs from Tuesday after Septuagesima, the Prayer on Mount Olivet, onward. It covers the Crown of Thorns on Lent's first Friday, first kept when Louis IX brought the crown to Paris in 1241. It also covers the Spear and Nails, the Winding Sheet, and further instruments across Lent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patriarchate-: The Patriarchate of the East Indies arose from a Holy See-Portugal agreement of 1886 that settled Goan Schism troubles. Both Goa's archbishop and Macao's bishop had claimed jurisdiction inside British India's districts, already expressly withdrawn from them, and Portugal had backed the archbishop, claiming royal patronage over all India's church. Under the settlement Goa's jurisdiction shrank sharply. As compensation its archbishop received the title of patriarch. His suffragans are Damao, Cochin, Macao, Mylapore, and the prelature nullius of Mozambique. The title honoured Goa's bishop, while his real sway grew smaller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peace-congres:
Peace congresses trace their modern genesis to 1623. French monk Emeric Cruce then wrote The New Cyneas, showing means to set up general peace and liberty of conscience for all the world. It was addressed to monarchs and sovereign princes. He proposed choosing a city, preferably Venice, where all Powers held ambassadors, for a universal union including all peoples. Careful order of precedence gave first place to the pope.

Two years later Hugo Grotius's Latin work On the Right of War and Peace pleaded to soften war's barbarous usages. William Penn, Pennsylvania's founder, planned a European Diet, Parliament, or Estates. Writers of many nations followed. Just after Napoleon I's fall a congress of great European powers met at Vienna, but it hardly counts as a peace congress. Its aim was adjusting borders and limiting spheres of nations that had joined to overthrow the French emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-augusti:
Peter Augustine Baines was a forceful English Benedictine bishop of the Emancipation era, born at Kirkby in Lancashire in 1787. Sent to the English monastery at Lampspring in Hanover, he followed its monks to Ampleforth after Prussian suppression, joined the order, and held nearly every office there. In 1817 he moved to Bath, where his sermons drew Protestants as well as Catholics, and his printed reply to Archdeacon Moysey became known as Baines's Defence.

Consecrated titular Bishop of Siga at Dublin in 1823, he became coadjutor of the Western District and dreamed on a grand scale. Seeing the district lacked a seminary, he bought Prior Park near Bath and built twin colleges for laymen and seminarians, hoping for a Catholic university. Fire in 1836 and clerical suspicion hampered the scheme. He died suddenly at Prior Park in 1843.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pharisees:
The Pharisees were a politico-religious party of later Judaism, rising as a class about the third century BC. After the exile, when monarchy had passed and a half-state, half-church community took its place, Hellenism threatened to dissolve Jewish life. The zealous drew apart as Chasidim, pious ones, devoted to Ezra's programme of separation from heathen neighbours and heathenizing ways, and in the Maccabean wars they hardened into the Pharisees.

Their work shaped Judaism. Synagogue schooling, missions to heathen tribes, the apocalypses of Daniel and Enoch, and the common belief in resurrection and future reward all owe them much. The entry credits them with clearing ground for Christianity. Yet pride, formalism, and an exclusive nationalism marred the achievement, valuing ceremony above the Law's weightier precepts and setting the party against prophetism and, finally, against the universal Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-de-c:
Philippe de Commines was a French historian and statesman, born in Flanders probably before 1447. Son of Burgundy's chief bailiff in Flanders, he was raised a knight, spoke Flemish and French but never learned Latin, and picked up Italian in travel. Presented at Burgundy's court in 1464, he served Charles the Bold, fought at Montlhéry in 1465, and became chamberlain in 1467. At Péronne in 1468 he entered Charles's confidence, then secretly warned Louis XI.

On 8 August 1472 he deserted Charles in Normandy for Louis, who showered him with favours, estates, and marriage to the heiress Hélène de Chambes. He became the king's confidant and chief diplomat. His Mémoires, a political history of Europe from 1464 to 1498, analyse causes rather than paint scenes, in abrupt, periphrastic prose with medieval manner and Renaissance realism. He died about 1511, his tomb now in the Louvre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philistines:
The Philistines were the seafaring people of Palestine's maritime plain from the Judges onward. Genesis counts them with the Caphtorim among Egypt's descendants, and scholars trace them with probability to Crete, as a piratical sea people. They first loom large when Samson, promised to begin Israel's deliverance from forty years of their rule, battles them along the western border.

Under Samuel they seized the Ark, only to return it when plague struck, and under Saul they pressed Israel until Jonathan's bravery checked them. David subdued them, Assyrians and Egyptians later crossed their land, and Alexander's siege of Gaza stands famous. After Assyria they fade from record, absorbed into surrounding peoples, their Semitic gods Dagon and Ishtar marking a Canaanite civilization. Herodotus already calls the coast's holders Arabians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-phylacteries:
Phylacteries, called tephillin by Jews, were small leather cases worn in prayer, named in the New Testament only once. In Matthew 23:5 Christ reproaches Pharisees who broaden their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes in ostentation. The Greek word means safeguard, amulet, or charm, and the Jewish name comes from tephillah, prayer.

Two cases make the set: one worn on the forehead with four compartments, one on the upper left arm with a single compartment. Both hold narrow parchment strips copied from the Pentateuch: Exodus 13:1-10 and Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and 11:13-21. Orthodox Jews still regard wearing them at stated moments as a sacred duty. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the object, its texts, and its rebuke.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-picture-bible:
Picture Bibles were the Middle Ages' illustrated Scriptures, made because books were costly manuscripts and reading belonged to few. Frescoes, stained glass, and painted pages taught the illiterate what writing could not. As the Synod of Arras said in 1025, the unlettered contemplated in painting's lines what they could never discern in script. The Church used pictures to spread Bible events and to pair Old and New Testament as type and antitype, prophecy and fulfilment.

Chief among surviving picture Bibles stands the thirteenth-century Bible Moralisée, also called the Bible Historiée or Allégorisée. At least two editions survive, alike in chosen texts and order but differing in allegorical and moral deductions drawn from them. Later sections trace other pictured Bibles and their circulation through medieval Christendom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-puvis-:
Pierre Puvis de Chavannes was a French painter who made large decorative wall paintings the centre of his art. He was born at Lyons in 1824 and was meant for the Polytechnic school. After a first trip to Italy he turned to painting at twenty-three. He studied briefly with Scheffer, Delacroix, and Couture.

A second stay in Italy fixed his aim: grand, simple compositions that express the shared beliefs and memories of a people. He painted them with calm colour and quiet landscapes. Rejected at the Salon for years after his first Pietà in 1852, he became, with Eugène Carrière, the leading defender of spiritual and religious art in an age of materialism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pilgrimages:
Pilgrimages are journeys to a holy place to honour it, seek supernatural help, or fulfil a religious duty. The practice is found in every religion. The entry traces the custom from ancient shrines. Egyptians went to Bubastis and Thebes, Greeks to Delphi and Epidaurus, Mexicans to Quetzal's temple, and Peruvians to Cuzco. Later, Christian Holy Places drew travellers across Europe.

It argues that once a god's appearances are tied to one spot, pilgrimage follows naturally from the human heart. That claim is set against older beliefs about local gods. The long article then surveys Christian pilgrimage through the centuries, its shrines, its motives, and the customs that grew up around the road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poles-in-the-:
Poles in the United States traces Polish immigration from early explorers to the great nineteenth-century waves. Tradition puts a Pole, John of Kolno, in Danish service off Labrador in 1476, and Albert Zborowski settled on the Hackensack River by 1662, founding the Zabriskie family of New York. A Polish schoolmaster was hired on Manhattan in 1659.

The champions of American independence included Thaddeus Kosciuszko and Casimir Pulaski, whose legion drew Polish noblemen. The Polish rising of 1830 then sent soldiers and lesser nobles across the Atlantic. By 1835 a Polish National Committee in the United States, led by prominent Americans, was rallying sympathy for Poland's cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polyglot-bibl:
Polyglot Bibles are Bibles printed in several languages side by side, and the entry begins with the first of them, the Complutensian Bible of Alcalá. Edited between 1502 and 1517 under Cardinal Ximenes at the university he founded, and published in 1520 with Leo X's sanction, it aimed to revive the languishing study of Scripture.

It gave the Old Testament in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin and the New Testament in Greek and Latin. It added a Chaldean Targum of the Pentateuch and a six-volume apparatus of dictionaries and grammars. Only six hundred copies were issued, yet they reached Europe's chief libraries and shaped later editions. Its Greek Old Testament was the first printed and the common text until Sixtus V's edition of 1587.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-au:
Pontifical Audiences are the receptions the pope grants to cardinals, sovereigns, princes, ambassadors, and others with business at the Holy See. They form a large part of the pope's daily duties, as bishops of every rite and nation come to Rome to honour the apostles' tombs and consult the supreme pastor.

Requests go to the master of the chamber, the grand chamberlain of the papal court, even those of ambassadors sent through the cardinal secretary of state. Each day the pope receives the prefect of one of the sacred congregations, signing decrees and giving counsel. Days and hours of regular audiences appear on a printed form changed every six months, while audiences for sovereigns carry special ceremony, with guards and officials doubled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-co:
Pontifical Colleges surveys the colleges and seminaries placed under the Holy See or the Propaganda, above all those founded to keep the faith alive in England, Ireland, and Scotland. Earlier foundations ranged widely. They include the English College at Valladolid of 1589 and the Irish College at Paris of 1592. They include English, Scots, Benedictine, Carmelite, and Jesuit houses at Douai, Saint-Omer, Liège, and Louvain.

Most emigrated to England or closed by the Revolution's end, and the entry distinguishes colleges that bear the honorary title Pontifical from those merely dependent on Rome. Only three hold the title. They are the Pontifical Seminary of Kandy in Ceylon, the Pontifical Seminary of Scutari, and the Pontifical College Josephinum at Columbus, Ohio. Sixteen further colleges are under consideration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-clares:
The Poor Clares, also called the Poor Ladies or Sisters of Saint Clare, are the Second Order of Saint Francis, the order of religious women beside the friars. It began at San Damiano, Assisi. Clare withdrew there in 1212 on Francis's advice. She was soon joined by ladies drawn by her holiness, among them her sister Agnes, her mother, aunt, and niece.

Clare became Francis's counsellor and, after his death, the supreme exponent of his ideal of poverty, exalting the beggar's state into spiritual liberty lived in dependence on God's providence. She won from Innocent III the privilege of absolute poverty for the community as a whole, not merely for individuals. The entry then follows the order's rules, from Ugolino's rule to Clare's definitive rule, its spread, the Colettine reform, and its life in England and America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-milti:
Miltiades was elected pope in 310 or 311 and died on 10 or 11 January 314. After Eusebius's banishment the see stood vacant, tangled in the lapsi disputes. On 2 July 310 or 311, Miltiades, an African by birth, rose to the papacy. The Liberian list dates his consecration 2 July 311, yet gives his death as 2 January 314 and his reign as three years, six months, and eight days. A copyist's slip probably turned two years into three, making 311 the likelier election year.

Around then an edict of Galerius, Licinius, and Constantine ended the great persecution. Christians could live openly and rebuild worship places, except where Maximinus Daia still persecuted in the East. Miltiades's reign thus opened in toleration's first light.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portraits-of-:
Portraits of the Apostles surveys the earliest painted images of Christ with his apostles. The oldest fresco of Christ enthroned among the apostles dates from the early fourth century, from the Domitilla cemetery. Christ sits enthroned, hand raised. Six more frescoes of Christ instructing the apostles survive in Rome's catacombs.

Two frescoes once showed only Peter and Paul beside Christ; one keeps Peter, the other Paul. A Priscilla fresco shows Christ giving the law to Peter, handing Peter a roll. The scene casts Peter as the New Law's Moses. A third-century Ad duas lauros fresco shows Peter seated, studying an open roll. Wilpert reads the steady types as a Roman tradition of their looks, and Eusebius mentions painted likenesses of both apostles and Christ. A second-century Domitilla bronze medal, now in the Vatican museum, shows Peter's curly hair and short beard beside Paul's longer beard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preadamites:
Preadamites are the supposed folk of earth ere Adam. Strictly the word should mark men who died out ere Adam was made. In common use it also covers Coadamites, folk of a stock older than Adam who lived on with him. Whether strict Preadamites, a race dead ere Adam, can be allowed touches no revealed dogma. The same holds for whether stars hold minds like man.

The common sense of the word stands otherwise. It holds that men ere Adam lived on with Adam and his seed, breaking the unity of the race. Palmieri calls that heresy, and Father Pesch backs the censure. La Peyrère's plea: Genesis tells the Gentiles formed on the sixth day, while Adam was formed on the seventh. Adam's sin outweighed Gentile sins, since he sinned against law, while they sinned but against nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protectories:
Protectories were homes that gave neglected or abandoned children shelter, food, clothing and a plain education. Pupils learned religion, morals, school subjects and a trade. This encyclopedia entry follows the idea from its first home, Saint Michele at Rome. Clement the Eleventh founded it in 1704. Two centuries later many such houses stood across American dioceses. Courts, above all the new juvenile courts, often sent young offenders to these houses for schooling rather than to prison.

Ireland and the United States supply most of the detail, with separate houses for boys and girls. Figures show who was committed and for how long. A note from 1904 records that 84.7 per cent of male delinquents in American houses could read and write. The share among girls ran higher still. Readers interested in child welfare or penal reform find here a snapshot of an age that began to treat wayward youth as pupils, not criminals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protestant-ep:
This encyclopedia history of the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States falls into two halves. The first covers its years under the Church of England. The second covers its later life with bishops of its own. English church life reached Virginia with the Jamestown colony in 1607. Earlier plantings in the Carolinas and Maine had failed. During the colonial age the church gained a near-establishment in Maryland and Virginia. New England long kept it at arm's length.

American independence broke the old tie. Bishops in England could not ordain men who owed no loyalty to the Crown. Parliament at last passed an act letting English bishops consecrate such men. William White, chosen for Pennsylvania, sailed to England with Samuel Provost, chosen for New York. Both received consecration from Archbishop Moore of Canterbury. The entry then traces the new church's growth through the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purgatorial-s:
Purgatorial societies are pious associations, or confraternities, whose purpose is to aid the poor souls in purgatory by every means possible. This long encyclopedia entry roots them in Catholic teaching on purgatory, the communion of saints, and the value of good works offered for others. From the beginning, brotherly love marked Christ's Church, and the earliest communities, down to the catacomb age, formed one great purgatorial society in practice.

Prayers for the dead in the oldest liturgies and breviaries, and the earliest Christian inscriptions, supply the clearest proof. Later centuries multiplied formal confraternities, and one Roman society gained power to aggregate sister societies across the world. Near the end of the nineteenth century it joined with a Requiem Mass association for deceased members. The Black Penitents, who marched through Rome under the banner of mercy from 1488 to aid the condemned, show how varied these brotherhoods could be.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quarantines: Quarantines is a term met in grants of indulgences, and it means a strict church penance of forty days, performed after the manner of the early Church. An indulgence of seven quarantines, for example, remits as much temporal punishment as would be wiped away by that amount of penance. That is seven times forty days of it. The entry is short because the term needs little more: a unit of ancient penitential discipline, carried over into the language of indulgences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ralph-baines:
Ralph Baines, Bishop of Lichfield and Coventry in England, was born at Knowsthorp in Yorkshire, though his birth date is uncertain, and died on 18 November 1559. This encyclopedia entry follows him from Saint John's College, Cambridge, to ordination at Ely in 1519. He served as rector of Hardwicke in Cambridgeshire until 1544, when he moved to Paris and became Professor of Hebrew. Returning to England in 1553, he was consecrated bishop on 18 November 1554.

Baines vigorously opposed the Reformers and stood among the eight defenders of Catholic doctrine at the Westminster Conference of 1558 to 1559.
