On Elizabeth's accession he lost his bishopric on 21 June 1559 and was placed in the care of Grindal, Protestant Bishop of London. He thus became one of the eleven imprisoned bishops. The Reverend G. Philips, whose research treats their imprisonment exhaustively, supplies the entry's modern source on that harsh episode.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphael-semme:
Raphael Semmes, naval officer, was born in Charles County, Maryland, on 27 September 1809 and died at Point Clear, Alabama, on 26 August 1877. This encyclopedia entry traces his family to one of the original Catholic colonists of Maryland, from which state he entered the United States Navy as a midshipman on 1 April 1826. He served until 1832, then took leave until July 1835, studying law and gaining admission to practice.

Rejoining the navy, he served with distinction and rose to commander. At the Civil War's outbreak he resigned and cast his lot with Alabama, where he had become a citizen in 1841. He became a commander in the Confederate States Navy on 25 March 1861, a captain on 21 August 1862, and a rear-admiral on 10 February 1865. After Johnston's surrender at Greensboro he returned to civil life, writing The Cruise of the Alabama and Sumter in 1864 and his Memoirs of Services Afloat in 1869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-d-agi:
Raymond d'Agiles was a chronicler and canon of Puy-en-Velay towards the close of the eleventh century. This encyclopedia entry follows him on the First Crusade of 1096 to 1099, accompanying the Count of Toulouse as chaplain to Adhémar, Bishop of Puy and legate of Pope Urban the Second. With Pons de Balazuc he undertook a history of the expedition, but Pons was killed, and Agiles had to carry the work on alone.

At a sortie during the siege of Antioch on 28 June 1098, Agiles walked before the column bearing the Sacred Lance in his hands. He shared the entry into Jerusalem, joined the Count of Toulouse on pilgrimage to the Jordan, and fought at Ascalon. After that he vanishes from sight. His Historia Francorum qui ceperunt Hierusalem gives an eyewitness account of most of the crusade. Molinier judged him partial, credulous, ignorant and prejudiced, usable only under close criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rechab-and-th:
Rechab was the father of Jonadab, who appears in the Second Book of Kings as a fervent backer of Jehu's attack on the House of Ahab. This short encyclopedia entry explains that Jehu aimed to root out the idolatrous worship that dynasty had fostered. The principles guiding Jonadab's descendants, the Rechabites, come from Jeremiah chapter 35, where the Rechabites, invited to drink wine, refuse in their father's words.

Jonadab commanded them to drink no wine, neither they nor their children, for ever. They must build no houses, sow no seed, plant no vineyards, and own none. They must live in tents all their days, so that they might live long in the land where they were strangers. Jonadab and his kin evidently believed that settled life and its civilized forms pulled them away from the Jewish faith. The First Book of Chronicles links the clan with the Kenites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemptoristi:
The Redemptoristines began at Scala, not far from Amalfi in Italy. This encyclopedia entry tells that Father Thomas Falcoia gathered nuns into a community there under a rule he gave them. He later became Bishop of Castellammare. While directing Saint Alphonsus, he heard that Sister Maria Celeste Crosterosa had received a new rule by revelation. The bishop backed the rule, asking Alphonsus to lead the nuns through spiritual exercises and shape the community as he saw fit.

Alphonsus readied them for the new rule through meditation on Christ's life and virtues. Daily life was to mirror phases of His life in its details. Zeal was to work through prayer, with each weekday given to an object touching the Church's well-being. They were to pray for the apostolic works of the Redemptorists. Bruges and Tournai histories supply the entry's sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reformed-chur:
Reformed Churches is the name for Protestant bodies that adopted the tenets of Zwingli and, later, the doctrinal principles of Calvin. This encyclopedia entry dates the distinctive title to 1561, at the colloquy of Poissy. The movement began in Switzerland and spread early to France, some German states, the Netherlands, England, Scotland, Hungary and Poland. Emigration and colonization later carried the Calvinistic system still wider. Some bodies under it, like Presbyterianism, receive separate treatment.

Others became national churches and appear under their countries' names. The bodies treated here include the Reformed Dutch Church in America. Its True Reformed offshoot, organized in 1822, joined the main church in the United States in 1890, numbering 138 ministers, 189 churches and 29,006 communicants. Early schools mark the story: Rutgers College, founded in 1770 as Queen's College at New Brunswick, New Jersey, with a theological seminary added in 1784, and Hope College at Holland, Michigan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reliquaries:
Reliquaries, in the sense any box, casket, or shrine made to receive relics, must have existed in some form almost from the beginning of Christianity. About their construction and materials in the early centuries nothing positive can be said. Even their names, capsa, capsella, theca, pyxis, and arca, are general, and the same names served for receptacles of the Eucharist, the holy oils, and other pious objects.

That generality makes some pieces hard to judge: certain circular ivory pyxes, the best known and earliest in the Berlin Museum, may or may not have served as reliquaries. Later masterpieces are easier to place. A silver casket nearly six feet long is shaped like a church with nave and two aisles. The enamelled and jewelled Marienschrein at Aachen is linked by tradition to Charlemagne, and the Ursula Shrine at Bruges is adorned with Hans Memling's paintings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-descarte:
René Descartes, philosopher and scientist, was born at La Haye, France, in 1596 and died at Stockholm in 1650. He studied at the Jesuit college of La Flèche and went to Paris in 1613, befriending Father Mersenne and meeting the mathematician Mydorge. After army service under Maurice of Nassau and the Duke of Bavaria, he resolved on 10 November 1619 to set aside childhood prejudices. He devoted his life to restoring decayed knowledge, taking the mission as mystical after a dream he read as revelation.

His method starts with doubt. Simple sums may deceive, but thought itself survives. From thought he passes to existence, Cogito, ergo sum, the rock on which knowledge must be built. His gift lies less in his theories than in the impetus of his genius, his method, and his discoveries. His quantitative picture gives way to quality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rennes:
Rennes was re-established by the Concordat of 1802. It drew on ancient Rennes, less three parishes given to Nantes, most of Dol and Saint Malo, and ten parishes from Vannes and Nantes. On 3 January 1859 it became an archiepiscopal see, suffragans Quimper, Vannes, and Saint Brieuc. Its archbishop later added the titles of Dol and Saint Malo by Leo the Thirteenth's permission. Rennes was Brittany's capital, in Roman times part of Third Lyonnesse.

The entry traces Breton church quarrels over the hierarchy Nomenoë set up against Tours. The Council of Savonnières in 859 had seven metropolitans write to the Bishop of Rennes. They wrote to the bishops of the new sees of Dol, Saint Brieuc, and Tréguier, reproaching disobedience to the Metropolitan of Tours. The bishops of Vannes, Quimper, Aleth, and Saint Pol de Léon, who held sees of bishops Nomenoë had deposed, received no such letter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-requiem-masse:
Requiem Masses are masses offered for the dead, named from the first word of their Introit. That word traces to the Fourth Book of Esdras among the Apocrypha and to Isaiah's promise that the Lord will give rest always. The entry works through eleven heads, from origins and formulary to vestment colour, conditions for celebrating, the rite, and the funeral Mass.

Later heads cover the Mass for All the Dead, the Mass on news of a death, and Masses of the third, seventh, and thirtieth days and on anniversaries. High and Low Mass close the list. Celebration is hedged with conditions. On the vigil of Pentecost when the font is blessed, and on the Major and Minor Litany days, a parish Mass must follow the day's own rubrics, not Requiem. On a feast day, the exequial Mass may stand only if the day's solemnity does not oppose it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reserved-case:
Reserved cases are sins whose absolution lies beyond every confessor's power, kept by a superior for himself or granted specially to another confessor. To reserve a case is to refuse jurisdiction for absolving a particular sin, a power traced to Christ's words, whose sins you shall retain, they are retained. Reservation presupposes jurisdiction: the pope alone reserves for the whole Church, bishops for their dioceses only, and certain regular prelates for their religious subjects.

A sin qualifies for reservation only when mortal, external, and consummated. The entry then treats the penitent who, with no intent to evade the law, confesses in another diocese where the sin is not reserved, and the limits that keep reservation narrow. Christ's commission to retain sins anchors the whole practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhodes:
Rhodes, a metropolitan of the Cyclades, is an island opposite Lycia and Caria, divided from them by an arm of the sea. It covers about 564 square miles, watered by streams and the river Candura, and rich in fruit, with a climate so genial that, as Pliny records, the sun shines ever. Carians lived there first, then Phoenicians about 1300 BC, then Dorian Greeks about 800 BC. In 408 BC the city of Rhodes was founded by the three towns, Lindus, Ialysus, and Camirus.

The island's knights and fleet stood as Christendom's bulwark against Islam. In 1480 Rhodes under Pierre d'Aubusson endured a siege by the lieutenants of Mahomet the Second. On 24 October 1522 Villiers de l'Isle Adam capitulated to Solyman the Second and gave the island to the Turks for good. From 1328 to 1546 Rhodes was a Latin metropolitan over Melos, Nicaria, Carpathos, Chios, Tinos, and Mycone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhymed-bibles:
Rhymed Bibles are almost entirely collections of psalms in verse. The oldest English rhymed psalter is a Vulgate psalm translation from before the Reformation, generally assigned to Henry the Second's reign and kept at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge. The Bodleian at Oxford holds another Catholic rhyming psalter in much the same style, dated by its inscription to Edward the Second's time.

Thomas Brampton turned the Seven Penitential Psalms from the Vulgate into rhyming verse in 1414, and his manuscript sits in the Cottonian collection at the British Museum. These pre-Reformation psalters witness a popular vernacular Scripture in England, against the claim that English psalm singing began with the Reformation. Sir Thomas Wyatt, who died in 1521, is said to have done the whole psalter, though only selected psalms survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rites:
Rite is defined here in two senses, and the distinction shapes the whole entry. In classical Latin, ritus meant the form of any religious observance. In English it can mean a single ceremony, such as the blessing of palms. Or it can mean the whole complex of services of a church or group of churches. In the second sense it is often treated as liturgy, though liturgy properly means the Eucharistic service.

A Christian rite, in this broad sense, covers all that is done to worship God and make people holy. It includes the sacraments, above all the Eucharist. It includes the Divine Office of psalms, lessons, and prayers divided into hours. It also includes the sacramentals, from blessings of persons and things to processions and vows. The Church never imposed uniformity of rite. Local and national rites grew to suit different peoples, as varied expressions of shared truths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rites-in-the-:
Eastern rites in the United States are the subject of this entry, written when immigration from eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa had brought whole worshipping communities across the Atlantic. These peoples arrived with their priests and forms of worship, and as they grew in number and wealth they built churches in cities and towns across the country. Rome once seemed the place to see every rite grouped together, but the entry argues that America offered the better field.

In Rome the rites survived mainly to train clergy and to display church unity, with no lay body following them. In America, by contrast, lay numbers and pressure created and sustained the churches. The chief rites established were the Armenian, the Greek or Byzantine, and the Syro-Maronite. Studying them side by side with dissident churches of the same rites gives, the entry claims, an unmatched chance for comparison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-jum:
Robert of Jumieges was Archbishop of Canterbury in 1051-52, a Norman caught in the struggle between Normans and Saxons at Edward the Confessor's court. A monk of St Ouen at Rouen, prior there in 1037, he became Abbot of Jumieges and began its Norman abbey church. He had served Edward in exile, and when Edward took the throne in 1043, Robert came with him as Bishop of London in 1044.

As bishop he led the Norman party against Godwin's Saxons. In 1051 he was named Archbishop of Canterbury and fetched his pall from Rome, though English clergy resented a foreigner as metropolitan. He helped drive Godwin into exile. Godwin's return in 1052 sent Robert fleeing to Rome, where he was outlawed. The pope restored him, yet he never regained his see, and William of Normandy used his exclusion as a pretext for invasion. The Missal of Robert of Jumieges was his gift to the abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-luz:
Robert of Luzarches was the architect of Amiens Cathedral, called the Gothic Parthenon. Born at Luzarches near Pontoise late in the twelfth century, Philip Augustus is said to have summoned him to Paris, where he shared in work on Notre Dame. His fame rests on Amiens. After fire destroyed the old cathedral in 1218, Bishop Evrard de Fouilloy had it rebuilt in Gothic.

A floor-labyrinth inscription of 1288 records that building began in 1220. It names Robert as architect, with Thomas de Cormont and his son as successors. Robert did not stay long on the work. Cormont appears as architect under Evrard's successor. The church, larger than Notre Dame in Paris and Reims, became a standard across France and beyond for balanced weight and Gothic style. Its nave runs about 470 feet long, 164 wide, and 141 high, with a five-aisle choir flanked by seven chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rolls-series:
The Rolls Series is the great British Government collection of medieval chronicles and memorials, titled The Chronicles and Memorials of Great Britain and Ireland during the Middle Ages. It followed a scheme of 1857 from the Master of the Rolls, Sir John Romilly. An earlier venture, the Monumenta Historica Britannica, had failed after one huge volume in 1848. Earnest appeals from the researcher Joseph Stevenson led to the new scheme.

Editors preferred the scarcest and most valuable materials first, treating each chronicle as an editio princeps. Each handy octavo volume carried a preface on the author's life and times and a description of the manuscripts. Some 255 volumes covering 99 works have appeared, save the Year Books of Edward I and Edward III. Nearly all the great medieval English chronicles are included. Luard's Matthew Paris, Stubbs's Hoveden, Brewer's Giraldus, and Robertson's Becket materials are singled out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-academi:
Roman academies were the learned associations of Renaissance Rome, surveyed here from the close of the Western Schism in 1418 to the mid-sixteenth century. With Florence, Rome formed one of two centres where scientific, literary, and artistic culture grew intense and varied. Italian academies were circles of learned men, not teaching institutes.

The Middle Ages left Rome no scientific or literary academies, while princely courts such as Charlemagne's were the nearest models. Constant turmoil blocked such growth: Hohenstaufen oppression, Gregory VII's fight for church liberty, the Guelph and Ghibelline wars, French domination, Avignon, and schism. Once unity returned and popes came home, Renaissance culture flourished. The academies revived Plato's model, treating philosophy as the broadest culture. Neo-Platonism, reacting against decadent Aristotelian scholasticism, was led by Gemistus Plethon at Florence and Cardinal Bessarion at Rome, whose house around 1450 centred a flourishing Platonic academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-college:
Roman colleges are the seminaries in Rome for training priests. College here means a Roman school for training priests, the same as a seminary. Rome's colleges also nurture loyal attachment to the Holy See. Popes encouraged national colleges where young men lived together and used the city's opportunities.

Several colleges grew as offshoots of the Propaganda's Urban College, splitting off once a nationality grew numerous enough for its own house. Colleges are halls of residence where students follow seminary exercises of piety and private study. Some add special courses in languages, music, or archaeology. Regular philosophy and theology are taught at central schools such as the Propaganda, the Gregorian University, and the Dominican Minerva. Each college has a rector named by its country's bishops and appointed by the pope, aided by a vice-rector and spiritual director. Discipline runs through the camerata system of student groups under prefects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-histori:
Roman historical institutes are bodies set up at Rome for historical research, notably in the Vatican archives. In business and diplomacy, church authorities always relied on their stored material. Thirteenth-century papal registers show references to documents once kept but since lost. Pure interest in the past was rare, arising when outsiders sought documents for their own work.

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, critical study drew scholars to the Vatican treasures. The most far-reaching use began with Caesar Baronius, later cardinal. His Annales ecclesiastici from Christ's birth to 1198, in twelve folio volumes of 1588-93, first revealed to the world the wealth of the Roman archives. Later continuations, papal decrees, and monographs on local churches all drew on Vatican material. Later historians were aided by archive officials who were often scholars themselves, notably Augustin Theiner, papal archivist from 1804 to 1874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sadducees:
Sadducees were a politico-religious sect among Jews of the late post-Exile and New Testament age. The old derivation from tsaddiqim, the righteous, is now generally discredited on philological grounds. The term is linked to Sadoc. Sadducee thus equals Sadokite. They became the dominant priestly party in the Greek and Roman period, claiming descent from Sadoc, high priest under David and Solomon.

As a political party they first appear under John Hyrcanus, 135 to 105 B.C. They espoused the hellenizing tendencies of Asmonean princes, strongly opposed by Pharisees, who abhorred Greek culture. Under Aristobulus I and Alexander Jannaeus their power was supreme. Though Pharisees gained favour under Alexandra Salome, 78 to 69 B.C., Sadducees regained ascendancy under Aristobulus II, 69 to 63 B.C., supporting him against Hyrcanus II, Antipater, and Romans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-nicomed:
Nicomedes, a martyr of the Roman Church whose feast falls on 15 September, is known almost entirely through his grave. His name is missing from the three oldest manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology. Yet later lists, seventh-century pilgrim guides, and a fifth-century Roman titular church all honour him. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gathers these thin traces with care.

Buried in a catacomb on the Via Nomentana, he gained a church over his tomb that Pope Adrian I later restored. Nothing survives about how he died, and the entry refuses to fill the gap with invention. A legend in the story of Nereus and Achilleus makes him a priest of the first century. The entry treats that dating as unproven and leaves the martyr in his proper obscurity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salazar-franc:
Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, born at Toledo probably in 1513 or 1514, sailed to Mexico in 1550 and died there in 1575. In Spain he had taught at Osuna, and in Mexico he became one of the first professors of the new university, formally opened on 25 January 1553 by order of Charles V. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia honours a scholar of solid learning and wide influence.

Holding the chair of rhetoric, Cervantes wrote histories of Mexico City and New Spain. His Latin Dialogues are best known: three parts describing the young city as it stood about 1554, prized by historians and archaeologists alike. His Túmulo Imperial of 1560 records the funeral honours for Charles V in minute detail, from ceremony to monument, and was reprinted in 1886. Readers meet a humanist shaping a colonial capital's memory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salmanticense:
Salmanticenses and Complutenses are the shared names for the authors of the great courses in philosophy, theology, and moral theology made by teachers of the Discalced Carmelites at Alcalá and Salamanca. Though written mainly to train younger friars, the courses reached outsiders too, since both colleges belonged to the universities of Alcalá, ancient Complutum, and Salamanca. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a publishing feat.

In the Middle Ages the Carmelites had mostly followed the Dominicans against Franciscan and Augustinian schools, and in the sixteenth century they kept that loyalty against the Jesuits. Strict fidelity to Thomas Aquinas became their watchword, carried out more steadily than by any other commentators of the neo-Scholastic age. The entry surveys the three courses and their many unnamed contributors, a monument of teamwork.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-luiz-de-c:
São Luiz de Cáceres, a Brazilian diocese suffragan of Cuiabá, was split from that diocese by papal decree of 10 March 1910. Its city, also called Villa Maria, stands in Mato Grosso on the Paraguay river's left bank, about 115 miles west-south-west of Cuiabá and fifty miles from Bolivia. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a river port's rise.

Luiz de Albuquerque de Mello Pereira e Cáceres founded it in 1776 as a fort against the Spaniards, naming it Maria for Portugal's queen, and it gained town rank in 1859. In 1895 only about 1,500 people, mostly Indians, lived there. River trade between Mato Grosso and the south, carried wholly by water, then made São Luiz into an important centre. It is the most southerly Brazilian port on the Paraguay, with its cathedral dedicated to St Aloysius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarabaites:
Sarabaites were a class of monks widespread before Benedict's time, living either at home like the earliest ascetics or together in or near cities. They answered to no superior, followed no fixed rule, and kept the earnings of their own handiwork for themselves. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia reports a byword for lax monastic life.

Jerome called them Remoboth, and John Cassian described their spread across Egypt and other lands. Both writers judged their conduct harshly, and Benedict's Rule, in its first chapter, speaks of them in the same vein. Later the name, whose original meaning cannot be fixed, came to mean degenerate monks in general. The entry gives readers the ancient witnesses and lets their verdict stand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sardes:
Sardes, a titular see of Lydia in Asia Minor, was probably Homer's Hyde, at the foot of Mount Tmolus. Its later name seems drawn from the Shardani, a people of the cuneiform records. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a Lydian capital through empires.

Early kings ruled from 766 to 687 before Christ, and the Mermnad dynasty founded by Gyges in 687 lasted until Croesus fell to Cyrus in 546. Persian satraps then ruled from Sardes. Its capture by Ionians and Athenians in 498 sparked the Persian wars with Greece. Alexander took it without a fight in 334, Antigonus held it until 301, and then the Seleucids ruled, until Rome defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scoto-hiberni:
Scoto-Hibernian monasteries is a handy term for houses founded in sixth-century Scotland, though Scotland did not bear its modern meaning for four hundred years more. They owe their rise to Columba, whose work among Picts and Scots ran nearly forty years. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia groups a monastic family around Iona.

Adamnan, Iona's ninth abbot and Columba's biographer, is the chief authority, though his list of foundations is likely incomplete and their dates uncertain. What is certain is that these houses clustered around Iona as centre and stayed closely linked with her. Like Columban houses in Ireland, they answered to Iona as mother-house. Together they formed the wide organisation called the family of Iona, or muinter Ioe, though not every house was Columba's own founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scribes:
Scribes, Greek grammateis or teachers of the law, were the professional interpreters of the Law in New Testament synagogues. Their profession dates from the return from captivity, and its growth followed naturally from the formal, legalistic bent of post-exilic Jewish piety. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains why a whole class arose to expound the Law.

The Law was revered as God's will in precise form, and its many rules governed every pious Jew's daily life in minute detail. Love of the Law was the heart of piety, and the just were those who walked in all the Lord's commandments without blame. But the commandments were numerous, tangled, and often obscure, so popular guidance needed specialists. Ezra is the first called a ready scribe in the law of Moses, and the entry follows the class to Gospel times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptural-gl:
Scriptural glosses take their name from the Latin glossa, itself from the Greek glossa, tongue. In classical Greek the word meant the tongue or organ of speech, then figuratively a language. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows the word from grammar to Bible study.

Greek scholars commenting on authors used glossa first for a word needing explanation, then for the explanation itself. Christian writers took the word in that last sense for Holy Writ: a gloss explains a purely verbal difficulty, not doctrinal, ritual, or historical obscurity. Words commonly glossed fall into five classes: foreign words, provincial dialect terms, obsolete words, technical terms, and words used in an unusual sense. The entry surveys gloss collections and their makers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-secret-societ:
Secret societies, a term whose exact sense has shifted over time, are defined in this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia first by an older meaning and then by a newer one. Formerly the phrase meant a society known to exist whose members and meeting places stayed hidden. Today it means a society with secrets: a ritual demanding an oath of loyalty and silence, with religious ceremonies using the Bible, prayers, hymns, signs, symbols, and special funerals.

Raich offers a fuller picture. Groups wholly hide rules, corporate acts, members' names, signs, passwords, and usages from outsiders, called the profane. Members are bound by oath, promise, or word of honour to strict silence about all the association's business. The entry then surveys such societies, above all Freemasonry, and the Church's condemnations, giving readers the Catholic case against secret oaths and hidden allegiances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-semites:
The Semites are a group of peoples closely linked by language, living in Asia and partly in Africa. Their name comes from the biblical table of nations, where most of them appear as descendants of Noah's son Sem. This long entry traces the term from Ludwig Schlözer's proposal in 1781 to its general use. Modern science widened it to cover peoples demonstrably of Semitic origin or fully Semitized.

Four chief divisions organize the survey. They are the Babylonian-Assyrian Semites of the east, the Chanaanitic Semites of the west, the Aramaic Semites of the north, and the Arabian Semites of the south. The entry follows their migrations, empires, and languages, from Hammurabi's Babylon and the Hyksos in Egypt to the Phoenicians, Hebrews, and Arabs who carried Semitic speech across the ancient Near East.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-servants-of-m:
The Servites, or Servants of Mary, were founded on the feast of the Assumption in 1233. The Virgin appeared to seven noble Florentines at a confraternity service. She told them to leave the world and live for God alone. On the feast of her Nativity that September, they withdrew to La Camarzia outside the city walls, then moved to Monte Senario, eleven miles from Florence. There Mary appeared again, holding a black habit and the Rule of Saint Augustine, with angels bearing the instruments of the Passion.

She named them her first Servants and charged them to tend her Son's vineyard, saying the dark habit would recall her pangs at the Cross. Saint Philip Benizi, born on the day of the first vision, became the order's great propagator. The entry follows the order's swift growth across Italy and beyond, down to the general chapter held in London in 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sibylline-ora:
The Sibylline Oracles are collections of supposed prophecies ascribed to the sibyls, divinely inspired seeresses widely circulated in antiquity. Early writers speak of one sibyl, while later authors name many by their dwelling places. Varro, quoted by Lactantius, lists ten, from the Persian and Libyan to the Cumaean and the Tiburtine. At Rome the sibyls of Cumae and Erythraea stood highest.

Because pagan oracles shaped religious views, Hellenistic Jews at Alexandria in the second century BC composed verses in the same form and fathered them on the sibyls, spreading Jewish teaching among pagans. Christians borrowed the custom in the second and third centuries, producing a new class of oracles. The entry sorts the surviving collections, weighs their dates and sources, and traces how Jewish and Christian writers turned a pagan voice to their own ends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socialistic-c:
This entry lists societies holding land, factories, and stores in common, sometimes extending common ownership to houses and food. Most groups treated here are strictly communistic rather than socialistic, though commonly called by the latter name. Reformation sects such as Anabaptists, Libertines, and Familists tried socialistic experiments without lasting or thorough practice. The Labadists founded a Westphalian community in 1672 and a Maryland colony, and both died within half a century.

American experiments dominate the list. Ephrata dates to 1732, the Shakers to Watervliet in 1776, the Harmonists to 1805, Zoar to 1818, and Robert Owen's New Harmony to 1824. It was the greatest attempt, lasting only two years with 900 members at most. The Amana community, organized in 1843 and moved to Iowa in 1845, alone grew steadily in wealth and numbers, which its members credit to its religious character. Later colonies mostly allowed private goods and family life, and few grew strong.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socrates:
Socrates, Greek philosopher and educational reformer of the fifth century before Christ, was born at Athens in 469 and died there in 399. After an Athenian education in music, geometry, and gymnastics, he worked briefly as a sculptor in his father's workshop. A divine call, as he told it, turned him to the moral and intellectual reform of his fellow citizens, and he styled himself a gadfly to the Athenian state.

Unconventional and deliberately shocking in manner, he provoked the Sophists and their friends, and faced formal charges of impiety and subverting moral traditions. Defiant before his judges, he refused to retract or apologize, and drank the hemlock with calm dignity. His method, Socratic irony followed by definition through questions, made knowledge through concepts the foundation of moral science, holding knowledge to be virtue and ignorance vice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spanish-ameri:
Spanish-American universities grew up under the joint care of Church and State. This entry traces their rise, revolution, and survival. Lima's University of St. Mark's claims the title of oldest in America, having begun by royal decree. Santo Domingo's university was the first founded by a papal bull, established by Paul III in 1538 at Dominican request, and given legal life by Philip II in 1558.

Similar foundations spread across the colonies, flourishing while Church and State acted together. At independence they passed to state control, with Havana's university the exception, staying in religious hands late into the nineteenth century. The entry offers a compact institutional history for readers tracing higher learning in Latin America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-species:
Species, in scholastic terminology, is the necessary determinant of every act of knowing, and this entry defends a doctrine often misunderstood and mocked. Knowledge, it argues, is the union of an object with the mind, so the known thing must somehow be present in the knower, in St. Thomas's phrase, the known exists in the knower.

Because no faculty starts with innate ideas, each begins as a mere capacity to acquire knowledge, indeterminate in two ways that the entry spells out. Modern psychology, using different words, offers an account essentially identical to the medieval one, the entry claims. And readers get a careful restatement of why the schoolmen thought a likeness of the thing must stand between mind and world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-caesarius-:
St. Caesarius of Arles was bishop, administrator, preacher, and theologian, born at Chalons in Burgundy in 470 or 471. He died at Arles on 27 August 543, according to Malnory. This entry follows a boy who entered Lerins when young, but whose health gave way, so the abbot sent him to Arles to recuperate. There he won the affection and esteem of Bishop Aeonus, who had him ordained deacon and priest.

On the bishop's death Caesarius was unanimously chosen successor in 502 or 503. He ruled Arles for forty years with apostolic courage and prudence, and stands out in that unhappy period's history as Gaul's foremost bishop. His episcopal city, near the Rhone's mouth and close to Marseilles, kept its importance in the social, commercial, and industrial life of Gaul and the Mediterranean world. As a political centre it suffered all the vicissitudes of the early sixth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-de:
Francis de Sales, bishop of Geneva and doctor of the Church, preached his way back into Calvinist Savoy with gentleness rather than force. Born at Thorens on 21 August 1567 to old Savoyard aristocracy, he was eldest of six brothers, destined by his father for the magistracy. After Clermont in Paris, where a torment over predestination broke before an image of Our Lady, he studied law at Padua and took his doctorate in 1592. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Lyons to 28 December 1622.

With Jane Frances de Chantal he founded the Visitation in 1607, for girls and widows called to religion without strength for great austerities. His Lent and Advent courses at Dijon, Chambéry, and Grenoble drew crowds, and at Grenoble he converted the marshal Lesdiguières. Refusing Paris honours, he returned to Annecy, dying at Lyons in a gardener's small room after apoplexy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gertrude-o:
Gertrude of Nivelles, abbess from childhood's refusal of marriage, built a double monastery that welcomed Irish pilgrims. Born in 626 to Pepin I of Landen, younger sister of Begga of Andenne, she was ten when her father feasted King Dagobert and nobles. Asked to marry Austrasia's duke's son, she indignantly refused any man, declaring Christ alone her bridegroom. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 17 March 659.

After Pepin's death in 639, her mother Itta raised a double monastery at Nivelles. Amandus of Maastricht had advised the plan. The house held both men and women. Itta set Gertrude as first abbess, living there as a nun herself. Among its pilgrims came the Irish brothers Foillan and Ultan, travelling from Rome toward Peronne, where their brother Fursey lay buried. The entry joins a child's vow to a house of hospitality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-giles:
Giles, abbot of the forest near Nîmes, fled fame from Athens to Gaul and found it waiting at every retreat. Said to be born of illustrious Athenian parents about the middle of the seventh century, he gave himself early to spiritual things. Noble birth and high repute hindered his perfection at home, so he crossed to Gaul, settling first near the Rhone's mouth, then by the Gard. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows him into deeper solitude.

Crowds followed again, so he withdrew to a dense forest near Nîmes, living many years with only a hind for company. The king's hunters, pursuing the hind, discovered his refuge. Legend names the king Wamba of the Visigoths, though Franks had expelled Visigoths from Nîmes a century and a half earlier. The king esteemed him highly, but Giles's humility refused honours. The entry joins legend, chronology, and a hermit's flight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hermes:
Hermes, martyr and supposed bishop of Salona in Dalmatia, is a name tangled among several early Christians. Very little is known about him with certainty. Paul's greeting in Romans 16:14 names a Hermes among others, and many suppose that name refers to this article's subject. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 reports he is also said to have followed Titus as bishop of Dalmatia and to have been martyred.

Other threads pull apart. A Hermas appears in the Bollandists under Herodion. Pape calls him one of the seventy-two disciples. Migne counts him among seventy disciples with Patrobas, Linus, Gaius, and Philologus. Canisius tells of a presbyter Hermaeus, lacerated and hanged with Nicander of Myra. Hermes was a common slave name, and the entry leaves the identities honestly unresolved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilary-of-:
Hilary of Arles, archbishop from 429 to 449, was seized for office while returning to his hermitage. Born about 401 to a notable northern Gallic family, likely the same house as Honoratus, his predecessor, he was learned and rich, with every prospect of worldly success. At Honoratus's urgent pleading he abandoned honours and wealth, followed him to the Lérins hermitage, and gave himself to austerity and Scripture study. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 5 May 449.

When Honoratus lay dying as archbishop of Arles, Hilary attended his last moments. About to return to Lérins, he was retained by force and proclaimed archbishop in Honoratus's place. Yielding to constraint, he took up the heavy charge resolutely and attended councils at Riez, Orange, Vaison, and Arles. A dispute with Pope Leo then began, which the entry follows into the politics of Gallic church government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isaac-jogu:
Isaac Jogues, French Jesuit martyr of New York, was the first Catholic priest to reach Manhattan Island. Born at Orléans on 10 January 1607, he entered the Society in 1624, taught literature at Rouen, and sailed for Canada in 1636 with Montmagny, Champlain's successor. From Quebec he worked the Great Lakes country with Brébeuf and others for six dangerous years. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his martyrdom at Ossernenon to 18 October 1646.

Practical by temper, he aimed to fix his peoples in permanent homes, not merely to visit them. With Garnier among the Petuns, he and Raymbault reached Sault Ste. Marie, first missionaries, in Bancroft's words, to preach a thousand miles inland. Taken prisoner on 3 August 1642 and cruelly tortured, he endured thirteen months' slavery at Ossernenon, escaping through Dutch help at Fort Orange before returning to the mission that killed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ives-yves:
Ives of Brittany, ecclesiastical judge turned parish priest, earned the title advocate and patron of the poor. Born at Kermartin near Tréguier on 17 October 1253, he was son of Helori, lord of Kermartin, and Azo du Kenquis. He studied civil law at Paris from 1267, then canon law at Orléans from 1277. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Louannec to 19 May 1303.

In minor orders he became official, or church judge, of Rennes archdeaconry in 1280, studying Scripture meanwhile, and likely joining the Franciscan Tertiaries at Guingamp later. Tréguier's bishop invited him to serve as his official in 1284. He showed zeal and rectitude, resisting the king's unjust taxation as an encroachment on church rights. Ordained, he held Tredrez from 1285 and Louannec from 1293, dying in that parish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ivo-yves-o:
Ivo of Chartres, bishop for twenty-five years, was the West's most important canonist before Gratian. Born to a noble family about 1040 near Beauvais, he studied at Paris, then at Bec in Normandy with Lanfranc, at the same time as Anselm of Canterbury. About 1080 his bishop made him prior of St-Quentin's canons at Beauvais, where he ranked among France's best teachers. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death to 1116.

Appointed bishop of Chartres in 1090, after Geoffroy's deposition for simony, he faced opposition from Geoffroy's tenants at first. His government ranged over twenty-five years of Investiture struggle. No man is better portrayed in his own writing than Ivo in his letters and sermons, faithful to duty, high-minded, zealous, pious, and sound in judgment. The entry follows a teacher who became a bishop of letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-james-of-t:
James of the Marches, Franciscan preacher for half a century, is pictured with a chalice from which a snake escapes. Born poor at Monteprandone in 1391 to the Gangala family, he studied at Offida under his priest uncle, then at Ascoli, and took a doctorate in civil law at Perugia. After tutoring a noble family at Florence and judging sorcerers, he entered the Friars Minor at the Portiuncula on 26 July 1416. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Naples to 28 November 1476.

After novitiate at the Carceri hermitage and theology at Fiesole under Bernardine of Siena, he was ordained on 13 June 1420. Then he preached through Tuscany, the Marches, and Umbria for fifty years, with miracles marking his labours. The chalice and snake recall attempts to poison him, or, less likely, a dispute over the Precious Blood. The entry follows a lawyer turned wandering preacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-of-a:
Peter of Arbues, inquisitor of Aragon, was murdered in Saragossa cathedral in 1485 for his office. Born in 1441 or 1442 to the nobleman Antonio Arbues and Sancia Ruiz, he studied philosophy probably at Huesca. He then studied theology and law at Bologna's Spanish College of St Clement, where he was a model of learning and piety.

Returning to Spain, he became a canon regular at Saragossa and professed in 1474. Torquemada named him inquisitor provincial of Aragon in 1484, and he worked with zeal and justice. The entry insists no death sentence can be traced to him. Marranos he had punished plotted his killing, and assassins struck him down at prayer in Saragossa cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-prin:
Peter, prince of the Apostles, receives the fullest biographical treatment in this long Catholic Encyclopedia article. Simon son of Jona, born at Bethsaida, fished Lake Genesareth from Capernaum, where he lived with his mother-in-law. His brother Andrew brought him to Jesus, who renamed him Peter, the rock.

Sections follow him through the Gospels, his confession and denial, and his leadership at Jerusalem after the Ascension. They trace his missionary journeys in the East, the Council of the Apostles, and his activity and death at Rome. Tradition places his martyrdom under Nero and his burial on the Vatican hill. Feasts, relics, and artistic images close a survey worthy of the Church's first pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-theophanes:
Theophanes, chronicler of Constantinople, wrote the great Byzantine chronicle that carries history from 284 to 813. Born at Constantinople about 758 to Isaac, imperial governor of the islands of the White Sea, he came to court under Constantine Copronymus. Married at twelve, he persuaded his wife to a life of virginity, and in 799 they separated by consent for religion.

She entered a convent near Constantinople, while he joined Polychronius monastery near Cyzicus. He built a house on his own lands at Calonymus, then founded the abbey of the Great Acre at Sigriano and ruled it as abbot. Present at Nicaea in 787, he signed its decrees for images. Under Leo the Armenian's renewed iconoclasm he was exiled to Samothrace, where he died, probably on 12 March 817.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-hawes:
Stephen Hawes, a court poet of Henry VII, wrote the allegory The Passetyme of Pleasure in rime royal. Born in Suffolk about 1474 and dead about 1523, very little is known of his life. He was schooled at Oxford, travelled, and visited foreign universities, studying English literature and foreign languages. Returning home, he became groom of the chamber to Henry VII.

Anthony à Wood credits him with wit and a memory that could repeat many English poets by heart, above all Chaucer and Lydgate. At court, about 1506, he wrote The Passetyme of Pleasure, the poem for which he is best known, which ran through several editions over the next half century. Nearly six thousand lines in forty-five divisions, it revives medieval allegory from the Romaunt of the Rose, tracing a man's life in seven-line stanzas. Its verse marks, on the whole, a low ebb of English poetry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-theodorus:
Theodorus and Theophanes, brothers from Jerusalem, are called the Grapti, the written upon. This entry follows their defence of images in the second Iconoclastic controversy. Monks of St Sabas, trained in theology and strict in ascetic life, they reached Constantinople about 812 and opposed the emperor Leo V, who exiled them.

Under Michael II they were housed at Sosthenes, but Theophilos exiled them again, recalled them in 836, had them scourged, and cut twelve lines of verse into their skin. Exiled once more, Theodorus died, while Theophanes lived to see the controversy end in 842 and became archbishop of Nicaea. His poems, including one for his brother, remain unpublished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stylites:
Stylites were solitaries who lived on top of a pillar, and this entry traces that harsh calling to its roots. Pillar life crowned a wave of Eastern asceticism in the later fourth century, when fasts and self-restraint grew extreme. Palladius tells of a hermit who spent twenty-five years in a mountain cave without turning his face west, and Theodoret saw a man pass ten years in a tub hung from poles.

Simeon the Elder first climbed a pillar in 423, and imitators followed across Syria and Palestine, Daniel among them. A pagan parallel in Lucian, a man ascending a column at Hierapolis twice a year, probably never reached Simeon. The entry closes by defending such excess as a witness to penance in an age of corruption.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suburbicarian:
Suburbicarian dioceses are the sees nearest Rome, whose bishops form the order of cardinal bishops. This entry works through all seven: Albano, Frascati, Palestrina, Sabina, Ostia and Velletri, and Porto with St Rufina. Albano, on the Appian Way ten miles out, holds twelve parishes and 41,000 people, while Frascati in the Alban Hills holds eight parishes and 16,000, including Grottaferrata abbey.

Palestrina, ancient Praeneste, counts twenty-four parishes and 45,700 souls, and Sabina, largest of the group, counts thirty-five parishes and 55,000. Ostia, ancient seaport of Rome, joined with Velletri, counts sixteen parishes and 34,000, and Porto, the port built by Claudius, counts eighteen parishes. Rules for vacancies and funerals of cardinal bishops close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sulpicians-in:
The Sulpicians reached the United States at the birth of the American hierarchy, and this entry traces their first foothold. Their superior, Father Emery, first eyed Gallipolis on the Ohio as a refuge from revolution, but the papal nuncio at Paris urged Baltimore instead, the newly erected first American see.

Bishop Carroll, consecrated in England in 1790, welcomed Emery's offer, and on 10 July 1791 four Sulpicians landed at Baltimore. They bought the One Mile Tavern, opened classes that October with five students from France, and founded St Mary's, the first American seminary, on the same spot. Reinforcements in 1792 and 1795, including Flaget and Dubourg, joined a tiny priesthood serving a diocese from the Atlantic to the Mississippi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sylvestrines:
The Sylvestrines are a small monastic congregation following the Rule of Benedict, yet distinct from the Black monks and outside the Benedictine confederation. St Sylvester Gozzolini founded them on Monte Fano near Fabriano in 1231, keeping Benedict's Rule in its primitive form and going beyond it in austerity, above all in strict poverty.

At his death in 1267 eleven houses stood under him, and Innocent IV had sanctioned the congregation twenty years earlier. Houses spread through Ancona, Tuscany, and Umbria, and Rome's San Stefano del Cacco has been theirs since 1568. A Ceylon mission from 1855, centred on Kandy, and about a hundred members in 1911 complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-symeon-metaph:
Symeon Metaphrastes was the chief compiler of saints' legends for the Byzantine Menologia, and his name became famous among medieval Greek writers. Metaphrastes means compiler, from the word for such arrangements of saints' lives. Little is certain about his life, beyond his period in the later tenth century.

Psellus, who wrote his life, calls him a Logothete, a secretary of state with the title Magister, and a favourite of the emperor who ordered the collection. Most authorities now identify him with Symeon Magister the Logothete, chronicler under Nicephorus Phocas, on grounds of name, period, and inner likeness between chronicle and legends. An Arab chronicler of Antioch confirms the identification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabernacle-so:
Anne de Meeûs founded the Association of Perpetual Adoration at Brussels in 1848, to work for poor churches. Belgian bishops approved it by 1851, and within a few years members formed the Sisters of Perpetual Adoration, with de Meeûs as first superior general. In 1853 it became an archconfraternity for Belgium, spreading quickly to neighbouring countries.

Pius IX granted the Brussels mother-society power to affiliate confraternities worldwide in 1863, except in Rome itself, a restriction lifted when the sisters' mother-house moved to Rome. Statutes won approval in 1880, Leo XIII confirmed the transfer in 1881, and a brief of 1895 gave the title Prima Primaria. Members give an hour a month in adoration and yearly dues that buy vestment materials, sewn by women members for poor churches in many lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarbes:
Tarbes is a diocese of the Hautes-Pyrénées, the old land of Bigorre. It was absorbed into Bayonne in 1802. The Concordat of 1817 restored it in theory, and the bull of October 1822 did so in fact. It lost twenty-one parishes to Bayonne and twenty to Auch. It gained instead the Quatre Vallées and Louron valley from Auch and Comminges, as suffragan of Auch. Tradition names Girinus and Evex as Bigorre's first martyrs.

Vandals wasted the district until the priest Missolinus routed them. Priscillianism troubled it, and Arian Visigoths under Ewarik persecuted the clergy. Duchesne counts Aper, at Agde in 506, as first historically known bishop, discounting Justin and Faustus. Later bishops include Landeolus in 870 and William I, who helped frame the ancient For de Bigorre. Gramont tried to mediate between Henry VIII and Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teaching-of-m:
Moses ben Maimun, or Maimonides, was a Jewish commentator and philosopher born at Cordova in 1135. After sojourning in Spain, Palestine, and North Africa, he settled at Old Cairo in 1165. There he served as court physician and headed Egypt's Jewish communities, expounding the Talmud. He died at Cairo on 13 December 1204 and was buried at Tiberias. His commentaries include the Kitáb al-Siraj on the Mishnah and the Mishneh Torah, or Yad ha-Hazakah.

His chief philosophical work, the Guide of the Perplexed, first written in Arabic, reached Hebrew as Moreh Nebûkîm and Latin as Doctor Perplexorum. Munk's French edition ran to thirteen volumes, and Friedländer gave the whole work in English in 1889. Through the Guide and his Mishnah introductions, Maimonides deeply influenced the Scholastics, above all Albert the Great, St Thomas, and Duns Scotus. Minor works cover God's unity, happiness, logic, resurrection, medicine, and the calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tertiaries: Tertiaries, or Third Orders, are persons living by the Third Rule of religious orders, either in the world outside a monastery or in a religious community. The idea is that persons who cannot enter a religious order strictly so-called may still enjoy, as far as possible, the advantages and privileges of religious orders. This appears clearest in the Third Order of St Francis, which, though not the oldest, has become the model for almost all other Third Orders. Tertiaries divide into Regular and Secular.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bernardin:
Cistercian sisters who laboured to restore the strict observance of their rule take the stage here, under the name Bernardines. In Spain the Bernardine Recollects led the way. They were joined in France and Savoy by the Bernardines of Divine Providence, of the Precious Blood, and of Flines and Lille, with scattered houses in Belgium and Peru.

Reform began with the abbesses of Las Huelgas at Burgos, who renewed Gradefes, Perales, and Saint Anne of Valladolid toward the end of the sixteenth century. Saint Anne became mother-house of the new reform in 1601, and Paul V approved its constitutions in 1606. From there the movement reached the Indies and the Canary Islands, carrying Cistercian austerity into a new age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bohemians:
Bohemian emigrants to America, surprising in number for so beautiful and resourceful a homeland, are traced here through political, religious, and economic causes. Religious strife after John Hus's preaching produced sects that were crushed following the Battle of White Mountain near Prague in 1620. Many fled abroad, some as far as America.

Augustyn Herman and Frederick Filip stand out among the earliest arrivals. Herman, trusted by Governor Stuyvesant of New Amsterdam with important missions, drew the first map of Maryland, a copy of which survives in the British Museum. Later waves, parishes, schools, societies, and newspapers carry the story into the twentieth century, when Bohemians formed a visible strand of American Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-books-of-:
Four books sharing the Machabee name are sorted here, though only the first two count as canonical for Catholics. The other two, like all four for Protestants, rank as apocryphal. First Machabees earned its title from the family's revolt, the fourth from its martyrs, and the third, unrelated to that period, from a persecution of Jews it recounts.

First Machabees tells the Jewish struggle for religious and political freedom under Judas Machabeus, from Persian rule through Seleucid domination to revolt under Mathathias. Second Machabees retells part of the same history with edifying purpose. Authorship, sources, versions, and canonicity are weighed for each book in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-court-of-:
Canterbury's chief and oldest court, the Court of Arches, is the tribunal explained in this short entry. Its name comes from Saint Mary le Bow, Sancta Maria de Arcubus, in Cheapside, where it anciently sat. Judge of the court, the Official Principal of the Arches, heard causes across the province and appeals from the Dean of the Arches.

Dean's peculiar covered thirteen parishes, including Saint Mary le Bow, inside London diocese yet free of its bishop. Dean and Principal in time merged into one office. Public Worship Regulation Act of 1874 gave Canterbury and York provincial judges, deeming all later Canterbury province proceedings taken in the Arches Court. Appeals beyond it to the Privy Council close the sketch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-eight-bea:
Solemn blessings opening the Sermon on the Mount, the Eight Beatitudes of Matthew chapter 5, verses 3 to 10, are the Gospel text expounded here. Four recur in slightly different form in Luke chapter 6, verse 22, at a sermon's start parallel to Matthew 5 to 7, matched there by four woes in verses 24 to 26. Matthew's fuller account and pride of place fit the First Gospel's spiritual view of the Messianic kingdom.

Poetic parallelism of thought and phrase, hallmark of biblical poetry, makes the Beatitudes perhaps the only strictly poetical sayings of the Lord. Text, translation, and each blessing's sense follow: poor in spirit, mourners, meek, hungry for justice, merciful, pure of heart, peacemakers, and persecuted. Their promise of the kingdom crowns Christian ethics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-machabees:
Priestly rebels who won Jewish freedom give this entry its family. Mathathias launched the revolt against Antiochus IV Epiphanes of Syria, and his house ruled the commonwealth until Herod the Great overthrew it. Machabee began as the surname of Judas, third son of Mathathias, then spread to all his descendants and to all who joined the rising.

Hammer explains the name best, from Aramaic maqqaba, earned by Judas's valour against Israel's foes. Hasmoneans, from ancestor Hashmon, serves as the family name in old Jewish writers and now labels Simon's dynasty. Martyrs of Second Machabees, chapter 6 and 7, also bear the name, linking war and witness in one proud title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-organic-a:
Napoleon's law for public worship, voted with the Concordat itself, is the subject here. Seventy-seven articles touched Catholicism and forty-four Protestantism, presented to Tribunate and legislative body together and published as law on 8 April 1802 under one title and preamble. French governments down to 1905 treated them as inseparable from the Concordat.

Pius VII protested on 24 May 1802 that they had issued without his knowledge and needed change before he could accept them. Catholic articles fall under four titles, the first covering the Church's government in relation to state rights and constitution. State approval for papal acts, seminaries, and appointments shows a concordat fenced by police power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-synods-of:
Church councils at Arles, across five centuries, are gathered here in order. The first, in 314, aimed to end the Donatist row, backing Rome’s council of 313: Caecilian of Carthage stood rightly chosen, Donatus of Casae Nigrae stood cast out. Twenty-two rules on abuses since Diocletian’s persecution rank among early church law’s key texts.

A council of 353, with two papal envoys present, leaned Arian, drawn into shunning communion with Athanasius and refusing to condemn Arius, to Pope Liberius’s grief. The synod of 443, or 452, framed fifty-six rules, mostly repeats of old discipline: new converts barred from high orders, married men seeking priesthood vowing continence, and rules for making bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ursulines:
Angela de Merici's teaching order for girls, the first of its kind for women in the Church, is the subject here. Convinced of a divine call to found an educational institute, Angela spent seventeen years guiding young women known as the Company of Saint Ursula. They lived at home with their families yet met at set times for conferences and devotions. 

Hindrances at last gave way, and in 1535 twelve members formed a community with episcopal approval, Angela as superioress. Enthusiasm carried the movement swiftly through Italy, Germany, and France, with houses soon multiplying, each independent. Constitutions fitted to the institute's special work followed, shaping girls' schooling for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theatines:
Clerks Regular known as Theatines, founded to recall clergy and laity to holy living, are introduced here. Gaetano dei Conti di Tiene, Paolo Consiglieri, Bonifacio da Colle, and Giovanni Pietro Carafa, later Paul IV, founded the order. Carafa, Bishop of Chieti or Theate in the Abruzzi, gave the congregation its distinctive name among later-modelled groups such as Jesuits, Barnabites, and Somaschi. 

Gaetano consecrated the order to the Cross as its emblem. Foundation fell on the Finding of the Holy Cross, 3 May 1524, approved by Clement VII on 24 June in the brief Exponi Nobis. Solemn profession before Saint Peter's papal altar followed on 14 September. Reform of clergy, preaching, and pastoral care fill the order's early story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoric-thi:
Schoolman Theodoric of Chartres, lover of the classics, fought a lone battle for good Latin and Greek learning. Born in France early in the twelfth century, he died at Chartres about 1150. He likely learned at Chartres under his brother Bernard and led its school in 1121. Paris teaching came next, with John of Salisbury among his pupils, and Chartres teaching again in 1141.

His books were the Eptateuchon on the seven liberal arts, De Sex Dierum Operibus, and a note on De Inventione Rhetorica ad Herennium. The first still lies in manuscript at Chartres, the rest saw print in 1884 and 1890. He loved the classics with zeal, took an interest in nature lore through Herman's Ptolemy Planisphere, and held a Platonic view of reality that gave ideas full being.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theological-c:
Church judgments that brand teachings harmful to faith or morals are the censures explained here. They differ from canonical censures such as excommunication, suspension, and interdict, which punish offenders. Theological censure judges doctrine, not persons, and the Church has claimed that right from Saint Paul onward.

Paul declared anathema on perverters of Christ's Gospel and warned against profane novelties and false knowledge. Newman saw the teaching office work in two ways: stating truth plainly and condemning error. Popes, councils, Roman congregations, universities, and special commissions all share in the task, down to Pius X's condemnation of Modernism. Grades of censure, from heretical to rash, fill the rest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-willia:
Thomas William Allies, an English writer born in 1813, moved from Anglican ministry to Catholic letters. A lonely boy at a country parsonage, he loved books more than company. He won the Newcastle Scholarship at Eton at sixteen, studied at Oxford, and took Anglican orders. His poetry and philosophy blended in a mind that prized clear thought.

Newman's departure from the Church of England in 1845 left Allies without his guiding star, yet he pressed on. His Journal drew a sharp rebuke from the Bishop of Oxford. On 11 September 1850 he converted, giving up his living, his work and his prospects with a wife and three sons to face the world. He then gave his mind to Catholic truth in a long career as a writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tithes:
Tithes are the tenth part of the increase from land and stock, set apart for the clergy or for religious and charitable uses. The word comes from the Anglo-Saxon teotha, meaning a tenth. Scripture already shows the custom: Abraham gives tithes of spoil to Melchizedek, and Jacob vows a tenth of all he gains. Under the Mosaic Law the tenth of field produce, tree fruit and firstborn livestock went to God.

God in turn assigned the tithes to the Levites for their service in the tabernacle. Later law divided tithes into predial tithes from crops, mixed tithes from cattle, milk, cheese and wool, and personal tithes from work or trade. Charlemagne's capitularies first enforced payment by civil law, and English statutes from Westminster in 1285 onward recognized the tithe as a legal charge on the land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tralles:
Tralles was a titular see subject to Ephesus in Asia Minor, founded, so tradition says, by Argians and Thracians on a slope of Mount Messogis in the Meander valley. It ranked among the richest and most populous cities of Lydia, and King Attalus kept a splendid palace there. Zeus Larasios was its local god, with Apollo Pythius and others also worshipped.

An earthquake destroyed Tralles, and Augustus rebuilt it as Caesarea. Christianity came very early: Ignatius of Antioch, writing to its church, notes that Bishop Polybius visited him at Smyrna and warns the people against Docetism, showing a church already well organized. Its bishops run from Heracleon in 431 to John in 1230. About 1270 Andronicus rebuilt and repeopled it to 36,000 souls, but the Turks soon retook and demolished it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trocmades:
A titular see of Galatia Secunda, suffragan of Pessinus, named for no city any geographer or historian mentions. Hierocles gives a "regio Trocnades" instead, likely the Galatian name of a tribe on the left bank of the Sangarius, centred near the present village of Kaimez.

All the episcopal lists up to the thirteenth century place the see among Pessinus's suffragans, the latest calling it Lotinou, perhaps Plotinou after St. Plotinus. Le Quien lists four bishops. They run from Cyriacus at the Robber Synod of Ephesus in 449 to Constantine in 879. A Cyriacus said to have attended Nicaea in 325 is absent from the authentic lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-troyes:
A diocese covering the Department of Aube, re-established in 1802 as a suffragan of Paris. At first it also held Yonne, and its bishop bore the titles of Troyes, Auxerre and Châlons-sur-Marne. Châlons became a separate see in 1822, and Auxerre passed to Sens, leaving Troyes a suffragan of Sens.

Its bishop list, known since the ninth century, is judged trustworthy by Duchesne. Among its bishops are St. Lupus, who forced the Huns to spare Troyes and was carried off as Attila's hostage, and St. Prudentius, who wrote against Gottschalk, while the Lirey Winding Sheet, once exposed here, is now honoured at Turin. The diocese also honours Saint Mathia and Saint Helena as patronesses of the town, their relics found at Troyes in 980 and transferred there in 1209.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universities:
This general entry treats universities as a whole, while particular Catholic foundations get their own articles. It runs in five parts: origin and organization, academic work and development, Renaissance and Reformation, the modern period, and Catholic action. The name is sometimes given to the famed schools of Athens and Alexandria, but universities properly arose in the Middle Ages. Legends long credited Oxford to King Alfred, Paris to Charlemagne, and Bologna to Theodosius II.

For thirteenth-century foundations dates and charters can be fixed, but the earliest beginnings stay obscure. The entry follows the schools from cathedral and monastic roots through the dialectical method and Scholasticism, shaped by Peter Lombard and crowned in St Thomas's Summa. At Bologna the new learning turned practical, toward civil and canon law under Irnerius and Gratian. Later parts carry the story through humanism, reform, and the modern Catholic university.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vannes:
Vannes covers the Department of Morbihan in Brittany and was restored by the Concordat of 1802. It was formed from the old Diocese of Vannes, minus parishes east of the Oust River given to Rennes. It also took the district of Roche-Bernard from Nantes, the southern part of old St Malo, and the district of Gourin from Quimper. It answered to Tours until 1859 and since then to Rennes.

Morbihan holds more monuments of old Gallic worship than any part of France, with the famed long avenues of menhirs at Carnac. By tradition St Clair, first Bishop of Nantes, died in the third century while preaching in the region. The entry follows the diocese's bishops, its shrines, and its modern parishes, a compact history of a Breton see rich in stone and legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-christoph:
Christopher Bales, also called Bayles or Evers, was a priest and martyr born at Coniscliffe near Darlington about 1564, executed on 4 March 1590. He entered the English College at Rome on 1 October 1583, but poor health sent him to Reims, where he was ordained on 28 March 1587. Sent to England on 2 November 1588, he was soon seized, racked, and tortured by Topcliffe, and hung by his hands for twenty-four hours at a time, bearing all with patience.

Tried at last for high treason, on the charge of ordination overseas and coming to England to exercise his office, he put a question to Judge Anderson. He asked whether St Augustine, Apostle of the English, was also a traitor. The judge answered no, but said the act had since been made treason by law. Bales suffered on 4 March 1590, about Easter, in Fleet Street, London.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-jo:
Edward Jones was a priest and martyr born in the Diocese of St Asaph in Wales at an unknown date, who died in London on 6 May 1590. Raised Anglican, he was received into the church at the English College, Reims, in 1587, ordained priest in 1588, and went to England the same year. In 1590 a priest-catcher posing as a Catholic seized him in a Fleet Street shop.

Jailed in the Tower and brutally tortured by Topcliffe, he at last admitted he was a priest and had been an Anglican. Those admissions were used at his trial, yet he mounted a skilful and learned defence, arguing that a confession wrung out by torture could not lawfully convict. The court praised his courageous bearing but convicted him of high treason as a priest entering England, and he suffered the same day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-d:
William Davies was one of the most celebrated Welsh priests to suffer under Elizabeth, executed at Beaumaris in July 1593. Born in North Wales, he reached Reims in 1582, was ordained in 1585. Laboured with great zeal in Wales until his arrest at Holyhead in 1592, while sending four students by way of Ireland to Valladolid.

Thrown into a foul dungeon in Beaumaris Castle, he frankly owned that he was a priest. His patience won easier confinement, and he could celebrate Mass and receive visitors, Catholics seeking counsel and Protestant ministers coming to dispute. Condemned at the assizes, he intoned the Te Deum, a hymn of praise, which his companions took up. After examinations at Ludlow and Bewdley, where he outwitted attempts to trap him into a Protestant service, he was put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veneration-of:
This long doctrinal article defends the Catholic veneration, or reverent honour, of sacred images against the charge of idolatry. It opens with the First Commandment's apparent ban on graven things, noting the golden calf as proof of how easily Israel might slide from making a statue to worshipping it.

Insists the law's thrust is against strange gods and adoration, not against every picture. From there the survey moves through the Old Testament, the early Church, and the iconoclast controversies, distinguishing the honour paid to an image from worship owed to God alone. Later sections describe popular devotion in practice, icons crowned, incensed, and kissed, lamps burning before them. Images reputed not made by hands, while arguing that such reverence passes through the image to the holy person it portrays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-versailles:
Versailles is a French diocese covering Seine-et-Oise, created in 1790 by the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and maintained by the Concordat of 1802, losing Eure-et-Loir to restored Chartres in 1822. It was pieced together from parts of the old dioceses of Paris, Chartres, Rouen, Sens, Beauvais, Senlis, and Evreux.

The town itself was a mere village when Louis XIII bought it in 1632 and built a small château. Under Louis XIV, Mansart raised the great palace from 1661, Lenôtre laid out the gardens. Lebrun directed the interiors; the king lived there constantly from 1682. French monarchs resided at Versailles for over a century, and there the 1783 treaty recognized American independence and, in 1789, the Third Estate constituted itself a national assembly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-canes:
Vincent Canes, in religion John Baptist, was an English Franciscan controversialist who died in London in June 1672. Raised Protestant on the Nottingham and Leicestershire borders, he embraced Catholicism at twenty, went to Douai, joined the Friars Minor. Became lecturer in philosophy and then professor of theology in their convent.

Back in England he laboured strenuously for the faith and was chosen by Catholics to answer Dr Stillingfleet. His ability as a controversialist was strengthened, the entry notes, by an absence of bitterness toward opponents, and his elegant, graceful style made his writings effective. His works include The Reclaimed Papist of 1655, Fiat Lux of 1662, a plea for moderation and quiet after England's religious tumults. Dedicated to the Countess of Arundel, and Infallibility of 1665 as its appendix.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-votive-office:
A votive office is an office not entered in the general calendar but adopted to satisfy a special devotion. By Pius X's constitution Divino Afflatu of November 1911 all votive offices were abolished. Before that action such an office might be celebrated, under rules the entry summarizes, either by privilege or by custom predating St Pius V's bull.

They were called votive because recitation remained optional in principle, as the object of a privilege, even when, after the privilege was obtained, it became accidentally obligatory. They differed from offices ad libitum properly so called. Held a place in a calendar under the rubric ad libitum and might be indicated at will by the compiler of the Ordo. Two classes existed: votive offices granted to petitioners but obligatory after concession, such as the Office of the Blessed Sacrament for Thursdays, and others the entry goes on to detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-waldenses:
The Waldenses were a religious group arising in the second half of the twelfth century and living on, much changed, to the present day. Their name comes from Waldes, their founder, with variants Valdesii and Vallenses. Their vow of extreme poverty earned them the name Poor, their Lyons origin Leonistae, and their sandals or wooden shoes Sandaliati, Insabbatati, and Sabotiers.

Some Waldenses claimed apostolic origins, with Paul founding their Piedmont valley churches on his way to Spain. Later sections follow their structure, a yearly synod checking districts, taking men into ministry, and casting out the unworthy. The Lombard communities, more radical than the French, who held sacramental validity depended on the minister's worthiness and rejected the Catholic Church as Satan's community.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wales:
Wales is the western portion of Great Britain between the Irish Sea and the Dee, the English border counties, the Severn estuary, the Bristol Channel, and St George's Channel. Its name was given not by its inhabitants but by Teutonic occupiers, meaning territory of the alien race. The Welsh have ever called themselves Cymry, and their country in poetry alone Gwalia.

After a 330-year invasion, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes drove the earlier Britons into the western hills, and the entry follows Welsh history, language. Religion from pre-Aryan nature worship and Celtic deities, equations of Greek and Latin gods, through Roman occupation and Llandaff, the oldest episcopal see, to Cardiff's recognition as capital. Its religion sections trace nature cults deifying abstract ideas rather than material objects, and the long Christian story that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-henry:
William Henry Coombes was an English priest and scholar who escaped Revolutionary France and served one parish for nearly forty years. Born in 1767, he died in 1850. Raised at Meadgate in Somerset under his Douai-trained uncle, he entered Douai at twelve, took orders in 1791, and fled from Dourlens to England in October 1793 as the Revolution raged. A doctor of theology, he worked with Bishop Douglass at Old Hall seminary as teacher and vice-president.

From 1810 Coombes served Shepton Mallet until retiring to Downside monastery in 1849. Friends called him spiritual, self-denying, and deeply learned. His books include Sacred Eloquence from Basil and Chrysostom, and an Escape from France memoir with the sufferings of Pius VI. Lives of Saint Francis de Sales and Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, and The Essence of Religious Controversy of 1827 complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-co:
William of Conches was a twelfth-century thinker who carried Arab science and Platonic cosmology into Christian schools. Born about 1100, he taught theology at Paris, then about 1122 became tutor to Henry Plantagenet. A friend's warning about the risks in his Platonic realism as applied to theology turned him toward philosophy and the natural science of the Arabs. When and where he died is uncertain.

Authorship of his works is debated, but he likely wrote glosses on Plato's Timaeus, a commentary on Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue called Dragmaticon, and a treatise, Magna de Naturis Philosophia. A pupil of Bernard of Chartres, he shared the Chartrain love of Plato, humane letters, and nature study. He ranks among the first medieval Christian thinkers to use Arab physics and physiology, reaching him through Constantine the African's translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ju:
William of Jumièges, surnamed Calculus, was an eleventh-century Benedictine historian of the Normans. Practically nothing is known of his life beyond Norman birth, monkhood at the royal abbey of Jumièges, and death about 1090. His fame rests wholly on the Historia Normannorum in eight books, the chief source for Norman history from 851 to 1137. An early manuscript survived at Rouen until the Revolution and now sits in Paris's Bibliothèque Nationale.

William built his first four books on Dudon of Saint Quentin, praising his predecessor yet pruning his romancing and errors and using all that was sound. Only seven books are William's own, running to 1087; an anonymous hand added the eighth, reaching Abbot Boson's death in 1137. Ordericus Vitalis and Thomas Walsingham drew heavily on him, and the work first reached print at Frankfurt in 1603.
