catholic-encyclopedia-1913-williamites:
Williamites was the name of two small religious families, one rooted at Monte Vergine and one at Maleval. The Monte Vergine branch sprang from William of Vercelli's houses in Naples, including a double house at Guglieto. Celestine III confirmed the congregation in November 1197. By 1611 it counted forty-five houses; Benedict XIV confirmed new constitutions in 1741, and in 1879 the mother-house alone joined the Cassinese Congregation, keeping its white habit.

The Hermits of Saint William were founded by Albert, companion and biographer of Saint William of Maleval, and Renaldus, a physician at Maleval. It spread swiftly over Italy, Germany, France, Flanders, and Hungary until Gregory IX softened its harsh rule in 1229. Many houses took Benedictine or Augustinian rule, and in 1256 Alexander IV's new Augustinian Hermits drew some away while others stayed apart, numbering fifty-four houses in three provinces by 1435.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yellow-knives:
The Yellow Knives are a sub-arctic Déné people, called Copper Indians by Hearne and Red Knives by Mackenzie and Franklin. About five hundred strong, they now roam the bleak wastes northeast of Great Slave Lake, though 250 years ago they hunted along the Coppermine River. Their name comes from knives they once made from copper scattered on a mountain slope, which drew Hudson Bay fur traders and prompted Hearne's trek to the Coppermine's mouth.

Legend says a woman showed them the copper, then sank into the ground, taking most of it with her. When whites first met them, they were bold and unscrupulous, often bullying gentler neighbours until bloody revenge fell on them. Remote habitat has left them among the least civilized-touched tribes. They are now Catholics, served by Oblate missionaries from two missions on Great Slave Lake's north shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zionites:
Zionites were a sect of visionary fanatics who flourished in the eighteenth century at Ronsdorf in the Duchy of Berg, now in Prussia's Rhine province. The sect sprang from a Philadelphian society founded at Elberfeld in 1726 by Elias Eller and Pastor Daniel Schleiermacher.

The society's prophetess was Anna van Bushel, a baker's daughter, who had dreams, visions, and apparitions. After his wife's death Eller married her; she called herself mother of Zion, her husband father of Zion, and prophesied she would bear the world's saviour. Her first child was a daughter, but Eller consoled the society with Scripture texts; a son born in 1733 died two years later. In 1737 the sect left Elberfeld and founded Ronsdorf, raised to city rank in 1745 through Eller's influence. Eller took the chief offices, lived in great pomp, and governed tyrannically until death.
cautionary-tales: Cautionary Tales, Hilaire Belloc's comic verses for children. Jim and Matilda. This book preserves that classic. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
celibates:
Celibates, by George Moore, collects three long stories about people who renounce love, in a 1915 New York printing with an introduction by Temple Scott. Scott looks back twenty years to the book's first publication in 1895 and finds the Moore of both dates the same artist. Moore, he says, is never a reporter or a philosopher, but a man expressing himself through whatever personalities stir his imagination to create.

The three tales study their celibates from inside. One is a young woman artist in London. One is a man whose single passion curdles into religion and routine. Others turn purity into a kind of self worship. Moore writes desire denied with slow, exact attention to rooms, clothes, and weather of mind. The introduction warns that fact matters less here than rendering, at the moment English fiction was learning new candor.
cenci-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas recounted the Cenci horror in this piece from his Celebrated Crimes, dated by its heading to 1598. Dumas starts as a tourist in Rome, following a guide through St. Peter in Montorio, before the story takes him: Francesco Cenci, a rich Roman noble of monstrous cruelty, kept his family in terror, and his daughter Beatrice became the center of the case. The family turned on the tyrant, and murder answered tyranny.

Rome then tried the Cenci, and pope and people took opposite sides on the executions that followed. Dumas tells the tale as documented melodrama, with the famous portrait of Beatrice hanging over it. His Celebrated Crimes series mined real dossiers for exactly this mixture: history, pity, and judicial cruelty in gorgeous prose.
charmides:
Plato's Charmides, in Benjamin Jowett's translation with his analyses and introductions, stages Socrates fresh from the battle of Potidaea meeting the beautiful young Charmides in a wrestling school. The question is temperance, sophrosyne, and each definition fails in turn: quietness, modesty, doing one's own business, self-knowledge. Critias, the boy's guardian and a future tyrant, defends the argument.

Jowett's introduction notes the dialogue's puzzle: Plato here asks whether a knowledge of knowledge is possible or useful, almost in Aristotle's spirit, though elsewhere he identifies good and knowledge. The Charmides matters for that puzzle and for its portrait of Socratic irony playing on Athenian beauty and ambition just before the city's great war.
checkmates-for-three-pieces: William Brett Fishburne's Checkmates for Three Pieces is a data file of chess endgame positions rather than a prose book. Each line gives one board position in FEN, a compact notation that records where the pieces stand and whose move it is. Every position uses only three pieces: the two kings plus a queen or a rook. The side to move faces checkmate, the trapped king with no legal escape.
chess-history-and-reminiscences:
H. E. Bird's Chess History and Reminiscences condenses his forty-six years at the board into one gossipy volume. Bird, an English master, admits in his preface that the work is the essence of a much larger one. He mixes what can be discovered about the origin of chess with his own memories. The dedication honours an opponent and patron of nearly forty years.

Three Indian traditions compete in his account of the game's invention. Progress runs through China, Egypt, Persia, and Arabia into medieval Europe. Chaucer, Caxton, and Elizabeth's reign mark the English chapters. Philidor's ascendency introduces the modern masters, Simpson's club, and the congresses of Bird's own century. Specimens of play and a review of Steinitz follow. Bird writes as a participant, not a scholar, and his reminiscences of players' temperaments are the book's living core.
chinese-sketches:
Herbert A. Giles knew China from eight years of travel and consular work when he gathered these sketches, first printed in a Shanghai newspaper. Giles opens with the death of the young emperor in January 1875 and the secret accession of a child successor. Other pieces take up customs, names, examinations, and street life as he met them with pencil and notebook in hand.

His preface fights the English habit of calling the Chinese a degraded race. Giles answers that he found a hardworking, sober, and happy people, placed between Western wealth and Western misery. The sketches mix reportage, folklore, and argument. They read as one informed foreigner's attempt to correct his countrymen, anecdote by anecdote.
chronicles-of-the-canongate-1st-series:
Walter Scott framed Chronicles of the Canongate through Mr Chrystal Croftangry, an elderly Edinburgh gentleman who edits other people's manuscripts. The publisher's crisis of 1826 had ended Scott's anonymity, as his 1827 introduction explains. The first series contains two long tales plus that introduction and an appendix on the Theatrical Fund dinner.

The Highland Widow tells of Elspat MacTavish, whose son's soldiering ends on the scaffold. The Two Drovers follows English and Scottish cattle men whose quarrel turns on honor and a concealed dirk. Bruce's vengeance in the Highland pass appears inside the widow's back-story of cateran raids. Scott's late tales trade his early romance for tragic compression, and they still cut deep.
cinderella-or-the-little-glass-slipper-a:
Anonymous authors fill this children's story collection headed by Cinderella, or the Little Glass Slipper, printed without credits for its many contributors. The contents run to dozens of short pieces: Fanny's Telephone Order, Sir Gobble, A Sad Thanksgiving Party, Mean Boy, Naughty Pumpkin's Fate, The Ice-King's Reign, and Christmas in California among them. Moral tales and holiday stories mix freely.

One story follows Hiram, who catches shrimp early and late to buy his mother a ring costing three dollars and twenty-two cents. Another sets four dolls before a dressing-case mirror at a children's party. The volume typifies nineteenth-century Sunday-school and gift-book fare: brief, improving, and varied enough to hold a child's whole winter of evenings.
clotelle-a-tale-of-the-southern-states:
William Wells Brown, who escaped slavery himself, wrote Clotelle as a tale of the southern states built from the legend of Thomas Jefferson's enslaved daughter. His contents announce the machinery of the system chapter by chapter: the slave's social circle, the negro sale, the slave speculator, the slave-holding parson, and today a mistress, tomorrow a slave. Clotelle, the quadroon heroine, is sold away from her mother and lover.

The middle chapters move through slave hunts, prisons, and self-sacrifice, with servants carrying compliments between great houses in the ordinary courtesies that slavery hollowed out. Brown revised the novel across four versions over fourteen years. It stands among the first novels published by an African American.
cobwebs-and-cables: Cobwebs and Cables, Hesba Stretton's tale. Its story unfolds. This book preserves that novel. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
complete-works-of-plutarch-volume-3-essa:
Plutarch's essays and miscellanies fill this third volume of his complete works in English, the Moralia beyond the famous Lives. The contents divide into philosophical essays and literary essays. The philosophical set opens with an attack on Epicurus, arguing that his doctrine makes a pleasant life impossible, and continues against the Stoics.

The Symposiacs preserve table talk on dozens of questions, and short pieces treat fate, the eating of flesh, and Plato's problems. The literary essays include the Life and Poetry of Homer, advice on how a young man ought to hear poems, and the Banquet of the Seven Wise Men. The Malice of Herodotus closes the list, a prosecution of the father of history for bias. The old translation's thee-and-thou manner is part of the flavour.
condensed-novels-new-burlesques:
Bret Harte turned parodist in Condensed Novels: New Burlesques, shrinking the popular novels of his day into mocking miniatures. Rupert the Resembler deflates Anthony Hope's Prisoner of Zenda romances, with a hero proud of resembling everybody and being nobody. The Stolen Cigar Case imitates Conan Doyle, and other pieces take off Hall Caine, Marie Corelli, and Kipling, their authors' names printed in coy dashes.

Harte copies each writer's tricks so exactly that the joke needs no explaining: the mannerisms were the message all along. These burlesques first made his name in California magazines. Read beside his mining tales, they show a second gift, literary mimicry sharp enough to wound and fond enough to entertain.
crucial-instances:
Edith Wharton's Crucial Instances gathers seven stories, opening with The Duchess at Prayer. Wharton asks whether the reader has ever questioned the shuttered front of an old Italian house, a motionless mask as smooth and mute as a priest's face behind which buzz confessional secrets.

Other houses declare their activities, Wharton writes, but the old palace down its narrow street stays as closed as death, its tall windows like blind eyes. Contents also include The Angel at the Grave, The Recovery, Copy: A Dialogue, The Rembrandt, The Moving Finger, and The Confessional. Readers of Wharton will find these instances finely observed studies of conscience and society.
david-crockett-his-life-and-adventures:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this biography of David Crockett for the American Pioneers and Patriots series. Abbott says plainly in his preface that Crockett was no model man. He presents him instead as a representative frontiersman whose wild life shows a whole class of early Americans. The narrative runs from Crockett's birth in Tennessee to his fame.

Early chapters cover a runaway boyhood, work as a farm labourer, and a scant schooling. Marriage and settlement follow, then soldiering under Andrew Jackson in the Creek War. Abbott takes Crockett through Indian warfare, a justice of the peace's bench, and election to Congress. Hunting tales, bear fights, and tall talk fill the later pages. The book closes with Crockett's restless move west and his death in Texas, told as popular history.
david-poindexter-s-disappearance-and-oth:
Julian Hawthorne's David Poindexter's Disappearance and Other Tales gathers mystery stories rooted in real cases. Hawthorne notes that English state trials hold many strange stories, but that local cases of small legal notice can stimulate imagination just as much.

The title tale retells the disappearance of David Poindexter, much discussed near the scene of its events, in the simple form in which Hawthorne heard it years before. Other tales in the contents include Ken's Mystery, When Half-Gods Go, the Gods Arrive, Set Not Thy Foot on Graves, and My Friend Paton. Readers who enjoy Victorian mystery with a documentary flavour will find Hawthorne's handling quiet and effective.
dead-men-tell-no-tales: Dead Men Tell No Tales, E, w, hornung's novel, the silent dead. This book preserves that story. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
definitions-essays-in-contemporary-criti:
Definitions, essays in contemporary criticism by Henry Seidel Canby, gathers the work of a Yale English professor who also edited the Literary Review of the New York Evening Post. Canby thanks the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's, the Century, the Nation, and the North American Review for leave to reprint. His preface explains the title. Literature in a civilization trying to be sophisticated and democratic at once has too many sources for one theory. Each essay opens a door by defining its term.

An informal definition, Canby says, is his whole method: approach a word like fiction, poetry, or realism through the books that embody it, and let writer and reader enter together. This first series surveys the literary scene of the early nineteen twenties. It asks what novelists, poets, and critics are trying to do.
derues-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas retells the career of Antoine Derues, the Paris poisoner, as one tale in his Celebrated Crimes series. The story opens in September 1751 with schoolboys at Chartres, where the young Derues is already marked out by cruelty and cunning. Dumas follows the boy as apprenticeship and marriage carry him to the capital.

derzhavin-spiritual-odes:
Russia's great eighteenth-century poet Gavrila Derzhavin speaks in his Spiritual Odes, given here in Russian. Derzhavin bridged classicism and the age of Pushkin, serving empresses while writing verse of startling personal force. His famous ode God stands among the landmarks of Russian poetry, translated across Europe in his lifetime.

Odes to God and meditations on death combine lofty philosophy with sudden, intimate feeling. A courtier who had seen favor and disgrace alike, Derzhavin writes about power's vanity from inside the palace. The Russian text preserves his bold, uneven music exactly. Modern Russian poetry effectively begins on this foundation stone. Readers with Russian will find the odes grand, strange, and unexpectedly tender.

Anthony Hope's Dolly Dialogues present twenty short conversations between the narrator and Miss Dolly Foster, a married flirt of perfect assurance. The first, A Liberal Education, opens with Dolly crying ingratitude at a smart young man passing their seat. Titles like Retribution, My Last Chance, and The Other Lady map the game.

Dolly teases, confesses, and corners her partner while husbands, lovers, and rivals pass through the talk. Hope, who wrote The Prisoner of Zenda, shows his other gift here: society comedy in pure dialogue, hardly a line wasted. Dolly's bashful, knowing smiles drive men to angry patronage and back. The dialogues were 1890s drawing-room favorites and still sparkle.
douglass-life-and-times:
Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, first published in 1881 and revised in 1892, is his third and fullest autobiography. Douglass had become a statesman of Reconstruction, a marshal, a diplomat, and the leading Black voice in America. This is the capstone of his life's writing.

He retells his enslavement and escape, then follows his public career through the Civil War and beyond. His meetings with Lincoln, his recruiting of Black troops, and his posts in Washington fill the second half. Douglass looks back with pride and continued fight. The book completes the greatest life story written by an American born enslaved.
dramatic-romances:
Robert Browning's Dramatic Romances, in the Porter and Clarke edition drawn from Crowell's 1898 Poetic Works, gathers the great monologues and tale-poems. My Last Duchess opens the muster of voices: a duke showing a portrait and burying a wife in a sentence. The Pied Piper of Hamelin follows as the volume's child's story, with the Incident of the French Camp and The Patriot for the crowd's two faces. Count Gismond, In a Gondola, and The Flight of the Duchess carry the romance half of the title. The Last Ride Together carries its philosophy.

Browning's method is the book: speakers who reveal more than they intend, in verse that thinks at talking speed. Porter and Clarke's notes made this the standard American school Browning. Readers get the essential Browning in one volume, the poems through which most English readers first hear that famous, rapid, sidelong voice.
drift-from-two-shores:
Bret Harte called this gathering Drift from Two Shores, fourteen short pieces from his California years and after. The Man on the Beach opens the book with a solitary figure living beside a river mouth near Trinidad Head, indifferent miners his only neighbors. Other titles promise saints of the foothills, a ghost of the Sierras, a hoodlum band, a tramp, an office seeker, and a sleeping-car experience.

Harte ranges from mining camps to city avenues, mixing sketches, tales, and character studies. Some pieces run only a few pages; each turns on a revealed trait or a quiet reversal. For readers sampling Harte beyond his two or three famous stories, this miscellany shows the variety he could manage inside a single volume.
edinburgh-picturesque-notes:
Robert Louis Stevenson, born in Edinburgh, wrote these picturesque notes on his native city, here in the 1903 Seeley people's edition. He walks the reader through the Old Town and New Town, the castle hill, closes, wynds, and gardens. History sits close beside daily street life in every chapter.

Stevenson recalls famous residents, executions, kirks, and the windy views toward the Firth of Forth and the May lighthouse. He loves the city's beauty while noting its dirt, poverty, and stern past. Anyone who wants Edinburgh explained by one of its most gifted sons, with affection and clear eyes, will find the short book rewarding.
elder-conklin-and-other-stories:
Frank Harris's Elder Conklin and Other Stories gathers American tales of the prairie and the mining West. The title story opens after supper, as the Elder's daughter and the new schoolmaster step onto the verandah of a frame house on a roll in the prairie.

Cottonwood Creek runs below, fringed with trees, and the sun sinks like a ball of orange fire beyond spears of yellow maize. Other stories include The Sheriff and His Partner, A Modern Idyll, Eatin' Crow, and The Best Man in Garotte. Harris writes with a journalist's eye and a storyteller's warmth. Readers of Western short fiction will find these tales vigorous and unpolished in the best sense.
english-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs's English Fairy Tales collects the folk tales of England, answering those who said English folk had no fairy tales of their own. Jacobs found traces of some 140 tales in the country, a quarter of them collected in the ten years before publication.

The preface notes that France and Italy were likewise said to lack folk tales until 1870, yet within fifteen years over a thousand tales had been collected in each. Jacobs hopes his volume will stir equal activity in England, and begs readers to send him more. Children and folklorists will find here the classic English collection, with its playful invitation to knock, take down the key and walk in.
enoch-soames-a-memory-of-the-eighteen-ni:
Max Beerbohm invents Enoch Soames, a forgotten poet of the eighteen-nineties, and mourns that Holbrook Jackson's thorough history of the decade omits him entirely. Soames wrote obscure books with titles like Fungoids and a preface urging readers to lean near to life. Nobody read them, and Beerbohm claims to be the only mourner.

The story turns fantastic when Soames, desperate to know his future fame, bargains with the devil to visit the British Museum a hundred years hence. He drones that the museum will still stand where it stands, and finds his reward waiting there. Beerbohm's tale mixes parody, pity, and a perfect literary hoax: later readers hunted catalogs for Soames's works.
eric-brighteyes:
H. Rider Haggard wrote Eric Brighteyes as a saga of Viking Iceland, and dedicated it to the Empress Frederick, whose dying husband had found pleasure in his stories. Eric, a golden-haired hero of great strength, loves Gudruda the Fair. Her father Asmund opposes the match. So does the witch-born Swanhild, who wants Eric herself. The berserk Skallagrim instead becomes his sworn companion. Deeds fill the chapter heads: winning the sword Whitefire, riding down Golden Falls, outlawry, and a-viking to London town.

Haggard imitates the Icelandic sagas' manner, fate-heavy and laconic, while loading the plot with witchcraft, sea fights, and a wedding feast that ends in blood. Eric's doom is foretold and unavoidable. The book stands beside King Solomon's Mines as proof of Haggard's second gift, the northern romance.
essays-and-lectures:
Oscar Wilde's Essays and Lectures, in its fourth Methuen edition of 1913, collects his early criticism and platform talks, pieces he never meant to reprint. The literary executor's preface says only the closing Poems in Prose are excepted from that judgment. The Rise of Historical Criticism, Wilde's Oxford prize essay, opens the volume.

Lectures on the English Renaissance of art, house decoration, and the craftsman follow, plus a lecture to art students and the sketch London Models. Wilde argues that art shapes life more than life shapes art, and that criticism itself is creative. Readers can watch his epigrammatic style forming here, years before the plays made it famous across London.
essays-and-tales:
Joseph Addison's periodical essays fill this Cassell volume of 1888, drawn from the Tatler and the Spectator. The introduction explains the plan of the series: an earlier volume took the Isaac Bickerstaff papers, another the Sir Roger de Coverley set. This one leaves Addison speaking alone, on subjects from public credit to household superstitions.

The contents show his range in one list. Six papers examine wit, two celebrate the ballad of Chevy Chase, and others treat friendship, censure, genius, and good nature. The Vision of Mirza gives the volume its most famous allegory, a dream of human life as a bridge over a tide. Short tales like Theodosius and Constantia close the set. These are the essays that taught English prose its ease.
everybody-s-business-is-nobody-s-busines:
Daniel Defoe published Everybody's Business Is Nobody's Business in 1725 under the name Andrew Moreton, Esquire, as this fifth edition's title page shows. Its subtitle promises private abuses and public grievances, exemplified in the pride, insolence, and exorbitant wages of women servants and footmen. A proposal for amendment accompanies the complaint.

Defoe, speaking as a master of a family, tells how a visitor's fine lady proved a common servant-wench asking eight pounds a year, dressed cleaner than her mistress. He also proposes clearing London's streets of shoe-cleaner vermin by employing the starving industrious poor instead. The pamphlet shows Defoe the social engineer, half indignant, half scheming, in his last productive decade.
fables:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these Fables across his career, and they were gathered in print in the 1890s, after his death. Like Aesop, he tells short tales of animals, sailors, devils, and kings, each ending in a moral that often turns the expected lesson on its head. A tadpole and a frog debate progress. A devil keeps an inn. A singer and his song meet their reckoning.

Stevenson packs wit, dread, and tenderness into a page or two at a time. Some tales read as jokes with teeth; others, like the tale of the man and the yellow paint, feel like small parables about art itself. Readers who know him from Treasure Island will find the same clear spring of story, here at its most concentrated.
famous-men-of-the-middle-ages:
John H. Haaren, a New York school superintendent, and A. B. Poland wrote Famous Men of the Middle Ages as history for young readers. Their preface argues that children learn the past best through lives, as peaks give shape to a landscape. Clear stories replace dates and king lists. The book served elementary classrooms as reading text and history.

Teuton gods and the Nibelung legends open the volume, mixing myth with history. Alaric the Visigoth, Attila the Hun, and Genseric the Vandal march through the chapters. Theodoric, Clovis, and Justinian show kingdoms rising from the empire's wreckage. Mohammed, Charles Martel, Pepin, and Charlemagne carry the story into a new Europe of faith and empire. Harun-al-Raschid of Baghdad adds the Muslim world in its golden age. Teachers liked the design: one vivid life per chapter, told plainly enough for a child to retell after one reading.
fantastic-fables:
Ambrose Bierce collected Fantastic Fables in 1899, very short satirical tales modeled on Aesop but aimed at modern politics, business, law, and religion. The contents list pieces such as The Moral Principle and the Material Interest, The Ingenious Patriot, and Two Kings. Each fable runs a page or less and ends in a sting.

Politicians promise, officials dodge, big nations bully small ones, and reformers expose themselves, all in Bierce's dry, exact prose. Animals still talk, but senators, editors, and financiers now share the stage with them. Readers who enjoy the bitter wit of his Devil's Dictionary will find the same mind here, working in miniature and rarely sparing anyone.
father-brown-stories: Father Brown Stories, G, k, chesterton's priest-detective tales, the clerical sleuth. This book preserves that collection. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
fenimore-cooper-s-literary-offences:
Mark Twain's most famous piece of literary criticism opens with the praise he means to destroy. Professors Lounsbury and Brander Matthews and the novelist Wilkie Collins call Cooper's Pathfinder and Deerslayer perfect works of art. Twain replies that the professors cannot have read the books, and proceeds to the evidence.

There are nineteen rules, he says, governing romantic fiction, and Cooper violated eighteen of them in The Deerslayer. In two-thirds of a page he counts 114 offences against literary art out of a possible 115. The rules are then applied one by one: the tale must accomplish something, its people must talk like humans, its woodcraft must be possible. The essay is demolition performed as comedy, and it fixed Cooper's reputation for a century.
fifty-famous-fables:
Lida Brown McMurry retold Fifty Famous Fables as a reader for children, drawing on the old Aesop tradition. Each short tale uses animals or country folk to act out a single fault or virtue. The stories are grouped under plain moral headings. A brief telling keeps every episode within a few pages.

Young readers meet the tortoise and the ducks, the shepherd boy who cried wolf, and the goose that laid golden eggs. Other tales warn against pride, greed, quarrelling, and deceit. Some praise deeds over words and urge contentment with one's lot. McMurry's groupings make the lesson of each story easy to find and discuss. The book served schools and families who wanted classic fables in simple modern English.
fifty-famous-people-a-book-of-short-stor:
Fifty Famous People, a book of short stories by James Baldwin, tells true incidents from great lives for young readers. Baldwin's prefatory note makes a careful claim: the stories are not biographical, but they are about real persons who actually lived and played their parts in history. Each, he says, has a basis of truth and an ethical lesson, and he has given good measure, a few more than fifty people, into the bargain.

The contents open with bird stories and schoolroom pieces, speaking a piece and writing a composition among them. Benjamin Franklin's whistle, the famous bought lesson in paying too much for a pleasure, stands for the method. Caliphs and poets, the Ettrick Shepherd, and kings and inventors follow in short chapters sized for reading aloud. Baldwin believed children delight in the real when it is told as story. He built the book to prove that doctrine false.
five-tales:
John Galsworthy gathered Five Tales in 1919. His contents page itself tells a publishing story. The fifth tale in this edition is Indian Summer of a Forsyte, later moved into The Forsyte Saga. The other tales are The First and Last, A Stoic, The Apple Tree, and The Juryman. The First and Last opens in a barrister's firelit library, where Keith Darrant rests from court and a family crisis assembles itself offstage.

Galsworthy's tales turn on conscience under pressure: a brother's crime, an old clerk's loyalty, a young man's holiday love, a juror's doubt. His method is quiet accumulation, detail by detail, until duty and desire cannot both be served. Readers of the Forsytes will find Soames's world here in concentrated, short-story form.
flames: Flames, Robert Hichens's occult novel. The fires burn. This book preserves that story. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
flower-fables:
Louisa May Alcott wrote Flower Fables as a girl of sixteen, and it became her first published book, in 1854. She wrote the tales for Ellen Emerson, the daughter of her father's friend Ralph Waldo Emerson. The hosted text gathers her fairy stories, each built around flowers, elves, and the small moral weather of kindness, pride, and patience.

In the title tale, the elf Thistledown must learn gentleness before the flower spirits will welcome him. Other tales follow a violet, a little bud, and fairy queens through trials that test their hearts. Alcott's love of nature and her gift for plain, warm telling show early here, years before Little Women made her famous. The book stays sweet without going soft.
fly-leaves: Charles Stuart Calverley's 1884 verse book gathers light and reflective poems on morning and evening, shelter, the palace, first love and sad memories. Schoolmasters, railway stations, examinations, the beach and the organ all supply subjects, treated with wit and a sharp ear for metre. The collection moves easily between humour and tenderness, never settling long in either mood.
four-arthurian-romances:
Chretien de Troyes, court poet of twelfth-century France, wrote the four verse romances gathered here in English prose: Erec et Enide, Cliges, Yvain, and Lancelot. Chretien effectively invented Arthurian romance, turning Welsh legend into courtly French storytelling. Knights leave Arthur's court to test love against adventure.

Erec must prove marriage has not softened him, Yvain the lion knight goes mad and is healed by service, and Lancelot rides in a cart for Guinevere's sake. The scholarly notes discuss even the chastity-testing horn at Arthur's court. Chretien's irony and psychology shaped Malory and every Arthurian writer after him. These translations let modern readers meet the source, graceful, strange, and foundational.
four-weird-tales: Four Weird Tales, Algernon Blackwood's collection. The weird quartet. This book preserves that horror. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
freckles:
Gene Stratton-Porter, an Indiana writer and naturalist, wrote Freckles, published in 1904, one of her best-loved novels. Its hero is Freckles, a young orphan with one hand, raised in a children's home with no knowledge of his family. He is hired to guard a stretch of precious timber in the Limberlost swamp, walking a lonely line each day against thieves who want the trees.

In the swamp he finds beauty, birdsong, and work that gives him pride. He also finds the Swamp Angel, a girl whose singing and kindness match his love of the wild place, and a friend in the Bird Woman who studies nature. A logging boss's plot and a question of birth drive the tale to its close. The book helped save the real Limberlost in readers' hearts.
friends-in-council-first-series:
Arthur Helps's Friends in Council, First Series, presents moral and social discussion in the form of conversations among friends. Helps was born at Streatham in July 1813, went to Eton at sixteen and then to Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating in 1835.

He served as aide to two cabinet ministers, published Essays Written in the Intervals of Business in 1841, and took a post settling French, Danish and Spanish claims. Friends in Council applies that experience to questions of conduct, work and society, in dialogue rather than lecture. Readers who enjoy Victorian essays in conversational dress will find Helps thoughtful, urbane and quietly wise.
gallegher-and-other-stories:
Gallegher and Other Stories, by Richard Harding Davis, collects the newspaper tales that made his name, in an 1891 Scribner's volume illustrated by Charles Dana Gibson. Davis opens his title story in a newsroom worn down by office boys. So many sleepy, lazy, and too smart boys had passed through that the staff called them all by one name, until Gallegher arrived and became an individual at once.

Around Gallegher, Davis sets A Walk Up the Avenue, My Disreputable Friend Mr Raegen, The Other Woman, and The Trailer for Room No 8. Three Van Bibber stories close the book, following his elegant young man of society through swan boats, a burglar, and duty as best man. Davis wrote from inside the newspaper world he had just conquered, and the copy boy who solves a crime became the pattern for a generation of reporter heroes.
galton-memories:
Francis Galton published Memories of My Life in 1908, summing up one of the most varied careers in Victorian science. Galton was Darwin's cousin, and his interests seemed endless. Travel, weather, heredity, and measurement all drew his restless mind.

He recalls exploring in southwest Africa, mapping weather patterns, and inventing the fingerprint method for identification. His work on heredity and human ability, which he named eugenics, fills later chapters and now draws sharp criticism. Galton writes with dry humor about his many failures and fixes. The memoir shows the making of modern statistics, for better and for worse.
geoffrey-monmouth-history-kings-britain-:
Geoffrey of Monmouth completed his History of the Kings of Britain around 1136, and it became a medieval bestseller. J. A. Giles's translation is the text here, from his Six Old English Chronicles. Geoffrey claimed to translate a very ancient book in the British tongue. What he really did was invent much of Britain's past.

From Brutus of Troy, his kings run through Lear, Cymbeline, and the long line to Arthur, whose reign fills the book's center. Merlin's prophecies thread the story. Shakespeare drew Lear and Cymbeline from Geoffrey's pages, and Arthur's world starts here. Historians scolded the book for centuries while everyone read it. It is myth-making of the first order.
gildas-on-the-ruin-of-britain-giles:
Gildas, a British monk of the sixth century, wrote On the Ruin of Britain as a sermon of blame against his own kings and priests. J. A. Giles translated the Latin for the modern reader. The work is the only connected narrative source for Britain after the Romans left. Everything else for those years is scraps and saints' tales.

Gildas tells of Roman rule, the coming of the Saxons as hired swords, their revolt, and the wars of Ambrosius and the siege of Badon. Then he turns on the five kings of his day and scourges their sins. His Latin is hot, tangled, and full of scripture. Later ages mined him for Arthur's age, though he never names Arthur.
glasses:
Henry James opens Glasses with a narrator resolving, pen in hand, to follow a thread of colored beads back to a first impression at Folkestone. The story he reconstructs concerns Flora Saunt, a beautiful young woman whose face all London watches through opera glasses. She sustains fifty tentative glasses at the theater with admirable serenity.

Flora is secretly going blind and hides her glasses, the instruments of her vanity and shame, behind subterfuges her friend gradually perceives. James studies the terror of being seen versus the need to see, in a society that prices a woman's face. The 1916 Secker text preserves the tale's delicate cruelty: a small subject worked to novella depth.
govdocs-archive_org-PaulFosterCaseGreatS:
Paul Foster Case, an American occultist and founder of the Builders of the Adytum, wrote The Great Seal of the United States. His subject is the history, symbolism, and message of the national emblem. Case read public symbols as carriers of hidden teaching. The Great Seal, with its pyramid and eye, drew him strongly.

He traces the seal's making in the 1780s and reads its parts: the eagle, the shield, the unfinished pyramid, and the Latin mottos Annuit Coeptis and Novus Ordo Seclorum. For Case the seal announces a new age for mankind. The book decodes the nation's emblem for readers of his school, in the archive's collection.
govdocs-archive_org-SpanishUFOFiles_Span:
Spain investigated unidentified flying objects through official channels for decades, and its files on those cases were later released to the public. The Spanish UFO Files gather that material: reports and investigations kept in the government's own records.

The papers cover sightings brought to official attention and the inquiries that followed, recorded in the dry language of state paperwork. Read together, they show how a modern government handled reports it could not easily explain. For UFO researchers, official releases like these matter because they rest on documents rather than retellings, and claims can be checked against the record.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFBIAndCISPES_The_:
In July 1989 the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence issued its report on the FBI's investigation of CISPES, the Committee in Solidarity with the People of El Salvador. The inquiry, from the 101st Congress, reviewed how the Bureau had treated an American group opposed to United States policy in Central America.

The report sets out what the FBI did, on whose authority, and where the committee found fault with the investigation. It became part of the wider record of 1980s fights over domestic surveillance of political groups. Readers get Congress's own oversight findings, drawn from the Bureau's files and testimony.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Part2HowHelpC:
Cisco Wheeler, who presented herself as a survivor of Illuminati mind control, wrote Deeper Insights into the Illuminati Formula as a companion to the conspiracy literature around that book. Part 2, How Help Comes About, turns from the alleged system itself to escape from it.

Wheeler writes about how help supposedly reaches people caught in the programming she describes, drawing on her own claimed experience. The volume assumes readers know the earlier Illuminati Formula books and their framework of handlers, alters, and secret networks. It is held as an archive holding, without endorsement, as part of the 1990s mind-control literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BankRobberies_B:
The FBI's King assassination file, MURKIN, generated teletypes long after the shooting, as agents ran down leads to build and close the case. This teletype, dated November 14, 1968, reports a registration-records check at a motel in Indiana, under file 44-38861.

Agents were looking for any record of James Earl Ray or his associates at the motel, and the check found none. Negative results fill much of the MURKIN file, because proving where Ray had not been mattered to a case built on his movements. The single teletype is preserved as issued, one page of the Bureau's legwork.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurkeJW_Burke_J:
On June 8, 1977, an angry citizen wrote to J. W. Burke Jr. about the House Select Committee on Assassinations, then in the first year of its reinvestigation of the Kennedy and King murders. The author's name is garbled in the scan, but the temper survived intact.

The letter denounces the committee as dishonest and irresponsible, a charge the HSCA heard from both directions: some thought it a whitewash, others a witch hunt. Citizen mail in the files shows the second investigation never enjoyed the public's full trust. The single letter is preserved as written, heat and all, for researchers of the committee's reception.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
A news article reports a demand from Maryland Governor Marvin Mandel. Mandel ordered Baltimore Police Commissioner Donald Pomerleau to deliver a full report on his department's secret intelligence and surveillance activities. The governor wanted the covert work of the city police brought into the open.

The demand put a police commissioner under public pressure from his own governor. Domestic intelligence units in American cities operated with little oversight in this period, and Baltimore's was no exception. The article records the moment that secrecy was challenged from the top of state government.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FoxJames_Fox_Ja: A personal letter dated August 6, 1991 was written to a man named David. The writer enclosed a copy of another letter and mentioned Sciambra, a member of Jim Garrison's staff, and the judge in the Shaw case. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text, so the letter survives as an unsigned note among researchers still trading Shaw case material in 1991.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GochenauerJames: nsia-GochenauerJames Gochenauer James: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonHaynes_J:
Haynes Johnson reported from New Orleans for the Washington Star in 1967 on two vacant offices on Lafayette Square. One had been used by Cuban exiles. The other was the headquarters of Guy Banister Associates, the detective agency of a former FBI man. Johnson explains their place in the Kennedy assassination story.

An address can carry a case. The square put exile politics and Banister's office within steps of each other, and Oswald's New Orleans summer ran through that ground. Johnson's article walks readers through the geography while the Garrison investigation made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KirkwoodJames_K: James Kirkwood's interview with Clay Shaw survives in this file, under the heading 'Surviving.' Shaw was the New Orleans businessman whom District Attorney Jim Garrison put on trial in 1969 over the Kennedy assassination. He was acquitted. Beyond the title and Kirkwood's name, the file gives little detail about when the interview was made or what Shaw said in it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeavelleJames_L: Canada's Maclean's magazine devoted its November 22, 1993 issue to the Kennedy assassination, thirty years after Dallas. The special issue appeared under the line 'JFK — 30 Years Later.' Anniversary issues like this one gathered essays, photographs, and argument about the case for a general audience. The file preserves the issue as a record of how the anniversary was marked in print, though the evidence here does not list its individual articles.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Queries_Queries: A letter filed under the heading 'Queries' concerns geese donated to Peace Corps projects. The project was nicknamed 'Geese for Peace.' The letter discusses the publicity the donations generated. Geese went abroad as breeding stock and as symbols, and the press noticed. The file gives the project, the nickname, and the letter's concern with coverage. It does not name the writer, so the letter stands as one page of that project's correspondence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Sources_Sources: Days after President Kennedy was shot in November 1963, FBI staff in Dallas faced a legal problem. Their report, filed as DL 89-43 and linked to Anton Pavrlka Jr., records the search for a federal statute that actually covered an assassination. At the time, killing a president was not clearly a federal crime. The report shows investigators working through the law books while the case was already underway.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Turtles_Turtles: nsia-Turtles Turtles: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Witnesses_Witne: Howard Leslie Brennan was the witness who said he saw a rifleman in the Texas School Book Depository window. A study examines his Warren Commission testimony, given in March 1964. Brennan's account helped the commission place a shooter in that building. Because so much rested on his words, researchers have tested them for decades. The study works through what he said and how well it holds up.
govdocs-archive_org-the-odessa-signal-si: The Odessa Signal SIGMA 6 UMBRA: the declassified government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated material, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers, a single volume.
govdocs-archive_org-topdeclassified_Top_:
The CIA wrote the Human Resource Exploitation Training Manual in 1983 to teach its officers the work of interrogation. It covers techniques for questioning prisoners and human sources, set out in the agency's own calm, procedural language.

Once secret, the manual was later declassified and became one of the most notorious training texts of the Cold War. Human rights groups cite it in debates over coercive questioning, because later detention programs echoed its methods and its euphemisms. The library presents the full text as an archive holding. Readers can study exactly what the agency taught its people, rather than rely on summaries or accusations about it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH: CHILE: The Barnes House - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records, filed. An obscure item and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Colombia set up a Truth Commission to account for decades of armed conflict, alongside a special court and a unit hunting for the disappeared. A Constitutional Court ruling said all three bodies could see every record they needed. This briefing book reports that the promise ran into a wall.

Despite the ruling, Colombia's armed forces kept key files off limits. The blocked records included military intelligence files tied to serious abuses. Those same agencies were linked to illegal paramilitary groups and drug traffickers. The posting shows how access to paper can decide whether a truth process can do its job.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
How should a military choose targets for cyber operations? Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, number 683, published in September 2019. It presents a freedom of information release on that question.

The released material discusses considerations inside United States military targeting doctrine as applied to cyberspace. Targeting rules decide what may be hit, what must be avoided, and who approves. Seeing those considerations in an official release helps readers understand how cyber attacks are planned as formal military operations, not improvised hacks. Releases of this kind are uncommon, since targeting doctrine is usually kept classified.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia-int:
Gina Haspel ran a CIA black site where detainees were tortured, and cables from that program were later declassified. The evidence for this posting centers on the legal cover the program needed. Top CIA lawyer John Rizzo worked the Justice Department for secret opinions approving the proposed methods.

Those opinions were ultimately repudiated by the Justice Department itself, but only years later. That sequence is the core of the record: lawyers blessed harsh methods in secret, the blessing was withdrawn long after the acts, and the cables survived to be read. The posting ties Haspel's name to the paper trail of the program she oversaw.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Ira: Iran's 1979 Revolution Revisited: Failures (and a Few Successes) - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
great-catherine-whom-glory-still-adores:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Great Catherine, a short play about Catherine the Great of Russia, prefaced by an author's apology for his title. Shaw confesses that Catherine's diplomacy and conquests bore him. Her character fascinates him instead. In his portrait she outplays every statesman at court intrigue. Her favorite Patiomkin fools her with sham villages built for her tours.

The play brings a stiff young English officer, Captain Edstaston, into Catherine's court. He represents respectable England in a palace run on appetite and wit. Claire and the Princess Dashkoff move through the court scenes. Catherine toys with the captain's prudery while ruling Russia between love affairs. Shaw treats history as farce with a serious edge. Readers get an empress shown as a great comic performer, shrewder than the diplomats who thought they managed her.
grim-tales:
E. Nesbit was famed for bright tales for young readers, such as her books of child quests. In 1893 she showed a far more dark face in this set of horror tales. The change shocked some fans who knew just the gay side of her pen.

The best known tale, 'Man-Size in Marble,' turns on two stone knights in a church who may not stay still. Dread in wed life, in homes, and in love runs through the set as its core theme. The set is the dark twin of her famed books for the young.
half-past-seven-stories:
Robert Gordon Anderson's Half-Past Seven Stories gathers bedtime tales, illustrated in colour by Dorothy Hope Smith. Anderson dedicates the book to Sarah Davis Anderson, whose young admirers called her Aunt Sally, in tribute to a loving heart that made many little ones happy.

Contents include The Little Lost Fox, The Big Bobsled, The Jolly Roger, The Old Woman Who Lived on the Canal, Two o' Cat, The Fairy Lamp, and The Animals' Birthday Party. Later tales bring Dr. Philemon Pipp the patent medicine man, Ole Man Pumpkin, the Norway spruce, and the hole that ran to China. Children will find these stories whimsical, warm and made for reading aloud.
hans-brinker-or-the-silver-skates:
Mary Mapes Dodge set Hans Brinker, or The Silver Skates in Holland, announcing in her preface a book of travels joined to a domestic tale. Hans and his sister Gretel Brinker are poor, honest children whose father Raff lies injured and senseless after a fall from a dike. A famous skating race offers silver skates as its prize.

The children seek the surgeon Dr Boekman, visit Amsterdam and Haarlem at Saint Nicholas season, and learn their father's hidden story. Dodge checked her Dutch customs, dress, and scenery with scrupulous care and Dutch friends' help. Generations of American children learned Holland from this book: canals, windmills, tulip mania, and the boy who held the dike.
heart-histories-and-life-pictures:
T. S. Arthur's Heart-Histories and Life-Pictures came out in New York in 1853. His introduction argues that every heart has its history, sad or bright. We cross paths daily with sober faces whose stories we never ask. Arthur wrote, he says, to awaken sympathy rather than to win literary elegance.

The Book of Memory opens the tales with an old man's counsel to Edwin. Memory, he warns, records every act on pages that cannot be erased. Jenny Lawson, The Wife, and The Married Sisters treat women's lots. Unredeemed Pledges and Going to the Springs mix money and fashion. Arthur dates his preface from Philadelphia in December 1852. The pictures are brief and direct, built to make readers kinder to the strangers beside them.
heckewelder-lenape-dialogues:
Words, Phrases, and Short Dialogues in the Lenape tongue appeared in 1819. Heckewelder gathered the material at Moravian stations on the frontier. Missionaries there had to preach and teach in the people's own language.

Word lists give the core terms of daily Lenape life and speech. Useful phrases cover travel, trade, food, and greetings between strangers. Short talks between speakers show the tongue in real use. The slim book was a working tool, not a work of show. Today it keeps early Lenape speech on record for new students of the tongue. Linguists still value its plain, field-gathered forms and phrases.
helen-s-babies:
John Habberton's Helen's Babies begins with a letter that traps a bachelor. Harry Burton, salesman of white goods, aged twenty-eight, is choosing where to spend his fortnight's vacation. His sister Helen writes from Hillcrest: come to us, she says, since Tom and she are invited away. The man she needs is an uncle for ten days. Budge and Toddie, her two toddlers, are the babies of the title, promised by the subtitle to be innocent, crafty, angelic, impish, witching, and impulsive by turns.

Inside, Harry's journal of the ten days became one of America's best-selling comic books. The children wreck his books, his courtship prospects, and his dignity in rotation. He records it all with a salesman's eye. Readers get the Victorian nursery's favorite comedy here.
hell-fer-sartain-and-other-stories:
John Fox Jr wrote these Kentucky mountain stories, collected under the title of the first, 'Hell fer Sartain.' The contents promise tales of dances, feuds, courtship, and preaching: Through the Gap, Courtin' on Cutshin, Preachin' on Kingdom-Come, and The Passing of Abraham Shivers among them. Fox renders mountain speech in heavy dialect throughout.

The opening story explains its creek's name at a Christmas dancing party where Rich Harp and Harve Hall carry old grudges into the room. Others follow moonshiners, mountain preachers, and young lovers in the Cumberland hills Fox knew from his family's Kentucky home. His stories helped define the local-color picture of Appalachia for magazine readers of the 1890s.
hieroglyphic-tales: Hieroglyphic Tales, Horace Walpole's fables. The pictured tales. This book preserves that collection. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
hinton-scientific-romances-first-series:
Charles Howard Hinton, a British mathematician, issued his Scientific Romances in essays between 1884 and 1886. Hinton coined the word 'tesseract' for a four-dimensional cube. His tales were the first great push to make the fourth dimension known to general readers.

The essays mix story and study: flat worlds, beings who pass through solid walls, and drills for picturing four dimensions. Hinton thought training the mind to see past three dimensions could free it. His work fed later writers of higher-space fiction, and Abbott's Flatland appeared in the same years.
homespun-tales:
Kate Douglas Wiggin gathered three long stories in Homespun Tales, all set in an imaginary village in York County, Maine. Wiggin explains in her introduction that two first appeared as decorated gift-books. The Saco River runs through the first tale and through her summers. She calls the river its real principal character. A meeting house and a church society anchor the second.

Rose o' the River follows a country girl and a river-driving romance. The Old Peabody Pew tells of a Dorcas Society that scrubs its church clean and of Nancy Wentworth returning at nightfall to mend a pew tied to her lost love. Village neighbors, hymn singing, and parish pride fill the pages. Readers get Wiggin's Maine at its warmest: small places, stubborn hearts, and kindness treated as a form of local knowledge.
hospital-sketches:
Louisa May Alcott, not yet famous for Little Women, nursed Union soldiers in Washington and turned the work into Hospital Sketches. James Redpath published the book in Boston in 1863, after the sketches ran in the Commonwealth newspaper. Alcott hides inside a mask, Miss Tribulation Periwinkle, and calls her family the Periwinkles. Five cents from each copy went to war orphans.

Obtaining Supplies shows her fighting red tape to reach the hospital. A Forward Movement carries her to the wards, where a day and a night of nursing fill two chapters. Wounded men arrive in batches, and she washes, feeds, writes letters, and sits with the dying. Off Duty gives the nurses' meals, jokes, and sorrows between the crises. A postscript sums up what the work taught her about courage and waste. Civil War readers value the sketches as a nurse's record, unsparing about pain that glory talk hides.
hunt-popular-romances-west-england-1865-:
Robert Hunt, a Cornish man of science, made this first set of the folk tales of the west of England in 1865. He heard most of the tales in Cornwall, from miners, fish wives, and old folk. His aim was to save the lore of old Cornwall before it died out.

The set holds the famed tale of the Mermaid of Zennor, who lured a choir man to the sea. Giants, saints, mine sprites, and strange dreams fill the rest of the Cornish store. Hunt's work is the chief book of the folk lore of the Cornish coast.

Robert Hunt brought out the second set of his Cornish folk tales in 1865, in the Hotten print of that year. It stands as mate to the first set of the same year. Hunt spent years in the lanes and ports of Cornwall to gather his store.

More drolls, as Cornish folk name their sly tales, fill this set with fresh lore. Saints, giants, sea tales, and old rites of the Cornish year all find a place here. With the first set, it forms the full record of old Cornwall as its folk told it.
hunting-sketches:
Anthony Trollope wrote Hunting Sketches as short character studies of the fox-hunting field he loved. His eight sketches sort the crowd by type. There are men who hunt and dislike it, men who love it, and the lady who rides to hounds. The hunting farmer, the man who never jumps, the hunting parson, and the master of hounds complete the field. A closing piece teaches how to ride to hounds.

Trollope insists the men who dislike hunting outnumber its lovers, since fashion and business drag many into the field. Gates, rails, and pretty sporting pictures get his dry practical treatment. Barsetshire's creator knew this world from his own saddle, and the sketches mix comedy, class observation, and genuine riding instruction.
in-divers-tones:
Charles G. D. Roberts's In Divers Tones is a book of poems by the Canadian poet, then professor of English at the University of King's College, Windsor. Roberts dedicates the verses to his friend Edmund Collins, promising a medley of song in many tones.

Contents range from a Collect for Dominion Day and poems on Canada, Actaeon and the Pipes of Pan to pieces on Fredericton, the Tantramar marshes, the potato harvest and a slave woman. Serious things mix with light laughter, and Roberts warns that a tear may hide where laughter rings. Readers of Canadian poetry will find here an early, confident Roberts, singing far and near themes in varied keys.
in-midsummer-days-and-other-tales:
August Strindberg's In Midsummer Days and Other Tales gathers short stories in Ellie Schleussner's English translation. The title story opens in the northern summer, when meadows are still uncut and birds sing, and a dove alights before the cottage of a bedridden old grandmother.

Other tales in the contents include The Big Gravel-Sifter, The Sluggard, The Pilot's Troubles, Photographer and Philosopher, Half a Sheet of Foolscap, and The Story of the St. Gotthard. Strindberg moves between country life, work and sly philosophical turns, often letting a small incident open onto a larger human truth. The collection suits readers who want Strindberg in brief, vivid pieces rather than in his long dramas.
in-the-days-when-the-world-was-wide-and-:
Henry Lawson, Australia's best-loved bush poet, gathered his verses in this book, published in 1896 under the title In the Days When the World Was Wide, and Other Verses. Lawson wrote from the world he knew: shearing sheds, gold towns, long roads, and the pubs and camps of the outback. The title poem looks back to younger, wider days on the track, when the world seemed open and mates were close.

Other pieces sing of roaring gold days, teamsters, drought, and the humor and sorrow of bush life. Lawson's plain speech and short, strong lines made him the voice of working Australia. He wrote much of the book while poor and often on the road himself, and its success fixed his place in the nation's letters.
in-the-heart-of-the-rockies: In the Heart of the Rockies, G, a, henty's western tale, the mountain adventure. This book preserves that novel. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
indian-fairy-tales:
Joseph Jacobs's Indian Fairy Tales, selected and edited by Jacobs and illustrated by John D. Batten, gathers the folk tales of India for English readers. The London edition of 1892, printed in part on Japanese vellum, presents the stories with Batten's distinctive illustrations.

Princess Labam and other tales of princes, demons, clever animals and magical transformations fill the volume, chosen from the rich store of Indian oral tradition. Jacobs, editor of Folk Lore, adds notes that help readers place each tale. Children and folklorists alike will enjoy this collection, which remains one of the classic English renderings of India's fairy tales.
irish-fairy-tales:
James Stephens retells the old Irish heroic tales in this collection, in prose that keeps the flavour of the sagas. The contents move from the Story of Tuan Mac Cairill through the Boyhood of Fionn to Mongan's Frenzy. Bran's birth, Oisin's mother, and the Wooing of Becfola stand between the greater stories.

Tuan, who has lived through ages in shifting animal shapes, tells Ireland's invasions to Saint Finnian, who came to convert him. Fionn's boyhood gives the hero his wisdom from the salmon and his first feats. Becuma of the White Skin and the Enchanted Cave of Cesh Corran bring in the fairy world at full strength. Stephens wrote for readers new to the Fenian cycle, and his telling is lyrical, funny, and swift.
japanese-fairy-tales:
Yei Theodora Ozaki's Japanese Fairy Tales, compiled in Tokyo and prefaced in 1908, retells twenty-three stories from Japanese sources for young Western readers. Ozaki says the tales follow Sadanami Sanjin's modern versions, faithful in story rather than literal. The collection opens with My Lord Bag of Rice and the Tongue-Cut Sparrow. Urashima Taro the fisher lad, Kintaro the golden boy, and Princess Hase follow in the contents.

Inside, Momotaro is born from a peach, the bamboo-cutter finds a moon-child, and an old man makes withered trees flower. The mirror of Matsuyama, the goblin of Adachigahara, and the white hare and the crocodiles fill the middle tales. Ozaki closes with Prince Yamato Take and the five colored stones of the Empress Jokwa. Readers get the standard English gateway to Japanese folklore, the book, suggested by Andrew Lang, through which generations of children first met Japan's story world.
jeanne-of-the-marshes:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Jeanne of the Marshes opens in a princess's London rooms, where the maid Annette risks her place to announce a visitor. Major Forrest has come on a very urgent matter, and princesses are not disturbed for less. Behind it stands the other world: the flat Norfolk marshes, where Jeanne lives among fishermen, an heiress whose inheritance draws plotters like marsh lights. Oppenheim, the prolific English thriller writer, binds the two Englands together with a country-house mystery.

Inside, a weekend party at a great house on the marsh turns on money, a missing fortune, and a girl whose simplicity defeats drawing-room weapons. Forrest, the soldier of fortune, must decide which side of the intrigue deserves him. Readers get Oppenheim in his Edwardian prime: brisk chapters, veiled identities, and romance conducted like espionage, with the salt wind of the marshes blowing through every ballroom scene.
joan-of-naples-celebrated-crimes:
Joan of Naples is Alexandre Dumas's account of Queen Joan of Naples, covering the years 1343 to 1382. It forms one piece of his Celebrated Crimes set, here in eight chapters. The story opens on the night of January 15, 1343. Bells from three hundred churches wake sleeping Naples to pray for a passing soul.

The dying man is the king, and dread has gripped Castel Nuovo for days. Crown officers meet twice daily, and courtiers leave the royal rooms bowed with grief. Dumas builds the scene like a novel, with a whole city listening in the dark. From this deathbed, the tale moves into Joan's reign of splendor, love, and crime in medieval Naples.
joe-tilden-s-recipes-for-epicures:
Joe Tilden's Recipes for Epicures is a cookbook printed at San Francisco in 1907. Major Joseph Tilden was famed on the Pacific Coast as a Bohemian and a fine cook, an epicurean. After his death, friends hunted for the recipes behind his famous dinners. One close companion, among the few who held them, gave this full set for publication.

The book opens with soups and chowders. Onion soup stews four white onions slowly in butter, then adds stock, milk, and egg yolks beaten with Parmesan. Palestine soup uses Jerusalem artichokes, rubbed through a colander and finished with flour, butter, and milk. The recipes are short, rich, and written for cooks who already know their kitchen.
joe-wilson-and-his-mates:
Joe Wilson and His Mates is a set of stories by Henry Lawson, Australia's bush writer. The sample opens with a glossary of Australian and older terms for far-off readers. It explains words like jackaroo, a newcomer learning station work, and Anniversary Day, now Australia Day. Even slang for pubs, possums, and visiting cards gets a careful note.

That care shows how foreign Lawson's world once seemed to outsiders. His Joe Wilson is a working man of the outback, moving through drought, loneliness, and mateship. Lawson's tales are spare and dry-humored, built on the code of mates helping mates. This glossary stands at the front like a guide, preparing readers for the plain speech of the bush stories.
john-bull-on-the-guadalquivir-from-tales:
John Bull on the Guadalquivir is a story by Anthony Trollope, taken from his Tales from All Countries in the 1864 edition. The narrator is John Pomfret, an Englishman whose family traded with Spain for years. His father's firm had works at Seville, and one partner always lived there. The Daguilars, the firm's Spanish partners, became family to the Pomfrets.

Maria Daguilar visited the Pomfret house at seventeen, and John soon decided to go after her. Their match met no resistance; both families plainly wanted the alliance. Yet John felt something lacking, the flower of romance that a little opposition adds. Maria herself had a quiet decision of character unlike English girls he knew. Trollope turns an Anglo-Spanish marriage into gentle comedy about national habits.
john-ingerfield-and-other-stories:
John Ingerfield, and Other Stories gathers five tales by Jerome K. Jerome. The contents list the title story, The Woman of the Saeter, and Silhouettes. Variety Patter and The Lease of the Cross Keys complete the set. In a note to the gentle reader, Jerome warns that three of the tales are not meant to be amusing.

He tells of a critic who praised one solemn tale as not as funny as his other things. So he asks readers to judge the serious stories by another measure than humor. The title story, a tale of old London, remembers John Ingerfield and Anne, his wife. Jerome, famous for laughter, here shows his grave and tender side on purpose.
joinville-memoirs-st-louis-johnes:
Jean de Joinville, a French knight, finished his Memoirs of Louis IX in 1309, nearly sixty years after the events. Thomas Johnes's English translation is the text here, from Bohn's Chronicles of the Crusades. Joinville sailed with King Louis on the Seventh Crusade and knew him as a friend.

The memoir mixes the king's holy sayings and just deeds with Joinville's own adventures in Egypt: battles on the Nile, captivity after Mansourah, and ransom talks. Louis appears praying, judging under an oak, and washing the feet of the poor. The book is the most intimate life of any medieval king. Its appendix adds knight lists and a Saracen account of the crusade.
jorrocks-jaunts-and-jollities:
Jorrocks' Jaunts and Jollities is Robert Smith Surtees's comic book about a London sportsman. Thirteen chapters follow Mr. Jorrocks through the Surrey hunt, shooting, and the turf at Newmarket. Other jaunts take him to Cheltenham, Margate, Paris, and a ride to Brighton. A dinner party and the day after the feast close the set.

The opening chapter asks what true-bred city sportsman has not put off urgent business for the Surrey foxhounds. Surtees writes as the bard of Eastcheap, cheering the hardy exploits of his fellow Londoners. Jorrocks, a cockney grocer with a passion for sport, became one of English fiction's great comic figures. The book's slang, pace, and hunting lore made it a sporting classic.
karl-ludwig-sand-celebrated-crimes:
Karl-Ludwig Sand is Alexandre Dumas's account of the German student who murdered the writer Kotzebue in 1819. It belongs to Dumas's Celebrated Crimes set, in the 1910 edition. The tale opens on March 22, 1819, about nine in the morning. Sand, twenty-three or twenty-four, pauses on the road between Kaiserthal and Mannheim, within sight of his goal.

Dumas paints him closely: smallpox-marked face, gentle eyes, long black hair over a broad forehead. Sand lifts his cap to feel the fresh air from the Neckar valley. He notes in his little book that he left Wanheim at five that morning. Then, lips moving as if in prayer, he walks on firmly toward Mannheim. Dumas builds dread by calm, step by step.
katherine-s-sheaves:
Katherine's Sheaves is a novel by Mrs. George Sheldon, copyrighted by the author in her later name, Mrs. George Sheldon Downs. She dedicates it to her teacher, F.S.K., placing the book wholly in his keeping. Marginal references to Mary Baker Eddy's Science and Health run through the text. The story is set at Hilton Seminary, and opens in Katherine's room there.

Hilton matters at once: Katherine talks with her roommate, and Dorothy Gordon's strength of character wins early praise. Dr. Phillip Harris Stanley stands central in the cast named by chapter titles. A chapter called Katherine Makes a Demonstration signals the book's Christian Science teaching. Mrs. Seabrook's problem and the Hilton Volunteers carry the later action. Sheldon's novels often mixed romance with moral instruction, and this one teaches openly.
keckley-behind-the-scenes:
Elizabeth Keckley published Behind the Scenes in 1868, with a subtitle that sums her life: thirty years a slave, four years in the White House. Keckley bought her freedom with her needle, then became Mary Todd Lincoln's dressmaker. She was also the First Lady's closest confidante.

She tells of slavery in Virginia and North Carolina, her son's death in Union uniform, and the Lincoln household at war. Lincoln's assassination and his widow's grief fill the closing chapters. The book caused a scandal for its private details. Today it is prized as a rare insider view of the Civil War White House.
king-john-of-jingalo-the-story-of-a-mona:
King John of Jingalo: The Story of a Monarch in Difficulties is Laurence Housman's satirical novel, published by Henry Holt in 1912. Sixteen chapters follow a king whose crown sits uneasily. Early titles include A Domestic Interior, Popular Monarchy, and Church and State. A Royal Commission and a game of heads or tails come next.

Later chapters name a deed without a name, a new bishop, and Maximilian. Housman, known for fairy tales and plays, here mocks modern monarchy gently. His king of the imaginary Jingalo faces parliaments, bishops, and newspapers like any real ruler. The satire stays playful: a fairy-tale kingdom used to tease the politics of Housman's own England.
king-of-the-khyber-rifles:
King of the Khyber Rifles is Talbot Mundy's romance of adventure on India's northwest frontier, in its 1916 Imperial edition. Captain Athelstan King, the hero, serves among the hill tribes of the Khyber country. The sample opens deep in the book, at chapter nine, inside a tunnel action. A verse headpiece tells of Abdul standing guard at a gate.

Rifle-fire sweeps the tunnel's floor on both sides, and terrified men huddle in the dark. A mule breaks loose in panic, and the hillman guide tries to master the scene. Mundy drops the reader into frontier fighting at full speed. His King moves through spies, secret missions, and tribal politics in the passes between India and Afghanistan.
king-solomons-mines:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this adventure tale in a rush of work in 1885, to match a bet on the style of Treasure Island. It was his first big hit, and it made his name at a stroke. Allan Quatermain, a dry and tough hunter, tells the tale in his own voice.

Quatermain leads two English men deep in Africa to find the lost mines of King Solomon. Maps, deserts, a lost tribe, and a vast hoard of gems fill the road there and back. The book made the lost world tale a set form for a hundred years of thrills.
kitty-s-class-day-and-other-stories:
Louisa May Alcott, author of Little Women, wrote the short stories gathered here. The book first appeared as Proverb Stories in 1882. Its eight tales include Aunt Kipp, Psyche's Art, and A Country Christmas.

The title story follows Kitty, who longs to attend a class day with her cousin Jack. She worries most about what she should wear. Other stories cover picket duty, a baron's gloves, and what bells saw and said. Each tale opens under a proverb, giving young readers a lesson inside a lively story. Alcott writes for young people without talking down to them. Work, duty, and kindness recur across the varied settings.
knock-knock-knock-and-other-stories:
Ivan Turgenev's short fiction fills this volume, translated from Russian by Constance Garnett. It gathers five pieces: Knock, Knock, Knock, The Inn, and Lieutenant Yergunov's Story. The Dog and The Watch complete the set.

The title story is framed as a tale told among friends. Its narrator recalls his student days in Petersburg in the 1830s. He stayed with his brother, an officer stationed near Krasnoe Selo. Turgenev builds quiet unease from memory, talk, and small events, which suits readers who like subtle, eerie stories. Garnett's translation keeps Turgenev's calm surface and quiet dread. Small gestures and pauses do much of the work in these tales.
korolenko-birds-of-heaven-and-other-stor:
Exiles, wanderers, and ordinary people enduring great hardship fill Birds of Heaven and Other Stories by Vladimir Korolenko, in English. Korolenko wrote as the humane conscience of Russian literature, and Chekhov counted him a favorite among living writers. Siberian roads and steppe villages supply most of the settings in this selection.

His tales observe convicts, pilgrims, and peasants with moral clarity and steady sympathy. No character is too small for his full attention, a quality readers noticed at once. The title story lifts its eyes from hard lives to the birds passing over them. Together the stories show why contemporaries trusted Korolenko's judgment on Russia itself. His kindness on the page was earned in a life of exile and advocacy.
korolenko-makar-s-dream-and-other-storie:
A Siberian peasant dies drunk before Christmas and argues his case in heaven in Korolenko's famous tale Makar's Dream, which heads this English collection. Makar, a poor dreamer cheated by life and by the local powers, pleads before the Great Toyon with peasant cunning. His scales of sins and good deeds produce the story's famous, tender verdict.

Funny, moving, and profound at once, the tale ranks among the great Russian short stories. Other pieces in the volume carry Korolenko's Siberian exile experience into fiction. He knew the taiga settlements he describes from years of banishment there. The collection makes a perfect doorway into his work. Few writers judge their characters so justly and forgive them so much.
la-constantin-celebrated-crimes:
Alexandre Dumas wrote La Constantin as part of his Celebrated Crimes series. This printing comes from the eight-volume set issued in 1910. The tale is set in the year 1660.

Dumas warns readers not to hunt for its people in real records. Marie Leroux, widow of Jacques Constantin, was no great criminal of history. Her accomplice Claude Perregaud was likewise obscure. Dumas builds nine chapters of drama from their small, dark story, in his lively storyteller's manner. Dumas openly prefers a good story to strict record keeping here. That honesty helps readers enjoy the tale on its own terms.
la-le-gende-des-sie-cles:
Victor Hugo's La Légende des Siècles is a vast French poem cycle. This school and university edition was edited by G. F. Bridge. It appeared in the Oxford Higher Series of French works.

The series aimed at upper forms of public schools and private students. Hugo's poems sweep across the ages of human history. They retell legends, Bible stories, and great events in verse. Even in extracts, the cycle shows Hugo's huge range and his faith in human progress. Bridge's edition suits students who read French with help. Notes and selection make Hugo's vast design easier to approach.
la-mere-bauche-from-tales-of-all-countri:
